heading: SECTION 12.5
body: SECTION 12.5 Confidentiality • Share results only with people who need to know: the designated program contact, the employee's decision-maker, and legal counsel. • Never discuss a result with coworkers. • Release results to outside parties only with the employee's written consent or as law requires. SECTION 12.6 Helping employees: EAPs and second chances • An Employee Assistance Program offers confidential counseling and referral. Many employers encourage selfreferral before a test by promising no discipline for coming forward first. • A last chance agreement lets an employee keep their job after a violation if they complete treatment, pass a returnto-duty test, and accept follow-up testing. Any later violation ends employment. • Second chances can help retention in tight labor markets, but they must be offered consistently. SECTION 12.7 Auditing your program Once a year, review: positivity and refusal rates by test reason, whether random selections were completed on schedule, supervisor training records, vendor performance, policy changes needed for new laws, and any complaints or claims. SECTION 12.8 Budgeting and cost Testing costs vary widely by region, volume, specimen and vendor, so get written quotes. Published figures give a starting point: lab-based tests often start around $50 and hair tests around $125 (Checkr), and published fee schedules for a DOT urine test including collection, lab analysis and MRO review cluster around $65 to $80. What goes into the cost of a lab-based test: • Collection fee (higher for observed, after-hours or on-site mobile collections) • Laboratory screen, plus confirmation for non-negatives • MRO review • TPA or consortium fees: annual membership, random selection, reporting • Travel time and lost work while employees go to a collection site What goes into the cost of an on-site rapid program: • Rapid devices, temperature strips and collection supplies • Collector time and training • Lab confirmation and MRO fees for each non-negative (usually a small share of tests) • Shipping or courier to the lab • Any state registration or CLIA certificate fees • Less travel and lost work, which is often the biggest saving Building an annual budget. Estimate the number of tests by reason, then multiply by the cost per test:

Comparing vendor quotes. Ask every vendor for the all-in price for the same test, and check: • What is included: collection, lab screen, confirmation, MRO, reporting • Fees for after-hours, observed, shy bladder and cancelled collections • Turnaround time for negatives and for MRO-verified results • Minimums, contract length and price changes • Who owns the records, and what it costs to get them if you leave The cheapest price per test is rarely the cheapest program. A cancelled test, a lost specimen or a slow result that delays a hire costs more than a few dollars per test. SECTION 12.9 Contractors, temps and staffing agencies ** People who work at your site but are not your employees create two risks: an impaired contractor can hurt your people, and testing someone else's employee directly can make you look like their employer. • Put testing in the contract. Require contractors and staffing agencies to run a program that meets your standards: which tests, which panel, an MRO and who is excluded from your site after a positive or refusal. • Let the contractor test its own people and certify compliance to you, rather than testing them yourself. Testing, disciplining and controlling another company's workers is one factor in finding joint employment. • Ask for proof: a written policy, a certificate of compliance, or aggregate results. Do not ask for individual results unless the contract and law clearly allow it and the worker has consented. • Site access rules can still apply to everyone: "No one may work on site while impaired, and anyone involved in an incident may be required to test under the contractor's program." • Customer requirements flow down. If your customer requires your workers to be tested, write the same requirement into your subcontracts and staffing agreements.

heading: T EST REASON
body: • DOT contractors must be in a compliant DOT program, often through a consortium. Verify before they drive or work under your DOT authority. NEW AND DEVELOPING LAW ** Laws in these areas are new and developing. Please confirm any policy decisions regarding these issues that you may include in your program with your attorneys. SECTION 12.10 Privacy and data security Drug test results are some of the most sensitive records an employer holds, and they increasingly live in software systems. • Who can see results: limit system access to the program owner and named backups. Check that your HR system, TPA portal and email do not quietly give supervisors or IT staff access. • Separate storage: keep results out of the general personnel file and general HR system, as the ADA requires for medical information. heading: • HIPAA: usually does not apply to an employer acting as an employer. It may apply to your
body: • HIPAA: usually does not apply to an employer acting as an employer. It may apply to your MRO, clinic or health plan. Do not assume either way; ask your counsel. • State privacy laws may cover employee data, such as California's privacy law for employee information, and some states regulate biometric data if your systems use fingerprints or facial images. • Vendors: require confidentiality, data security, breach notice and return or destruction of records in every vendor contract. • Email and texts: never send results or names of donors by unencrypted email or text. • Retention and destruction: keep records for the required periods (above), then destroy them securely, unless a lawsuit or claim is pending. • Litigation hold: once a claim or lawsuit is likely, stop routine destruction of every related record, including emails, logs and images. Use the vendor and privacy rules above together: most data problems in testing programs come from vendor systems and email, not from paper files. heading: PART IV | BUILDING YOUR PROGRAM
body: PART IV | BUILDING YOUR PROGRAM Communicating the Program A program succeeds when everyone involved understands it and trusts it. As the program owner, you are its spokesperson: you explain why the company tests, how it works and what happens next, to people with very different concerns. The rule that runs through every conversation: talk freely about the program, and never about an individual's result except with those who need to know. 13.1 Who you will talk to 13.2 Core talking points 13.3 Reporting to leadership 13.4 Scripts for hard conversations 13.5 Answering common employee questions 13.6 Employee FAQ handout 13.7 Do's and don'ts Check your understanding SECTION 13.1 Who you will talk to S TAKEHOLDER W HAT THEY NEED TO KNOW W HAT THEY WORRY ABOUT W HAT YOU MUST NOT SHARE Employees Why the company tests, how it Privacy, fairness, prescriptions, Other employees' results works, their rights, where to get marijuana, losing their job help Applicants That an offer depends on a test, Being turned away for legal use Reasons beyond the result, unless and how to complete it or a prescription required Supervisors and Reasonable suspicion signs, how Getting it wrong, confronting Results of employees they do not managers to act, what not to say employees, liability manage Executives, owners Program costs, results trends, Lawsuits, productivity, hiring, cost Individual results, except for a and board legal risk, compliance status leader who is the decision-maker on that case Union Policy terms, changes, Fairness, discipline, bargaining Individual results without the procedures rights employee's consent Collection sites and Your account setup, test reasons, Correct paperwork, payment, Nothing beyond what is needed clinics panels, authorizations, after- scheduling to collect hours needs, where results go Chapter 13: Communicating the Program © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. Prescriptions are discussed privately with the doctor, not with your supervisor." • Help: "If you have a problem, ask for help before you are tested. We have an EAP, and asking for help early is protected under our policy." SECTION 13.3 Reporting to leadership Executives want to know whether the program is working, what it costs and whether the company is exposed. heading: M EASURE
body: M EASURE W HY IT MATTERS Workplace incidents and workers' comp claims Shows impact over time Policy changes needed for new laws Legal risk SECTION 13.4 Scripts for hard conversations Adapt these to your policy. Keep conversations private, calm and short, and have a second manager present for anything involving discipline. Announcing a new program: "Starting [DATE], we are launching a drug and alcohol testing program for [WHO]. Here is why we are doing it, how it works, and what your rights are. Everyone will get a copy of the policy and a chance to ask questions before any testing starts." Notifying a random selection: "You've been randomly selected for a test today. This is computer-generated, not based on anything you've done. Please go to [LOCATION] now; [NAME] will go with you." Reasonable suspicion: "I've noticed [SPECIFIC OBSERVATIONS] today. Because of what I've seen, our policy requires a test. I'm not accusing you of anything. We will take you to the collection site, and you will not be able to work until we have the result." Do not argue, diagnose or ask what they took. Post-accident: "Our policy requires testing after incidents like this one, for everyone whose actions could have contributed. It isn't a judgment about what happened. Once you've received any medical care you need, [NAME] will take you to the collection site." Delivering a verified positive: "The doctor who reviews our tests has verified your test as positive for [SUBSTANCE]. Under our policy, [CONSEQUENCE]. Here is a written notice, including how to request a test of your split specimen and how to reach our EAP." Do not debate the science; refer questions to the MRO. A coworker asks about someone's test: "I can't discuss anyone's personal information, just as I wouldn't discuss yours." An employee asks for help: "Thank you for coming to me. Under our policy, asking for help before you're selected for a test is protected. Let's get you connected with [EAP]." Then follow the self-referral section of your policy.

heading: M EASURE
body: SECTION 13.5 Answering common employee questions • "Marijuana is legal in my state. Why can you test for it?" State law may protect some off-duty use, and our policy follows the law where you work. No state protects use or impairment at work, and DOT rules prohibit marijuana for covered jobs regardless of state law. • "Can CBD make me test positive?" It can. Many CBD products contain THC, even when labeled otherwise, and hempderived THC products such as delta-8 test positive for marijuana. Neither is a legitimate medical explanation. Federal limits on hemp-derived THC products are due to take effect on December 11, 2026 (Chapter 2). • "What about my prescriptions?" Discuss them privately with the MRO if your test is non-negative. A valid prescription taken as directed is reported as negative. • "Can poppy seeds or secondhand smoke make me fail?" Poppy seeds can cause an opiate screen to show nonnegative, especially at the lower cutoffs many private programs use. That is why every non-negative goes to the lab and the MRO, who considers poppy seeds before verifying a result. Normal secondhand marijuana smoke exposure is very unlikely to reach the cutoff. • "Who sees my results?" Only the people listed in the policy who need to know. • "What if I refuse?" A refusal is treated the same as a positive result. Chapter 13: Communicating the Program © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 13.6

Any non-negative screen is confirmed by a certified lab and reviewed by a physician (MRO) before any decision. • Prescriptions: Discussed only with the MRO, privately. • Your results: Confidential and kept separate from your personnel file. • Refusing or tampering: Treated the same as a positive result. • Getting help: Contact [EAP NAME, PHONE] any time. heading: PART V | DOT AND PRACTICE
body: PART V | DOT AND PRACTICE DOT Testing Requirements If any of your employees perform DOT safety-sensitive work, federal rules decide almost everything about their testing: who is tested, when, how, by whom and what happens after a violation. You cannot opt out of, add to or relax these rules. The rest of this guidebook describes best practice for non-DOT programs; wherever DOT differs, a DOT note points here. Always check the current rules at the DOT Office of Drug and Alcohol Policy and Compliance (ODAPC), transportation.gov/ odapc. 15.1 How the rules fit together 15.2 Where DOT differs from this guidebook 15.3 What the employer must do 15.4 Required tests 15.5 2026 minimum random testing rates 15.6 Drug testing under DOT 15.7 DOT drug panel and cutoffs 15.8 DOT collection rules 15.9 DOT results, MRO and refusals 15.10 Alcohol testing under DOT 15.11 Violations and the SAP process 15.12 The FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse 15.13 DOT recordkeeping 15.14 Common DOT audit findings Check your understanding SECTION 15.1 How the rules fit together • 49 CFR Part 40 sets the testing procedures for every DOT agency: collection, labs, MROs, alcohol testing, SAPs and records. • Each DOT agency's own rule decides who is covered, which tests are required, and specific duties. A GENCY A GENCY RULE W HO IS COVERED FMCSA 49 CFR Part 382 CDL drivers of commercial motor vehicles FAA 14 CFR Part 120 Flight crew, flight attendants, mechanics, dispatchers, air traffic controllers and other aviation safety jobs Chapter 15: DOT Testing Requirements © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 70 of 94

heading: A GENCY

heading: • Name a Designated Employer Representative (DER) to receive results and remove employees
body: • Name a Designated Employer Representative (DER) to receive results and remove employees from duty. • Contract with qualified service agents: collectors, an HHS-certified lab, an MRO, a SAP and optionally a consortium/ third-party administrator (C/TPA). • Check every new hire's drug and alcohol violation history with previous DOT-regulated employers: the past two years under Part 40, and three years for CDL drivers. For FMCSA drivers, a full Clearinghouse pre-employment query now satisfies this check for prior FMCSA employers; ask employers regulated by other DOT agencies directly. • Run a limited Clearinghouse query on every CDL driver at least once a year. • Train supervisors: at least 60 minutes on drugs and 60 minutes on alcohol for reasonable suspicion. • Give employees the required education materials. • Keep records for the required periods and file annual testing data (MIS) reports when your agency requires them. • Keep DOT and non-DOT testing completely separate. SECTION 15.4 Required tests T EST D OT REQUIREMENT Pre-employment A negative drug test before first safety-sensitive work. Pre-employment alcohol testing is optional for most agencies. Random Unannounced, spread through the year, at least the agency's minimum rate. Reasonable suspicion Based on a trained supervisor's specific, current observations made just before, during or just after duty. Alcohol test within 2 hours if possible, and never after 8. Post-accident Required when the agency's accident criteria are met. For FMCSA, for example: any fatality, or an injury treated away from the scene or a vehicle towed away, when the driver receives a citation. Alcohol within 8 hours (ideally 2), drugs within 32 hours. Return-to-duty Directly observed, after the SAP process, before returning to safety-sensitive work. Follow-up Directly observed, unannounced, at least 6 in the first 12 months, for up to 5 years, as the SAP directs. SECTION 15.5 2026 minimum random testing rates Rates are set each year by each agency and posted by ODAPC. These apply to calendar year 2026: A GENCY R ANDOM DRUG RATE R ANDOM ALCOHOL RATE FMCSA 50% 10% FAA 25% 10% FRA (covered service and maintenance-of-way)

heading: SECTION 15.6
body: The rate is a percentage of your average number of covered positions. With 100 FMCSA drivers, you must complete at least 50 random drug tests and 10 random alcohol tests during the year. SECTION 15.6 Drug testing under DOT • Urine only, for now. DOT has authorized oral fluid testing, but employers cannot use it until HHS certifies at least two oral fluid laboratories; none had been certified when DOT last addressed this in May 2026. Under a rule effective June 10, 2026, in the limited situations where DOT would otherwise require an oral fluid test, a directly observed urine collection is required instead. Check transportation.gov/odapc for current status. • The fixed DOT panel: marijuana, cocaine, amphetamines (including methamphetamine, MDMA and MDA), opioids (codeine, morphine, 6-AM, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, oxycodone, oxymorphone) and PCP. Fentanyl was proposed in September 2025 but is not yet part of the panel. Employers may not add drugs to a DOT test or apply company cutoffs. • An HHS-certified lab tests the specimen; every non-negative goes to the MRO. SECTION 15.7 DOT drug panel and cutoffs DOT laboratories must use these urine cutoffs, in ng/mL (49 CFR 40.85): C OMPARED WITH TYPICAL NON-DOT D RUG (TARGET ANALYTE) D OT SCREEN D OT CONFIRM Marijuana metabolite (THC-COOH) Same Cocaine metabolite (benzoylecgonine) Same Codeine / morphine 2,000 2,000 each Different: many non-DOT programs screen P RACTICE at 300 6-acetylmorphine (heroin) Same Hydrocodone / hydromorphone 100 each Same Oxycodone / oxymorphone 100 each Same Phencyclidine (PCP) Same Amphetamine / methamphetamine 250 each Same MDMA / MDA 250 each Same Fentanyl Not tested Not tested Different: many non-DOT programs test for it The opiate difference. DOT screens and confirms codeine and morphine at 2,000 ng/mL, mainly so that poppy seeds do not cause positives. Many private programs screen at 300 ng/mL to detect more use. The same specimen can be negative on a DOT test and non-negative on a company test. Never apply company cutoffs or company drugs to a DOT test; if you want broader testing for a DOT employee, it must be a separate non-DOT test under your company policy, on a non-federal form, where law allows.

heading: SECTION 15.6
body: Federal agencies are different again. Federal agency programs (not DOT) follow the HHS panel, which since July 2025 includes fentanyl and norfentanyl at 1 ng/mL and uses a 4,000 ng/mL morphine confirmation cutoff. DOT has not adopted those changes. Chapter 15: DOT Testing Requirements © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 15.8
body: SECTION 15.8 DOT collection rules • Federal form. Every DOT collection uses the federal Custody and Control Form, on paper or an approved electronic version. • Collector qualifications. Collectors must complete qualification training, pass five error-free mock collections, and take refresher training every five years. • Direct observation by a same-sex observer is required for return-to-duty and follow-up tests, when the temperature is out of range or tampering is suspected, when the MRO orders it, and in the other situations listed in 49 CFR 40.67. • Shy bladder. The donor may drink up to 40 ounces of fluid over up to 3 hours. If they still cannot provide 45 mL, the employer must arrange a medical evaluation within 5 days. If no medical condition explains it, it is a refusal. • Dilute specimens. If the MRO reports a dilute negative with creatinine of 2 to 5 mg/dL, the employee must be recollected immediately under direct observation. DOT treats these collection errors as follows: F LAW R ESULT UNDER DOT Specimen ID on the bottle does not match the form Fatal; test cancelled Seal broken or missing when the lab receives it Fatal; test cancelled Collector's printed name and signature missing Fatal; test cancelled Not enough specimen for the lab to test Fatal; test cancelled Collector forgot to sign the certification Correctable with a signed memo Non-federal form used for a DOT test Correctable with a signed memo SECTION 15.9 DOT results, MRO and refusals • MRO interview. The MRO interviews the employee before verifying a positive. A state medical marijuana card or a Schedule III marijuana product is not a legitimate medical explanation. • Reaching the employee. If the MRO cannot reach the employee, the DER tells the employee to call the MRO, without giving details. The employee then has 72 hours to call. If the employee does not, the MRO may verify the result without an interview.

heading: SECTION 15.8
body: • Split specimen. The employee may ask the MRO, within 72 hours, to have the split specimen tested at a second HHScertified lab. The employer may not delay action while waiting. • Refusals are defined in 49 CFR 40.191. They include failing to appear in a reasonable time, leaving before the test is complete, failing to provide enough specimen without a medical explanation, refusing an observed collection or failing to follow the observer, refusing to empty pockets, carrying or wearing a device to tamper, an adulterated or substituted result, admitting adulteration or substitution, and failing to cooperate. • Invalid and cancelled results. The MRO directs any required recollection, which may be observed. • Safety concerns. When the MRO believes a prescribed medication makes the employee medically unqualified or a safety risk, the MRO reports it, and the DOT agency's medical qualification rules govern what happens next. SECTION 15.10 Alcohol testing under DOT • Trained breath alcohol technicians or screening test technicians use DOT-approved devices. • A screening result of 0.02 or higher must be confirmed on an evidential breath testing device, after a waiting period of at least 15 minutes, starting within 30 minutes of the screen. heading: SECTION 15.11
body: • 0.04 or higher: a violation. Removal from safety-sensitive duty and the SAP process. • 0.02 to 0.039: not a violation, but the employee must be removed from safety-sensitive duty for a period set by the agency (24 hours for FMCSA). • Agencies also bar alcohol use within set hours before duty (for example, 4 hours for FMCSA drivers, 8 hours for FAA flight crew) and after an accident until tested. SECTION 15.11 Violations and the SAP process A DOT violation is a verified positive, an alcohol result of 0.04 or higher, a refusal, or alcohol or drug use on or before duty in violation of agency rules. After any violation: 1. Remove the employee from safety-sensitive duty immediately. 2. Give the employee a list of qualified Substance Abuse Professionals. This is required even if you terminate the employee. 3. The SAP evaluates the employee and requires education or treatment. 4. The SAP re-evaluates and, if the employee complied, sets a follow-up testing plan. 5. The employee passes a directly observed return-to-duty test. 6. The employee completes the follow-up testing plan, which travels with them to any new DOT employer. DOT does not require you to rehire or keep the employee. That is your company's decision, but if you do return them to safety-sensitive work, they must complete this process first. SECTION 15.12 The FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse For CDL drivers, employers, MROs and SAPs must report violations, refusals and return-to-duty steps to the Clearinghouse. Since November 2024, state licensing agencies downgrade the CDL of a driver in "prohibited" status until the return-toduty process is complete. Driving with a prohibited status is a serious violation for the driver and the carrier.

heading: SECTION 15.11
body: SECTION 15.13 DOT recordkeeping DOT records must be kept confidential, apart from personnel files, and released only as 49 CFR Part 40 allows. These are the minimum retention periods: R ECORD D OT RETENTION Positive results, refusals, SAP reports, follow-up schedules 5 years Collection process and supervisor training records 2 years Negative and cancelled results 1 year SECTION 15.14 Common DOT audit findings • Random rates not met, or tests bunched at one time of year • Missing previous employer checks or Clearinghouse queries • No supervisor training records • Non-DOT tests done on federal forms, or company drugs added to DOT tests • Employees allowed to keep working after a refusal or violation • Owner-operators not enrolled in a consortium Chapter 15: DOT Testing Requirements © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: PART V | DOT AND PRACTICE
body: PART V | DOT AND PRACTICE Case Scenarios These scenarios apply the guidebook to situations program owners face. Each is an example only; the right answer in your company depends on your policy and the law where the employee works. 16.1 Scenario 1: A non-negative on-site screen for an applicant 16.2 Scenario 2: A forklift accident 16.3 Scenario 3: The smell of alcohol after lunch 16.4 Scenario 4: A prescription and a crane 16.5 Scenario 5: "Why do I keep getting picked?" 16.6 Scenario 6: A cold specimen 16.7 Scenario 7: "It was only CBD" 16.8 Scenario 8: A DOT driver at 0.03 16.9 Scenario 9: A union representative 16.10 Scenario 10: Asking for help before a test Check your understanding SECTION 16.1 Scenario 1: A non-negative on-site screen for an applicant An applicant for an office job in New Jersey gives a urine specimen on site after a conditional offer. The rapid cup shows no test line for THC. What to do: Tell the applicant the screen needs lab confirmation, seal and send the specimen to the lab, and take no action. When the MRO reports the result, check New Jersey law before acting: New Jersey allows the test, but bars withdrawing the offer based only on a positive cannabis result without documented evidence of impairment, and a recent appellate decision lets applicants sue over offers withdrawn for a positive alone. For an office job, a positive THC result by itself is unlikely to support withdrawing the offer. Your policy should already say how marijuana is handled for this job in this state. Lesson: The screen is never final, and marijuana results must be read against state law where the person works. SECTION 16.2 Scenario 2: A forklift accident A forklift strikes a rack, causing $8,000 in damage. A coworker standing nearby twisted an ankle stepping away. Your policy requires testing for property damage over $5,000. What to do: Get the injured worker medical care first. Test the forklift operator, whose actions could have contributed. Do not test the coworker just because they were injured; that risks an OSHA violation for discouraging injury reporting.

heading: PART V | DOT AND PRACTICE
body: Chapter 16: Case Scenarios © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 78 of 94

heading: SECTION 16.3
body: Complete the post-accident decision record (Form B-4) and test promptly, ideally alcohol within 2 hours and drugs within 32. Lesson: Test the people whose actions could have contributed, not the people who got hurt. SECTION 16.3 Scenario 3: The smell of alcohol after lunch A supervisor notices an employee returning from lunch with a strong odor of alcohol, flushed face and loud, slurred speech. The employee drove back to work. What to do: Remove the employee from duty, have a second supervisor observe if possible, and complete the reasonable suspicion checklist (Form B-3). Arrange transport to the collection site, or test on site with an approved breath device. Do not let the employee drive. If the employee insists on driving away, do not restrain them; consider calling law enforcement for public safety. Lesson: Specific, current observations, documented before the test, are what make reasonable suspicion defensible. SECTION 16.4 Scenario 4: A prescription and a crane A crane operator's random test is reported by the MRO as negative because of a valid opioid prescription, with a safety concern noted. What to do: This is not a policy violation. Begin the ADA interactive process: confidentially, with the employee's release, ask the treating provider whether the employee can safely operate a crane on this medication, consider temporary reassignment or leave, and document the decision. Lesson: A safety concern is a fitness-for-duty question, not discipline. SECTION 16.5 Scenario 5: "Why do I keep getting picked?" An employee has been selected for random testing three times this year and complains that they are being targeted. What to do: Explain that selections are computer-generated by your TPA, that everyone has an equal chance at every draw, and that being picked several times, or not at all, is normal. Offer to show documentation that the selection method is scientifically valid, without revealing anyone else's selections. Lesson: True random selection does not even out over a year, and your records should prove the method. SECTION 16.6 Scenario 6: A cold specimen During an on-site collection, the cup's temperature strip shows no reading in the 90-100°F range.

heading: SECTION 16.3
body: What to do: Note the temperature, keep the first specimen, and immediately conduct a second collection under direct observation by a same-sex observer. Send both specimens to the lab. If the employee refuses the observed collection, document it as a refusal. Lesson: Temperature is the first line of defense against substituted urine. SECTION 16.7 Scenario 7: "It was only CBD" An employee's MRO-verified result is positive for marijuana. The employee says they only use a CBD product. Chapter 16: Case Scenarios © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 79 of 94

heading: SECTION 16.8
body: What to do: Follow the policy. CBD products can contain THC even when labeled otherwise, and CBD use is not a legitimate medical explanation. The MRO has already considered any explanation offered. Check whether state law protects off-duty cannabis use for this job before deciding the consequence. Lesson: The MRO process, not the employer, weighs explanations. SECTION 16.8 Scenario 8: A DOT driver at 0.03 A CDL driver's random breath alcohol confirmation is 0.03. What to do: This is not a DOT violation, but the driver must be removed from safety-sensitive duty for 24 hours under FMCSA rules. Your company policy may set its own consequence for non-DOT purposes, as long as it is applied consistently and labeled as a company rule. Lesson: Know the difference between a DOT violation and a DOT removal (Chapter 15). SECTION 16.9 Scenario 9: A union representative During a reasonable suspicion meeting, a union employee asks for a union representative. What to do: Honor the request for an investigatory interview that could lead to discipline. Follow your contract and counsel's guidance on proceeding with the test itself, which should not be delayed beyond the testing window. Lesson: Union rights and testing deadlines both apply; plan for both in advance. SECTION 16.10 Scenario 10: Asking for help before a test An employee tells HR they have a drinking problem and want help. The next morning, they are selected for random testing. What to do: If your policy protects self-referral before selection, honor it: refer the employee to the EAP and follow the selfreferral terms. The random test still happens; how a result is handled depends on what your policy says about selfreferral. Lesson: Write the self-referral rule clearly, and apply it exactly as written. heading: APPENDIX
body: APPENDIX Appendix A: Draft Drug and Alcohol Testing Policy This is a starting draft for a non-DOT company program. Replace every item in [brackets], delete options you do not use, and have an employment attorney review it for every state and city where you have employees before you adopt it. DOT-regulated employees need a separate policy that follows 49 CFR Part 40 and the rules of their DOT agency. [COMPANY NAME] Drug and Alcohol Testing Policy Effective date: [DATE] 1. Purpose. [COMPANY NAME] is committed to a safe, healthy and productive workplace. Drug and alcohol use can endanger employees, customers and the public. This policy sets the rules for a drug- and alcohol-free workplace and explains when and how testing will be done. 2. Who is covered. This policy applies to all employees and to applicants who receive a conditional offer of employment [, and to temporary workers and contractors working on company premises]. Employees covered by U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) rules are also subject to the company's separate DOT policy, which controls for DOT testing. 3. Prohibited conduct. While on duty, on company premises, in company vehicles, or while conducting company business, employees may not: • Use, possess, sell, distribute, or be under the influence of illegal drugs or controlled substances not lawfully prescribed to them; • Use or be under the influence of marijuana, regardless of state legality [modify where state law protects off-duty use]; • Use or possess alcohol, or be under the influence of alcohol (an alcohol concentration of [0.04] or higher), except at company-approved events where the employee is not on duty; • Misuse prescription or over-the-counter medications; • Refuse to submit to a test or tamper with a test. 4. Definitions. • Safety-sensitive position: a job in which impairment could cause injury to the employee or others, including [list positions or job categories]. • Reasonable suspicion: a belief, based on specific, current, observable facts about an employee's appearance, behavior, speech or odor, that the employee has violated this policy. • Refusal to test: any conduct listed in Section 9. • Verified positive: a result confirmed by a laboratory and verified by a Medical Review Officer (MRO). 5. When testing will be done. The company will test:

heading: APPENDIX
body: • Pre-employment: all applicants for [all positions / safety-sensitive positions] after a conditional offer of employment. The offer depends on a negative result. • Random: employees in [safety-sensitive positions / all positions], selected by a scientifically valid random method. Each employee in the pool has an equal chance of selection at each draw. Tests are unannounced, and selected employees must report immediately. • Reasonable suspicion: when a trained supervisor has reasonable suspicion, documented on the company's reasonable suspicion checklist and [confirmed by a second supervisor or manager when available]. • Post-accident: after any work-related incident involving [a fatality; an injury requiring medical treatment beyond first aid; property damage over $[AMOUNT]; or a moving traffic citation], for each employee whose actions could have contributed. Testing will not be used to discourage the reporting of injuries. • Return-to-duty and follow-up: before an employee returns after a violation, and unannounced for up to [24] months afterward, as set out in a written agreement. • [Periodic: as part of scheduled physical examinations for [positions].] Appendix A: Draft Drug and Alcohol Testing Policy © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 82 of 94

heading: 6. Testing procedures. Tests will be performed by qualified collectors using [urine / oral
body: 6. Testing procedures. Tests will be performed by qualified collectors using [urine / oral fluid / hair / breath] specimens under chain-of-custody procedures. The panel tests for [list drugs or panel]. [Rapid on-site screens may be used; every non-negative screen will be confirmed by an [HHS-certified / CAP-FDT-accredited] laboratory.] Every non-negative laboratory result will be reviewed by an MRO, who will give the employee an opportunity to provide a legitimate medical explanation before reporting the result to the company. 7. Prescription medications. Employees do not need to report prescriptions to their supervisor as part of testing. Prescriptions are discussed privately with the MRO. Employees in safety-sensitive positions who take a medication that may affect safe performance should [notify the company's designated health and safety contact], who will handle the matter confidentially and consider reasonable accommodation. 8. Consequences. An applicant with a verified positive result or a refusal will not be hired [and may reapply after [6] months]. An employee with a verified positive result or a refusal will be removed from duty immediately and [will be terminated / may, at the company's discretion, be offered one last chance agreement requiring evaluation, completion of any recommended treatment, a negative return-to-duty test and follow-up testing]. A second violation will result in termination. 9. Refusal to test. Each of the following is a refusal: failing to report for a test as directed without delay; leaving the collection site before the test is complete; failing to provide a sufficient specimen without a valid medical reason; refusing a required observed collection; failing to cooperate with the testing process; and providing an adulterated or substituted specimen. 10. Removal from duty pending results. An employee tested for reasonable suspicion or after an accident [or with a nonnegative rapid screen] will be removed from duty pending results. [Pay status during removal: specify.] An employee whose final result is negative will be returned to work [with back pay for scheduled time missed].

heading: 6. Testing procedures. Tests will be performed by qualified collectors using [urine / oral
body: 11. Employee assistance. Employees who believe they have a drug or alcohol problem are encouraged to seek help through [EAP NAME AND CONTACT] or their own provider. An employee who asks for help before being selected or notified for a test will not be disciplined for that request, but must follow treatment recommendations and remains responsible for job performance and conduct. 12. Confidentiality. Test results and related records are confidential, kept separate from personnel files, and shared only with those who need to know or as required by law. 13. Employee rights. An employee with a verified positive result may request, within [72 hours] of notice from the MRO, that the split specimen or retained portion be tested at another certified laboratory at [the employee's / the company's] expense. 14. Searches. [Optional, attorney review recommended:] The company may inspect company property, including vehicles, lockers and desks, when it has reasonable suspicion of a violation. 15. Changes to this policy. The company may change this policy at any time with notice to employees, as permitted by law. Nothing in this policy creates a contract of employment or changes at-will status [where applicable]. 16. Questions. Direct questions about this policy to [PROGRAM CONTACT NAME, TITLE, PHONE, EMAIL]. heading: SECTION 1.1
body: SECTION 1.1 The risk on the jobsite Construction is one of the most dangerous industries in the country, and it carries one of the heaviest burdens of substance use. A worker who is impaired on a scaffold, in a trench, or behind the controls of heavy equipment puts the whole crew at risk. HIGHEST OVERDOSE RATE ALL OCCUPATIONS OPIOIDS age-adjusted drug overdose deaths deaths per 100,000 across all Multiple studies identify construction per 100,000 construction and occupations in the same study. as having the highest rates of opioid- extraction workers aged 16 to 64 in Construction was nearly four times involved overdose death of any 2020 (46 states and New York City), higher. industry. 162.6 42.1 #1 the highest of any occupation group (CDC) Why construction is hit so hard • Physical work and injuries. Strains, falls, and repetitive work lead to pain, and pain often leads to prescription opioids. • Workforce patterns. Seasonal and project-based work, long travel, and time away from home add stress and isolation. • Safety-sensitive tasks everywhere. Heights, trenches, power tools, cranes, and vehicles leave little room for impaired judgment. • Hiring pressure. When crews are short, companies are tempted to put workers on site before screening is complete. GOVERNING RULE A screening program is a safety program. Treat it with the same discipline you give fall protection and lockout. Chapter 1: Why Screening Matters in Construction © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 1.2
body: SECTION 1.2 What a screening program protects A well-run program does more than catch drug use. It protects the crew, the project, the contract, and the company. WHAT IT PROTECTS HOW SCREENING HELPS Your people Keeps impaired workers off safety-sensitive tasks and gives others confidence in the crew beside them. Your projects Fewer incidents mean fewer stoppages, investigations, and schedule delays. Your contracts Many owners, general contractors, and prequalification platforms ask whether you have a drug and alcohol program, and some require one to bid. Your insurance costs Several states offer workers' compensation premium credits to employers with a certified drug-free workplace program, commonly about 5 percent. Confirm the rules with your carrier and state. Your legal position A consistent, documented program supports hiring and discipline decisions if they are challenged, and helps show you took reasonable care in hiring. Your reputation Customers, especially in occupied homes, schools, and hospitals, want to know who is on their site. NEGLIGENT HIRING If an employee harms someone and the employer knew, or should have known, that the employee was unfit for the job, the employer can be held responsible. Reasonable, job-related background screening and drug testing are important ways construction companies show they took care in hiring. EXERCISE 1.2 1. Which is one way a screening program can help your company win or keep work? A It helps you meet owner, GC and prequalification requirements B It guarantees you will win every bid you submit C It replaces the site safety plan that owners require D It lets you skip background checks for any workers the customer never meets in person Chapter 1: Why Screening Matters in Construction © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 1.4
body: SECTION 1.4 Outsourced or in-house? Most construction companies start by sending workers to an outside collection site. More are bringing testing in-house, at the office or the jobsite, to hire faster and keep crews working. FACTOR OUTSOURCED COLLECTION SITE IN-HOUSE WITH LABB STATION Time to result Travel, waiting room, and often Minutes for a negative screen, on site days for a laboratory result Lost work time Worker off the job for travel and Worker tested where they are waiting Post-incident timing Delays while you find an open site Test right away, while results still mean something Remote jobsites May be far from any collection site Test at your office or a jobsite trailer set up for testing Control You depend on the site's hours You control timing, with trained staff and staff Objectivity Laboratory and site procedures Digital reading, image record, and laboratory confirmation for non-negatives Regulated DOT tests Required Rapid drug tests not permitted. DOT tests follow the full federal process, usually at a qualified collection site. In-house testing is not a shortcut. It shifts responsibility to your company, which is why the rest of this guidebook focuses on training, procedures, and certification. EXERCISE 1.4 1. heading: SECTION 2.1
body: SECTION 2.1 DOT testing and company testing Many construction companies employ drivers who hold a commercial driver's license (CDL) to haul equipment, materials, or debris. Those drivers fall under federal Department of Transportation (DOT) rules, and their tests follow a separate, strict process. Who Procedures DOT-REGULATED TESTING COMPANY (NON-DOT) TESTING CDL drivers in safety-sensitive driving jobs, under All other employees and applicants, FMCSA rules (49 CFR Part 382) under your own policy 49 CFR Part 40: federal custody form, certified collector, Your written policy, within state law HHS-certified laboratory, MRO review Rapid tests Not permitted for drug tests. Drug tests must be Permitted in most states laboratory-based. Clearinghouse Pre-employment and annual queries of the FMCSA Not applicable Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse GOVERNING RULE Never use a rapid drug test for a DOT-required test. DOT tests must follow the full Part 40 process, and most companies send them to a qualified collection site. FEDERAL CONTRACTS Companies with federal contracts may have their own drug-free workplace duties. The Drug-Free Workplace Act of 1988 requires covered federal contractors to publish a policy and provide awareness programs, and Department of Defense contracts can require a drug testing program for employees in sensitive positions. Read your contract clauses. SECTION 2.2 OSHA and post-incident testing OSHA's recordkeeping rule bars employers from retaliating against workers who report injuries. In a 2018 interpretation, OSHA said most workplace drug testing is permitted, including random testing, testing under a state workers' compensation law, testing under federal rules such as DOT, and testing to find the root cause of an incident. When you test after an incident, test everyone whose conduct could have contributed, not only the worker who reported an injury. heading: SECTION 2.3
body: SECTION 2.3 State drug testing laws There is no single federal law for private-employer drug testing. States fill the gap, and their rules range from almost none to very detailed. WHAT STATES MAY REGULATE EXAMPLES OF WHAT YOU MAY SEE Written policy and notice A written policy given to employees in advance, sometimes with required content Who may be tested, and when Limits on random testing outside safety-sensitive jobs, or a requirement for reasonable suspicion On-site testing Some states restrict on-site rapid testing, require a permit, or require laboratory confirmation before any action Confirmation and retests Laboratory confirmation of non-negative screens and the employee's right to explain or request a retest Drug-free workplace programs Voluntary programs in states such as Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Mississippi, South Carolina, and Tennessee that offer workers' compensation credits when you follow the state's rules CHECK EVERY STATE WHERE YOU WORK Construction companies often work across state lines. The law of the state where the employee works generally applies. Before testing in a new state, confirm its rules with counsel. A few states, including Minnesota and Vermont, have detailed testing laws that change how an in-house program must run. EXERCISE 2.3 1. Your company wins a project in a new state. What should you confirm before testing workers there? A That state's testing law: notice, random limits, on-site rules, confirmation and drug-free programs B Nothing new, because your home state's law follows your workers to every project C Only the general contractor's site rules, since state law does not apply to subcontractors D Only whether the state has legalized recreational marijuana for adults Chapter 2: Laws and Rules That Shape Your Program © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 2.4
body: SECTION 2.4 Marijuana and prescriptions Marijuana is legal for adult or medical use in most states, but it is still a federal controlled substance. Prescription medications can also produce non-negative results. Both need a clear policy. Marijuana • Several states protect off-duty marijuana use or limit pre-employment marijuana testing, including California, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, and Washington. • Many of these laws exempt safety-sensitive jobs or certain industries. California's law limiting cannabis testing does not apply to employees in the building and construction trades, for example. • No state requires an employer to allow impairment at work. You may still act on impairment or on-the-job use. • DOT rules still prohibit marijuana use by CDL drivers, regardless of state law. Prescriptions • A legitimate prescription can explain a non-negative result. That is why non-negatives go to a laboratory for confirmation and a Medical Review Officer (MRO) for review. • Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), tests for illegal drugs are not medical exams, but questions about medications and conditions are, and so are alcohol tests. Do not give alcohol tests to applicants before a conditional offer, do not ask applicants about medications before a conditional offer, and let the MRO, not supervisors, handle prescription information. • An MRO may report a safety concern when a lawful medication could make safety-sensitive work unsafe. SECTION 2.5 Unions and collective bargaining If your workers are represented by a union, drug testing of current employees is generally a mandatory subject of bargaining under federal labor law. Check your collective bargaining agreement and any project labor agreement before changing how or when you test. Many trade agreements already include a testing program you must follow. heading: SECTION 3.3
body: SECTION 3.3 Choosing a panel and specimen The panel is the list of drugs a test detects. It should match the drugs that cause harm in your workforce, which in construction means including opioids, not just the five classic drugs. DRUG GROUP WHY IT MATTERS IN CONSTRUCTION Fentanyl Drives the overdose crisis. Not detected by standard opiate tests, so it needs its own test. Oxycodone and other opioids Common after injuries. Many need their own test. Methamphetamine and Stimulants that affect judgment and are associated with long-shift work. amphetamines Cocaine Short-acting stimulant common in workplace positives. Marijuana (THC) Check state law (Chapter 2). Many construction employers still test. Benzodiazepines Sedatives that slow reaction time. Alcohol Breath or saliva alcohol tests, especially for post-incident and reasonable suspicion. Oral fluid or urine? ORAL FLUID (RECOMMENDED) URINE • Collected in plain view, no restroom • Longer detection window for most drugs • Harder to adulterate or substitute • Needs a private restroom and integrity checks • Detects more recent use • Easier to substitute or adulterate • Easy on a jobsite • Harder to collect on a jobsite EXERCISE 3.3 1. Why should a construction panel include a separate fentanyl test? A Standard opiate tests do not detect fentanyl B Fentanyl causes false positives for cocaine C OSHA requires fentanyl testing in every plant D Fentanyl stays in urine for about 90 days Chapter 3: Building Your Written Policy © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 3.4
body: SECTION 3.4 Consequences and second chances Workers accept a program they see as fair. Fairness comes from clear rules, applied the same way to everyone, with a real review before any decision. • No action on a rapid screen alone. A non-negative screen is not a positive. Wait for laboratory confirmation and MRO review before discipline or rejection, except for removing the worker from safety-sensitive duty while you wait. • Same violation, same result. Apply consequences consistently across crews, trades, and jobsites. • Refusals are serious. Treat a refusal, an adulterated or substituted specimen, or leaving before testing as your policy states, usually the same as a positive. • Consider a path back. Many construction companies offer a last-chance agreement with assessment, treatment, return-to-duty testing, and follow-up testing. With labor shortages, keeping a skilled worker can be worth it. REMOVING A WORKER FROM DUTY When a worker is waiting for a confirmed result after a non-negative screen, keep them away from safetysensitive work, and make sure someone else drives them. Follow your policy on whether that time is paid. Chapter 3: Building Your Written Policy © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 4.1
body: SECTION 4.1 Roles in an in-house program An in-house program works when every person knows their job. In a small company one person may hold more than one role, but the duties stay separate. ROLE RESPONSIBILITIES Program administrator Owns the policy, schedules random selections, keeps records, receives verified results, and makes sure everyone is trained and certified. Trained collector Runs collections exactly as trained, keeps custody of the device, and documents everything. Never makes hiring or discipline decisions. Supervisors Send workers for testing, make documented reasonable suspicion referrals, and remove impaired workers from duty. Laboratory Confirms non-negative screens with a second, more specific method. Medical Review Officer A licensed physician who reviews laboratory results, talks to the donor about prescriptions, (MRO) and reports the verified result. SEPARATE COLLECTION FROM DECISIONS A collector who is also the worker's direct supervisor, relative, or friend creates a conflict of interest. Where you can, have someone outside the worker's crew collect, and never let the collector decide what happens next. EXERCISE 4.1 1. Your office manager is the only trained collector. Her brother works on one of your crews and is selected for a random test. What do you do? A She may collect, as long as a supervisor stands in the room and watches her do it B She may collect if she records the relationship C She should not collect; use another collector or a partner clinic D Skip his random selection and draw another name Chapter 4: Drug Testing Best Practices © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 4.4
body: SECTION 4.4 Non-negative results A rapid test is a screen. A non-negative result means the specimen needs more testing, not that the worker used drugs. The rapid test is non- Collect a laboratory The laboratory The MRO checks for a The administrator negative for one or specimen under confirms with a more legitimate medical receives the verified more drugs. chain of custody, as specific method. explanation. result and applies Screen Collect for the lab Confirm MRO review your program Verified result the policy. requires. • Do not tell the worker they "failed." Say the screen needs laboratory confirmation. • Remove the worker from safety-sensitive duty while you wait, if your policy says so. • Never guess which drug or why. Prescription questions belong to the MRO. • Give the worker a set window, stated in your policy, to ask for the specimen to be retested. DOT gives its drivers 72 hours. A fair retest window makes a result much harder to challenge. SECTION 4.5 Post-incident and reasonable suspicion timing Speed matters. Drugs and alcohol leave the body over hours, so a test that waits until the next day may miss what caused the incident. • Make sure injured workers get medical care first. Testing never delays treatment. • Test for alcohol within 2 hours when possible and document why if you cannot. Test for drugs as soon as possible. Many programs borrow the DOT limits of 8 hours for alcohol and 32 hours for drugs as outer limits. • Keep the worker away from safety-sensitive work and from driving until the result is known. heading: SECTION 4.6
body: SECTION 4.6 Confidentiality and records Drug test results are confidential. Mishandling them hurts workers, invites lawsuits, and destroys trust in the program. • Share results only with people who need them to make a decision: usually the program administrator. • Keep test records separate from personnel files, in a locked cabinet or a secure system. • Do not discuss results on the jobsite, in group texts, or over the radio. • Keep consent forms, custody forms, collection records, device lot numbers, test images, and MRO results long enough to defend a claim filed years later. Depending on the law, a worker may sue up to five or six years after a test. Confirm your retention period with counsel. WATCH WHAT YOU SAY In one real case, a supervisor told coworkers that an employee had failed a drug test. The result later turned out to be a false positive, and the employee sued. The company won only because its policy happened to define the result as a failure. Never discuss a result with anyone who does not need to know it, and never call a result "failed" until it is verified. HOW A READER HELPS With Labb Station, results are captured and stored digitally, and Labb's coded test devices keep drug names hidden from the person running the test. Chapter 6 explains how this protects both the worker and the company. Chapter 4: Drug Testing Best Practices © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 5.1
body: SECTION 5.1 The background check process step by step You don't run background checks yourself. You order them from a consumer reporting agency (CRA), a background screening company. Your duties come from the FCRA and from state and local law. # STEP WHAT YOU DO Set up your account The CRA verifies your business, and you certify that you will follow the FCRA. Make a conditional offer Where fair chance laws apply, check criminal history only after the offer. Disclose and authorize Give a standalone disclosure, with any state notices, and get written authorization. Most CRAs handle this electronically. Order the right package Order the searches set for that role (Section 5.2). Review the report Apply your written criteria for that role, consistently. Pre-adverse action If the report may lead you to reject or fire someone, send a copy of the report and the Summary of Rights first, with any state or local notices. Wait and listen Give a reasonable time to respond, commonly at least five business days. Some places require more. Final decision If the decision stands, send the adverse action notice with the CRA's contact information and the person's dispute rights. GOVERNING RULE No standalone disclosure, no authorization, no report. No pre-adverse notice, no rejection. Chapter 5: Background Screening Best Practices © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 5.2
body: SECTION 5.2 Matching searches to construction roles Good screening is relevant screening. Order the searches that relate to the job, and use the same package for everyone in that role. heading: SECTION 5.3
body: SECTION 5.3 Fair chance hiring in construction Construction has long offered a second chance to people with records, and the skilled labor shortage makes that pool more important. A fair chance approach keeps you compliant and helps you find good workers. • Ask at the right time. Where the law requires it, wait until after a conditional offer to check criminal history. • Look at the person, not the label. Consider the nature of the offense, how long ago it happened, and how it relates to the job. • Ask for context. Give the applicant a chance to explain, including work history and training since the offense. • Be consistent. Write criteria for each role and apply them the same way to everyone. • Do not consider arrests that did not lead to conviction as proof of conduct, or sealed and expunged records. BLANKET BANS ARE RISKY A policy such as "no felonies, ever" can screen out good workers and can violate federal and state antidiscrimination laws. Review your criteria with counsel. EXERCISE 5.3 1. heading: SECTION 6.1
body: SECTION 6.1 How a rapid test is read Almost every rapid drug test works the same way, and it works backward from what most people expect. Getting this wrong is the most common reading error. WHAT YOU SEE RESULT WHY Control line (C) and test line (T) Negative A line at T means the drug was not detected above the cut-off. Any line at T, even a very faint one, is negative. Control line (C), no test line Non-negative Drug in the specimen blocked the T line from forming. Send for laboratory confirmation. No control line Invalid The test did not run correctly. Retest with a new device. • Results must be read at the time the package insert states. Read too early and lines may not have formed. Read too late and the result is no longer valid. • Multi-panel devices may carry a dozen or more test lines, each read on its own. The same test, three readers Reader 1: "I see a line at T. Negative." Reader 2: "I don't see a line. Non-negative." T C Reader 3: "Too faint to call. Retest?" Figure 6.1 A faint test line. Under the package insert it is negative, but three people can read it three ways. They cannot all be right. heading: SECTION 6.2
body: SECTION 6.2 The problem with the human eye Reading a rapid test by eye turns a laboratory-style result into one person's opinion. On a busy jobsite, that opinion is shaped by many things besides the test. PROBLEM WHAT HAPPENS Faint lines The most common call is also the hardest to see. Readers disagree, and many wrongly call faint lines positive. Lighting and eyesight A dim trailer, glare, color vision, or tired eyes change what a reader sees. Timing A reader who is interrupted reads too late, or one who is rushed reads too early. Pressure A foreman who needs the worker today, or a worker the reader knows, can push a call one way. Knowledge of the drug When the device shows drug names, the reader learns private information and may treat the worker differently. No record Once the device is thrown away, there is nothing but a checkmark on a form. If the result is challenged, it is your word against theirs. Inconsistency Different readers at different jobsites apply different standards, which undermines a policy that must be applied equally. GOVERNING RULE Accuracy comes from reading the test correctly. Reliability comes from being able to prove it. Reading by eye gives you neither for certain. Chapter 6: Reading the Result: Why a Reader Wins © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Construction Edition Version 1.7.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 45 of 79

heading: SECTION 7.3
body: SECTION 7.3 A four-phase transition plan Most companies can move to in-house testing in about 90 days. Do not skip phases. Each one prevents a common failure. PHASE TIMING KEY STEPS 1. Plan Weeks 1 to 3 Choose a program administrator. Review state laws, union agreements, and customer contracts. Decide testing reasons, panel, and specimen. Separate DOTcovered drivers. 2. Build Weeks 3 to 6 Write or update the policy and have counsel review it. Set up Labb Station, laboratory confirmation, MRO review, and background screening. Prepare collection areas. 3. Train and pilot Weeks 6 to 10 Train collectors and supervisors, and complete certification. Announce the policy and collect signed acknowledgments. Pilot at one office or jobsite. 4. Roll out Weeks 10 to 13 Expand to all sites. Start random testing if your policy includes it. Review the first 30 days of records and fix gaps. GOVERNING RULE Announce before you test. Workers should receive the policy, and sign for it, before the first in-house test. EXERCISE 7.3 1. Why pilot at one site before rolling out to all of them? heading: SECTION 8.1
body: SECTION 8.1 Auditing your program Many construction companies already test. The question is whether the program would hold up if a result were challenged, an incident were investigated, or a customer audited it. AUDIT QUESTION YES NO Is the written policy current, reviewed by counsel, and signed for by every worker? Does the policy match what supervisors actually do? Are DOT-covered drivers in a separate DOT program? Does the panel include fentanyl and other opioids? Are pre-employment results back before the first shift? Are post-incident tests done within hours, not days? Are all non-negatives confirmed by a laboratory and reviewed by an MRO before action? Are results read objectively, with a stored record? Are supervisors trained in reasonable suspicion? Do background checks follow every FCRA step, including both notices? Are screening packages set by role and applied consistently? Are drug test and background records kept separately and securely? Are collectors trained and certified, with records of it? Every "No" is a gap. Section 8.2 shows how to close the most common ones. heading: SECTION 8.2
body: SECTION 8.2 Ten common failures and how to fix them # FAILURE FIX Workers start before results come back Test in-house the same day, and make "no result, no start" a firm rule. Post-incident tests happen the next day Test in-house right after medical care. Train supervisors on the timing. Faint lines read as positive Train on the competitive format, and use Labb Station to read objectively. Action taken on a rapid screen alone Confirm every non-negative at a laboratory, with MRO review, and give the worker a set window to request a retest. Panel misses fentanyl Add fentanyl and other opioids to the panel. Results shared on the jobsite Limit access to the administrator. Use coded devices that hide drug names. Background checks ordered without a standalone disclosure Use the CRA's electronic consent flow. Never add waivers or other content. Applicants rejected without notices Always send the pre-adverse notice, wait, then send the final notice. Different rules on different jobsites One policy, one package per role, one reading standard. DOT drivers tested on rapid tests Keep DOT tests with a qualified collection site. EXERCISE 8.2 1. How should you choose the three biggest risks from the list of common program failures? A By choosing the ones your competitors have had trouble with B By an honest self-assessment tied to your audit results C By picking the three listed first in the guidebook D By picking the failures that are cheapest to fix first Chapter 8: Improving an Existing Program © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: APPENDICES
body: APPENDICES A Glossary Definitions of the terms used in this guidebook. Section references point to where each term is explained in depth. A F Adverse action. A decision, such as not hiring, that is based in whole or in part on a background report. Requires FCRA notices (2.6, 5.1). Fair chance law. A state or local law that limits when and how employers consider criminal history (2.6, 5.3). Authorization. The applicant's written permission to obtain a background report (5.1). B FCRA. The Fair Credit Reporting Act, the federal law that governs background checks (2.6, 5.1). Fentanyl. A potent synthetic opioid that standard opiate tests do not detect (3.3). Background screening. Checks of identity, criminal history, driving records, licenses, and other job-related information through a consumer reporting agency (1.3, 5.2). I C L CDL. Commercial driver's license. CDL drivers in safety-sensitive driving jobs are covered by DOT testing rules (2.1). Chain of custody. The documented record of who handled a specimen, from collection to the laboratory (4.4). Clearinghouse. The FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse, a database of CDL drivers' DOT drug and alcohol violations (2.1). Collector. A trained person who runs in-house collections and keeps custody of the test (4.1). Conditional offer. A job offer that depends on passing the drug test and background check (1.3, 5.4). Confirmation. Laboratory testing of a non-negative screen with a more specific method (4.4). Invalid result. A rapid test with no control line. Retest with a new device (6.1). Labb Station. Labb's patented digital reader system that identifies the donor, records consent, captures and reads each test, and stores the record (6.3). Last-chance agreement. An agreement allowing a worker to return after a violation, with treatment and follow-up testing (3.4). M MRO (Medical Review Officer). A licensed physician who reviews laboratory results and prescription explanations (4.1, 4.4). MVR (motor vehicle record). A state driving record (5.2). N Control line (C). The line that shows a rapid test ran correctly. No control line means the test is invalid (6.1). Negligent hiring. Employer liability for harm caused by an employee the employer knew, or should have known, was unfit (1.2). CPP (Labb Channel Partner Program). A network of independent clinic owners who use Labb Station in their own facilities and support construction companies (9.2).

heading: APPENDICES
body: Non-negative. A rapid screen result that needs laboratory confirmation and MRO review. Not the same as a positive (4.4, 6.1). CRA (consumer reporting agency). A background screening company that prepares background reports (5.1). D DOT. U.S. Department of Transportation. DOT-regulated tests follow 49 CFR Part 40. DOT drug tests cannot be run on rapid tests (2.1). Drug-free workplace program. A state program that may offer workers' compensation premium credits to employers who follow its rules (1.2, 2.3). The recommended specimen for in-house construction testing (3.3, 4.3). P Package insert. The manufacturer's instructions for a test device, including storage and read time (4.2, 6.1). Panel. heading: Post-incident test. A test after an incident that caused, or could
body: Post-incident test. A test after an incident that caused, or could have caused, injury or damage (3.2, 4.5). Pre-adverse action notice. The person who owns the policy, records, and verified results (4.1). R Random test. An unannounced test of workers selected from a pool by a neutral method (3.2). Read time. The time stated in the package insert when a rapid test must be read (6.1). Reasonable suspicion test. A test based on specific, documented observations of possible impairment (3.2). Refusal. Failing to test when directed, leaving early, or providing an adulterated or substituted specimen (3.4). Appendix A: Glossary © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. S Safety-sensitive. Work where impairment could cause serious injury or damage (1.1, 3.4). Standalone disclosure. The FCRA notice, in a document by itself, that a background report may be obtained (2.6, 5.1). T Test line (T). On most rapid tests, any line at T, even faint, means negative for that drug (6.1). True Privacy. Labb's coding of rapid tests so the person running the test does not see drug names (6.3). V Verified result. heading: SECTION 1.1
body: SECTION 1.1 The risk on the plant floor Manufacturing puts people next to presses, saws, conveyors, robots, forklifts, and chemicals for full shifts, often around the clock. A worker whose judgment or reaction time is impaired puts themselves, their coworkers, and the product at risk. URINE POSITIVITY HAIR TESTING OSHA'S TOP 10 of urine drug tests in manufacturing of general U.S. workforce hair drug Lockout/tagout, powered industrial were positive in 2025, about 1 in 24 tests were positive in 2025, nearly 1 in trucks, and machine guarding are all (Quest Diagnostics Drug Testing Index, 5, a sign of ongoing use that short- on OSHA's preliminary list of the 10 general U.S. workforce) window tests can miss (Quest) most cited standards for fiscal year 4.2% 19.1% 3 of 10 2026. Why manufacturing is exposed • Machines that do not forgive. Presses, saws, and rotating equipment cause amputations and crush injuries in an instant. • Safety-critical tasks. Lockout/tagout, forklift operation, and chemical handling depend on a clear head every time. • Shift work. Night and weekend shifts have less supervision and fewer places to send a worker for a test. • Product quality. An impaired worker can let a defect through, which can lead to scrap, recalls, and lost customers. GOVERNING RULE A screening program is a safety program. Treat it with the same discipline you give lockout/tagout and machine guarding. Chapter 1: Why Screening Matters in Manufacturing © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 1.2
body: SECTION 1.2 What a screening program protects A well-run program does more than catch drug use. It protects your people, your product, your customer contracts, and your company. WHAT IT PROTECTS HOW SCREENING HELPS Your people Keeps impaired workers off machines and forklifts, and gives coworkers confidence in the people beside them. Your product Fewer errors, less scrap, and fewer quality escapes. Your customers OEMs, defense primes, and regulated buyers often require a drug and alcohol program, and some set specific screening standards in their contracts. Your insurance costs Several states offer workers' compensation premium credits to employers with a certified drug-free workplace program, commonly about 5 percent. Confirm the rules with your carrier and state. Your legal position A consistent, documented program supports hiring and discipline decisions if they are challenged, and helps show you took reasonable care in hiring. Your output Fewer incidents mean fewer line stoppages, investigations, and missed shipments. NEGLIGENT HIRING If an employee harms someone and the employer knew, or should have known, that the employee was unfit for the job, the employer can be held responsible. Reasonable, job-related screening is how you show you took care in hiring. EXERCISE 1.2 1. Which is one way a screening program can help you win or keep a customer? A It helps you meet the customer's screening requirements and pass its audits B It guarantees the customer will renew its contract every year C It replaces the safety training the customer requires on its contracts D It lets you skip background checks for any workers the customer never meets in person Chapter 1: Why Screening Matters in Manufacturing © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Manufacturing Edition Version 1.7.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 6 of 79

heading: SECTION 2.1
body: SECTION 2.1 DOT drivers and company testing Many manufacturers run trucks to move raw materials and finished goods. Drivers who need a commercial driver’s license (CDL) fall under federal Department of Transportation (DOT) drug and alcohol rules. Production, maintenance, warehouse, and office staff do not. Who Procedures DOT-REGULATED TESTING COMPANY (NON-DOT) TESTING CDL drivers in safety-sensitive driving jobs, Production, maintenance, warehouse, office, under FMCSA rules (49 CFR Part 382) and non-CDL drivers, under your own policy 49 CFR Part 40: federal custody form, qualified Your written policy, within state law collector, HHS-certified laboratory, MRO review Rapid tests Not permitted for drug tests. Drug tests must Permitted in most states be laboratory-based. Clearinghouse Pre-employment and annual queries of the Not applicable FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse GOVERNING RULE Never use a rapid drug test for a DOT-required test. DOT tests must follow the full Part 40 process, and most companies send them to a qualified collection site. FEDERAL AND DEFENSE CONTRACTS Manufacturers with federal contracts may have their own drug-free workplace duties. The Drug-Free Workplace Act of 1988 requires covered federal contractors to publish a policy and provide awareness programs, and Department of Defense contracts can require a drug testing program for employees in sensitive positions. Defense manufacturers may also have personnel security requirements. Read your contract clauses and any requirements your customers flow down to you.
