heading: SECTION 2.2
body: SECTION 2.2 Temporary and staffing agency workers Many manufacturers rely on temporary and staffing agency workers, especially when production ramps up. Decide in writing who screens them, because an agency worker on your floor is still a risk on your floor. • Put it in the contract. Your staffing agreement should say who tests, which panel, which background searches, and how results are shared. • Same standard. Require agency workers to meet the same screening standard as your own hires for the same job. • Post-incident and reasonable suspicion. Agree in advance whether you or the agency tests an agency worker after an incident on your site. • Shared responsibility. You and the agency can both be liable for discriminatory screening and for safety training. Under OSHA, the host site usually provides site-specific training, including forklift training. • Background checks. If you order checks on agency workers yourself, the FCRA steps in Section 2.6 apply to you. SECTION 2.3 OSHA and post-incident testing OSHA's recordkeeping rule bars employers from retaliating against workers who report injuries. In a 2018 interpretation, OSHA said most workplace drug testing is permitted, including random testing, testing under a state workers' compensation law, testing under federal rules such as DOT, and testing to find the root cause of an incident. When you test after an incident, such as a machine injury or a forklift collision, test everyone whose conduct could have contributed, not only the worker who reported an injury. EXERCISE 2.2 1. An agency worker on a packaging line is injured when a guard is bypassed. Who tests the worker, and how should you know before it happens? A Whoever the staffing agreement names, decided in writing in advance B The staffing agency always tests, and you never need to ask C Your company always tests, whatever the staffing agreement says about who is responsible D No one tests agency workers, because they are not your employees Chapter 2: Laws and Rules That Shape Your Program © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Manufacturing Edition Version 1.7.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 13 of 79

heading: SECTION 2.4
body: SECTION 2.4 State laws and marijuana There is no single federal law for private-employer drug testing. States fill the gap, and marijuana laws are the fastest-changing part. WHAT STATES MAY REGULATE EXAMPLES OF WHAT YOU MAY SEE Written policy and notice A written policy given to employees in advance, sometimes with required content Who may be tested, and when Limits on random testing outside safety-sensitive jobs On-site testing Some states restrict on-site rapid testing, require a permit, or require laboratory confirmation before any action Drug-free workplace programs Voluntary programs in states such as Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Mississippi, South Carolina, and Tennessee that offer workers' compensation credits Marijuana • California bars most employers from acting on off-duty cannabis use or on tests that detect only nonpsychoactive metabolites, which is what urine and hair tests detect, and from asking applicants about past cannabis use. Tests that detect the parent compound THC, such as oral fluid tests, remain an option for applicants. Unlike construction, manufacturing has no industry exemption. Jobs that federal law requires to be tested, such as DOT drivers, are exempt. • Washington bars hiring decisions based on lawful off-duty cannabis use or non-psychoactive metabolites, except for jobs the employer identifies as safety-sensitive before the person applies. • New York generally bars cannabis testing unless federal or state law requires it. New Jersey, Nevada, and other states protect off-duty use or limit marijuana testing in different ways. • No state requires you to allow impairment at work, and DOT still prohibits marijuana use by CDL drivers. MULTI-PLANT COMPANIES A company with plants in several states faces several sets of rules, each with its own rules. The law where the employee works generally applies. Build your panel and procedures site by site with counsel. Chapter 2: Laws and Rules That Shape Your Program © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Manufacturing Edition Version 1.7.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 14 of 79

heading: SECTION 2.5
body: SECTION 2.5 Prescriptions, unions, and customer contracts Prescriptions and the ADA • A legitimate prescription can explain a non-negative result. That is why non-negatives go to a laboratory for confirmation and a Medical Review Officer (MRO) for review. • Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), tests for illegal drugs are not medical exams, but questions about medications and conditions are disability-related inquiries, and alcohol tests are medical exams. Do not give alcohol tests to applicants before a conditional offer, do not ask applicants about medications before an offer, and let the MRO handle prescription information. Unions If your workers are represented by a union, drug testing of current employees is generally a mandatory subject of bargaining. Check your collective bargaining agreement before changing how or when you test. Customer contracts Customers such as OEMs, defense prime contractors, and food and pharmaceutical buyers may set their own screening standards or flow contract clauses down to you. Read your customer agreements before you move testing in-house, and keep a copy of each customer's requirements with your policy. SECTION 2.6 Background check law in brief When you use an outside company to run background checks, the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) applies. You must give a standalone disclosure and get written authorization, send a pre-adverse action notice with a copy of the report and the Summary of Rights before rejecting anyone based on it, wait a reasonable time, and then send a final adverse action notice. Many states and cities also have fair chance laws that limit when you may ask about criminal history. Chapter 5 covers the details. Chapter 2: Laws and Rules That Shape Your Program © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 3.3
body: SECTION 3.3 Choosing a panel and specimen The panel is the list of drugs a test detects. It should match the drugs that cause harm in your workforce, which in manufacturing means including opioids and stimulants, not just the five classic drugs. DRUG GROUP WHY IT MATTERS IN MANUFACTURING Fentanyl Drives the overdose crisis. Not detected by standard opiate tests, so it needs its own test. Oxycodone and other opioids Common after injuries. Many need their own test. Methamphetamine and Stimulants that affect judgment and are associated with long-shift work. amphetamines Cocaine Short-acting stimulant common in workplace positives. Marijuana (THC) Check state law (Chapter 2). California and some other states limit metabolite testing. Benzodiazepines Sedatives that slow reaction time. Alcohol Breath or saliva alcohol tests, especially for post-incident and reasonable suspicion. Oral fluid or urine? ORAL FLUID (RECOMMENDED) URINE • Collected in plain view, no restroom • Longer detection window for most drugs • Harder to adulterate or substitute • Needs a private restroom and integrity checks • Detects more recent use • Easier to substitute or adulterate • Detects THC itself, which matters under • Detects metabolites that California law limits California's law EXERCISE 3.3 1. Why should a manufacturing panel include a separate fentanyl test? A Fentanyl causes false positives for cocaine B OSHA requires fentanyl testing in every plant C Fentanyl stays in urine for about 90 days D Standard opiate tests do not detect fentanyl Chapter 3: Building Your Written Policy © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 3.4
body: SECTION 3.4 Consequences and second chances Workers accept a program they see as fair. Fairness comes from clear rules, applied the same way to everyone, with a real review before any decision. • No action on a rapid screen alone. A non-negative screen is not a positive. Wait for laboratory confirmation and MRO review before discipline or rejection, except for removing the worker from safety-sensitive duty while you wait. • Same violation, same result. Apply consequences consistently across shifts, departments, and facilities. • Refusals are serious. Treat a refusal, an adulterated or substituted specimen, or leaving before testing as your policy states, usually the same as a positive. • Consider a path back. Many manufacturers offer a last-chance agreement with assessment, treatment, return-toduty testing, and follow-up testing. When good workers are hard to find, keeping a trained machine operator or skilled tradesperson can be worth it. REMOVING A WORKER FROM DUTY When a worker is waiting for a confirmed result after a non-negative screen, keep them away from safetysensitive work, and make sure someone else drives them. Follow your policy on whether that time is paid. Chapter 3: Building Your Written Policy © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 4.1
body: SECTION 4.1 Roles in an in-house program An in-house program works when every person knows their job. In a small company one person may hold more than one role, but the duties stay separate. ROLE RESPONSIBILITIES Program administrator Owns the policy, schedules random selections, keeps records, receives verified results, and makes sure everyone is trained and certified. Trained collector Runs collections exactly as trained, keeps custody of the device, and documents everything. Never makes hiring or discipline decisions. Supervisors Send workers for testing, make documented reasonable suspicion referrals, and remove impaired workers from duty. Laboratory Confirms non-negative screens with a second, more specific method. Medical Review Officer A licensed physician who reviews laboratory results, talks to the donor about prescriptions, (MRO) and reports the verified result. SEPARATE COLLECTION FROM DECISIONS A collector who is also the worker's direct supervisor, relative, or friend creates a conflict of interest. Where you can, have someone outside the worker's department collect, and never let the collector decide what happens next. EXERCISE 4.1 1. Your office manager is the only trained collector. Her brother works on second shift and is selected for a random test. What do you do? A She may collect, as long as a supervisor stands in the room and watches her do it B She should not collect; use another collector or a partner clinic C She may collect if she records the relationship D Skip his random selection and draw another name Chapter 4: Drug Testing Best Practices © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 4.4
body: SECTION 4.4 Non-negative results A rapid test is a screen. A non-negative result means the specimen needs more testing, not that the worker used drugs. The rapid test is non- Collect a laboratory The laboratory The MRO checks for a The administrator negative for one or specimen under confirms with a more legitimate medical receives the verified more drugs. chain of custody, as specific method. explanation. result and applies Screen Collect for the lab Confirm MRO review your program Verified result the policy. requires. • Do not tell the worker they "failed." Say the screen needs laboratory confirmation. • Remove the worker from safety-sensitive duty while you wait, if your policy says so. • Never guess which drug or why. Prescription questions belong to the MRO. • Give the worker a set window, stated in your policy, to ask for the specimen to be retested. DOT gives its drivers 72 hours. A fair retest window makes a result much harder to challenge. SECTION 4.5 Post-incident and reasonable suspicion timing Speed matters. Drugs and alcohol leave the body over hours, so a test that waits until the next day may miss what caused the incident. • Make sure injured workers get medical care first. Testing never delays treatment. • Test for alcohol within 2 hours when possible and document why if you cannot. Test for drugs as soon as possible. Many programs borrow the DOT limits of 8 hours for alcohol and 32 hours for drugs as outer limits. • Keep the worker away from safety-sensitive work and from driving until the result is known. heading: SECTION 4.6
body: SECTION 4.6 Confidentiality and records Drug test results are confidential. Mishandling them hurts workers, invites lawsuits, and destroys trust in the program. • Share results only with people who need them to make a decision: usually the program administrator. • Keep test records separate from personnel files, in a locked cabinet or a secure system. • Do not discuss results on the floor, in group texts, or over the radio. • Keep consent forms, custody forms, collection records, device lot numbers, test images, and MRO results long enough to defend a claim filed years later. Depending on the law, a worker may sue up to five or six years after a test. Confirm your retention period with counsel. WATCH WHAT YOU SAY In one real case, a supervisor told coworkers that an employee had failed a drug test. The result later turned out to be a false positive, and the employee sued. The company won only because its policy happened to define the result as a failure. Never discuss a result with anyone who does not need to know it, and never call a result "failed" until it is verified. HOW A READER HELPS With Labb Station, results are captured and stored digitally, and Labb's coded test devices keep drug names hidden from the person running the test. Chapter 6 explains how this protects both the worker and the company. Chapter 4: Drug Testing Best Practices © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 5.1
body: SECTION 5.1 The background check process step by step You don't run background checks yourself. You order them from a consumer reporting agency (CRA), a background screening company. Your duties come from the FCRA and from state and local law. # STEP WHAT YOU DO Set up your account The CRA verifies your business, and you certify that you will follow the FCRA. Make a conditional offer Where fair chance laws apply, check criminal history only after the offer. Disclose and authorize Give a standalone disclosure, with any state notices, and get written authorization. Most CRAs handle this electronically, which makes hiring events manageable. Order the right package Order the searches set for that role (Section 5.2). Review the report Apply your written criteria for that role, consistently. Pre-adverse action If the report may lead you to reject or fire someone, send a copy of the report and the Summary of Rights first, with any state or local notices. Wait and listen Give a reasonable time to respond, commonly at least five business days. Some places require more. Final decision If the decision stands, send the adverse action notice with the CRA's contact information, a statement that the CRA did not make the decision, the right to a free copy of the report within 60 days, and the person's dispute rights. GOVERNING RULE No standalone disclosure, no authorization, no report. No pre-adverse notice, no rejection. A production ramp-up is not an exception. heading: SECTION 5.3
body: SECTION 5.3 Fair chance hiring in manufacturing Manufacturers have long given people with records a path to steady, skilled work. With open production jobs hard to fill, a fair chance approach keeps you compliant and widens a hiring pool you need. • Ask at the right time. Where the law requires it, wait until after a conditional offer to check criminal history. • Look at the person, not the label. Consider the nature of the offense, how long ago it happened, and how it relates to the job. • Ask for context. Give the applicant a chance to explain, including work history and training since the offense. • Be consistent. Write criteria for each role and apply them the same way to everyone. • Do not consider arrests that did not lead to conviction as proof of conduct, or sealed and expunged records. BLANKET BANS ARE RISKY A policy such as "no felonies, ever" can screen out good workers and can violate federal and state antidiscrimination laws. Review your criteria with counsel. EXERCISE 5.3 1. heading: SECTION 6.1
body: SECTION 6.1 How a rapid test is read Almost every rapid drug test works the same way, and it works backward from what most people expect. Getting this wrong is the most common reading error. WHAT YOU SEE RESULT WHY Control line (C) and test line (T) Negative A line at T means the drug was not detected above the cut-off. Any line at T, even a very faint one, is negative. Control line (C), no test line Non-negative Drug in the specimen blocked the T line from forming. Send for laboratory confirmation. No control line Invalid The test did not run correctly. Retest with a new device. • Results must be read at the time the package insert states. Read too early and lines may not have formed. Read too late and the result is no longer valid. • Multi-panel devices may carry a dozen or more test lines, each read on its own. The same test, three readers Reader 1: "I see a line at T. Negative." Reader 2: "I don't see a line. Non-negative." T C Reader 3: "Too faint to call. Retest?" Figure 6.1 A faint test line. Under the package insert it is negative, but three people can read it three ways. They cannot all be right. heading: SECTION 6.2
body: SECTION 6.2 The real problem: human bias Most collectors read well. The bigger problem is that every reader is human, and a human read is shaped by what the reader expects, feels, and needs. Bias is harder to see than a faint line. BIAS HOW IT SHOWS UP Expectation A worker mentions something before the test: an antibiotic, an over-the-counter pain reliever, or use from months ago. Many people don't know what a test detects or for how long. The collector now expects a positive, and a faint line may get called non-negative. Sympathy The collector knows the worker is struggling or needs this job, and a borderline line could be called negative. Assumptions about people Everyone carries assumptions about who "looks like" a drug user, often without knowing it. Any judgment call can be challenged as influenced by who the donor is. A reader takes that argument away. Production pressure When a line is short, supervisors need people at their stations. A collector who knows the shift is short can feel pressure to call it negative. Conditions make it worse Faint lines, poor lighting, tired eyes, interruptions that push a read past its time, and drug names printed on the device all give bias more room to work. When the device is thrown away, nothing is left but a checkmark. GOVERNING RULE The question is not whether your collectors are good. It is whether any person should be the one deciding what a line means. Chapter 6: Reading the Result: Why a Reader Wins © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 7.1
body: SECTION 7.1 Is in-house testing right for you? In-house testing pays off most for companies that hire often, work far from collection sites, or need fast post-incident testing. heading: SECTION 7.3
body: SECTION 7.3 A four-phase transition plan Most companies can move to in-house testing in about 90 days. Do not skip phases. Each one prevents a common failure. PHASE TIMING KEY STEPS 1. Plan Weeks 1 to 3 Choose a program administrator. Review state laws, union agreements, and customer contracts. Decide testing reasons, panel, and specimen. Separate DOTcovered drivers. 2. Build Weeks 3 to 6 Write or update the policy and have counsel review it. Set up Labb Station, laboratory confirmation, MRO review, and background screening. Prepare collection areas. 3. Train and pilot Weeks 6 to 10 Train collectors and supervisors, and complete certification. Announce the policy and collect signed acknowledgments. Pilot at one plant or shift first. 4. Roll out Weeks 10 to 13 Expand to all sites. Start random testing if your policy includes it. Review the first 30 days of records and fix gaps. GOVERNING RULE Announce before you test. Workers should receive the policy, and sign for it, before the first in-house test. EXERCISE 7.3 1. Why pilot at one site before rolling out to all of them? A Because counsel must approve each site separately before any in-house testing can begin there B Because the CPP requires one site to test for a full year first C To find procedure, space and training problems before they repeat everywhere D To delay the cost of buying Labb Station devices for every site Chapter 7: Transitioning to In-House Testing © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 7.4

heading: SECTION 8.1
body: SECTION 8.1 Auditing your program Many manufacturers already test. The question is whether the program would hold up if a result were challenged, an incident were investigated, or a customer audited it. AUDIT QUESTION YES NO Is the written policy current, reviewed by counsel, and signed for by every worker? Does the policy match what supervisors actually do? Are DOT-covered drivers in a separate DOT program? Does the panel include fentanyl and other opioids? Are pre-employment results back before the first shift? Are post-incident tests done within hours, not days? Are all non-negatives confirmed by a laboratory and reviewed by an MRO before action? Are results read objectively, with a stored record? Are supervisors trained in reasonable suspicion? Do background checks follow every FCRA step, including both notices? Are screening packages set by role and applied consistently? Are drug test and background records kept separately and securely? Are collectors trained and certified, with records of it? Every "No" is a gap. Section 8.2 shows how to close the most common ones. heading: SECTION 8.2
body: SECTION 8.2 Ten common failures and how to fix them # FAILURE FIX Workers start before results come back Test in-house the same day, and make "no result, no start" a firm rule. Post-incident tests happen the next day Test in-house right after medical care. Train supervisors on the timing. Faint lines read as positive Train on the competitive format, and use Labb Station to read objectively. Action taken on a rapid screen alone Confirm every non-negative at a laboratory, with MRO review, and give the worker a set window to request a retest. Panel misses fentanyl Add fentanyl and other opioids to the panel. Results shared on the floor Limit access to the administrator. Use coded devices that hide drug names. Background checks ordered without a standalone disclosure Use the CRA's electronic consent flow. Never add waivers or other content. Applicants rejected without notices Always send the pre-adverse notice, wait, then send the final notice. Different rules at different facilities One policy, one package per role, one reading standard. DOT drivers tested on rapid tests Keep DOT tests with a qualified collection site. EXERCISE 8.2 1. heading: APPENDICES
body: APPENDICES A Glossary Definitions of the terms used in this guidebook. Section references point to where each term is explained in depth. A E Adverse action. A decision, such as not hiring, that is based in whole or in part on a background report. Requires FCRA notices (2.6, 5.1). Expectation bias. Reading a result the way you expect it to come out, for example after a worker mentions taking a medication (6.2). Authorization. The applicant's written permission to obtain a background report (5.1). B Background screening. Checks of identity, criminal history, driving records, licenses, and other job-related information through a consumer reporting agency (1.3, 5.2). C CDL. Commercial driver's license. CDL drivers in safety-sensitive driving jobs are covered by DOT testing rules (2.1). F Fair chance law. A state or local law that limits when and how employers consider criminal history (2.6, 5.3). FCRA. The Fair Credit Reporting Act, the federal law that governs background checks (2.6, 5.1). Fentanyl. A potent synthetic opioid that standard opiate tests do not detect (3.3). I Invalid result. A rapid test with no control line. Retest with a new device (6.1). Chain of custody. The documented record of who handled a specimen, from collection to the laboratory (4.4). L Clearinghouse. The FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse, a database of CDL drivers' DOT drug and alcohol violations (2.1). Labb Station. Labb's patented digital reader system that identifies the donor, records consent, captures and reads each test, and stores the record (6.3). Collector. A trained person who runs in-house collections and keeps custody of the test (4.1). Conditional offer. A job offer that depends on passing the drug test and background check (1.3, 5.4). Confirmation. Laboratory testing of a non-negative screen with a more specific method (4.4). Control line (C). The line that shows a rapid test ran correctly. No control line means the test is invalid (6.1). CPP (Labb Channel Partner Program). A network of independent clinic owners who use Labb Station in their own facilities and support manufacturers (9.2). CRA (consumer reporting agency). A background screening company that prepares background reports (5.1). Last-chance agreement. An agreement allowing a worker to return after a violation, with treatment and follow-up testing (3.4).

heading: APPENDICES
body: Lockout/tagout. Procedures that keep machines from starting during service or maintenance. Workers who perform it hold safety-critical authority (1.1, 5.2). M MRO (Medical Review Officer). A licensed physician who reviews laboratory results and prescription explanations (4.1, 4.4). MVR (motor vehicle record). A state driving record (5.2). N D Negligent hiring. Employer liability for harm caused by an employee the employer knew, or should have known, was unfit (1.2). DOT. U.S. Department of Transportation. DOT-regulated tests follow 49 CFR Part 40. DOT drug tests cannot be run on rapid tests (2.1). Non-negative. A rapid screen result that needs laboratory confirmation and MRO review. Not the same as a positive (4.4, 6.1). Drug-free workplace program. A state program that may offer workers' compensation premium credits to employers who follow its rules (1.2, 2.4). Appendix A: Glossary © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Manufacturing Edition Version 1.7.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 76 of 79

heading: Read time. The time stated in the package insert when a rapid test
body: O Read time. The time stated in the package insert when a rapid test must be read (6.1). Oral fluid. Saliva collected from the mouth. The recommended specimen for in-house manufacturing testing. It detects THC itself rather than only metabolites (2.4, 3.3, 4.3). Reasonable suspicion test. A test based on specific, documented observations of possible impairment (3.2). P Package insert. The manufacturer's instructions for a test device, including storage and read time (4.2, 6.1). Refusal. Failing to test when directed, leaving early, or providing an adulterated or substituted specimen (3.4). S Panel. The list of drugs a test detects (3.3). Safety-sensitive. Work where impairment could cause serious injury or damage (1.1, 3.4). Powered industrial truck. A forklift or similar vehicle. OSHA requires the employer to train and evaluate operators (5.2). Standalone disclosure. The FCRA notice, in a document by itself, that a background report may be obtained (2.6, 5.1). Post-incident test. A test after an incident that caused, or could have caused, injury or damage (3.2, 4.5). Staffing agency worker. A temporary worker employed by an agency and assigned to your facility. Screening duties should be set in the staffing agreement (2.2). Pre-adverse action notice. The notice, with a copy of the report and the Summary of Rights, sent before a final decision based on a background report (5.1). T Program administrator. The person who owns the policy, records, and verified results (4.1). Test line (T). On most rapid tests, any line at T, even faint, means negative for that drug (6.1). R True Privacy. Labb's coding of rapid tests so the person running the test does not see drug names (6.3). Random test. An unannounced test of workers selected from a pool by a neutral method (3.2). V Verified result. The final result reported by the MRO after laboratory confirmation and review (4.4). Appendix A: Glossary © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 1.1
body: SECTION 1.1 The risk on the dock and the floor Logistics and fulfillment work is fast, physical, and full of moving equipment. Forklifts, reach trucks, conveyors, dock plates, trailers, and delivery vehicles leave little room for a worker whose judgment or reaction time is impaired. URINE POSITIVITY RETAIL TRADE HAIR TESTING of urine drug tests in transportation urine positivity in retail trade, including of general U.S. workforce hair drug and warehousing were positive in retailers that run their own store and tests were positive in 2025, nearly 1 in 2025 (Quest Diagnostics Drug Testing e-commerce fulfillment, in the same 5, a sign of ongoing use that short- Index, general U.S. workforce) data window tests can miss (Quest) 4.2% 5.4% 19.1% Why logistics is exposed • Powered equipment everywhere. Forklifts and other powered industrial trucks are among the most common sources of serious warehouse injuries. • High-volume hiring. Peak season can double a headcount in weeks. Every hire who skips screening, or starts before results are back, is a risk. • Around-the-clock shifts. Night and weekend shifts have less supervision and fewer places to send a worker for a test. • Valuable freight. Inventory loss, cargo theft, and package tampering make background screening as important as drug testing. GOVERNING RULE A screening program is a safety program. Treat it with the same discipline you give forklift certification and lockout. Chapter 1: Why Screening Matters in Logistics © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 1.2
body: SECTION 1.2 What a screening program protects A well-run program does more than catch drug use. It protects your people, your freight, your customer contracts, and your company. WHAT IT PROTECTS HOW SCREENING HELPS Your people Keeps impaired workers off equipment and docks, and gives coworkers confidence in the people beside them. Your freight Background screening and a strong testing program reduce theft, loss, and damage. Your customers Shippers, retailers, and carriers often require a drug and alcohol program, and some set specific screening standards in their contracts. Your insurance costs Several states offer workers' compensation premium credits to employers with a certified drug-free workplace program, commonly about 5 percent. Confirm the rules with your carrier and state. Your legal position A consistent, documented program supports hiring and discipline decisions if they are challenged, and helps show you took reasonable care in hiring. Your service levels Fewer incidents mean fewer shutdowns, investigations, and missed shipments. NEGLIGENT HIRING If an employee harms someone and the employer knew, or should have known, that the employee was unfit for the job, the employer can be held responsible. A delivery driver with a poor driving record or a warehouse worker with a relevant history are classic examples. Reasonable, job-related screening is how you show you took care in hiring. heading: SECTION 1.4
body: SECTION 1.4 Outsourced or in-house? Most logistics companies start by sending applicants to an outside collection site. More are bringing testing in-house so they can hire on the spot, test every shift, and keep peak-season hiring moving. FACTOR OUTSOURCED COLLECTION SITE IN-HOUSE WITH LABB STATION Time to result Travel, waiting room, and often Minutes for a negative screen, at your facility days for a laboratory result Applicant drop-off Applicants who must go Test during the hiring visit elsewhere often never show up Night and weekend shifts Few sites open Test on every shift with trained staff Post-incident timing Delays while you find an open site Test right away, while results still mean something Peak season Sites get backed up when Capacity grows with your hiring events everyone hires at once Objectivity Laboratory and site procedures Digital reading, image record, and laboratory confirmation for non-negatives Regulated DOT tests Required Rapid drug tests not permitted. DOT tests follow the full federal process, usually at a qualified collection site. In-house testing is not a shortcut. It shifts responsibility to your company, which is why the rest of this guidebook focuses on training, procedures, and certification. EXERCISE 1.4 1. heading: SECTION 2.1
body: SECTION 2.1 DOT drivers and company testing Many logistics companies run trucks. Drivers who need a commercial driver's license (CDL) fall under federal Department of Transportation (DOT) drug and alcohol rules. Most warehouse workers and many delivery van drivers do not. Who Procedures DOT-REGULATED TESTING COMPANY (NON-DOT) TESTING CDL drivers in safety-sensitive driving jobs, under Warehouse, dock, office, and non-CDL FMCSA rules (49 CFR Part 382) delivery staff, under your own policy 49 CFR Part 40: federal custody form, qualified Your written policy, within state law collector, HHS-certified laboratory, MRO review Rapid tests Not permitted for drug tests. Drug tests must be Permitted in most states laboratory-based. Clearinghouse Pre-employment and annual queries of the FMCSA Not applicable Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse GOVERNING RULE Never use a rapid drug test for a DOT-required test. DOT tests must follow the full Part 40 process, and most companies send them to a qualified collection site. NON-CDL DELIVERY DRIVERS Drivers of vans and box trucks that do not require a CDL are generally not covered by DOT drug and alcohol testing. You can and should test them under your company policy, and check their driving records. Confirm vehicle weights and routes with a DOT compliance advisor, because some vehicles and operations bring other FMCSA rules into play. Chapter 2: Laws and Rules That Shape Your Program © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 2.2
body: SECTION 2.2 Temporary and staffing agency workers Logistics relies heavily on temporary and staffing agency workers, especially at peak. Decide in writing who screens them, because an agency worker on your floor is still a risk on your floor. • Put it in the contract. Your staffing agreement should say who tests, which panel, which background searches, and how results are shared. • Same standard. Require agency workers to meet the same screening standard as your own hires for the same job. • Post-incident and reasonable suspicion. Agree in advance whether you or the agency tests an agency worker after an incident on your site. • Shared responsibility. You and the agency can both be liable for discriminatory screening and for safety training. Under OSHA, the host site usually provides site-specific training, including forklift training. • Background checks. If you order checks on agency workers yourself, the FCRA steps in Section 2.6 apply to you. SECTION 2.3 OSHA and post-incident testing OSHA's recordkeeping rule bars employers from retaliating against workers who report injuries. In a 2018 interpretation, OSHA said most workplace drug testing is permitted, including random testing, testing under a state workers' compensation law, testing under federal rules such as DOT, and testing to find the root cause of an incident. When you test after an incident, such as a forklift striking a rack or a person, test everyone whose conduct could have contributed, not only the worker who reported an injury. EXERCISE 2.2 1. An agency worker drives a pallet jack into a dock door. Who tests the worker, and how should you know before it happens? A Whoever the staffing agreement names, decided in writing in advance B The staffing agency always tests, and you never need to ask C Your company always tests, whatever the staffing agreement says about who is responsible D No one tests agency workers, because they are not your employees Chapter 2: Laws and Rules That Shape Your Program © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Logistics Edition Version 1.7.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 13 of 79

heading: SECTION 2.4
body: SECTION 2.4 State laws and marijuana There is no single federal law for private-employer drug testing. States fill the gap, and marijuana laws are the fastest-changing part. WHAT STATES MAY REGULATE EXAMPLES OF WHAT YOU MAY SEE Written policy and notice A written policy given to employees in advance, sometimes with required content Who may be tested, and when Limits on random testing outside safety-sensitive jobs On-site testing Some states restrict on-site rapid testing, require a permit, or require laboratory confirmation before any action Drug-free workplace programs Voluntary programs in states such as Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Mississippi, South Carolina, and Tennessee that offer workers' compensation credits Marijuana • California bars most employers from acting on off-duty cannabis use or on tests that detect only nonpsychoactive metabolites, which is what urine and hair tests detect, and from asking applicants about past cannabis use. Tests that detect the parent compound THC, such as oral fluid tests, remain an option for applicants. Unlike construction, warehousing has no industry exemption. Jobs that federal law requires to be tested, such as DOT drivers, are exempt. • Washington bars hiring decisions based on lawful off-duty cannabis use or non-psychoactive metabolites, except for jobs the employer identifies as safety-sensitive before the person applies. • New York generally bars cannabis testing unless federal or state law requires it. New Jersey, Nevada, and other states protect off-duty use or limit marijuana testing in different ways. • No state requires you to allow impairment at work, and DOT still prohibits marijuana use by CDL drivers. MULTI-STATE NETWORKS A distribution network may span many states, each with its own rules. The law where the employee works generally applies. Build your panel and procedures site by site with counsel. Chapter 2: Laws and Rules That Shape Your Program © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Logistics Edition Version 1.7.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 14 of 79

heading: SECTION 2.5
body: SECTION 2.5 Prescriptions, unions, and customer contracts Prescriptions and the ADA • A legitimate prescription can explain a non-negative result. That is why non-negatives go to a laboratory for confirmation and a Medical Review Officer (MRO) for review. • Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), tests for illegal drugs are not medical exams, but questions about medications and conditions are disability-related inquiries, and alcohol tests are medical exams. Do not give alcohol tests to applicants before a conditional offer, do not ask applicants about medications before an offer, and let the MRO handle prescription information. Unions If your workers are represented by a union, drug testing of current employees is generally a mandatory subject of bargaining. Check your collective bargaining agreement before changing how or when you test. Customer contracts Retailers, shippers, and carrier programs may set their own screening standards, and some limit who may conduct testing for workers on their freight or routes. Read your customer agreements before you move testing in-house, and keep a copy of each customer's requirements with your policy. SECTION 2.6 Background check law in brief When you use an outside company to run background checks, the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) applies. You must give a standalone disclosure and get written authorization, send a pre-adverse action notice with a copy of the report and the Summary of Rights before rejecting anyone based on it, wait a reasonable time, and then send a final adverse action notice. Many states and cities also have fair chance laws that limit when you may ask about criminal history. Chapter 5 covers the details. heading: SECTION 3.1
body: SECTION 3.1 What the policy must cover Every in-house program starts with a written policy. It tells workers what to expect, tells supervisors what to do, and is your first defense if a decision is challenged. TOPIC WHAT TO DECIDE AND WRITE DOWN Purpose and scope Why you test and who is covered: applicants, employees, and any temporary or leased workers Prohibited conduct Use, possession, sale, or being under the influence at work, on the dock and floor, and in company vehicles Testing reasons Pre-employment, post-incident, reasonable suspicion, random, and return-to-duty and follow-up Panel and specimen Which drugs, which specimen (oral fluid or urine), and alcohol testing Procedures Who collects, where, how results are read, and how non-negatives are confirmed and reviewed Refusals What counts as a refusal and its consequences Consequences What happens after a verified positive or refusal Confidentiality Who sees results and how records are kept Background screening Which roles get which searches, consent, and the adverse action process Help available Any employee assistance program or treatment resources Acknowledgment Signed receipt of the policy by every worker GOVERNING RULE If it is not in the policy, do not do it. If it is in the policy, do it the same way every time. Chapter 3: Building Your Written Policy © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 3.2
body: SECTION 3.2 Testing reasons for logistics Each reason for testing has a different purpose and timing. Logistics programs usually use all of them. REASON WHEN LOGISTICS NOTES Pre-employment After a conditional offer, before work starts Test before the first shift, not after. No one goes on the floor waiting for a result, even at peak. Post-incident As soon as possible after an incident that Test everyone whose conduct could have caused, or could have caused, injury or damage contributed. Alcohol within 2 hours is best. Inhouse testing makes speed possible. Reasonable suspicion When a trained supervisor observes specific Document what was seen, heard, and signs of impairment smelled. Remove the worker from duty. Never let them drive. Random Unannounced, from a pool, by a neutral The strongest deterrent. Check state law and selection method any union agreement first. Return-to-duty and Before return after a violation, then Usually part of a last-chance agreement follow-up unannounced for a set period REASONABLE SUSPICION TRAINING Supervisors who make reasonable suspicion calls should be trained to recognize signs of impairment and to document them. A good record lists specific observations (slurred speech, unsteady walking, the smell of alcohol), the time, and a second witness when possible. EXERCISE 3.2 1. A forklift strikes a racking upright and a picker is hurt. The driver, a spotter, and two pickers were in the aisle. Who should be tested? A Everyone who was present in the area when it happened, whether or not they took part B No one until the incident investigation is complete C Each worker whose conduct could have contributed to the incident D Only the injured worker, since the injury triggered the test Chapter 3: Building Your Written Policy © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Logistics Edition Version 1.7.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 20 of 79

heading: SECTION 3.3
body: SECTION 3.3 Choosing a panel and specimen The panel is the list of drugs a test detects. It should match the drugs that cause harm in your workforce, which in logistics means including opioids and stimulants, not just the five classic drugs. DRUG GROUP WHY IT MATTERS IN LOGISTICS Fentanyl Drives the overdose crisis. Not detected by standard opiate tests, so it needs its own test. Oxycodone and other opioids Common after injuries. Many need their own test. Methamphetamine and Stimulants that affect judgment and are associated with long-shift work. amphetamines Cocaine Short-acting stimulant common in workplace positives. Marijuana (THC) Check state law (Chapter 2). California and some other states limit metabolite testing. Benzodiazepines Sedatives that slow reaction time. Alcohol Breath or saliva alcohol tests, especially for post-incident and reasonable suspicion. Oral fluid or urine? ORAL FLUID (RECOMMENDED) URINE • Collected in plain view, no restroom • Longer detection window for most drugs • Harder to adulterate or substitute • Needs a private restroom and integrity checks • Detects more recent use • Easier to substitute or adulterate • Detects THC itself, which matters under • Detects metabolites that California law limits California's law EXERCISE 3.3 1. Why should a logistics panel include a separate fentanyl test? A Fentanyl causes false positives for cocaine B OSHA requires fentanyl testing in every plant C Fentanyl stays in urine for about 90 days D Standard opiate tests do not detect fentanyl Chapter 3: Building Your Written Policy © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Logistics Edition Version 1.7.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 21 of 79

heading: SECTION 3.4
body: SECTION 3.4 Consequences and second chances Workers accept a program they see as fair. Fairness comes from clear rules, applied the same way to everyone, with a real review before any decision. • No action on a rapid screen alone. A non-negative screen is not a positive. Wait for laboratory confirmation and MRO review before discipline or rejection, except for removing the worker from safety-sensitive duty while you wait. • Same violation, same result. Apply consequences consistently across shifts, departments, and facilities. • Refusals are serious. Treat a refusal, an adulterated or substituted specimen, or leaving before testing as your policy states, usually the same as a positive. • Consider a path back. Many logistics companies offer a last-chance agreement with assessment, treatment, return-to-duty testing, and follow-up testing. When good workers are hard to find, keeping a trained equipment operator can be worth it. REMOVING A WORKER FROM DUTY When a worker is waiting for a confirmed result after a non-negative screen, keep them away from safetysensitive work, and make sure someone else drives them. Follow your policy on whether that time is paid. Chapter 3: Building Your Written Policy © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 4.1
body: SECTION 4.1 Roles in an in-house program An in-house program works when every person knows their job. In a small company one person may hold more than one role, but the duties stay separate. ROLE RESPONSIBILITIES Program administrator Owns the policy, schedules random selections, keeps records, receives verified results, and makes sure everyone is trained and certified. Trained collector Runs collections exactly as trained, keeps custody of the device, and documents everything. Never makes hiring or discipline decisions. Supervisors Send workers for testing, make documented reasonable suspicion referrals, and remove impaired workers from duty. Laboratory Confirms non-negative screens with a second, more specific method. Medical Review Officer A licensed physician who reviews laboratory results, talks to the donor about prescriptions, (MRO) and reports the verified result. SEPARATE COLLECTION FROM DECISIONS A collector who is also the worker's direct supervisor, relative, or friend creates a conflict of interest. Where you can, have someone outside the worker's department collect, and never let the collector decide what happens next. EXERCISE 4.1 1. Your office manager is the only trained collector. Say the screen needs laboratory confirmation. • Remove the worker from safety-sensitive duty while you wait, if your policy says so. • Never guess which drug or why. Prescription questions belong to the MRO. • Give the worker a set window, stated in your policy, to ask for the specimen to be retested. DOT gives its drivers 72 hours. A fair retest window makes a result much harder to challenge. SECTION 4.5 Post-incident and reasonable suspicion timing Speed matters. Drugs and alcohol leave the body over hours, so a test that waits until the next day may miss what caused the incident. • Make sure injured workers get medical care first. Testing never delays treatment. • Test for alcohol within 2 hours when possible and document why if you cannot. Test for drugs as soon as possible. Many programs borrow the DOT limits of 8 hours for alcohol and 32 hours for drugs as outer limits. • Keep the worker away from safety-sensitive work and from driving until the result is known. heading: SECTION 4.6
body: SECTION 4.6 Confidentiality and records Drug test results are confidential. Mishandling them hurts workers, invites lawsuits, and destroys trust in the program. • Share results only with people who need them to make a decision: usually the program administrator. • Keep test records separate from personnel files, in a locked cabinet or a secure system. • Do not discuss results on the floor, in group texts, or over the radio. • Keep consent forms, custody forms, collection records, device lot numbers, test images, and MRO results long enough to defend a claim filed years later. Depending on the law, a worker may sue up to five or six years after a test. Confirm your retention period with counsel. WATCH WHAT YOU SAY In one real case, a supervisor told coworkers that an employee had failed a drug test. The result later turned out to be a false positive, and the employee sued. The company won only because its policy happened to define the result as a failure. Never discuss a result with anyone who does not need to know it, and never call a result "failed" until it is verified. HOW A READER HELPS With Labb Station, results are captured and stored digitally, and Labb's coded test devices keep drug names hidden from the person running the test. heading: SECTION 5.1
body: SECTION 5.1 The background check process step by step You don't run background checks yourself. You order them from a consumer reporting agency (CRA), a background screening company. Your duties come from the FCRA and from state and local law. # STEP WHAT YOU DO Set up your account The CRA verifies your business, and you certify that you will follow the FCRA. Make a conditional offer Where fair chance laws apply, check criminal history only after the offer. Disclose and authorize Give a standalone disclosure, with any state notices, and get written authorization. Most CRAs handle this electronically, which makes high-volume hiring events manageable. Order the right package Order the searches set for that role (Section 5.2). Review the report Apply your written criteria for that role, consistently. Pre-adverse action If the report may lead you to reject or fire someone, send a copy of the report and the Summary of Rights first, with any state or local notices. Wait and listen Give a reasonable time to respond, commonly at least five business days. Some places require more. Final decision If the decision stands, send the adverse action notice with the CRA's contact information, a statement that the CRA did not make the decision, the right to a free copy of the report within 60 days, and the person's dispute rights. GOVERNING RULE No standalone disclosure, no authorization, no report. No pre-adverse notice, no rejection. Peak season is not an exception. heading: SECTION 5.3
body: SECTION 5.3 Fair chance hiring in logistics Warehousing and fulfillment are among the largest employers of people with records. A fair chance approach keeps you compliant and widens a hiring pool you need, especially at peak. • Ask at the right time. Where the law requires it, wait until after a conditional offer to check criminal history. • Look at the person, not the label. Consider the nature of the offense, how long ago it happened, and how it relates to the job. • Ask for context. Give the applicant a chance to explain, including work history and training since the offense. • Be consistent. Write criteria for each role and apply them the same way to everyone. • Do not consider arrests that did not lead to conviction as proof of conduct, or sealed and expunged records. BLANKET BANS ARE RISKY A policy such as "no felonies, ever" can screen out good workers and can violate federal and state antidiscrimination laws. Review your criteria with counsel. EXERCISE 5.3 1. An applicant for a packer job has an 8-year-old conviction for possession and steady work since. What should you consider? heading: SECTION 6.1
body: SECTION 6.1 How a rapid test is read Almost every rapid drug test works the same way, and it works backward from what most people expect. Getting this wrong is the most common reading error. WHAT YOU SEE RESULT WHY Control line (C) and test line (T) Negative A line at T means the drug was not detected above the cut-off. Any line at T, even a very faint one, is negative. Control line (C), no test line Non-negative Drug in the specimen blocked the T line from forming. Send for laboratory confirmation. No control line Invalid The test did not run correctly. Retest with a new device. • Results must be read at the time the package insert states. Read too early and lines may not have formed. Read too late and the result is no longer valid. • Multi-panel devices may carry a dozen or more test lines, each read on its own. The same test, three readers Reader 1: "I see a line at T. Negative." Reader 2: "I don't see a line. Non-negative." T C Reader 3: "Too faint to call. Retest?" Figure 6.1 A faint test line. Under the package insert it is negative, but three people can read it three ways. They cannot all be right. heading: SECTION 6.2
body: SECTION 6.2 The real problem: human bias Most collectors read well. The bigger problem is that every reader is human, and a human read is shaped by what the reader expects, feels, and needs. Bias is harder to see than a faint line. BIAS HOW IT SHOWS UP Expectation A worker mentions something before the test: an antibiotic, an over-the-counter pain reliever, or use from months ago. Many people don't know what a test detects or for how long. The collector now expects a positive, and a faint line may get called non-negative. Sympathy The collector knows the worker is struggling or needs this job, and a borderline line could be called negative. Assumptions about people Everyone carries assumptions about who "looks like" a drug user, often without knowing it. Any judgment call can be challenged as influenced by who the donor is. A reader takes that argument away. Staffing pressure At peak, managers need people on the floor. A collector who knows the building is short can feel pressure to call it negative. Conditions make it worse Faint lines, poor lighting, tired eyes, interruptions that push a read past its time, and drug names printed on the device all give bias more room to work. When the device is thrown away, nothing is left but a checkmark. GOVERNING RULE The question is not whether your collectors are good. It is whether any person should be the one deciding what a line means. Chapter 6: Reading the Result: Why a Reader Wins © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. body: SECTION 7.1 Is in-house testing right for you? In-house testing pays off most for companies that hire often, work far from collection sites, or need fast post-incident testing. heading: SECTION 7.3
body: SECTION 7.3 A four-phase transition plan Most companies can move to in-house testing in about 90 days. Do not skip phases. Each one prevents a common failure. PHASE TIMING KEY STEPS 1. Plan Weeks 1 to 3 Choose a program administrator. Review state laws, union agreements, and customer contracts. Decide testing reasons, panel, and specimen. Separate DOTcovered drivers. 2. Build Weeks 3 to 6 Write or update the policy and have counsel review it. Set up Labb Station, laboratory confirmation, MRO review, and background screening. Prepare collection areas. 3. Train and pilot Weeks 6 to 10 Train collectors and supervisors, and complete certification. Announce the policy and collect signed acknowledgments. Pilot at one facility, outside peak season. 4. Roll out Weeks 10 to 13 Expand to all sites. Start random testing if your policy includes it. Review the first 30 days of records and fix gaps. GOVERNING RULE Announce before you test. Workers should receive the policy, and sign for it, before the first in-house test. EXERCISE 7.3 1. Why pilot at one site before rolling out to all of them? heading: SECTION 8.1
body: SECTION 8.1 Auditing your program Many logistics companies already test. The question is whether the program would hold up if a result were challenged, an incident were investigated, or a customer audited it. AUDIT QUESTION YES NO Is the written policy current, reviewed by counsel, and signed for by every worker? Does the policy match what supervisors actually do? Are DOT-covered drivers in a separate DOT program? Does the panel include fentanyl and other opioids? Are pre-employment results back before the first shift? Are post-incident tests done within hours, not days? Are all non-negatives confirmed by a laboratory and reviewed by an MRO before action? Are results read objectively, with a stored record? Are supervisors trained in reasonable suspicion? Do background checks follow every FCRA step, including both notices? Are screening packages set by role and applied consistently? Are drug test and background records kept separately and securely? Are collectors trained and certified, with records of it? Every "No" is a gap. Section 8.2 shows how to close the most common ones. Chapter 8: Improving an Existing Program © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Logistics Edition Version 1.7.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 61 of 79

heading: SECTION 8.2
body: SECTION 8.2 Ten common failures and how to fix them # FAILURE FIX Workers start before results come back Test in-house the same day, and make "no result, no start" a firm rule. Post-incident tests happen the next day Test in-house right after medical care. Train supervisors on the timing. Faint lines read as positive Train on the competitive format, and use Labb Station to read objectively. Action taken on a rapid screen alone Confirm every non-negative at a laboratory, with MRO review, and give the worker a set window to request a retest. Panel misses fentanyl Add fentanyl and other opioids to the panel. Results shared on the floor Limit access to the administrator. Use coded devices that hide drug names. Background checks ordered without a standalone disclosure Use the CRA's electronic consent flow. Never add waivers or other content. Applicants rejected without notices Always send the pre-adverse notice, wait, then send the final notice. Different rules at different facilities One policy, one package per role, one reading standard. DOT drivers tested on rapid tests Keep DOT tests with a qualified collection site. EXERCISE 8.2 1. A By an honest self-assessment tied to your audit results B By choosing the ones your competitors have had trouble with C By picking the three listed first in the guidebook D By picking the failures that are cheapest to fix first Chapter 8: Improving an Existing Program © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: APPENDICES
body: APPENDICES A Glossary Definitions of the terms used in this guidebook. Section references point to where each term is explained in depth. A E Adverse action. A decision, such as not hiring, that is based in whole or in part on a background report. Requires FCRA notices (2.6, 5.1). Expectation bias. Reading a result the way you expect it to come out, for example after a worker mentions taking a medication (6.2). Authorization. The applicant's written permission to obtain a background report (5.1). B Background screening. Checks of identity, criminal history, driving records, licenses, and other job-related information through a consumer reporting agency (1.3, 5.2). C CDL. Commercial driver's license. CDL drivers in safety-sensitive driving jobs are covered by DOT testing rules (2.1). F Fair chance law. A state or local law that limits when and how employers consider criminal history (2.6, 5.3). FCRA. The Fair Credit Reporting Act, the federal law that governs background checks (2.6, 5.1). Fentanyl. A potent synthetic opioid that standard opiate tests do not detect (3.3). I Invalid result. A rapid test with no control line. Retest with a new device (6.1). Chain of custody. The documented record of who handled a specimen, from collection to the laboratory (4.4). L Clearinghouse. The FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse, a database of CDL drivers' DOT drug and alcohol violations (2.1). Labb Station. Labb's patented digital reader system that identifies the donor, records consent, captures and reads each test, and stores the record (6.3). Collector. A trained person who runs in-house collections and keeps custody of the test (4.1). Conditional offer. A job offer that depends on passing the drug test and background check (1.3, 5.4). Confirmation. Laboratory testing of a non-negative screen with a more specific method (4.4). Control line (C). The line that shows a rapid test ran correctly. No control line means the test is invalid (6.1). CPP (Labb Channel Partner Program). A network of independent clinic owners who use Labb Station in their own facilities and support logistics and fulfillment companies (9.2). CRA (consumer reporting agency). A background screening company that prepares background reports (5.1). D DOT. U.S. Department of Transportation. DOT-regulated tests follow 49 CFR Part 40. DOT drug tests cannot be run on rapid tests (2.1).

body: P Refusal. Failing to test when directed, leaving early, or providing an adulterated or substituted specimen (3.4). Package insert. The manufacturer's instructions for a test device, including storage and read time (4.2, 6.1). S Panel. The list of drugs a test detects (3.3). Safety-sensitive. Work where impairment could cause serious injury or damage (1.1, 3.4). Powered industrial truck. A forklift, reach truck, or similar vehicle. OSHA requires the employer to train and evaluate operators (5.2). Post-incident test. A test after an incident that caused, or could have caused, injury or damage (3.2, 4.5). Pre-adverse action notice. The notice, with a copy of the report and the Summary of Rights, sent before a final decision based on a background report (5.1). Standalone disclosure. Screening duties should be set in the staffing agreement (2.2). T Program administrator. The person who owns the policy, records, and verified results (4.1). Test line (T). On most rapid tests, any line at T, even faint, means negative for that drug (6.1). R True Privacy. Labb's coding of rapid tests so the person running the test does not see drug names (6.3). Random test. An unannounced test of workers selected from a pool by a neutral method (3.2). Read time. The time stated in the package insert when a rapid test must be read (6.1). V Verified result. The final result reported by the MRO after laboratory confirmation and review (4.4). Reasonable suspicion test. A test based on specific, documented observations of possible impairment (3.2). heading: BEFORE YOU BEGIN
body: BEFORE YOU BEGIN About This Guidebook This guidebook teaches employers how to set up and run a lawful, defensible drug and alcohol testing program. It is written for the people who own the program inside a company: HR managers, personnel managers, safety directors, owners, CEOs and presidents. It is the employer companion to the LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook and the LabbPO Criminal Justice course. Those books teach the people who collect and run tests. This one teaches the people who decide who gets tested, when, and what happens next. This Healthcare Edition contains everything in the general Employer's Guidebook, geared to hospitals, health systems, long-term care, home health, clinics and pharmacies. Three added chapters cover drug diversion, licensed professionals and the medical staff, and running a program in a clinical setting. Look for Healthcare Note boxes throughout the book. How to use it • Read Chapters 1 through 10 to understand the rules, the drugs, how testing works, on-site testing, recognizing signs of use and handling results. • Read Chapters 11 through 13 for the issues unique to healthcare. • Use Chapters 14 through 17 to build or audit your own program, Chapter 18 for the DOT rules if you employ CDL drivers (for example, in transport fleets), and Chapter 19 to test your judgment against real situations. • Adapt the draft policy (Appendix A) and forms (Appendix B) to your company, then have your attorney review them before use. • Answer the review questions at the end of each chapter; the answer key is in Appendix D. • Sections marked ** cover areas where the law is new and developing or varies by state; see the note at the end of each. • This guidebook describes best practice for non-DOT (private employer) programs. Chapter 18 covers the separate rules for DOT-regulated employees, and DOT note boxes throughout the book point to it wherever DOT rules differ. Important disclaimers Read these before using this guidebook or the online course built from it. • General education only, not legal advice. This guidebook is general educational information. It is not legal advice, and using it does not create an attorney-client relationship with Labb or anyone else.

heading: BEFORE YOU BEGIN
body: • Always check current law. Drug and alcohol testing law differs by federal, state, county and city jurisdiction and changes often, especially for marijuana. Before you adopt a policy, test anyone, or act on a result, check the current federal, state, county and local laws that apply where each employee works. • Examples are examples only. Any state, city, case or practice named in this guidebook is an example. Your laws may differ. • Draft policy and forms require attorney review. The draft policy and forms in Appendices A and B are starting points only. Have a qualified employment attorney review and adapt them for every jurisdiction where you operate before you use them. • Not DOT-required training or certification. This guidebook explains DOT rules, but completing it does not qualify anyone as a DOT collector, breath alcohol technician, screening test technician, Medical Review Officer or Substance Abuse Professional. It does not by itself satisfy DOT's supervisor reasonable suspicion training requirement. DOTregulated employers must follow 49 CFR Part 40 and their DOT agency's rules, available at transportation.gov/odapc. • Not medical advice. Information about drugs, medications, detection windows and test results is general. heading: PART I | FOUNDATIONS
body: PART I | FOUNDATIONS Why Employers Test A testing program exists to keep impaired people out of jobs where they can hurt themselves or others, and to give the employer a fair, documented way to act when drug or alcohol use shows up. Done well, it lowers risk. Done badly, it creates new legal risk. 1.1 What the numbers show 1.2 What a program protects against 1.3 What a program cannot do Check your understanding SECTION 1.1 What the numbers show The Quest Diagnostics Drug Testing Index, published every year since 1988, is the most widely cited source on workforce drug use. Its 2026 edition (covering 2025 tests) found: • About 1 in 23 urine tests in the combined U.S. workforce was positive (4.3%), a rate that has stayed above 4% for more than a decade. • Hair tests, which look back about 90 days, were positive 19.1% of the time, up from 13.1% in 2021. • Marijuana remains the main driver of positives across all specimen types. • Healthcare had the highest positivity of any industry, at 5.8%. • Fentanyl positivity in urine roughly halved from 2024 to 2025. The gap between urine (4.3%) and hair (19.1%) is not a contradiction. Each specimen sees a different window of use, which Chapter 4 explains. HEALTHCARE NOTE Healthcare has the highest overall positivity of any industry in the 2026 Quest Diagnostics Drug Testing Index: 5.8% for 2025, up from 5.1% in 2021. Healthcare workers also have something most workers do not: direct access to controlled substances. That is why diversion (Chapter 11) is as important as testing. SECTION 1.2 What a program protects against • Accidents and injuries to employees, customers and the public, and the workers' compensation costs that follow. • Negligent hiring and retention claims, where an employer is sued because it knew, or should have known, an employee was unsafe. • Lost productivity: absenteeism, turnover, theft and poor work quality. • Contract and insurance requirements: many customers, government contracts and insurers require a program. • Regulatory penalties for employers covered by Department of Transportation (DOT) or other federal rules.

heading: SECTION 1.3
body: SECTION 1.3 What a program cannot do A drug test shows that a substance or its metabolite was present above a cutoff. Except for alcohol breath and blood tests, it does not measure impairment at the moment of the test. This matters more every year as states legalize marijuana, and it is why reasonable suspicion training (Chapter 9) and clear policy language (Chapter 14) carry so much weight. heading: PART I | FOUNDATIONS
body: PART I | FOUNDATIONS The Legal Landscape No single law governs workplace testing. An employer's rights come from a stack of federal, state and local laws, and the most restrictive layer that applies to you usually decides the question. Check every layer before you test. 2.1 Federal laws that require or shape testing 2.2 State and local laws 2.3 State law quick reference 2.4 Marijuana: the fastest-changing area ** 2.5 Remote, traveling and multistate employees 2.6 Unions and collective bargaining 2.7 FCRA in practice 2.8 Workers' compensation and unemployment 2.9 Practical legal rules for every program Check your understanding SECTION 2.1 Federal laws that require or shape testing L AW W HAT IT MEANS FOR EMPLOYERS Drug-Free Workplace Act of 1988 Applies to federal grantees and many federal contractors. Requires a written policy, an awareness program, and employee notice of drug convictions. It does not require testing. DOT rules (49 CFR Part 40) Mandatory testing for safety-sensitive transportation employees, with procedures set by federal rule. See Chapter 18. Other federal mandates Nuclear (NRC, 10 CFR Part 26) and some Department of Defense contracts carry their own testing requirements. Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Current illegal drug use is not protected, and a drug test is not a "medical exam." But people in recovery and people using lawful prescriptions are protected, and an alcohol test is a medical exam, so it cannot be given to applicants before a conditional job offer. Title VII and other anti-discrimination laws Testing must be applied consistently. Testing one group more than another invites discrimination claims. Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) Eligible employees may take protected leave for substance abuse treatment, though not for the use itself. Chapter 2: The Legal Landscape © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Healthcare Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 10 of 108

heading: L AW
body: L AW W HAT IT MEANS FOR EMPLOYERS National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) In a unionized workplace, testing is a mandatory subject of bargaining. You generally cannot start or change a program without bargaining. OSHA (29 CFR 1904.35) You may not use post-accident testing to discourage employees from reporting injuries. Testing to evaluate the cause of an incident is permitted. Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) If a third-party screening company reports results to you, those results can be a "consumer report." FCRA disclosure, authorization and adverse action steps then apply. HEALTHCARE NOTE Healthcare employers also answer to the DEA, which requires registrants to guard controlled substances, screen employees with access and report thefts and significant losses, and to accreditors such as The Joint Commission, which requires a separate, non-disciplinary process for practitioner health (Chapters 11 and 12). Many hospitals and clinics also receive federal grants, which can bring them under the Drug-Free Workplace Act. SECTION 2.2 State and local laws State laws fall into three broad groups, and some states fit more than one: • Restrictive states limit who may be tested and when. Some allow random testing only for safety-sensitive jobs, require reasonable suspicion for current employees, or require a lab confirmation before any action. Minnesota, Vermont, Connecticut, Maine and Rhode Island are commonly cited examples. • Voluntary "drug-free workplace" states offer benefits, such as a workers' compensation premium discount or a defense to injury claims, to employers that follow a defined program. • Silent states have little or no general testing law, leaving most decisions to employer policy. Some states also limit rapid (point-of-care) testing or require specific lab certifications, and some cities add their own rules. New York City, for example, bars most pre-employment marijuana testing. Check state and local law where each employee works, not only where your headquarters is. SECTION 2.3 State law quick reference This table shows examples of states with notable rules. It is not complete, it changes often, and it is not legal advice. Verify every state where you have employees before testing. S TATE N OTABLE RULES (EXAMPLES) California Protects off-duty cannabis use and tests that detect only non-psychoactive metabolites; limits asking about past cannabis use. Random testing generally limited to safety-sensitive jobs.

heading: L AW
body: Connecticut Protects off-duty cannabis use for most jobs. Random testing generally limited to safety-sensitive jobs or where federal law requires it. Hawaii Detailed testing procedures. On-site rapid non-negatives must be confirmed by a certified laboratory. Maine Testing policy generally must be filed with the state labor agency. Random testing restricted. Maryland Tests must go to a state-permitted laboratory. On-site rapid testing is limited (commonly cited as pre-employment only).
