heading: S TATE
body: S TATE N OTABLE RULES (EXAMPLES) Minnesota Restrictive testing law: written policy, signed acknowledgment, random testing only for safetysensitive jobs, confirmation by an independent lab. Off-duty cannabis protected; pre-employment cannabis testing limited to listed exceptions. Montana Protects lawful off-duty cannabis use. Restrictive testing law for current employees. Nevada Bars refusing to hire most applicants for a pre-employment marijuana positive. On-site rapid testing is regulated through laboratory licensing. New Jersey Allows pre-employment, random, reasonable suspicion and post-accident testing, but bars adverse action based only on a positive cannabis result without documented evidence of impairment (state guidance describes a Workplace Impairment Recognition Expert, or WIRE, evaluation). A recent Appellate Division decision (Sanders) lets applicants sue over offers withdrawn for a positive cannabis test alone. New York Protects lawful off-duty cannabis use. New York City bars most pre-employment marijuana testing. Oregon On-site drug screens require registration with the Oregon Health Authority and lab confirmation before adverse action. Limits on breath alcohol testing. Rhode Island Protects off-duty cannabis use; restrictive testing law. Vermont Most restrictive: random or company-wide testing generally prohibited unless federal law requires it; most testing needs an individualized, documented basis; lab testing required. Washington Bars refusing to hire most applicants for off-duty cannabis use or a test showing non-psychoactive metabolites. Sources for this section include Ogletree, GovDocs, Justia's 50-state survey and DISA's oral fluid law map, current as of fall 2026. SECTION 2.4 Marijuana: the fastest-changing area ** Marijuana is the biggest source of legal risk in a modern program. • State protections. A growing group of states protects lawful off-duty marijuana use or limits pre-employment marijuana testing for most jobs. Commonly cited examples include California, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Minnesota, Montana, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island and Washington. Sources count between 9 and 20 jurisdictions depending on how they define protection, so verify your states directly. • Medical marijuana. More states protect registered medical marijuana patients, typically from discrimination for offduty use, not from discipline for on-duty use or impairment. • Common exceptions. Protections usually exclude DOT-regulated and other federally mandated testing, federal contractors and jobs a state defines as safety-sensitive.

heading: S TATE
body: • What no state protects. Using, possessing or being impaired by marijuana at work. • Hemp-derived THC products. DUE TO TAKE EFFECT. Delta-8 THC, THCA and other hemp-derived THC products are sold widely, including as gummies and drinks, and they cause marijuana positives; a drug test cannot tell them apart from marijuana. A 2025 federal law narrows the definition of hemp in two steps. Hemp products containing synthesized cannabinoids that the plant does not naturally produce lose hemp status on November 12, 2026. On December 11, 2026, hemp products with more than 0.4 mg of total THC per container are due to become federally controlled as marijuana. Congress has already delayed the second step once (from November 12 to December 11, 2026) and may delay it again, and some states have their own limits. Whatever the status of the product, a hemp product is not a legitimate medical explanation for a positive test. Chapter 2: The Legal Landscape © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Healthcare Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 12 of 108

heading: NEW AND DEVELOPING LAW
body: • Federal rescheduling. Effective April 28, 2026, a federal order moved FDA-approved marijuana products and statelicensed medical marijuana into Schedule III. All other marijuana remains Schedule I, and a broader rescheduling proceeding is still pending. Non-DOT employers still set their own marijuana rules, subject to state law. DOT rules did not change (Chapter 18). NEW AND DEVELOPING LAW ** Laws in these areas are new and developing. Please confirm any policy decisions regarding these issues that you may include in your program with your attorneys. HEALTHCARE NOTE Many states that protect off-duty or medical marijuana use exclude safety-sensitive jobs. Patient-care roles and roles with access to controlled substances are strong candidates for that exception, but only if your policy defines them before you rely on it. SECTION 2.5 Remote, traveling and multistate employees • Which law applies: generally the law of the state, and city, where the employee actually works, not where the company is headquartered. A remote employee in Minnesota is usually covered by Minnesota's testing law even if your office is in Texas. • Traveling employees who work in several states raise harder questions. Ask counsel which state's law to follow, and consider the most protective one when in doubt. • Applicants are usually governed by the law where the job will be performed. • One policy, state addenda: most multistate employers use one core policy with a state addendum for each state that has special rules. • Testing at a distance: use a TPA or a national collection network so employees can test at a nearby site, schedule electronically with a deadline, and track no-shows. For remote jobs, ask whether testing is needed at all for that role, and what reason you would give. • Post-accident testing for traveling employees needs a plan in advance: which collection network to call, after-hours options, and who arranges it. SECTION 2.6 Unions and collective bargaining In a unionized workplace, the National Labor Relations Board has long treated drug testing of current employees as a mandatory subject of bargaining (Johnson-Bateman Co., 1989). Testing of job applicants generally is not, because applicants are not yet in the bargaining unit (Star Tribune, 1989). In practice:

heading: NEW AND DEVELOPING LAW
body: • Bargain before you start or change testing for current union employees, including adding drugs, changing specimens or adding random testing. • Read the contract. Many collective bargaining agreements already set testing rules, discipline standards and grievance steps. The contract controls where it speaks. • Expect "just cause" review. Arbitrators look at whether the rule was reasonable, known to the employee, applied consistently, and whether the investigation and test were fair. • Weingarten rights. A union employee may ask for a union representative at an investigatory interview that could lead to discipline, such as a reasonable suspicion meeting. Honor the request. You may hold the interview once the representative arrives, or decide not to interview; either way, the request should not push the test past its testing window. Agree on this approach with counsel and the union before it comes up. • Last chance agreements for union employees should be signed by the union as well as the employee. heading: SECTION 2.7
body: SECTION 2.7 FCRA in practice When a third-party screening company, such as a TPA or background screening firm, reports drug test results to you, those results may be a "consumer report." If so, the Fair Credit Reporting Act requires these steps: 1. Disclosure: give the applicant or employee a clear written disclosure that a report may be obtained, in a stand-alone document with nothing else on it. 2. Authorization: get their written permission before ordering the report. 3. Pre-adverse action notice: before acting on the result, give them a copy of the report and the federal Summary of Your Rights Under the FCRA, and wait a reasonable time (commonly five business days) so they can dispute errors. 4. Adverse action notice: after the decision, tell them in writing, including the screening company's contact information and their right to dispute. Whether a result counts as a consumer report depends on who reports it and how. Ask your attorney and your screening vendor how they classify their reports, and build these steps into your process if they apply. Some states add their own requirements. SECTION 2.8 Workers' compensation and unemployment • Drug-free workplace programs. Several states, including Alabama, Florida, Georgia and Ohio, offer workers' compensation premium discounts to employers that follow a state-defined program. The program rules are specific: required tests, notice, training and labs. Follow them exactly to get the benefit. • Intoxication defenses. Many states reduce or deny workers' compensation benefits when an injury was caused by drug or alcohol use. Some create a presumption of causation when an employee tests positive after an accident under a compliant program. A sloppy post-accident test can lose this defense. • Unemployment benefits. Many states deny unemployment benefits to employees fired for a verified positive or a refusal, but only if the employer can prove the policy, the notice and the test. Your paperwork is your proof. SECTION 2.9 Practical legal rules for every program • Put your program in a written policy and give every employee a copy before testing starts. • Get written consent before each test. • Apply the policy the same way to everyone in the same job category.

heading: SECTION 2.7
body: • Confirm every non-negative screen with a laboratory and have a Medical Review Officer (MRO) review it before taking final action. • Keep results confidential and separate from personnel files. • Have an employment attorney review the policy for each state where you have employees, and review it again every year. heading: PART II | TESTING SCIENCE
body: PART II | TESTING SCIENCE The Drugs A drug test does not look for "drugs" in general. Each test looks for specific target compounds, called analytes, at or above a set concentration, called the cutoff. To run a program, you need to know which drugs your panel covers, what each test actually detects, and what it misses. 3.1 Parent drugs and metabolites 3.2 Opiates vs. opioids: a common gap 3.3 Drug classes, targets, cutoffs and windows 3.4 Expanded and emerging drugs 3.5 Detection windows are estimates Check your understanding SECTION 3.1 Parent drugs and metabolites When a person takes a drug, the body breaks it down into metabolites. Many tests look for a metabolite rather than the drug itself, because metabolites stay in the body longer and prove the drug was taken and processed, not just touched. • Marijuana tests look for THC-COOH, a metabolite of THC, in urine. Oral fluid tests look for THC itself. • Cocaine tests look for benzoylecgonine, a metabolite, in urine. • Heroin breaks down into 6-acetylmorphine (6-AM), then morphine. Only 6-AM proves heroin; morphine alone could come from heroin, a prescription or poppy seeds. SECTION 3.2 Opiates vs. opioids: a common gap "Opiates" are drugs from the poppy plant (morphine, codeine) and drugs made directly from them (heroin). "Opioids" is the wider family that also includes semi-synthetic and synthetic drugs. A standard opiate screen mainly detects morphine and codeine. It does not reliably detect oxycodone, fentanyl, methadone, buprenorphine or tramadol. Each of those needs its own test. Many employers believe they are testing for fentanyl when they are not. SECTION 3.3 Drug classes, targets, cutoffs and windows Cutoffs below are for urine, in ng/mL, and show the screen / confirmation levels typical of non-DOT (private employer) programs. They vary by laboratory and device, so confirm the cutoffs your lab and devices use. Detection windows are typical for occasional use. heading: SECTION 3.4
body: SECTION 3.4 Expanded and emerging drugs Non-DOT employers can add tests for drugs that standard panels miss. Common additions include: • Synthetic cannabinoids (K2, Spice): hundreds of changing compounds; tests catch only some. • Kratom (mitragynine): a plant sold legally in many states with opioid-like effects. • Xylazine and medetomidine: veterinary sedatives mixed into the illicit fentanyl supply. • Nitazenes: synthetic opioids stronger than fentanyl; few rapid tests exist, so lab testing is usually needed. • Ketamine, LSD, psilocybin, gabapentin, carisoprodol and others, chosen based on local trends. • Alcohol biomarkers such as EtG, which shows drinking over the past few days (Chapter 4). Check local drug trend data, your workers' compensation history, and your MRO's advice before adding drugs. Every added drug raises cost and the number of prescription positives the MRO must sort out. HEALTHCARE NOTE Standard panels miss many of the drugs most often diverted in healthcare, including fentanyl, meperidine, tramadol, ketamine, propofol, nalbuphine and butorphanol. Healthcare programs usually need an expanded panel for roles with controlled-substance access and for diversion investigations (Chapter 13). SECTION 3.5 Detection windows are estimates How long a drug shows up depends on the dose, how often it is used, body fat (for marijuana), hydration, metabolism and the cutoff. A low cutoff extends the window; a high one shortens it. Never promise an employee, or a court, an exact window. Chapter 3: The Drugs © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: PART II | TESTING SCIENCE
body: PART II | TESTING SCIENCE Specimens The specimen decides what question the test can answer. Oral fluid and breath answer "did this person use recently?" Hair answers "has this person used over the last few months?" Urine sits in between. Choose the specimen to fit the reason for the test, your cheating risk, your budget and your state's law. 4.1 Comparison at a glance 4.2 Urine 4.3 Oral fluid (saliva) 4.4 Hair 4.5 Alcohol testing 4.6 Hair testing and discrimination risk ** Check your understanding SECTION 4.1 Comparison at a glance S PECIMEN Urine Oral fluid Hair W HAT IT T YPICAL WINDOW C OLLECTION C HEATING RISK C OST AND SPEED Past use, 1-3 days for most drugs; Private restroom; Highest: substitution, Low cost; rapid or lab mostly weeks for heavy observed only in dilution, adulterants metabolites marijuana use special cases Recent use, About 24-48 hours Swab in the mouth, S HOWS mostly parent always observed, drug anywhere Pattern of use About 90 days (1.5 inches Small hair sample cut of head hair) near the scalp Low Low to moderate; rapid or lab Low Higher cost; lab only; several days Breath Alcohol now Current Breath into a device Low Low; immediate Blood Drug or Hours Needle draw by Very low High; lab only Low to moderate Moderate; used alcohol trained staff present now Sweat Use while patch worn Days to weeks Patch worn on skin mainly in courts and treatment Nails Pattern of use Several months Clippings Low Lab only; used when hair is unavailable Chapter 4: Specimens © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 4.2
body: SECTION 4.2 Urine Urine is the most common workplace specimen. Drugs and metabolites collect in urine, so it usually detects use for one to three days. Its weakness is privacy: because collections are normally unobserved, urine is the easiest specimen to cheat with synthetic urine, someone else's urine, dilution, or chemicals. Specimen validity checks (Chapter 6) are essential. DOT NOTE DOT drug tests use urine only for now. See Chapter 18 (Drug testing under DOT). SECTION 4.3 Oral fluid (saliva) Oral fluid shows drugs circulating in the body now, so it is the best fit for post-accident and reasonable suspicion tests. Every collection happens in front of the collector, which makes cheating much harder. Its window is shorter, and the person must not eat, drink or put anything in their mouth for about 10 minutes before collection. Some states limit oral fluid testing, so check before you switch. SECTION 4.4 Hair Drugs enter hair from the blood as it grows, about half an inch a month. A standard 1.5-inch sample covers about 90 days, which is why hair catches far more users than urine. Hair does not show use from the last 7 to 10 days, because that hair has not grown out yet. Body hair can be used if head hair is too short, but it covers a longer, less precise period. Hair is a strong pre-employment tool; it is weak for post-accident testing. HEALTHCARE NOTE Hair testing is useful in healthcare for pre-employment screening of roles with controlled-substance access and in diversion investigations, because it shows a pattern of use over about 90 days. Ask your lab which healthcare drugs it can test in hair before you rely on it. SECTION 4.5 Alcohol testing • Breath devices measure current alcohol concentration. Best practice is to screen with a device on the federal Conforming Products List and confirm any screen at or above your policy threshold on an evidential breath testing device (EBT) operated by a trained technician. • Oral fluid alcohol screening devices are a practical alternative for screening. Confirm any result at or above your threshold on an EBT before acting. • Urine alcohol is not recommended for workplace decisions; it is unreliable for showing current impairment.

heading: SECTION 4.2
body: • EtG and EtS are alcohol metabolites in urine that show drinking in the past several days. They are useful for return-toduty, follow-up and treatment monitoring, not for proving impairment. • PEth is a blood marker showing heavy drinking over the past few weeks. DOT NOTE DOT alcohol testing has its own devices, technician qualifications, thresholds and timing. See Chapter 18 (Alcohol testing under DOT). heading: SECTION 4.6
body: SECTION 4.6 Hair testing and discrimination risk ** Hair testing has been challenged as having a disparate impact on Black employees, because drugs bind more readily to darker, more melanin-rich hair, and hair treatments can also affect results. In Jones v. City of Boston (1st Cir. 2014), the federal appeals court held that Black officers had shown a statistically significant disparate impact from the department's hair testing and sent the case back to decide whether the test was job-related and whether a less discriminatory alternative was available. If you use hair testing: • Be able to explain why hair fits the job and the test reason, such as pre-employment screening for safety-sensitive work. • Use an accredited lab that applies wash procedures and cutoffs designed to reduce outside contamination. • Send every non-negative to an MRO, and consider allowing a confirming urine or oral fluid test when an employee disputes a hair result. • Track results by group where your data allows, so you would see a pattern before a plaintiff does. • Ask your attorney to review hair testing before adopting it, especially for current employees. NEW AND DEVELOPING LAW ** Laws in these areas are new and developing. Please confirm any policy decisions regarding these issues that you may include in your program with your attorneys. heading: PART II | TESTING SCIENCE
body: PART II | TESTING SCIENCE How Testing Works Every defensible drug test has two steps: a fast, inexpensive screen that sorts specimens, and a precise confirmation that identifies exactly what is there. Understanding both lets you choose vendors wisely and explain results to employees, managers and lawyers. 5.1 Step 1: The screen (immunoassay) 5.2 Reading a rapid test strip 5.3 Why screens are not final: cross-reactivity 5.4 Step 2: Confirmation (GC-MS and LC-MS/MS) 5.5 Laboratory vs. point-of-care testing 5.6 What a number does and does not mean 5.7 Laboratory credentials to look for Check your understanding SECTION 5.1 Step 1: The screen (immunoassay) Screens use antibodies, proteins built to grab a specific drug shape. In a competitive immunoassay, drug in the specimen competes with a labeled drug for a limited number of antibodies. The more drug in the specimen, the less labeled drug binds, and the test reads that difference. • Laboratory screens run on automated analyzers (EIA, EMIT, CEDIA and similar methods). They are consistent, documented and give a numeric reading against the cutoff. • Rapid or point-of-care (POCT) screens use the same principle on a test strip inside a cup, card or swab. Results appear in minutes. SECTION 5.2 Reading a rapid test strip W HAT YOU SEE W HAT IT MEANS Control line and test line both visible, even faint Negative for that drug Control line visible, no test line Non-negative; send to the lab No control line Invalid; the test did not work; retest with a new device The line logic surprises people: a line means negative, and a missing line means the drug may be present. Faint lines cause most reading errors. Digital readers remove human judgment, read each strip the same way every time, and create an electronic record. Chapter 5: How Testing Works © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Healthcare Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 24 of 108

heading: SECTION 5.3
body: SECTION 5.3 Why screens are not final: cross-reactivity Antibodies grab shapes, and some legal medications have similar shapes. This cross-reactivity can cause a screen to show non-negative when the drug is not there. Examples that labs and MROs see: • Some cold medicines, ADHD medications and bupropion can trigger amphetamine screens. • Dextromethorphan (cough syrup) can trigger PCP screens. • Some antidepressants and antipsychotics can trigger benzodiazepine, methadone or tricyclic screens. • Poppy seeds contain real morphine and codeine. At the 300 ng/mL opiate cutoff many private programs use, poppy seeds can cause a non-negative screen and sometimes a confirmed result; the MRO sorts these out. DOT uses a 2,000 ng/mL cutoff largely for this reason (Chapter 18). Screens can also miss drugs, called false negatives, when the drug is below the cutoff, outside the window, not covered by the antibody (many benzodiazepine screens miss clonazepam and lorazepam), or masked by tampering. SECTION 5.4 Step 2: Confirmation (GC-MS and LC-MS/MS) Confirmation tests are done only in a laboratory and are the legal standard of proof. 1. Chromatography separates the specimen into its individual chemicals. In gas chromatography (GC) the sample is vaporized and carried through a column; in liquid chromatography (LC) it is carried by a liquid. Each chemical comes out at a characteristic time. 2. Mass spectrometry (MS) breaks each chemical into charged fragments and weighs them. The pattern of fragments is a molecular fingerprint unique to each drug. M ETHOD N OTES GC-MS The long-time gold standard. Often needs extra preparation steps. LC-MS/MS (tandem mass spectrometry) Now the most common. More sensitive, handles more drugs, including fentanyl and other low-level drugs, with less preparation. Confirmation identifies the exact drug, not just the class, and measures the amount using known reference standards. A confirmed result tells you, for example, that a positive amphetamine screen was actually methamphetamine, or was a prescribed drug the MRO can verify.

heading: DOT NOTE
body: A common, defensible model is rapid screening for speed, with every non-negative sent to an HHS-certified or CAP-FDTaccredited laboratory for confirmation and MRO review. DOT NOTE DOT drug tests must be laboratory tests; rapid drug tests are not allowed. See Chapter 18 (Drug testing under DOT). SECTION 5.6 What a number does and does not mean A confirmed concentration shows the drug was present above the cutoff. It does not show how much was taken, when, or whether the person was impaired. Urine concentration also changes with how much the person drank. Avoid statements like "the level was high, so they were high at work." SECTION 5.7 Laboratory credentials to look for • HHS-certified: certified through SAMHSA's National Laboratory Certification Program (formerly called NIDA-certified). The strongest credential for workplace testing, and required for DOT and federal testing. • CAP Forensic Drug Testing accreditation: a strong credential for non-federal testing. • CLIA certification: the basic federal lab license; required for many clinical tests, but by itself not a forensic credential. heading: PART II | TESTING SCIENCE
body: PART II | TESTING SCIENCE Collection and Chain of Custody Most drug test challenges are won or lost at the collection, not at the lab. A result is only as strong as the paperwork that proves the specimen came from the right person, was not tampered with, and reached the lab sealed. That paperwork is the chain of custody. 6.1 The custody and control form 6.2 A standard urine collection, step by step 6.3 Oral fluid and hair collections 6.4 Specimen validity and problem collections 6.5 Fatal flaws and correctable flaws 6.6 Choosing and auditing collectors 6.7 Cheating and specimen tampering Check your understanding SECTION 6.1 The custody and control form Every forensic test uses a custody and control form, on paper or electronic. It records: • The donor's identity and the reason for the test • The employer, collector, collection site, lab and MRO • A unique specimen ID number that also appears on the specimen seals • Specimen temperature and any problems or remarks • The signatures and dates of every person who handled the specimen Non-DOT tests must use a non-federal custody form. The federal Custody and Control Form (CCF) is reserved for federally regulated tests; never use it for a company test. DOT NOTE DOT tests must use the federal CCF. See Chapter 18 (DOT collection rules). SECTION 6.2 A standard urine collection, step by step 1. Before the donor arrives, secure the restroom: blue dye in the toilet, water sources taped or turned off, no soap or cleaners available. 2. Verify the donor's identity with photo ID. If the donor has no acceptable ID, the employer must identify them. 3. Explain the process. Have the donor remove outer clothing such as coats and hats, and empty their pockets. Chapter 6: Collection and Chain of Custody © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Healthcare Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 28 of 108

heading: 4. Have the donor wash and dry their hands.
body: 4. Have the donor wash and dry their hands. 5. Give the donor a sealed collection cup and ask for at least 45 mL (enough for a split specimen). 6. Within 4 minutes, check the temperature. It must be 90-100°F (32-38°C). 7. Inspect for unusual color, odor or foreign objects. 8. In front of the donor, pour into bottles (for split specimens, 30 mL in A and 15 mL in B), seal with tamper-evident labels, and have the donor initial the seals. 9. Complete the form; collector and donor sign and date. 10. Package and ship to the lab, or run the rapid test according to the device instructions. A rapid test collection follows the same identity, security and documentation steps. Record the device name, lot number and expiration date, and keep any image or digital reading. SECTION 6.3 Oral fluid and hair collections • Oral fluid: the collector watches the donor for about 10 minutes with nothing in the mouth, then the donor places the swab as directed until the indicator shows enough sample. The collector seals the device in front of the donor. • Hair: the collector cuts a pencil-thick lock close to the scalp, usually from the back of the head, wraps it with the root end marked, and seals it in a foil and envelope set. SECTION 6.4 Specimen validity and problem collections • Temperature out of range, or signs of tampering, require an immediate second collection under direct observation. Both specimens are sent to the lab. • Directly observed collections are done by a same-sex observer. Best practice is to also observe return-to-duty and follow-up collections, and any collection the MRO directs. • Shy bladder: if the donor cannot provide enough urine, give them a reasonable amount of fluid over a set time; many programs follow the federal model of up to 40 ounces over up to 3 hours. If the donor still cannot provide a specimen, have a physician evaluate whether a medical condition explains it; if not, treat it as a refusal. Where your policy allows, an oral fluid test is a practical alternative.

heading: 4. Have the donor wash and dry their hands.

heading: Signs at the collection: a specimen too cold or too hot, no condensation, an unusual color
body: Signs at the collection: a specimen too cold or too hot, no condensation, an unusual color or no odor, a donor who takes too long or insists on keeping a bag, heat packs or tubing found when emptying pockets, or sounds of a container being opened in the stall. Document what you observe; do not accuse. Oral fluid and hair collections are always observed, so these methods largely remove substitution and adulteration. Employers with a cheating problem often switch some test reasons to oral fluid. State laws. At least 18 states make it a crime to sell, possess or use synthetic urine or products designed to defeat a drug test, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. Examples include Arkansas, Florida, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Texas and Virginia. Your policy should treat tampering as a refusal whether or not your state has such a law. HEALTHCARE NOTE Healthcare workers know how drug tests work and have access to substances that can be used to tamper with urine. For diversion investigations and for monitored professionals, use directly observed urine collections, oral fluid or hair testing. heading: PART III | TESTING IN THE WORKPLACE
body: PART III | TESTING IN THE WORKPLACE Testing On Site With Rapid Tests Many employers can screen employees and applicants at their own workplace with rapid point-of-care (POCT) tests, getting negative results in minutes instead of days. Done right, on-site testing saves time, travel and lost work. Done wrong, it creates legal exposure fast. The rule to remember: an on-site rapid test is only a screen. Every non-negative goes to a laboratory for confirmation and to a Medical Review Officer before any final decision. Employers who choose to act on rapid screens alone should read the rapid-test-only section later in this chapter. 7.1 When on-site testing fits 7.2 The law for on-site testing ** 7.3 Setting up an on-site program 7.4 The on-site collection, step by step 7.5 Reading and talking about results 7.6 Sending a non-negative to the lab 7.7 The MRO's role in an on-site program 7.8 Risks and how to manage them 7.9 If you choose a rapid-test-only program ** 7.10 Alcohol testing on site Check your understanding SECTION 7.1 When on-site testing fits O N-SITE TESTING WORKS WELL WHEN U SE A COLLECTION SITE OR LAB INSTEAD WHEN You hire in volume and need fast negatives The test is a DOT-required drug test Employees work at remote sites far from clinics Your state bans or tightly restricts on-site testing You need post-accident or reasonable suspicion tests at odd You cannot provide a private, secure collection area hours You can train and dedicate reliable collectors No one on staff can collect without a conflict of interest Your policy and state allow acting on lab-confirmed results The result is likely to be disputed in court or arbitration from the only start Many employers use a hybrid: on-site rapid screens for pre-employment and post-accident testing, and a collection site for DOT tests and anything likely to be contested. heading: HEALTHCARE NOTE
body: HEALTHCARE NOTE Employee health or occupational health offices are natural collection sites, but the collector must not be a close colleague of the donor. Do not run employee tests through the emergency department or patient registration; that creates a patient record and a bill for what should be an employment test. SECTION 7.2 The law for on-site testing ** • DOT: rapid drug tests cannot be used for DOT drug tests, and DOT alcohol tests have their own device and technician rules. See Chapter 18. • State law: some states ban, restrict or license on-site testing. Examples: Oregon requires registration with the state health authority and lab confirmation before adverse action; Hawaii requires lab confirmation of rapid non-negatives; Maryland limits on-site testing; Vermont generally requires lab testing; some states apply laboratory licensing laws to on-site testing. Check the state law table in Chapter 2 and confirm your state before you buy a single device. • CLIA: the federal Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments regulate laboratory testing. Federal rules exempt forensic testing and employment drug testing done by HHS-certified labs, and some state agencies have said employment-only drug screening does not need a CLIA certificate. Others, and many device sellers, advise a CLIA Certificate of Waiver for any on-site testing. A Certificate of Waiver is obtained by filing CMS Form 116 with your state CLIA agency and paying a modest fee every two years. Ask your state CLIA agency in writing; many employers simply get the waiver to be safe. • Device labeling: rapid drug tests are sold under different labels: FDA-cleared (often CLIA-waived), "employment and insurance" (E&I) exempt, or "forensic use only." Some states require FDA-cleared devices. Match the device's intended use to your program and state, and keep the package insert. • Cutoffs: choose devices whose screening cutoffs match your lab's, so a non-negative screen has a fair chance of confirming. • Consent, notice and confidentiality apply exactly as they do for lab testing. On-site testing does not relax any rule in Chapters 2 and 14.

heading: HEALTHCARE NOTE
body: NEW AND DEVELOPING LAW ** Laws in these areas are new and developing. Please confirm any policy decisions regarding these issues that you may include in your program with your attorneys. SECTION 7.3 Setting up an on-site program People • Choose collectors who are reliable, discreet and not the direct supervisor or close coworker of the people they test. Train at least two, plus backups for nights and weekends. • Train every collector on your procedure and the device instructions, have them complete practice collections, and keep written proof of training and competency. • Use a same-sex observer for any observed collection. Place • A private, single-occupancy restroom you can secure: blue dye in the toilet, water turned off or taped, no soap or cleaners, nothing to hide a specimen in. • A clean, private table area for reading devices and completing forms, out of view of coworkers. • For oral fluid, any private space works. heading: Supplies
body: Supplies • Rapid devices (urine cups or oral fluid swabs) with temperature strips, gloves, tamper-evident seals, lab specimen bottles or kits, non-federal custody forms, lab shipping supplies, and a locked storage cabinet. • Store devices as the package insert directs (temperature, humidity), track lot numbers and expiration dates, and never use an expired device. Paperwork and partners • A written standard operating procedure that follows the device insert and your policy. • An account with a confirming laboratory and an MRO before the first test, with shipping or courier arranged. • A confidential on-site testing log (Form B-8 in Appendix B). SECTION 7.4 The on-site collection, step by step 1. Confirm the reason for the test and that the donor received your policy and signed consent (Form B-2). 2. Verify identity with photo ID. 3. Have the donor remove outer clothing and empty pockets, then wash and dry their hands. 4. Check the device: correct panel, sealed pouch, not expired. Record the lot number. 5. Give the donor the sealed cup; ask for enough urine to fill to the line (enough for lab confirmation). 6. Read the temperature strip within 4 minutes. Out of range (outside 90-100°F) means an immediate second collection under direct observation. 7. Keep the specimen in view of the donor at all times. 8. Start the test as the insert directs and read it at the time the insert specifies, not earlier and not later. Late readings can change. 9. Record every drug's result, the device, lot, time and collector, and capture an image or digital reading if you have one. 10. Have the donor initial and sign where your form requires. For oral fluid: watch the donor for about 10 minutes with nothing in the mouth, have them place the swab as directed until the indicator shows enough sample, then run and read the device the same way. SECTION 7.5 Reading and talking about results • A visible test line, even a faint one, means negative for that drug. No test line means non-negative. No control line means invalid: retest with a new device.

heading: Supplies
body: • Never call a rapid result "positive." Say: "This screen needs laboratory confirmation. Nothing is final until a doctor reviews the lab result." • Do not ask the donor what they took or what medications they use. That conversation belongs to the MRO. • Record the result only in the confidential log, never in a personnel file or email to a supervisor. SECTION 7.6 Sending a non-negative to the lab 1. Tell the donor the specimen will go to a laboratory for confirmation. 2. Prepare the specimen for the lab exactly as your lab instructs: some labs accept the sealed device, others require pouring into lab bottles. Do it in front of the donor. 3. Seal with tamper-evident labels and have the donor initial the seals. 4. Complete the lab's non-federal custody form, including the specimen ID number on both the form and the seals. 5. Package and ship the same day, or store securely as the lab directs until pickup. Chapter 7: Testing On Site With Rapid Tests © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Healthcare Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 35 of 108

heading: SECTION 7.7
body: 6. If your policy and state law allow, remove a safety-sensitive employee from duty pending results. Take no final action. 7. Wait for the MRO's verified result. SECTION 7.7 The MRO's role in an on-site program The laboratory reports confirmed non-negative results to the MRO, not to you. The MRO reviews the chain of custody and lab report, interviews the donor about legitimate medical explanations, and only then reports a verified result to your program owner. Without an MRO, an employer would have to judge prescriptions and medical explanations itself, which creates ADA and privacy risk and weakens every result in a dispute. Some employers also have the MRO review on-site negatives for program oversight; ask your MRO what they recommend. SECTION 7.8 Risks and how to manage them R ISK H OW TO MANAGE IT Acting on an unconfirmed screen Written rule: no final action until MRO verification Reading errors, especially faint lines Train collectors, read at the exact time, use a digital reader Collector bias or conflicts Collectors do not test people they supervise or work closely with Privacy breaches Private collection area, confidential log, need-to-know only Cheating with substituted or adulterated urine Secure restroom, temperature check, observed recollection when indicated, or switch to oral fluid State law violations Confirm your state's on-site rules before buying devices Expired or mishandled devices Storage rules, lot and expiration tracking Broken chain of custody to the lab Seal in front of the donor, matching specimen IDs, same-day shipping SECTION 7.9 If you choose a rapid-test-only program ** This guidebook recommends lab confirmation and MRO review for every non-negative screen. Some employers, usually to save cost or time, act on rapid screens alone, most often for applicants. If you make that choice, understand what you give up and reduce the risk where you can. What you give up: • Defensibility. A rapid screen identifies a drug class, not the drug. Without confirmation you cannot rule out crossreactivity, and false positives are where most drug testing lawsuits come from.

heading: SECTION 7.7
body: • The medical explanation. Without an MRO, no one can verify a prescription privately. Asking the person yourself creates ADA and privacy risk. • State law compliance. Several states require lab confirmation before adverse action, and some restrict on-site testing altogether (Chapter 2). In those states a rapid-test-only program is not an option. • Legal protections. Drug-free workplace premium discounts, workers' compensation defenses and unemployment benefit denials usually depend on confirmed results. How to reduce the risk: • Use rapid-only results only where your state allows it, and generally only for pre-employment decisions, not for discipline or termination of current employees. • Use FDA-cleared devices with cutoffs at or below your lab's, and a digital reader that records the result. heading: • Before any decision, give the person a private chance to disclose prescriptions, ideally
body: • Before any decision, give the person a private chance to disclose prescriptions, ideally to a contracted MRO or other physician who reviews the screen, not to HR. • Offer lab confirmation on request. Keep the specimen sealed and stored so it can be sent to a lab if the person disputes the result. • Consider a second screen with a different device or method before acting. It raises confidence, but it is not a confirmation and should not be called one. • Write the rapid-test-only approach, its limits and the person's right to request confirmation into your policy, and apply it the same way every time. • Use full lab confirmation and MRO review for any current employee, any safety-sensitive decision, and any result likely to be disputed. NEW AND DEVELOPING LAW ** Laws in these areas are new and developing. Please confirm any policy decisions regarding these issues that you may include in your program with your attorneys. SECTION 7.10 Alcohol testing on site • Breath alcohol devices give immediate results. For non-DOT programs, use devices that meet your state's rules, and confirm any screen at or above your policy threshold on an evidential breath testing device if you will act on it. • Oral fluid alcohol screening devices are another option for screening. • Some states limit employer breath testing (Oregon, for example, requires consent or reasonable grounds). Check yours. DOT NOTE DOT alcohol tests require DOT-approved devices and qualified technicians. See Chapter 18 (Alcohol testing under DOT). heading: PART III | TESTING IN THE WORKPLACE
body: PART III | TESTING IN THE WORKPLACE Types of Testing Your policy must say exactly when testing happens. Each reason for testing has its own purpose, legal risks and procedures, and the most common mistakes happen in reasonable suspicion and post-accident testing. 8.1 Pre-employment 8.2 Random 8.3 Reasonable suspicion (for cause) 8.4 Post-accident 8.5 Return-to-duty and follow-up 8.6 Other reasons 8.7 Applicants and edge cases Check your understanding SECTION 8.1 Pre-employment Purpose: keep drug users from being hired. • Test every applicant for the same job category, never selected individuals. • Test after a conditional job offer. This is required for alcohol tests under the ADA, and it simplifies prescription questions, which should go to the MRO, not to HR. • State the offer is contingent on a negative result, and do not let the person start safety-sensitive work before the result. • Check state and local marijuana rules before testing applicants for marijuana (Chapter 2). SECTION 8.2 Random Purpose: deterrence. Random testing is the strongest deterrent because employees cannot plan around it. • Use a scientifically valid method, usually a computer program run by a third party, so every person in the pool has an equal chance at every draw. • Spread tests through the year, on different days and shifts, and keep them unannounced. • Send selected employees for testing immediately once notified. • A person may be picked more than once, or not at all, in a year. That is how true random selection works. • Some states allow random testing only for safety-sensitive jobs. Define who is in the pool in your policy. Chapter 8: Types of Testing © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Healthcare Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 39 of 108

heading: DOT NOTE
body: DOT NOTE DOT sets minimum yearly random testing rates. See Chapter 18 (2026 minimum random testing rates). SECTION 8.3 Reasonable suspicion (for cause) Purpose: remove and test an employee who shows signs of use or impairment now. You may see this called "probable cause." Probable cause is a criminal law standard for police. In employment, the standard is reasonable suspicion: specific, current, observable facts that a trained supervisor can describe. • Base the decision on what you see, hear and smell now: speech, balance, behavior, odor, appearance, or direct evidence of use or possession. Do not rely on rumor, past history or a hunch. • Have a trained supervisor make the call, ideally confirmed by a second person. • Write it down before the test, using the checklist in Appendix B (Form B-3). • Never let the employee drive to the collection site. Arrange transport. • Remove the employee from duty pending results. DOT NOTE DOT requires trained supervisors and sets time limits for reasonable suspicion tests. See Chapter 18 (Required tests). HEALTHCARE NOTE In healthcare, for-cause testing is often triggered by diversion signals, such as dispensing cabinet discrepancies or unwitnessed waste, combined with behavior. Chapter 11 covers how to handle these. SECTION 8.4 Post-accident Purpose: determine whether drugs or alcohol may have contributed to an incident. • Define in the policy exactly which events trigger a test, such as a fatality, an injury needing medical treatment beyond first aid, property damage over a set dollar amount, or a citation. • Test the employees whose actions could have contributed, not everyone who reports an injury. OSHA prohibits using post-accident testing to discourage injury reporting. • Test fast. Best practice is an alcohol test within 2 hours and no later than 8, and a drug specimen within 32 hours. Record the reason for any delay on the post-accident decision record. • Medical care for the injured always comes first. • Use the post-accident decision record (Form B-4). DOT NOTE DOT defines which accidents require testing and sets firm deadlines. See Chapter 18 (Required tests). Chapter 8: Types of Testing © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Healthcare Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 40 of 108

heading: HEALTHCARE NOTE
body: HEALTHCARE NOTE In healthcare, serious patient-harm events and medication errors can be post-incident triggers. Use them carefully: most patient safety programs depend on staff reporting errors freely, so test based on specific concerns about the people involved, not automatically after every reported error, the same way OSHA expects injury reporting to be protected. SECTION 8.5 Return-to-duty and follow-up Purpose: confirm an employee who violated the policy is clean before returning, then keep confirming. • Return-to-duty: a negative test required before the employee goes back to work, after any required evaluation or treatment. • Follow-up: unannounced tests for a set period after return, commonly at least six in the first 12 months, over 12 to 24 months. Best practice is to observe these collections directly. • Put the terms in a written last chance or return-to-work agreement (Form B-7). DOT NOTE DOT's return-to-duty and follow-up rules, including the SAP process, are set by rule. See Chapter 18 (Violations and the SAP process). SECTION 8.6 Other reasons • Periodic or annual: scheduled tests, often with a physical. Weak deterrent because they are announced. • Blanket or company-wide: testing everyone at once, such as when a program starts. Check state law first. SECTION 8.7 Applicants and edge cases • Deadlines: give applicants a firm, written deadline to test, commonly 24 to 48 hours after the conditional offer, and say that missing it will be treated as withdrawing from the process or as a refusal. A long gap lets a drug clear the system. • No-shows: decide in advance whether a no-show is a refusal or a withdrawn application, apply the rule consistently, and document the deadline you gave. • Dilute or invalid results: say in the policy whether an applicant gets one recollection, and whether it will be observed. • Minors: check your state's rules before testing employees under 18; some states add consent or notice requirements, and federal child labor rules already bar minors from many hazardous, safety-sensitive jobs. • Language and literacy: give the policy, notices and consent forms in a language each employee can read, or explain them and document that you did. A consent the employee could not understand is weak evidence.

heading: HEALTHCARE NOTE
body: • Disability accommodations at collection: an applicant who cannot provide urine for a medical reason, or needs help, should be offered another specimen type or an accommodation, not treated as a refusal. heading: PART III | TESTING IN THE WORKPLACE
body: PART III | TESTING IN THE WORKPLACE Recognizing Signs of Drug and Alcohol Use Reasonable suspicion testing depends on what a supervisor sees, hears and smells. Supervisors are not expected to diagnose anyone or name the drug. They are expected to notice specific, current signs, describe them accurately, and follow the policy. This chapter gives them the vocabulary. 9.1 Two kinds of signs 9.2 Signs by drug type 9.3 Medical emergencies come first 9.4 What to document 9.5 What not to do 9.6 Impairment and performance tests ** Check your understanding SECTION 9.1 Two kinds of signs • Acute signs happen now: slurred speech, stumbling, odor, pinpoint pupils, nodding off. These support a reasonable suspicion test today. • Pattern signs build over time: lateness, absences, missed deadlines, mood changes, accidents, money problems. On their own, they do not support a test today. They support a performance conversation and an EAP referral, and they help a supervisor know what to watch for. Many signs have innocent causes: illness, diabetes, fatigue, medication, stress or a disability. That is why the decision rests on documented observations, a second observer when possible, and a test, not on a supervisor's conclusion. SECTION 9.2 Signs by drug type S UBSTANCE P HYSICAL SIGNS B EHAVIOR AND SPEECH O THER CLUES Alcohol Odor of alcohol, flushed face, Slurred or loud speech, poor Mints or mouthwash to mask red or glassy eyes, poor judgment, mood swings, odor, frequent breaks, empty balance and coordination drowsiness containers Red eyes, dry mouth, slowed Slowed or rambling speech, Burnt-rope odor on clothing or reactions, poor coordination laughing inappropriately, poor in a vehicle, eye drops, vape short-term memory, devices Marijuana drowsiness Chapter 9: Recognizing Signs of Drug and Alcohol Use © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. body: S UBSTANCE P HYSICAL SIGNS B EHAVIOR AND SPEECH O THER CLUES Stimulants (cocaine, Dilated pupils, sweating, Rapid speech, agitation, Long periods without sleep, jaw methamphetamine, restlessness, runny nose or paranoia, overconfidence, clenching, grinding teeth amphetamines) nosebleeds (cocaine), weight irritability; later, a crash with loss, skin sores exhaustion (methamphetamine) Opioids (heroin, fentanyl, Pinpoint pupils, drooping Nodding off mid-task, slowed Long sleeves in warm weather, oxycodone and others) eyelids, slow or shallow speech, confusion, very calm foil or straws, frequent breathing, itching, flushed skin or detached restroom trips Benzodiazepines and other Poor coordination, drowsiness, Slurred speech, confusion, Pill bottles not prescribed to sedatives unsteady walk poor memory, looks drunk the person without the odor of alcohol Hallucinogens and PCP Dilated pupils (LSD), rapid eye Confusion, disorientation, Extreme reactions to normal movement (PCP), sweating unpredictable or violent situations behavior (PCP), seeing or hearing things Synthetic cannabinoids Rapid heart rate, sweating, Agitation, confusion, paranoia, Effects can be stronger and (K2, Spice) vomiting sudden aggression less predictable than marijuana HEALTHCARE NOTE Watch for diversion behaviors as well as impairment: volunteering for narcotic duty, frequent unwitnessed waste, high controlled-substance pulls compared with peers, patients whose pain stays uncontrolled, coming in on days off, and long or frequent restroom breaks after accessing medications. SECTION 9.3 Medical emergencies come first Some signs mean danger, not a policy question. Call 911 immediately if a person is unresponsive, has slow or stopped breathing, blue lips or fingertips (signs of an opioid overdose), a seizure, chest pain, or extreme agitation. Many employers keep naloxone (Narcan) on site and train staff to use it. Testing waits until the person is safe. SECTION 9.4 What to document • The date, time and place of each observation. • Exactly what you saw, heard and smelled, in plain words: "slurred speech when answering questions," not "he was high." • How long it lasted and who else observed it. • What the employee said, word for word if possible. • Any direct evidence, such as drugs or alcohol seen. Use the reasonable suspicion checklist (Form B-3) and complete it before the test. SECTION 9.5 What not to do • Do not accuse, diagnose or guess the drug.

heading: S UBSTANCE
body: • Do not argue, threaten or physically restrain the employee. Chapter 9: Recognizing Signs of Drug and Alcohol Use © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Healthcare Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 44 of 108

heading: SECTION 9.6
body: • Do not search the employee's person or belongings unless your policy allows it and law enforcement is not a better choice. • Do not let the employee drive, return to safety-sensitive work, or leave alone. • Do not discuss the situation with coworkers. • Do not delay. Signs fade, and the test window closes. SECTION 9.6 Impairment and performance tests ** Because a marijuana test shows past use rather than impairment, employers in states that protect off-duty use are asking about tools that try to measure impairment directly: tablet-based reaction and attention tests, eye-tracking devices, and balance or coordination tasks. • What they can do: flag a worker who is performing below their own baseline right now, from any cause, including fatigue, illness, medication or drugs. • What they cannot do: identify which substance is involved, or prove legal impairment. Most have limited independent validation for marijuana. • How to use them: as a supplement to trained supervisor observation and, where allowed, testing, not as a replacement. A low score supports a fitness-for-duty conversation and possibly a reasonable suspicion test. • Watch the law: some states, such as New Jersey, have created or proposed formal impairment-recognition roles for workplaces. Check your state's current rules, and treat these tools as medical-type information under the ADA. NEW AND DEVELOPING LAW ** Laws in these areas are new and developing. Please confirm any policy decisions regarding these issues that you may include in your program with your attorneys. heading: PART III | TESTING IN THE WORKPLACE
body: PART III | TESTING IN THE WORKPLACE Handling Results The result you receive should already be MRO-verified, and your response should already be written in your policy. Decide consequences in advance, apply them the same way every time, and document every step. 10.1 The MRO process, step by step 10.2 Result types and what to do 10.3 Refusals to test 10.4 Prescriptions and the ADA 10.5 Prescriptions in safety-sensitive jobs: the ADA interactive process 10.6 Employees in medication-assisted treatment (MAT) ** 10.7 Giving employees a fair process 10.8 Licensed professionals and reporting duties Check your understanding SECTION 10.1 The MRO process, step by step What happens between the laboratory result and your phone call: 1. The lab reports to the MRO, not to you, along with the custody form. This includes positives, adulterated, substituted and invalid results. 2. The MRO reviews the paperwork for collection and lab errors. A fatal flaw cancels the test. 3. The MRO contacts the donor privately. If the MRO cannot reach them, the MRO may ask the employer's program contact to tell the employee, without giving any detail, to call the MRO. Your policy should give the employee a short deadline to call, commonly 72 hours. 4. The interview. The MRO confirms identity, explains the result, and asks whether there is a legitimate medical explanation, such as a prescription. The MRO verifies it with the pharmacy or prescriber. 5. The decision. Verified negative, verified positive, refusal (for adulterated or substituted specimens), cancelled, or negative with a safety concern. 6. The report. The MRO reports only the verified result to your program contact. Medical details stay with the MRO, except information needed to address a safety concern. 7. Split specimen window. The employee may ask the MRO to test the split specimen at another lab (commonly within 72 hours). If the employee refuses to talk to the MRO, or cannot be reached after reasonable efforts within the time the rules allow, the MRO may verify the result without an interview. Your policy should tell employees to keep their phone numbers current for this reason. Chapter 10: Handling Results © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Healthcare Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 47 of 108

heading: DOT NOTE
body: DOT NOTE DOT sets the MRO's contact rules, deadlines and split specimen procedures. See Chapter 18 (DOT results, MRO and refusals). SECTION 10.2 Result types and what to do R ESULT W HAT IT MEANS E MPLOYER ACTION Negative No drugs found above cutoffs No action. File the result confidentially. Negative-dilute Negative, but the urine was watered down Follow your policy. Best practice is an immediate recollection, directly observed when the MRO reports very low creatinine. Non-negative (rapid Preliminary only screen) Send to the lab. Take no final action. Safetysensitive employees may be removed from duty pending results if the policy says so. Verified positive Lab-confirmed and MRO-verified, with no Apply the policy consequence: removal from legitimate medical explanation duty, then termination, last chance agreement or referral to treatment. Adulterated or The specimen was tampered with or is not substituted human urine Invalid The lab cannot get a valid result Treated as a refusal to test. The MRO decides the next step, usually a recollection, sometimes observed. Cancelled A procedural or lab problem voided the test Treat as neither positive nor negative. Retest only if required. Negative, safety concern The MRO verified negative due to a prescription Follow up through a fitness-for-duty evaluation, but believes the drug may make the person not discipline. unsafe DOT NOTE DOT sets exact rules for dilute, invalid and cancelled results. See Chapter 18 (DOT results, MRO and refusals). SECTION 10.3 Refusals to test A refusal is treated the same as a verified positive. Common refusals include failing to report for testing in a reasonable time, leaving before the test is finished, failing to give enough specimen without a valid medical reason, refusing an observed collection when required, and tampering. Spell out your own list of refusals in your policy. DOT NOTE DOT's list of refusals is set by rule and is longer. See Chapter 18 (DOT results, MRO and refusals). heading: SECTION 10.4
body: SECTION 10.4 Prescriptions and the ADA • Do not ask applicants or employees to list their medications as part of testing. Let the MRO handle prescription questions privately. • A lawfully prescribed medication taken as directed is a legitimate explanation, and the MRO will report the test as negative. • If a prescribed drug may make someone unsafe in a safety-sensitive job, handle it as a fitness-for-duty and reasonable accommodation question under the ADA, not as a policy violation. • Marijuana is different: under most non-DOT policies a medical marijuana card is not a legitimate medical explanation, but some states protect registered patients' off-duty use. Check state medical marijuana protections. DOT never accepts it (Chapter 18). SECTION 10.5 Prescriptions in safety-sensitive jobs: the ADA interactive process When a lawfully prescribed medication may make an employee unsafe, the ADA requires an individualized, good-faith process, not a blanket rule. 1. Start confidentially. The trigger is usually an MRO safety concern or an employee's own request. Only the people who need to know are involved. 2. Get medical facts, not guesses. With the employee's written release, ask the treating provider whether the employee can safely perform the essential functions of the job on this medication, and with what limits. 3. Consider accommodations, such as temporary reassignment to non-safety-sensitive work, schedule changes, leave, or time for the provider to adjust the medication. 4. Apply the "direct threat" standard before excluding anyone: a significant risk of substantial harm, based on objective medical evidence about this person, that cannot be reduced by reasonable accommodation. 5. Document each step and the reasons for the decision. 6. Keep medical information separate from the personnel file. Avoid rules such as "no one on opioids may work here." Blanket medication bans invite ADA claims. Post-offer, employers may ask applicants for a job category about medications only if they ask everyone in that category; for current employees, questions must be job-related and consistent with business necessity. Involve your attorney early.

heading: SECTION 10.4
body: SECTION 10.6 Employees in medication-assisted treatment (MAT) ** Medication-assisted treatment uses buprenorphine (Suboxone, Sublocade), methadone or naltrexone (Vivitrol), with counseling, to treat opioid use disorder. As more employers add buprenorphine and methadone to their panels, program owners will see these results, and handling them wrong is one of the clearest legal risks in testing today. The EEOC's 2020 guidance on opioids and the ADA (Use of Codeine, Oxycodone, and Other Opioids: Information for Employees) makes these points: • Opioid use disorder can be an ADA disability. People in recovery who are not currently using illegal drugs are protected. • MAT taken as prescribed is lawful use. An employer generally cannot refuse to hire or fire someone just because they are in a MAT program, unless they cannot do the job safely and effectively or federal law disqualifies them. • Testing: an employee should have the chance to explain lawful use that causes a result. In a properly run program, the MRO does this and reports the result as negative. • Safety concerns require an individualized assessment and the interactive process (above), not a blanket rule. • Accommodations may include schedule changes or time off for treatment, counseling or support meetings, or leave for treatment. Chapter 10: Handling Results © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Healthcare Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 49 of 108

heading: In practice:
body: • What employers never have to do: excuse current illegal drug use, lower performance standards, or remove essential job functions. In practice: • Never write a policy that bans everyone on MAT, or everyone taking buprenorphine or methadone. • Let the MRO handle the medical explanation; do not ask employees whether they are in treatment. • If the MRO reports a safety concern, use the interactive process with the treating provider. • Train HR and supervisors that a verified negative means negative, whatever medication caused the screen. • DOT-regulated jobs have their own medical qualification rules; an MRO's DOT safety concern follows those rules (Chapter 18). NEW AND DEVELOPING LAW ** Laws in these areas are new and developing. Please confirm any policy decisions regarding these issues that you may include in your program with your attorneys. HEALTHCARE NOTE Clinicians in recovery are usually monitored through a state alternative-to-discipline program or physician health program, and many return to practice successfully. Chapter 12 covers return-to-work agreements and medication access limits for licensed professionals. SECTION 10.7 Giving employees a fair process • Tell the employee the result privately, in writing (Form B-6 is a notice template). • Explain the right to have the split specimen or a retained portion tested at a second lab. Best practice is to offer it in your policy. • If you used a third-party screening company, follow FCRA adverse action steps before final action. • Keep everything confidential and limited to those who need to know. SECTION 10.8 Licensed professionals and reporting duties Some employees hold licenses that bring their own rules. Healthcare employers, for example, may have duties to report a nurse, pharmacist or physician's diversion or impairment to a state licensing board, and many boards run confidential peer assistance or alternative-to-discipline programs. Commercial drivers have FMCSA Clearinghouse reporting (Chapter 18). If your employees hold licenses, ask your attorney what reporting your state and their board require, and write it into your policy so the duty is known before it arises. heading: PART IV | HEALTHCARE FOCUS
body: PART IV | HEALTHCARE FOCUS Drug Diversion and Testing Drug diversion is the transfer of a controlled substance from its lawful use to an unlawful one, such as a nurse taking a patient's fentanyl for personal use. It harms patients through untreated pain, tampered or substituted medications and infection, and it exposes the facility to DEA and licensing action. Infection outbreaks have been traced to workers who diverted injectable opioids. In healthcare, testing works best as part of a diversion program, not on its own. 11.1 DEA duties for registrants 11.2 Signals of diversion 11.3 Building a diversion program 11.4 For-cause testing in a diversion investigation 11.5 The investigation interview 11.6 Reporting after diversion ** Check your understanding SECTION 11.1 DEA duties for registrants • Maintain effective controls against theft and diversion of controlled substances. • Do not employ, in a position with access to controlled substances, a person convicted of a felony involving controlled substances, or who had a DEA registration application denied or a registration revoked, suspended or surrendered for cause, without a DEA waiver. • Report theft or significant loss of controlled substances to the DEA within one business day of discovery, followed by DEA Form 106. • DEA rules state that an employee who knows of diversion by a fellow employee has an obligation to report it to a responsible security official. SECTION 11.2 Signals of diversion S OURCE S IGNALS Dispensing data Automated dispensing cabinet (ADC) discrepancies and overrides, pulls well above peers, frequent as-needed doses at shift end, pulls for patients not assigned or already discharged Waste Unwitnessed or late waste, waste witnessed by the same colleague every time, partial doses wasted often Patient care Patients reporting uncontrolled pain on one nurse's shifts, charting that does not match orders Chapter 11: Drug Diversion and Testing © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Healthcare Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 52 of 108

heading: S OURCE
body: S OURCE S IGNALS Behavior Volunteering for narcotic duty, working extra shifts or coming in on days off, long or frequent restroom breaks, signs of impairment (Chapter 9) A single signal is not proof. Patterns, confirmed by investigation, are what justify action. SECTION 11.3 Building a diversion program • Form a diversion committee with pharmacy, nursing, HR, security, compliance and risk management. • Use dispensing analytics to flag outliers, and review them on a set schedule. • Set a written investigation procedure: who reviews data, who interviews, when to remove someone from medication access, and when to test. • Train staff on signs of diversion and their duty to report, with a confidential way to report. • Audit waste, returns and pharmacy storage regularly. SECTION 11.4 For-cause testing in a diversion investigation • Test promptly when discrepancy data and behavior together create reasonable suspicion; drug levels and the evidence both fade quickly. • Order an expanded panel that includes the drugs involved, such as fentanyl, hydromorphone, morphine, oxycodone, meperidine, midazolam or ketamine. Arrange in advance with your lab for drugs that need special tests, such as propofol. • Consider hair testing as well as urine to show a pattern of use. • Remove the employee from medication access, and usually from duty, pending results and investigation. • Document the data reviewed, the observations and the chain of custody carefully; these cases often end up before a licensing board. SECTION 11.5 The investigation interview Interview with HR and pharmacy present, using the data and documents, not accusations. Allow a union representative if requested. Ask the employee to explain discrepancies. A negative test does not end a diversion investigation; diversion can be for sale or for someone else. SECTION 11.6 Reporting after diversion ** Depending on the facts and your state, you may need to report to the DEA, the state board that licenses the employee, the state board of pharmacy, the state health department and law enforcement. Patients may need clinical follow-up or notification. Bring in counsel and risk management early, and decide reporting before you finalize discipline.

heading: PART IV | HEALTHCARE FOCUS
body: PART IV | HEALTHCARE FOCUS Licensed Professionals and the Medical Staff Nurses, pharmacists, physicians and other licensed professionals bring licensing boards, reporting duties and monitoring programs into every testing decision. Handling them well protects patients and gives professionals a real path back to practice. 12.1 Employees versus medical staff 12.2 Board reporting and alternatives to discipline ** 12.3 Monitoring programs 12.4 Return to work for a licensed professional 12.5 The ADA and clinicians in recovery 12.6 Confidentiality Check your understanding SECTION 12.1 Employees versus medical staff Nurses, pharmacists, technicians and many advanced practice providers are employees, covered by your HR policy. Many physicians are not employees; they hold privileges through the medical staff, governed by medical staff bylaws. Testing and impairment concerns about privileged practitioners usually run through the medical staff process, not HR. HEALTHCARE NOTE The Joint Commission standard MS.11.01.01 requires the medical staff to have a process to identify and manage matters of individual health for licensed practitioners that is separate from discipline. It covers education, selfreferral, referral for evaluation and treatment, confidentiality, and monitoring until rehabilitation is complete. Coordinate your HR policy with that process so employed and privileged practitioners are treated consistently. SECTION 12.2 Board reporting and alternatives to discipline ** • Many states require facilities or licensees to report impaired or diverting licensed professionals to the licensing board. The rules, deadlines and who must report vary by state and profession. • Most states offer alternative-to-discipline programs for nurses and physician health programs (PHPs) for physicians. In many states, a professional who enrolls and complies can avoid public discipline. • Some states let a facility refer a professional to the alternative program instead of reporting to the board, if conditions are met. Others require both. • Write your state's rules into your policy, and have counsel confirm them for each profession you employ. heading: LAWS VARY BY STATE
body: LAWS VARY BY STATE ** This section states the general rule. Rules vary by state; check with your attorneys if you have any questions about the specific rules in your state. SECTION 12.3 Monitoring programs Alternative-to-discipline programs and PHPs typically require treatment, random testing with expanded panels, support meetings and a worksite monitor, often for several years. Your role as employer is usually to provide a worksite monitor, follow the program's practice restrictions, and report concerns to the program. SECTION 12.4 Return to work for a licensed professional C ONDITION C OMMON TERMS Fitness for duty Clearance from the treating provider and, where enrolled, the monitoring program Return-to-duty test Negative result before return, on an expanded panel Follow-up testing Random, observed testing as set by the program or agreement Controlled-substance access Often restricted at first: no access, or access only with a second person, for a set period Scheduling Often day shifts only at first, no overtime, no float or agency assignments Worksite monitor A named supervisor who meets with the professional and reports to the program Consequences Any relapse, refusal or diversion ends the agreement Put these terms in a written return-to-work agreement (Form B-10), signed by the professional, the manager and, where applicable, the union and the monitoring program. SECTION 12.5 The ADA and clinicians in recovery Professionals in recovery who are not currently using illegal drugs are protected by the ADA. Current illegal use is not protected. Decisions about restrictions, including for clinicians on medication-assisted treatment, must be individualized and based on objective evidence about safe practice (Chapter 10), not on a blanket rule. SECTION 12.6 Confidentiality Keep monitoring information in the confidential testing file, share it only with the people who need it to run the agreement, and do not disclose it to coworkers. Board reports and program reports are made under the law that requires them, not shared informally. heading: PART IV | HEALTHCARE FOCUS
body: PART IV | HEALTHCARE FOCUS Running a Program in a Healthcare Setting Hospitals and other healthcare employers run around the clock, rely on agency and contract staff, and hold patient records on their own employees. This chapter covers how to run a program in that setting. 13.1 Defining safety-sensitive roles 13.2 Expanded panels 13.3 HIPAA when your employees are also your patients 13.4 Collections in a hospital 13.5 Agency staff, students and residents ** 13.6 Unions 13.7 Medical marijuana and healthcare workers Check your understanding SECTION 13.1 Defining safety-sensitive roles In healthcare, define safety-sensitive roles by two features: direct patient care where impairment could cause harm, and access to controlled substances. Nurses, physicians and advanced practice providers, pharmacists and pharmacy technicians, anesthesia staff, respiratory therapists, paramedics and patient transport drivers usually qualify. List them in your policy (Attachment 1). SECTION 13.2 Expanded panels D RUG W HY IT MATTERS IN HEALTHCARE T ESTING NOTE Fentanyl Frequently diverted injectable opioid Needs its own test Oxycodone, hydrocodone, Widely stocked opioids Missed by opiate screens; confirm your hydromorphone panel includes them Meperidine Still stocked in some settings Not on standard panels Tramadol Common oral opioid Not on standard panels Ketamine Anesthesia and emergency use Not on standard panels Propofol Anesthesia; abuse can be fatal Specialized test; arrange with lab Nalbuphine, butorphanol Opioid agonist-antagonists Specialized tests Chapter 13: Running a Program in a Healthcare Setting © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: D RUG
body: D RUG W HY IT MATTERS IN HEALTHCARE T ESTING NOTE Midazolam and other Sedation Some screens miss certain benzodiazepines benzodiazepines Use the expanded panel for pre-employment testing of roles with controlled-substance access, for diversion investigations, and for monitoring. A standard panel is usually enough for other roles. SECTION 13.3 HIPAA when your employees are also your patients • Drug test results you hold as an employer are employment records, not protected health information (PHI) under HIPAA. They still must be kept confidential and apart from personnel files. • If an employee is treated as a patient at your facility, that medical record is PHI. Managers and HR may not look at it, or use it in an employment decision, without the employee's written authorization. • Keep employee health and occupational health records separate from the patient record system, and limit access by role. • Train managers that looking up a coworker's chart is a privacy violation, even with good intentions. SECTION 13.4 Collections in a hospital • Use employee health or occupational health as the collection site, with backup coverage on nights and weekends. • Do not process employee tests through the emergency department or patient registration. • Choose collectors who are not close colleagues of the donor, and use an outside collector for tests of employee health staff. • For a for-cause test at night, have an on-call collector or mobile collection service available. SECTION 13.5 Agency staff, students and residents ** • Travel and agency nurses: require the agency to test before assignment with an expanded panel for medicationaccess roles, certify eligibility, and agree how for-cause testing works on your premises. • Locum physicians: handle through credentialing and medical staff processes. • Students: the school's policy and the affiliation agreement govern; require testing for students with medication access. • Residents and fellows: follow the graduate medical education program's policy, coordinated with your HR policy. LAWS VARY BY STATE ** This section states the general rule. Rules vary by state; check with your attorneys if you have any questions about the specific rules in your state. SECTION 13.6 Unions Many nurses and other healthcare workers are unionized. Bargain testing changes, follow contract procedures for forcause testing and investigations, and honor requests for representation in diversion interviews.

heading: PART V | BUILDING YOUR PROGRAM
body: PART V | BUILDING YOUR PROGRAM Writing Your Policy Your written policy is the foundation of the program. Courts, arbitrators and state agencies judge a program first by whether the employer wrote clear rules, told employees in advance, and then followed its own rules. Appendix A is a draft you can adapt. 14.1 Decisions to make before you write 14.2 Required elements of a policy 14.3 Policy pitfalls 14.4 Executives and supervisors under the same rules Check your understanding SECTION 14.1 Decisions to make before you write D ECISION Q UESTIONS TO ANSWER Who is covered All employees?
