Reasons for testing Which of pre-employment, random, reasonable suspicion, post-accident, return-to-duty, follow-up and periodic will you use? Specimens and panel Urine, oral fluid, hair or breath? Which drugs, at what cutoffs? Marijuana Test for it in all jobs, only safety-sensitive jobs, or not pre-employment? What do your states allow? Rapid or lab On-site rapid screens with lab confirmation, or lab-only? Alcohol threshold What level is a violation? Consequences Termination, last chance agreement, or treatment for a first positive? Same for a refusal? Second chances Will you offer an Employee Assistance Program (EAP) referral or a last chance agreement? Self-referral Can an employee who asks for help before being tested keep their job? Vendors Who is your collector, lab, MRO, and (if used) third-party administrator? heading: 2. Prohibited conduct: use, possession, sale or being under the influence at work, and ref
body: 2. Prohibited conduct: use, possession, sale or being under the influence at work, and refusal to test. 3. Definitions of key terms (safety-sensitive, reasonable suspicion, refusal and others). 4. The circumstances for each type of test. 5. Drugs tested and the testing process, including MRO review. 6. Consequences for violations and refusals. 7. Assistance available, such as an EAP. 8. Confidentiality of results. 9. Employee rights, such as split specimen testing and explaining a result to the MRO. 10. A signed acknowledgment of receipt. 11. A reservation of the right to change the policy, with notice. SECTION 14.3 Policy pitfalls • Copying a template without changing it. A policy that does not match what you actually do is worse than no policy. • Promising something you won't do, such as "every positive will be offered treatment." • Ignoring state law where employees work, especially for marijuana and random testing. • Mixing DOT and non-DOT rules in a way that applies company rules to DOT tests. • Skipping notice. Many states require advance written notice, sometimes a set number of days, before testing starts. SECTION 14.4 Executives and supervisors under the same rules Decide in writing whether owners, executives and managers are covered, and cover them on the same terms as everyone else in the same kind of job. Leaders in safety-sensitive roles belong in the random pool. Exempting leadership tells employees the program is about control, not safety, and it weakens the employer's defense that the policy is applied consistently. If an executive tests positive, follow the policy exactly as written, with counsel involved, and keep it as confidential as any other result. body: PART V | BUILDING YOUR PROGRAM Running the Program A good policy fails without good execution. Most program failures come from poorly chosen vendors, untrained supervisors, sloppy records and inconsistent follow-through. 15.1 Building your vendor team 15.2 Setting up collection sites 15.3 Training 15.4 Recordkeeping 15.5 Confidentiality 15.6 Helping employees: EAPs and second chances 15.7 Auditing your program 15.8 Budgeting and cost 15.9 Contractors, temps and staffing agencies ** 15.10 Privacy and data security Check your understanding SECTION 15.1 Building your vendor team R OLE W HAT THEY DO W HAT TO CHECK Collection site Collects specimens and runs rapid tests or Trained, certified collectors; hours and breath alcohol tests locations that fit your shifts; after-hours and on-site options for post-accident tests Laboratory Screens and confirms specimens HHS-certified preferred, or at least CAP-FDT accredited; turnaround time; panel options Medical Review Officer Reviews non-negative results and talks to Certified MRO; how fast they reach donors; how donors they report safety concerns Third-party administrator Runs the program for you: random selections, Experience with your industry and states; FCRA (TPA) scheduling, recordkeeping, reporting compliance if reporting results; a secure online portal Consortium Pools small employers into one random pool Useful for small employers; check selection method and records. heading: SECTION 15.2
body: Get every vendor agreement in writing, including turnaround times, confidentiality, data security and who owns the records. SECTION 15.2 Setting up collection sites Collection sites are your partners in the field, and most testing problems start with unclear instructions. Before the first test: • Set up a written account with each site: your company name and account number, authorized contacts, payment terms and hours, including after-hours and weekend post-accident options. • Tell them exactly which tests to run for each reason: specimen, panel, DOT or non-DOT, and whether to use rapid tests. • Send donors with a written authorization or electronic order, never just a phone call from a supervisor. • Confirm where results go: to the MRO and then your DER, never to the supervisor who sent the employee. • Agree how the site will tell you about refusals, shy bladders, temperature problems and no-shows, and how fast. • Visit at least once a year. Check privacy, cleanliness, restroom security and wait times, and review a few completed forms. SECTION 15.3 Training • Supervisors: recognizing signs of impairment, documenting observations, making a reasonable suspicion decision, and handling the employee safely and respectfully. Best practice is at least 60 minutes on drugs and 60 minutes on alcohol, before a supervisor makes a reasonable suspicion decision, with periodic refreshers. • Employees: the policy, the dangers of drug and alcohol use, how testing works, and where to get help. Repeat at hiring and at least yearly. • HR and program staff: the policy, result handling, confidentiality and recordkeeping. DOT NOTE DOT requires this supervisor training for anyone supervising DOT employees. See Chapter 18 (What the employer must do). SECTION 15.4 Recordkeeping Keep testing records apart from personnel files, in a locked or access-controlled system. Use these retention periods, which match DOT's, as a minimum: R ECORD R ECOMMENDED RETENTION Positive results, refusals, SAP reports, follow-up schedules 5 years Collection process and supervisor training records 2 years Negative and cancelled results 1 year Check state law, which can require longer retention or specific handling.

heading: SECTION 15.5
body: SECTION 15.5 Confidentiality • Share results only with people who need to know: the designated program contact, the employee's decision-maker, and legal counsel. • Never discuss a result with coworkers. • Release results to outside parties only with the employee's written consent or as law requires. SECTION 15.6 Helping employees: EAPs and second chances • An Employee Assistance Program offers confidential counseling and referral. Many employers encourage selfreferral before a test by promising no discipline for coming forward first. • A last chance agreement lets an employee keep their job after a violation if they complete treatment, pass a returnto-duty test, and accept follow-up testing. Any later violation ends employment. • Second chances can help retention in tight labor markets, but they must be offered consistently. SECTION 15.7 Auditing your program Once a year, review: positivity and refusal rates by test reason, whether random selections were completed on schedule, supervisor training records, vendor performance, policy changes needed for new laws, and any complaints or claims. SECTION 15.8 Budgeting and cost Testing costs vary widely by region, volume, specimen and vendor, so get written quotes. Published figures give a starting point: lab-based tests often start around $50 and hair tests around $125 (Checkr), and published fee schedules for a DOT urine test including collection, lab analysis and MRO review cluster around $65 to $80. What goes into the cost of a lab-based test: • Collection fee (higher for observed, after-hours or on-site mobile collections) • Laboratory screen, plus confirmation for non-negatives • MRO review • TPA or consortium fees: annual membership, random selection, reporting • Travel time and lost work while employees go to a collection site What goes into the cost of an on-site rapid program: • Rapid devices, temperature strips and collection supplies • Collector time and training • Lab confirmation and MRO fees for each non-negative (usually a small share of tests) • Shipping or courier to the lab • Any state registration or CLIA certificate fees • Less travel and lost work, which is often the biggest saving Building an annual budget. Estimate the number of tests by reason, then multiply by the cost per test:

heading: T EST REASON
body: T EST REASON H OW TO ESTIMATE THE COUNT Post-accident and reasonable suspicion Last year's incidents, plus a cushion Return-to-duty and follow-up Number of employees on last chance agreements × required tests Add confirmation and MRO fees for the share of tests you expect to be non-negative, plus fixed costs such as TPA fees, training and supplies. Comparing vendor quotes. Ask every vendor for the all-in price for the same test, and check: • What is included: collection, lab screen, confirmation, MRO, reporting • Fees for after-hours, observed, shy bladder and cancelled collections • Turnaround time for negatives and for MRO-verified results • Minimums, contract length and price changes • Who owns the records, and what it costs to get them if you leave The cheapest price per test is rarely the cheapest program. A cancelled test, a lost specimen or a slow result that delays a hire costs more than a few dollars per test. SECTION 15.9 Contractors, temps and staffing agencies ** People who work at your site but are not your employees create two risks: an impaired contractor can hurt your people, and testing someone else's employee directly can make you look like their employer. • Put testing in the contract. Require contractors and staffing agencies to run a program that meets your standards: which tests, which panel, an MRO and who is excluded from your site after a positive or refusal. • Let the contractor test its own people and certify compliance to you, rather than testing them yourself. Testing, disciplining and controlling another company's workers is one factor in finding joint employment. • Ask for proof: a written policy, a certificate of compliance, or aggregate results. Do not ask for individual results unless the contract and law clearly allow it and the worker has consented. • Site access rules can still apply to everyone: "No one may work on site while impaired, and anyone involved in an incident may be required to test under the contractor's program." • Customer requirements flow down. If your customer requires your workers to be tested, write the same requirement into your subcontracts and staffing agreements.

heading: SECTION 15.10
body: SECTION 15.10 Privacy and data security Drug test results are some of the most sensitive records an employer holds, and they increasingly live in software systems. • Who can see results: limit system access to the program owner and named backups. Check that your HR system, TPA portal and email do not quietly give supervisors or IT staff access. • Separate storage: keep results out of the general personnel file and general HR system, as the ADA requires for medical information. • HIPAA: usually does not apply to an employer acting as an employer. It may apply to your MRO, clinic or health plan. Do not assume either way; ask your counsel. • State privacy laws may cover employee data, such as California's privacy law for employee information, and some states regulate biometric data if your systems use fingerprints or facial images. • Vendors: require confidentiality, data security, breach notice and return or destruction of records in every vendor contract. • Email and texts: never send results or names of donors by unencrypted email or text. • Retention and destruction: keep records for the required periods (above), then destroy them securely, unless a lawsuit or claim is pending. • Litigation hold: once a claim or lawsuit is likely, stop routine destruction of every related record, including emails, logs and images. Use the vendor and privacy rules above together: most data problems in testing programs come from vendor systems and email, not from paper files. body: PART V | BUILDING YOUR PROGRAM Communicating the Program A program succeeds when everyone involved understands it and trusts it. As the program owner, you are its spokesperson: you explain why the company tests, how it works and what happens next, to people with very different concerns. Prescriptions are discussed privately with the doctor, not with your supervisor." • Help: "If you have a problem, ask for help before you are tested. We have an EAP, and asking for help early is protected under our policy." SECTION 16.3 Reporting to leadership Executives want to know whether the program is working, what it costs and whether the company is exposed. Report quarterly, with no names: M EASURE W HY IT MATTERS Tests completed by reason (pre-employment, random, reasonable Shows the program is running as written suspicion, post-accident, follow-up) Positive and refusal rates by reason, compared with industry benchmarks Shows where risk is concentrated such as the Quest Drug Testing Index Random testing completed vs. the required or planned rate A key compliance and audit item Cancelled tests and collection errors Shows vendor quality Turnaround from collection to result Affects hiring speed Cost per test and total cost Budget Chapter 16: Communicating the Program © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: M EASURE
body: M EASURE W HY IT MATTERS Workplace incidents and workers' comp claims Shows impact over time Policy changes needed for new laws Legal risk SECTION 16.4 Scripts for hard conversations Adapt these to your policy. Keep conversations private, calm and short, and have a second manager present for anything involving discipline. Announcing a new program: "Starting [DATE], we are launching a drug and alcohol testing program for [WHO]. Here is why we are doing it, how it works, and what your rights are. Everyone will get a copy of the policy and a chance to ask questions before any testing starts." Notifying a random selection: "You've been randomly selected for a test today. This is computer-generated, not based on anything you've done. Please go to [LOCATION] now; [NAME] will go with you." Reasonable suspicion: "I've noticed [SPECIFIC OBSERVATIONS] today. Because of what I've seen, our policy requires a test. I'm not accusing you of anything. We will take you to the collection site, and you will not be able to work until we have the result." Do not argue, diagnose or ask what they took. Post-accident: "Our policy requires testing after incidents like this one, for everyone whose actions could have contributed. It isn't a judgment about what happened. Once you've received any medical care you need, [NAME] will take you to the collection site." Delivering a verified positive: "The doctor who reviews our tests has verified your test as positive for [SUBSTANCE]. Under our policy, [CONSEQUENCE]. Here is a written notice, including how to request a test of your split specimen and how to reach our EAP." Do not debate the science; refer questions to the MRO. A coworker asks about someone's test: "I can't discuss anyone's personal information, just as I wouldn't discuss yours." An employee asks for help: "Thank you for coming to me. Under our policy, asking for help before you're selected for a test is protected. Let's get you connected with [EAP]." Then follow the self-referral section of your policy.

heading: M EASURE
body: SECTION 16.5 Answering common employee questions • "Marijuana is legal in my state. Why can you test for it?" State law may protect some off-duty use, and our policy follows the law where you work. No state protects use or impairment at work, and DOT rules prohibit marijuana for covered jobs regardless of state law. • "Can CBD make me test positive?" It can. Many CBD products contain THC, even when labeled otherwise, and hempderived THC products such as delta-8 test positive for marijuana. Neither is a legitimate medical explanation. Federal limits on hemp-derived THC products are due to take effect on December 11, 2026 (Chapter 2). • "What about my prescriptions?" Discuss them privately with the MRO if your test is non-negative. A valid prescription taken as directed is reported as negative. • "Can poppy seeds or secondhand smoke make me fail?" Poppy seeds can cause an opiate screen to show nonnegative, especially at the lower cutoffs many private programs use. That is why every non-negative goes to the lab and the MRO, who considers poppy seeds before verifying a result. Normal secondhand marijuana smoke exposure is very unlikely to reach the cutoff. • "Who sees my results?" Only the people listed in the policy who need to know. • "What if I refuse?" A refusal is treated the same as a positive result. Chapter 16: Communicating the Program © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. body: SECTION 16.6 Employee FAQ handout Give this one-page summary to every employee with the policy, filled in with your details: NOTE Our Drug and Alcohol Testing Program: What You Need to Know • Why we test: To keep every employee, our customers and the public safe. • Who is tested: [WHO], under the same rules for everyone in the same job. • When: [Before hire / random / reasonable suspicion / after accidents / return-to-duty and follow-up]. • How: A [urine / oral fluid / hair / breath] sample collected privately by a trained collector. Any non-negative screen is confirmed by a certified lab and reviewed by a physician (MRO) before any decision. • Prescriptions: Discussed only with the MRO, privately. • Your results: Confidential and kept separate from your personnel file. • Refusing or tampering: Treated the same as a positive result. • Getting help: Contact [EAP NAME, PHONE] any time. heading: PART VI DOT AND PRACTICE
body: PART VI DOT AND PRACTICE DOT Testing Requirements If any of your employees perform DOT safety-sensitive work, federal rules decide almost everything about their testing: who is tested, when, how, by whom and what happens after a violation. You cannot opt out of, add to or relax these rules. The rest of this guidebook describes best practice for non-DOT programs; wherever DOT differs, a DOT note points here. Always check the current rules at the DOT Office of Drug and Alcohol Policy and Compliance (ODAPC), transportation.gov/ odapc. 18.1 How the rules fit together 18.2 Where DOT differs from this guidebook 18.3 What the employer must do 18.4 Required tests 18.5 2026 minimum random testing rates 18.6 Drug testing under DOT 18.7 DOT drug panel and cutoffs 18.8 DOT collection rules 18.9 DOT results, MRO and refusals 18.10 Alcohol testing under DOT 18.11 Violations and the SAP process 18.12 The FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse 18.13 DOT recordkeeping 18.14 Common DOT audit findings Check your understanding SECTION 18.1 How the rules fit together • 49 CFR Part 40 sets the testing procedures for every DOT agency: collection, labs, MROs, alcohol testing, SAPs and records. • Each DOT agency's own rule decides who is covered, which tests are required, and specific duties. A GENCY A GENCY RULE W HO IS COVERED FMCSA 49 CFR Part 382 CDL drivers of commercial motor vehicles FAA 14 CFR Part 120 Flight crew, flight attendants, mechanics, dispatchers, air traffic controllers and other aviation safety jobs Chapter 18: DOT Testing Requirements © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: • Name a Designated Employer Representative (DER) to receive results and remove employees
body: • Name a Designated Employer Representative (DER) to receive results and remove employees from duty. • Contract with qualified service agents: collectors, an HHS-certified lab, an MRO, a SAP and optionally a consortium/ third-party administrator (C/TPA). • Check every new hire's drug and alcohol violation history with previous DOT-regulated employers: the past two years under Part 40, and three years for CDL drivers. For FMCSA drivers, a full Clearinghouse pre-employment query now satisfies this check for prior FMCSA employers; ask employers regulated by other DOT agencies directly. • Run a limited Clearinghouse query on every CDL driver at least once a year. • Train supervisors: at least 60 minutes on drugs and 60 minutes on alcohol for reasonable suspicion. • Give employees the required education materials. • Keep records for the required periods and file annual testing data (MIS) reports when your agency requires them. • Keep DOT and non-DOT testing completely separate. SECTION 18.4 Required tests T EST D OT REQUIREMENT Pre-employment A negative drug test before first safety-sensitive work. Pre-employment alcohol testing is optional for most agencies. Random Unannounced, spread through the year, at least the agency's minimum rate. Reasonable suspicion Based on a trained supervisor's specific, current observations made just before, during or just after duty. Alcohol test within 2 hours if possible, and never after 8. Post-accident Required when the agency's accident criteria are met. For FMCSA, for example: any fatality, or an injury treated away from the scene or a vehicle towed away, when the driver receives a citation. Alcohol within 8 hours (ideally 2), drugs within 32 hours. Return-to-duty Directly observed, after the SAP process, before returning to safety-sensitive work. Follow-up Directly observed, unannounced, at least 6 in the first 12 months, for up to 5 years, as the SAP directs. SECTION 18.5 2026 minimum random testing rates Rates are set each year by each agency and posted by ODAPC. These apply to calendar year 2026: A GENCY R ANDOM DRUG RATE R ANDOM ALCOHOL RATE FMCSA 50% 10% FAA 25% 10% FRA (covered service and maintenance-of-way)

heading: SECTION 18.6
body: The rate is a percentage of your average number of covered positions. With 100 FMCSA drivers, you must complete at least 50 random drug tests and 10 random alcohol tests during the year. SECTION 18.6 Drug testing under DOT • Urine only, for now. DOT has authorized oral fluid testing, but employers cannot use it until HHS certifies at least two oral fluid laboratories; none had been certified when DOT last addressed this in May 2026. Under a rule effective June 10, 2026, in the limited situations where DOT would otherwise require an oral fluid test, a directly observed urine collection is required instead. Check transportation.gov/odapc for current status. • The fixed DOT panel: marijuana, cocaine, amphetamines (including methamphetamine, MDMA and MDA), opioids (codeine, morphine, 6-AM, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, oxycodone, oxymorphone) and PCP. Fentanyl was proposed in September 2025 but is not yet part of the panel. Employers may not add drugs to a DOT test or apply company cutoffs. • An HHS-certified lab tests the specimen; every non-negative goes to the MRO. SECTION 18.7 DOT drug panel and cutoffs DOT laboratories must use these urine cutoffs, in ng/mL (49 CFR 40.85): C OMPARED WITH TYPICAL NON-DOT D RUG (TARGET ANALYTE) D OT SCREEN D OT CONFIRM Marijuana metabolite (THC-COOH) Same Cocaine metabolite (benzoylecgonine) Same Codeine / morphine 2,000 2,000 each Different: many non-DOT programs screen P RACTICE at 300 6-acetylmorphine (heroin) Same Hydrocodone / hydromorphone 100 each Same Oxycodone / oxymorphone 100 each Same Phencyclidine (PCP) Same Amphetamine / methamphetamine 250 each Same MDMA / MDA 250 each Same Fentanyl Not tested Not tested Different: many non-DOT programs test for it The opiate difference. DOT screens and confirms codeine and morphine at 2,000 ng/mL, mainly so that poppy seeds do not cause positives. Many private programs screen at 300 ng/mL to detect more use. The same specimen can be negative on a DOT test and non-negative on a company test. Never apply company cutoffs or company drugs to a DOT test; if you want broader testing for a DOT employee, it must be a separate non-DOT test under your company policy, on a non-federal form, where law allows.

heading: SECTION 18.6
body: Federal agencies are different again. Federal agency programs (not DOT) follow the HHS panel, which since July 2025 includes fentanyl and norfentanyl at 1 ng/mL and uses a 4,000 ng/mL morphine confirmation cutoff. DOT has not adopted those changes. Chapter 18: DOT Testing Requirements © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 18.8
body: SECTION 18.8 DOT collection rules • Federal form. Every DOT collection uses the federal Custody and Control Form, on paper or an approved electronic version. • Collector qualifications. Collectors must complete qualification training, pass five error-free mock collections, and take refresher training every five years. • Direct observation by a same-sex observer is required for return-to-duty and follow-up tests, when the temperature is out of range or tampering is suspected, when the MRO orders it, and in the other situations listed in 49 CFR 40.67. • Shy bladder. The donor may drink up to 40 ounces of fluid over up to 3 hours. If they still cannot provide 45 mL, the employer must arrange a medical evaluation within 5 days. If no medical condition explains it, it is a refusal. • Dilute specimens. If the MRO reports a dilute negative with creatinine of 2 to 5 mg/dL, the employee must be recollected immediately under direct observation. DOT treats these collection errors as follows: F LAW R ESULT UNDER DOT Specimen ID on the bottle does not match the form Fatal; test cancelled Seal broken or missing when the lab receives it Fatal; test cancelled Collector's printed name and signature missing Fatal; test cancelled Not enough specimen for the lab to test Fatal; test cancelled Collector forgot to sign the certification Correctable with a signed memo Non-federal form used for a DOT test Correctable with a signed memo SECTION 18.9 DOT results, MRO and refusals • MRO interview. The MRO interviews the employee before verifying a positive. A state medical marijuana card or a Schedule III marijuana product is not a legitimate medical explanation. • Reaching the employee. If the MRO cannot reach the employee, the DER tells the employee to call the MRO, without giving details. The employee then has 72 hours to call. If the employee does not, the MRO may verify the result without an interview.

heading: SECTION 18.8
body: • Split specimen. The employee may ask the MRO, within 72 hours, to have the split specimen tested at a second HHScertified lab. The employer may not delay action while waiting. • Refusals are defined in 49 CFR 40.191. They include failing to appear in a reasonable time, leaving before the test is complete, failing to provide enough specimen without a medical explanation, refusing an observed collection or failing to follow the observer, refusing to empty pockets, carrying or wearing a device to tamper, an adulterated or substituted result, admitting adulteration or substitution, and failing to cooperate. • Invalid and cancelled results. The MRO directs any required recollection, which may be observed. • Safety concerns. When the MRO believes a prescribed medication makes the employee medically unqualified or a safety risk, the MRO reports it, and the DOT agency's medical qualification rules govern what happens next. SECTION 18.10 Alcohol testing under DOT • Trained breath alcohol technicians or screening test technicians use DOT-approved devices. • A screening result of 0.02 or higher must be confirmed on an evidential breath testing device, after a waiting period of at least 15 minutes, starting within 30 minutes of the screen. heading: SECTION 18.11
body: • 0.04 or higher: a violation. Removal from safety-sensitive duty and the SAP process. • 0.02 to 0.039: not a violation, but the employee must be removed from safety-sensitive duty for a period set by the agency (24 hours for FMCSA). • Agencies also bar alcohol use within set hours before duty (for example, 4 hours for FMCSA drivers, 8 hours for FAA flight crew) and after an accident until tested. SECTION 18.11 Violations and the SAP process A DOT violation is a verified positive, an alcohol result of 0.04 or higher, a refusal, or alcohol or drug use on or before duty in violation of agency rules. After any violation: 1. Remove the employee from safety-sensitive duty immediately. 2. Give the employee a list of qualified Substance Abuse Professionals. This is required even if you terminate the employee. 3. The SAP evaluates the employee and requires education or treatment. 4. The SAP re-evaluates and, if the employee complied, sets a follow-up testing plan. 5. The employee passes a directly observed return-to-duty test. 6. The employee completes the follow-up testing plan, which travels with them to any new DOT employer. DOT does not require you to rehire or keep the employee. That is your company's decision, but if you do return them to safety-sensitive work, they must complete this process first. SECTION 18.12 The FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse For CDL drivers, employers, MROs and SAPs must report violations, refusals and return-to-duty steps to the Clearinghouse. Since November 2024, state licensing agencies downgrade the CDL of a driver in "prohibited" status until the return-toduty process is complete. Driving with a prohibited status is a serious violation for the driver and the carrier.

heading: SECTION 18.11
body: SECTION 18.13 DOT recordkeeping DOT records must be kept confidential, apart from personnel files, and released only as 49 CFR Part 40 allows. These are the minimum retention periods: R ECORD D OT RETENTION Positive results, refusals, SAP reports, follow-up schedules 5 years Collection process and supervisor training records 2 years Negative and cancelled results 1 year SECTION 18.14 Common DOT audit findings • Random rates not met, or tests bunched at one time of year • Missing previous employer checks or Clearinghouse queries • No supervisor training records • Non-DOT tests done on federal forms, or company drugs added to DOT tests • Employees allowed to keep working after a refusal or violation • Owner-operators not enrolled in a consortium Chapter 18: DOT Testing Requirements © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: PART VI DOT AND PRACTICE
body: PART VI DOT AND PRACTICE Case Scenarios These scenarios apply the guidebook to situations program owners face. Each is an example only; the right answer in your company depends on your policy and the law where the employee works. 19.1 Scenario 1: A non-negative on-site screen for an applicant 19.2 Scenario 2: A forklift accident 19.3 Scenario 3: The smell of alcohol after lunch 19.4 Scenario 4: A prescription and a crane 19.5 Scenario 5: "Why do I keep getting picked?" 19.6 Scenario 6: A cold specimen 19.7 Scenario 7: "It was only CBD" 19.8 Scenario 8: A DOT driver at 0.03 19.9 Scenario 9: A union representative 19.10 Scenario 10: Asking for help before a test 19.11 Scenario 11: A dispensing cabinet pattern 19.12 Scenario 12: The surgeon and the odor of alcohol 19.13 Scenario 13: A nurse asks for help 19.14 Scenario 14: Back to nights too soon 19.15 Scenario 15: A prescription in the pharmacy 19.16 Scenario 16: The chart lookup Check your understanding SECTION 19.1 Scenario 1: A non-negative on-site screen for an applicant An applicant for an office job in New Jersey gives a urine specimen on site after a conditional offer. The rapid cup shows no test line for THC. What to do: Tell the applicant the screen needs lab confirmation, seal and send the specimen to the lab, and take no action. When the MRO reports the result, check New Jersey law before acting: New Jersey allows the test, but bars withdrawing the offer based only on a positive cannabis result without documented evidence of impairment, and a recent appellate decision lets applicants sue over offers withdrawn for a positive alone. For an office job, a positive THC result by itself is unlikely to support withdrawing the offer. Your policy should already say how marijuana is handled for this job in this state. Lesson: The screen is never final, and marijuana results must be read against state law where the person works. Chapter 19: Case Scenarios © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Healthcare Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 88 of 108

heading: SECTION 19.2
body: SECTION 19.2 Scenario 2: A forklift accident A forklift strikes a rack, causing $8,000 in damage. A coworker standing nearby twisted an ankle stepping away. Your policy requires testing for property damage over $5,000. What to do: Get the injured worker medical care first. Test the forklift operator, whose actions could have contributed. Do not test the coworker just because they were injured; that risks an OSHA violation for discouraging injury reporting. Complete the post-accident decision record (Form B-4) and test promptly, ideally alcohol within 2 hours and drugs within 32. Lesson: Test the people whose actions could have contributed, not the people who got hurt. SECTION 19.3 Scenario 3: The smell of alcohol after lunch A supervisor notices an employee returning from lunch with a strong odor of alcohol, flushed face and loud, slurred speech. The employee drove back to work. What to do: Remove the employee from duty, have a second supervisor observe if possible, and complete the reasonable suspicion checklist (Form B-3). Arrange transport to the collection site, or test on site with an approved breath device. Do not let the employee drive. If the employee insists on driving away, do not restrain them; consider calling law enforcement for public safety. Lesson: Specific, current observations, documented before the test, are what make reasonable suspicion defensible. SECTION 19.4 Scenario 4: A prescription and a crane A crane operator's random test is reported by the MRO as negative because of a valid opioid prescription, with a safety concern noted. What to do: This is not a policy violation. Begin the ADA interactive process: confidentially, with the employee's release, ask the treating provider whether the employee can safely operate a crane on this medication, consider temporary reassignment or leave, and document the decision. Lesson: A safety concern is a fitness-for-duty question, not discipline. SECTION 19.5 Scenario 5: "Why do I keep getting picked?" An employee has been selected for random testing three times this year and complains that they are being targeted. What to do: Explain that selections are computer-generated by your TPA, that everyone has an equal chance at every draw, and that being picked several times, or not at all, is normal. Offer to show documentation that the selection method is scientifically valid, without revealing anyone else's selections.

heading: SECTION 19.2
body: Lesson: True random selection does not even out over a year, and your records should prove the method. SECTION 19.6 Scenario 6: A cold specimen During an on-site collection, the cup's temperature strip shows no reading in the 90-100°F range. What to do: Note the temperature, keep the first specimen, and immediately conduct a second collection under direct observation by a same-sex observer. Send both specimens to the lab. If the employee refuses the observed collection, document it as a refusal. Lesson: Temperature is the first line of defense against substituted urine. Chapter 19: Case Scenarios © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Healthcare Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 89 of 108

heading: SECTION 19.7
body: SECTION 19.7 Scenario 7: "It was only CBD" An employee's MRO-verified result is positive for marijuana. The employee says they only use a CBD product. What to do: Follow the policy. CBD products can contain THC even when labeled otherwise, and CBD use is not a legitimate medical explanation. The MRO has already considered any explanation offered. Check whether state law protects off-duty cannabis use for this job before deciding the consequence. Lesson: The MRO process, not the employer, weighs explanations. SECTION 19.8 Scenario 8: A DOT driver at 0.03 A CDL driver's random breath alcohol confirmation is 0.03. What to do: This is not a DOT violation, but the driver must be removed from safety-sensitive duty for 24 hours under FMCSA rules. Your company policy may set its own consequence for non-DOT purposes, as long as it is applied consistently and labeled as a company rule. Lesson: Know the difference between a DOT violation and a DOT removal (Chapter 18). SECTION 19.9 Scenario 9: A union representative During a reasonable suspicion meeting, a union employee asks for a union representative. What to do: Honor the request for an investigatory interview that could lead to discipline. Follow your contract and counsel's guidance on proceeding with the test itself, which should not be delayed beyond the testing window. Lesson: Union rights and testing deadlines both apply; plan for both in advance. SECTION 19.10 Scenario 10: Asking for help before a test An employee tells HR they have a drinking problem and want help. The next morning, they are selected for random testing. What to do: If your policy protects self-referral before selection, honor it: refer the employee to the EAP and follow the selfreferral terms. The random test still happens; how a result is handled depends on what your policy says about selfreferral. Lesson: Write the self-referral rule clearly, and apply it exactly as written. SECTION 19.11 Scenario 11: A dispensing cabinet pattern Pharmacy analytics show a night-shift nurse pulls three times more hydromorphone than peers, with frequent late waste witnessed by the same colleague. A coworker reports she seems drowsy late in her shifts.

heading: SECTION 19.7
body: What to do: Under your diversion procedure, review the records, remove the nurse from medication access, and test for cause promptly with an expanded panel. Interview with HR and pharmacy using the data. Assess patients for uncontrolled pain, and bring in counsel on DEA and board reporting. Lesson: Data plus behavior supports action; testing is one part of a diversion investigation. Chapter 19: Case Scenarios © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Healthcare Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 90 of 108

heading: SECTION 19.12
body: SECTION 19.12 Scenario 12: The surgeon and the odor of alcohol Before a scheduled case, an operating room nurse smells alcohol on a privileged surgeon who is not your employee. What to do: Stop the surgeon from operating and notify the chief of staff or department chair under the medical staff bylaws, which govern testing and evaluation of privileged practitioners. HR policy does not apply directly, but patient safety comes first. Lesson: Know which process covers each practitioner before an incident. SECTION 19.13 Scenario 13: A nurse asks for help A nurse tells her manager she is struggling with opioid use and wants help. She has not been selected for testing and there is no investigation. What to do: Follow your self-referral provision: remove her from patient care and medication access pending a fitnessfor-duty evaluation, connect her with the EAP and, as your state allows, the alternative-to-discipline program. Check whether your state requires a board report or allows program referral instead. Lesson: Self-referral should lead to help, with reporting handled as state law requires. SECTION 19.14 Scenario 14: Back to nights too soon A nurse who returned to work six months ago under a monitoring agreement asks to move to nights, where she would have unsupervised narcotic access. What to do: Check the return-to-work agreement and the monitoring program's restrictions. If they limit nights or controlled-substance access, the answer is no until the program lifts the restriction. Lesson: The written agreement and the program decide, not the schedule. SECTION 19.15 Scenario 15: A prescription in the pharmacy A pharmacy technician's test is reported by the MRO as negative because of a valid hydrocodone prescription, with no safety concern noted. What to do: The result is negative. Take no action, and do not ask the technician about the prescription. If you later have specific safety concerns, use the fitness-for-duty process (Chapter 10). Lesson: A verified negative means negative, even in a pharmacy. SECTION 19.16 Scenario 16: The chart lookup An employee is treated in your emergency department for an overdose. Her manager asks HR to pull the ED record to decide whether to discipline her.

heading: SECTION 19.12
body: What to do: Refuse. The ED record is PHI and cannot be used for an employment decision without her written authorization. Address any work issue through the normal fitness-for-duty and policy process, and remind the manager not to access the chart. Lesson: Patient records and employment records must stay separate. heading: APPENDIX
body: APPENDIX Appendix A: Draft Drug and Alcohol Testing Policy This is a starting draft for a non-DOT company program. Replace every item in [brackets], delete options you do not use, and have an employment attorney review it for every state and city where you have employees before you adopt it. DOT-regulated employees need a separate policy that follows 49 CFR Part 40 and the rules of their DOT agency. [COMPANY NAME] Drug and Alcohol Testing Policy Effective date: [DATE] 1. Purpose. [COMPANY NAME] is committed to a safe, healthy and productive workplace. Drug and alcohol use can endanger employees, customers and the public. This policy sets the rules for a drug- and alcohol-free workplace and explains when and how testing will be done. 2. Who is covered. This policy applies to all employees and to applicants who receive a conditional offer of employment [, and to temporary workers and contractors working on company premises]. Employees covered by U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) rules are also subject to the company's separate DOT policy, which controls for DOT testing. 3. Prohibited conduct. While on duty, on company premises, in company vehicles, or while conducting company business, employees may not: • Use, possess, sell, distribute, or be under the influence of illegal drugs or controlled substances not lawfully prescribed to them; • Use or be under the influence of marijuana, regardless of state legality [modify where state law protects off-duty use]; • Use or possess alcohol, or be under the influence of alcohol (an alcohol concentration of [0.04] or higher), except at company-approved events where the employee is not on duty; • Misuse prescription or over-the-counter medications; • Refuse to submit to a test or tamper with a test. 4. Definitions. • Safety-sensitive position: a job in which impairment could cause injury to the employee or others, including [list positions or job categories]. • Reasonable suspicion: a belief, based on specific, current, observable facts about an employee's appearance, behavior, speech or odor, that the employee has violated this policy. • Refusal to test: any conduct listed in Section 9. • Verified positive: a result confirmed by a laboratory and verified by a Medical Review Officer (MRO). 5. When testing will be done. The company will test:

heading: APPENDIX
body: • Pre-employment: all applicants for [all positions / safety-sensitive positions] after a conditional offer of employment. The offer depends on a negative result. • Random: employees in [safety-sensitive positions / all positions], selected by a scientifically valid random method. Each employee in the pool has an equal chance of selection at each draw. Tests are unannounced, and selected employees must report immediately. • Reasonable suspicion: when a trained supervisor has reasonable suspicion, documented on the company's reasonable suspicion checklist and [confirmed by a second supervisor or manager when available]. • Post-accident: after any work-related incident involving [a fatality; an injury requiring medical treatment beyond first aid; property damage over $[AMOUNT]; or a moving traffic citation], for each employee whose actions could have contributed. body: 6. Testing procedures. Tests will be performed by qualified collectors using [urine / oral fluid / hair / breath] specimens under chain-of-custody procedures. The panel tests for [list drugs or panel]. [Rapid on-site screens may be used; every non-negative screen will be confirmed by an [HHS-certified / CAP-FDT-accredited] laboratory.] Every non-negative laboratory result will be reviewed by an MRO, who will give the employee an opportunity to provide a legitimate medical explanation before reporting the result to the company. 7. Prescription medications. Employees do not need to report prescriptions to their supervisor as part of testing. Prescriptions are discussed privately with the MRO. Employees in safety-sensitive positions who take a medication that may affect safe performance should [notify the company's designated health and safety contact], who will handle the matter confidentially and consider reasonable accommodation. 8. Consequences. An applicant with a verified positive result or a refusal will not be hired [and may reapply after [6] months]. An employee with a verified positive result or a refusal will be removed from duty immediately and [will be terminated / may, at the company's discretion, be offered one last chance agreement requiring evaluation, completion of any recommended treatment, a negative return-to-duty test and follow-up testing]. A second violation will result in termination. 9. Refusal to test. Each of the following is a refusal: failing to report for a test as directed without delay; leaving the collection site before the test is complete; failing to provide a sufficient specimen without a valid medical reason; refusing a required observed collection; failing to cooperate with the testing process; and providing an adulterated or substituted specimen. 10. Removal from duty pending results. An employee tested for reasonable suspicion or after an accident [or with a nonnegative rapid screen] will be removed from duty pending results. [Pay status during removal: specify.] An employee whose final result is negative will be returned to work [with back pay for scheduled time missed].

body: 11. Employee assistance. Employees who believe they have a drug or alcohol problem are encouraged to seek help through [EAP NAME AND CONTACT] or their own provider. An employee who asks for help before being selected or notified for a test will not be disciplined for that request, but must follow treatment recommendations and remains responsible for job performance and conduct. 12. Confidentiality. Test results and related records are confidential, kept separate from personnel files, and shared only with those who need to know or as required by law. 13. Employee rights. An employee with a verified positive result may request, within [72 hours] of notice from the MRO, that the split specimen or retained portion be tested at another certified laboratory at [the employee's / the company's] expense. 14. Searches. [Optional, attorney review recommended:] The company may inspect company property, including vehicles, lockers and desks, when it has reasonable suspicion of a violation. 15. Changes to this policy. The company may change this policy at any time with notice to employees, as permitted by law. Nothing in this policy creates a contract of employment or changes at-will status [where applicable]. 16. Questions. Direct questions about this policy to [PROGRAM CONTACT NAME, TITLE, PHONE, EMAIL]. Healthcare provisions (add to the policy above) Safety-sensitive positions. Positions involving direct patient care or access to controlled substances are safety-sensitive and are listed in Attachment 1. Expanded panel. body: BEFORE YOU BEGIN About This Guidebook This guidebook teaches employers how to set up and run a lawful, defensible drug and alcohol testing program. It is written for the people who own the program inside a company: HR managers, personnel managers, safety directors, owners, CEOs and presidents. It is the employer companion to the LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook and the LabbPO Criminal Justice course. Those books teach the people who collect and run tests. Three added chapters cover designing a program for a highturnover workforce, alcohol on the job, and drivers, security and other special roles. Look for Hospitality Note boxes throughout the book. heading: PART I | FOUNDATIONS
body: PART I | FOUNDATIONS Why Employers Test A testing program exists to keep impaired people out of jobs where they can hurt themselves or others, and to give the employer a fair, documented way to act when drug or alcohol use shows up. Done well, it lowers risk. Done badly, it creates new legal risk. 1.1 What the numbers show 1.2 What a program protects against 1.3 What a program cannot do Check your understanding SECTION 1.1 What the numbers show The Quest Diagnostics Drug Testing Index, published every year since 1988, is the most widely cited source on workforce drug use. Its 2026 edition (covering 2025 tests) found: • About 1 in 23 urine tests in the combined U.S. workforce was positive (4.3%), a rate that has stayed above 4% for more than a decade. • Hair tests, which look back about 90 days, were positive 19.1% of the time, up from 13.1% in 2021. • Marijuana remains the main driver of positives across all specimen types. • Healthcare had the highest positivity of any industry, at 5.8%. • Fentanyl positivity in urine roughly halved from 2024 to 2025. The gap between urine (4.3%) and hair (19.1%) is not a contradiction. Each specimen sees a different window of use, which Chapter 4 explains. HOSPITALITY NOTE Quest Diagnostics' industry data have long placed accommodation and food services among the industries with the highest marijuana positivity. Hospitality also has some of the highest turnover and the youngest workforce of any industry, which shapes every decision about who and when to test (Chapter 11). SECTION 1.2 What a program protects against • Accidents and injuries to employees, customers and the public, and the workers' compensation costs that follow. • Negligent hiring and retention claims, where an employer is sued because it knew, or should have known, an employee was unsafe. • Lost productivity: absenteeism, turnover, theft and poor work quality. • Contract and insurance requirements: many customers, government contracts and insurers require a program. • Regulatory penalties for employers covered by Department of Transportation (DOT) or other federal rules. Chapter 1: Why Employers Test © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 7 of 108

heading: SECTION 1.3
body: SECTION 1.3 What a program cannot do A drug test shows that a substance or its metabolite was present above a cutoff. Except for alcohol breath and blood tests, it does not measure impairment at the moment of the test. This matters more every year as states legalize marijuana, and it is why reasonable suspicion training (Chapter 9) and clear policy language (Chapter 14) carry so much weight. Chapter 1: Why Employers Test © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 8 of 108

heading: PART I | FOUNDATIONS
body: PART I | FOUNDATIONS The Legal Landscape No single law governs workplace testing. An employer's rights come from a stack of federal, state and local laws, and the most restrictive layer that applies to you usually decides the question. Check every layer before you test. 2.1 Federal laws that require or shape testing 2.2 State and local laws 2.3 State law quick reference 2.4 Marijuana: the fastest-changing area ** 2.5 Remote, traveling and multistate employees 2.6 Unions and collective bargaining 2.7 FCRA in practice 2.8 Workers' compensation and unemployment 2.9 Practical legal rules for every program Check your understanding SECTION 2.1 Federal laws that require or shape testing L AW W HAT IT MEANS FOR EMPLOYERS Drug-Free Workplace Act of 1988 Applies to federal grantees and many federal contractors. Requires a written policy, an awareness program, and employee notice of drug convictions. It does not require testing. DOT rules (49 CFR Part 40) Mandatory testing for safety-sensitive transportation employees, with procedures set by federal rule. See Chapter 18. Other federal mandates Nuclear (NRC, 10 CFR Part 26) and some Department of Defense contracts carry their own testing requirements. Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Current illegal drug use is not protected, and a drug test is not a "medical exam." But people in recovery and people using lawful prescriptions are protected, and an alcohol test is a medical exam, so it cannot be given to applicants before a conditional job offer. Title VII and other anti-discrimination laws Testing must be applied consistently. Testing one group more than another invites discrimination claims. Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) Eligible employees may take protected leave for substance abuse treatment, though not for the use itself. Chapter 2: The Legal Landscape © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 10 of 108

heading: L AW
body: L AW W HAT IT MEANS FOR EMPLOYERS National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) In a unionized workplace, testing is a mandatory subject of bargaining. You generally cannot start or change a program without bargaining. OSHA (29 CFR 1904.35) You may not use post-accident testing to discourage employees from reporting injuries. Testing to evaluate the cause of an incident is permitted. Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) If a third-party screening company reports results to you, those results can be a "consumer report." FCRA disclosure, authorization and adverse action steps then apply. SECTION 2.2 State and local laws State laws fall into three broad groups, and some states fit more than one: • Restrictive states limit who may be tested and when. Some allow random testing only for safety-sensitive jobs, require reasonable suspicion for current employees, or require a lab confirmation before any action. Minnesota, Vermont, Connecticut, Maine and Rhode Island are commonly cited examples. • Voluntary "drug-free workplace" states offer benefits, such as a workers' compensation premium discount or a defense to injury claims, to employers that follow a defined program. • Silent states have little or no general testing law, leaving most decisions to employer policy. Some states also limit rapid (point-of-care) testing or require specific lab certifications, and some cities add their own rules. New York City, for example, bars most pre-employment marijuana testing. Check state and local law where each employee works, not only where your headquarters is. SECTION 2.3 State law quick reference This table shows examples of states with notable rules. It is not complete, it changes often, and it is not legal advice. Verify every state where you have employees before testing. S TATE N OTABLE RULES (EXAMPLES) California Protects off-duty cannabis use and tests that detect only non-psychoactive metabolites; limits asking about past cannabis use. Random testing generally limited to safety-sensitive jobs. Connecticut Protects off-duty cannabis use for most jobs. Random testing generally limited to safety-sensitive jobs or where federal law requires it. Hawaii Detailed testing procedures. On-site rapid non-negatives must be confirmed by a certified laboratory. Maine Testing policy generally must be filed with the state labor agency. Random testing restricted. Maryland Tests must go to a state-permitted laboratory. On-site rapid testing is limited (commonly cited as pre-employment only).

heading: L AW
body: Minnesota Restrictive testing law: written policy, signed acknowledgment, random testing only for safetysensitive jobs, confirmation by an independent lab. Off-duty cannabis protected; pre-employment cannabis testing limited to listed exceptions. Montana Protects lawful off-duty cannabis use. Restrictive testing law for current employees. Nevada Bars refusing to hire most applicants for a pre-employment marijuana positive. On-site rapid testing is regulated through laboratory licensing. Chapter 2: The Legal Landscape © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 11 of 108

heading: S TATE
body: S TATE N OTABLE RULES (EXAMPLES) New Jersey Allows pre-employment, random, reasonable suspicion and post-accident testing, but bars adverse action based only on a positive cannabis result without documented evidence of impairment (state guidance describes a Workplace Impairment Recognition Expert, or WIRE, evaluation). A recent Appellate Division decision (Sanders) lets applicants sue over offers withdrawn for a positive cannabis test alone. New York Protects lawful off-duty cannabis use. New York City bars most pre-employment marijuana testing. Oregon On-site drug screens require registration with the Oregon Health Authority and lab confirmation before adverse action. Limits on breath alcohol testing. Rhode Island Protects off-duty cannabis use; restrictive testing law. Vermont Most restrictive: random or company-wide testing generally prohibited unless federal law requires it; most testing needs an individualized, documented basis; lab testing required. Washington Bars refusing to hire most applicants for off-duty cannabis use or a test showing non-psychoactive metabolites. Sources for this section include Ogletree, GovDocs, Justia's 50-state survey and DISA's oral fluid law map, current as of fall 2026. SECTION 2.4 Marijuana: the fastest-changing area ** Marijuana is the biggest source of legal risk in a modern program. • State protections. A growing group of states protects lawful off-duty marijuana use or limits pre-employment marijuana testing for most jobs. Commonly cited examples include California, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Minnesota, Montana, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island and Washington. Sources count between 9 and 20 jurisdictions depending on how they define protection, so verify your states directly. • Medical marijuana. More states protect registered medical marijuana patients, typically from discrimination for offduty use, not from discipline for on-duty use or impairment. • Common exceptions. Protections usually exclude DOT-regulated and other federally mandated testing, federal contractors and jobs a state defines as safety-sensitive.

heading: S TATE
body: • What no state protects. Using, possessing or being impaired by marijuana at work. • Hemp-derived THC products. DUE TO TAKE EFFECT. Delta-8 THC, THCA and other hemp-derived THC products are sold widely, including as gummies and drinks, and they cause marijuana positives; a drug test cannot tell them apart from marijuana. A 2025 federal law narrows the definition of hemp in two steps. Hemp products containing synthesized cannabinoids that the plant does not naturally produce lose hemp status on November 12, 2026. On December 11, 2026, hemp products with more than 0.4 mg of total THC per container are due to become federally controlled as marijuana. Congress has already delayed the second step once (from November 12 to December 11, 2026) and may delay it again, and some states have their own limits. Whatever the status of the product, a hemp product is not a legitimate medical explanation for a positive test. • Federal rescheduling. Effective April 28, 2026, a federal order moved FDA-approved marijuana products and statelicensed medical marijuana into Schedule III. All other marijuana remains Schedule I, and a broader rescheduling proceeding is still pending. Non-DOT employers still set their own marijuana rules, subject to state law. DOT rules did not change (Chapter 18). NEW AND DEVELOPING LAW ** Laws in these areas are new and developing. Please confirm any policy decisions regarding these issues that you may include in your program with your attorneys. Chapter 2: The Legal Landscape © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 12 of 108

heading: HOSPITALITY NOTE
body: HOSPITALITY NOTE Major hospitality states have some of the strongest marijuana protections. Nevada, for example, bars refusing to hire most applicants because of a pre-employment marijuana positive, with exceptions that include jobs that, in the employer's determination, could adversely affect the safety of others. California, New York and New Jersey also protect off-duty use. Nevada also gives employees tested within their first 30 days the right to a second test at their own expense, which the employer must accept and consider. Decide by state, and by job, before you test applicants for marijuana. SECTION 2.5 Remote, traveling and multistate employees • Which law applies: generally the law of the state, and city, where the employee actually works, not where the company is headquartered. A remote employee in Minnesota is usually covered by Minnesota's testing law even if your office is in Texas. • Traveling employees who work in several states raise harder questions. Ask counsel which state's law to follow, and consider the most protective one when in doubt. • Applicants are usually governed by the law where the job will be performed. • One policy, state addenda: most multistate employers use one core policy with a state addendum for each state that has special rules. • Testing at a distance: use a TPA or a national collection network so employees can test at a nearby site, schedule electronically with a deadline, and track no-shows. For remote jobs, ask whether testing is needed at all for that role, and what reason you would give. • Post-accident testing for traveling employees needs a plan in advance: which collection network to call, after-hours options, and who arranges it. SECTION 2.6 Unions and collective bargaining In a unionized workplace, the National Labor Relations Board has long treated drug testing of current employees as a mandatory subject of bargaining (Johnson-Bateman Co., 1989). Testing of job applicants generally is not, because applicants are not yet in the bargaining unit (Star Tribune, 1989). In practice: • Bargain before you start or change testing for current union employees, including adding drugs, changing specimens or adding random testing. • Read the contract. Many collective bargaining agreements already set testing rules, discipline standards and grievance steps. The contract controls where it speaks.

heading: HOSPITALITY NOTE
body: • Expect "just cause" review. Arbitrators look at whether the rule was reasonable, known to the employee, applied consistently, and whether the investigation and test were fair. • Weingarten rights. A union employee may ask for a union representative at an investigatory interview that could lead to discipline, such as a reasonable suspicion meeting. Honor the request. You may hold the interview once the representative arrives, or decide not to interview; either way, the request should not push the test past its testing window. Agree on this approach with counsel and the union before it comes up. • Last chance agreements for union employees should be signed by the union as well as the employee. HOSPITALITY NOTE Many hotels and casinos, especially in major markets, are unionized. Testing terms are often set in the collective bargaining agreement, so read it before changing testing or acting on a result, and bargain any changes (Chapter 11). Chapter 2: The Legal Landscape © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 13 of 108

heading: SECTION 2.7
body: SECTION 2.7 FCRA in practice When a third-party screening company, such as a TPA or background screening firm, reports drug test results to you, those results may be a "consumer report." If so, the Fair Credit Reporting Act requires these steps: 1. Disclosure: give the applicant or employee a clear written disclosure that a report may be obtained, in a stand-alone document with nothing else on it. 2. Authorization: get their written permission before ordering the report. 3. Pre-adverse action notice: before acting on the result, give them a copy of the report and the federal Summary of Your Rights Under the FCRA, and wait a reasonable time (commonly five business days) so they can dispute errors. 4. Adverse action notice: after the decision, tell them in writing, including the screening company's contact information and their right to dispute. Whether a result counts as a consumer report depends on who reports it and how. Ask your attorney and your screening vendor how they classify their reports, and build these steps into your process if they apply. Some states add their own requirements. SECTION 2.8 Workers' compensation and unemployment • Drug-free workplace programs. Several states, including Alabama, Florida, Georgia and Ohio, offer workers' compensation premium discounts to employers that follow a state-defined program. The program rules are specific: required tests, notice, training and labs. Follow them exactly to get the benefit. • Intoxication defenses. Many states reduce or deny workers' compensation benefits when an injury was caused by drug or alcohol use. Some create a presumption of causation when an employee tests positive after an accident under a compliant program. A sloppy post-accident test can lose this defense. • Unemployment benefits. Many states deny unemployment benefits to employees fired for a verified positive or a refusal, but only if the employer can prove the policy, the notice and the test. Your paperwork is your proof. SECTION 2.9 Practical legal rules for every program • Put your program in a written policy and give every employee a copy before testing starts. • Get written consent before each test. • Apply the policy the same way to everyone in the same job category.

heading: SECTION 2.7
body: • Confirm every non-negative screen with a laboratory and have a Medical Review Officer (MRO) review it before taking final action. • Keep results confidential and separate from personnel files. • Have an employment attorney review the policy for each state where you have employees, and review it again every year. HOSPITALITY NOTE Hospitality employers often have workers under 18. Check your state's rules on testing minors, including any parental consent requirements, before including them in a program (Chapter 11). Chapter 2: The Legal Landscape © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: PART II | TESTING SCIENCE
body: PART II | TESTING SCIENCE The Drugs A drug test does not look for "drugs" in general. Each test looks for specific target compounds, called analytes, at or above a set concentration, called the cutoff. To run a program, you need to know which drugs your panel covers, what each test actually detects, and what it misses. 3.1 Parent drugs and metabolites 3.2 Opiates vs. opioids: a common gap 3.3 Drug classes, targets, cutoffs and windows 3.4 Expanded and emerging drugs 3.5 Detection windows are estimates Check your understanding SECTION 3.1 Parent drugs and metabolites When a person takes a drug, the body breaks it down into metabolites. Many tests look for a metabolite rather than the drug itself, because metabolites stay in the body longer and prove the drug was taken and processed, not just touched. • Marijuana tests look for THC-COOH, a metabolite of THC, in urine. Oral fluid tests look for THC itself. • Cocaine tests look for benzoylecgonine, a metabolite, in urine. • Heroin breaks down into 6-acetylmorphine (6-AM), then morphine. Only 6-AM proves heroin; morphine alone could come from heroin, a prescription or poppy seeds. SECTION 3.2 Opiates vs. opioids: a common gap "Opiates" are drugs from the poppy plant (morphine, codeine) and drugs made directly from them (heroin). "Opioids" is the wider family that also includes semi-synthetic and synthetic drugs. A standard opiate screen mainly detects morphine and codeine. It does not reliably detect oxycodone, fentanyl, methadone, buprenorphine or tramadol. Each of those needs its own test. Many employers believe they are testing for fentanyl when they are not. SECTION 3.3 Drug classes, targets, cutoffs and windows Cutoffs below are for urine, in ng/mL, and show the screen / confirmation levels typical of non-DOT (private employer) programs. They vary by laboratory and device, so confirm the cutoffs your lab and devices use. Detection windows are typical for occasional use. Chapter 3: The Drugs © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 16 of 108

Many private programs screen codeine and morphine at 300 ng/mL, while DOT screens and confirms them at 2,000 ng/mL, mainly so that poppy seeds do not cause positives. The same specimen can therefore be negative on a DOT test and non-negative on a company test. DOT also does not test for fentanyl. See Chapter 18 (DOT drug panel and cutoffs) for the full DOT table. heading: SECTION 3.4
body: SECTION 3.4 Expanded and emerging drugs Non-DOT employers can add tests for drugs that standard panels miss. Common additions include: • Synthetic cannabinoids (K2, Spice): hundreds of changing compounds; tests catch only some. • Kratom (mitragynine): a plant sold legally in many states with opioid-like effects. • Xylazine and medetomidine: veterinary sedatives mixed into the illicit fentanyl supply. • Nitazenes: synthetic opioids stronger than fentanyl; few rapid tests exist, so lab testing is usually needed. • Ketamine, LSD, psilocybin, gabapentin, carisoprodol and others, chosen based on local trends. • Alcohol biomarkers such as EtG, which shows drinking over the past few days (Chapter 4). Check local drug trend data, your workers' compensation history, and your MRO's advice before adding drugs. Every added drug raises cost and the number of prescription positives the MRO must sort out. SECTION 3.5 Detection windows are estimates How long a drug shows up depends on the dose, how often it is used, body fat (for marijuana), hydration, metabolism and the cutoff. A low cutoff extends the window; a high one shortens it. Never promise an employee, or a court, an exact window. Chapter 3: The Drugs © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 18 of 108

heading: CHAPTER 3 REVIEW
body: CHAPTER 3 REVIEW Check your understanding These are the same questions as in the online course. Choose the best answer. Answers are in Appendix D. Which compound proves heroin use? A Codeine B 6-acetylmorphine (6-AM) C Morphine D Benzoylecgonine, the cocaine metabolite Does a standard opiate screen reliably detect fentanyl or oxycodone? A Yes, opiate screens detect all opioids B Only oxycodone C No, each needs its own test D Only fentanyl What opiate screen cutoff do many private programs use, compared with DOT? A 2,000 ng/mL, exactly the same as DOT's cutoff B 50 ng/mL, versus a DOT cutoff of 15 ng/mL C There is no opiate cutoff in private programs D 300 ng/mL, versus DOT's 2,000 ng/mL What is a cost of adding drugs to a panel? heading: PART II | TESTING SCIENCE
body: PART II | TESTING SCIENCE Specimens The specimen decides what question the test can answer. Oral fluid and breath answer "did this person use recently?" Hair answers "has this person used over the last few months?" Urine sits in between. Choose the specimen to fit the reason for the test, your cheating risk, your budget and your state's law. 4.1 Comparison at a glance 4.2 Urine 4.3 Oral fluid (saliva) 4.4 Hair 4.5 Alcohol testing 4.6 Hair testing and discrimination risk ** Check your understanding SECTION 4.1 Comparison at a glance S PECIMEN Urine Oral fluid Hair W HAT IT T YPICAL WINDOW C OLLECTION C HEATING RISK C OST AND SPEED Past use, 1-3 days for most drugs; Private restroom; Highest: substitution, Low cost; rapid or lab mostly weeks for heavy observed only in dilution, adulterants metabolites marijuana use special cases Recent use, About 24-48 hours Swab in the mouth, S HOWS mostly parent always observed, drug anywhere Pattern of use About 90 days (1.5 inches Small hair sample cut of head hair) near the scalp Low Low to moderate; rapid or lab Low Higher cost; lab only; several days Breath Alcohol now Current Breath into a device Low Low; immediate Blood Drug or Hours Needle draw by Very low High; lab only Low to moderate Moderate; used alcohol trained staff present now Sweat Use while patch worn Days to weeks Patch worn on skin mainly in courts and treatment Nails Pattern of use Several months Clippings Low Lab only; used when hair is unavailable Chapter 4: Specimens © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 4.2
body: SECTION 4.2 Urine Urine is the most common workplace specimen. Drugs and metabolites collect in urine, so it usually detects use for one to three days. Its weakness is privacy: because collections are normally unobserved, urine is the easiest specimen to cheat with synthetic urine, someone else's urine, dilution, or chemicals. Specimen validity checks (Chapter 6) are essential. DOT NOTE DOT drug tests use urine only for now. See Chapter 18 (Drug testing under DOT). SECTION 4.3 Oral fluid (saliva) Oral fluid shows drugs circulating in the body now, so it is the best fit for post-accident and reasonable suspicion tests. Every collection happens in front of the collector, which makes cheating much harder. Its window is shorter, and the person must not eat, drink or put anything in their mouth for about 10 minutes before collection. Some states limit oral fluid testing, so check before you switch. HOSPITALITY NOTE Oral fluid suits hospitality hiring: it can be collected in an HR office with no secured restroom, every collection is observed, and results come quickly. Its short window also fits post-accident and reasonable suspicion tests. SECTION 4.4 Hair Drugs enter hair from the blood as it grows, about half an inch a month. A standard 1.5-inch sample covers about 90 days, which is why hair catches far more users than urine. Hair does not show use from the last 7 to 10 days, because that hair has not grown out yet. Body hair can be used if head hair is too short, but it covers a longer, less precise period. Hair is a strong pre-employment tool; it is weak for post-accident testing. SECTION 4.5 Alcohol testing • Breath devices measure current alcohol concentration. Best practice is to screen with a device on the federal Conforming Products List and confirm any screen at or above your policy threshold on an evidential breath testing device (EBT) operated by a trained technician. • Oral fluid alcohol screening devices are a practical alternative for screening. Confirm any result at or above your threshold on an EBT before acting. • Urine alcohol is not recommended for workplace decisions; it is unreliable for showing current impairment.

heading: SECTION 4.2
body: • EtG and EtS are alcohol metabolites in urine that show drinking in the past several days. They are useful for return-toduty, follow-up and treatment monitoring, not for proving impairment. • PEth is a blood marker showing heavy drinking over the past few weeks. DOT NOTE DOT alcohol testing has its own devices, technician qualifications, thresholds and timing. See Chapter 18 (Alcohol testing under DOT). heading: SECTION 4.6
body: SECTION 4.6 Hair testing and discrimination risk ** Hair testing has been challenged as having a disparate impact on Black employees, because drugs bind more readily to darker, more melanin-rich hair, and hair treatments can also affect results. In Jones v. City of Boston (1st Cir. 2014), the federal appeals court held that Black officers had shown a statistically significant disparate impact from the department's hair testing and sent the case back to decide whether the test was job-related and whether a less discriminatory alternative was available. If you use hair testing: • Be able to explain why hair fits the job and the test reason, such as pre-employment screening for safety-sensitive work. • Use an accredited lab that applies wash procedures and cutoffs designed to reduce outside contamination. • Send every non-negative to an MRO, and consider allowing a confirming urine or oral fluid test when an employee disputes a hair result. • Track results by group where your data allows, so you would see a pattern before a plaintiff does. • Ask your attorney to review hair testing before adopting it, especially for current employees. NEW AND DEVELOPING LAW ** Laws in these areas are new and developing. Please confirm any policy decisions regarding these issues that you may include in your program with your attorneys.
