heading: PART II | TESTING SCIENCE
body: PART II | TESTING SCIENCE How Testing Works Every defensible drug test has two steps: a fast, inexpensive screen that sorts specimens, and a precise confirmation that identifies exactly what is there. Understanding both lets you choose vendors wisely and explain results to employees, managers and lawyers. 5.1 Step 1: The screen (immunoassay) 5.2 Reading a rapid test strip 5.3 Why screens are not final: cross-reactivity 5.4 Step 2: Confirmation (GC-MS and LC-MS/MS) 5.5 Laboratory vs. point-of-care testing 5.6 What a number does and does not mean 5.7 Laboratory credentials to look for Check your understanding SECTION 5.1 Step 1: The screen (immunoassay) Screens use antibodies, proteins built to grab a specific drug shape. In a competitive immunoassay, drug in the specimen competes with a labeled drug for a limited number of antibodies. The more drug in the specimen, the less labeled drug binds, and the test reads that difference. • Laboratory screens run on automated analyzers (EIA, EMIT, CEDIA and similar methods). They are consistent, documented and give a numeric reading against the cutoff. • Rapid or point-of-care (POCT) screens use the same principle on a test strip inside a cup, card or swab. Results appear in minutes. SECTION 5.2 Reading a rapid test strip W HAT YOU SEE W HAT IT MEANS Control line and test line both visible, even faint Negative for that drug Control line visible, no test line Non-negative; send to the lab No control line Invalid; the test did not work; retest with a new device The line logic surprises people: a line means negative, and a missing line means the drug may be present. Faint lines cause most reading errors. Digital readers remove human judgment, read each strip the same way every time, and create an electronic record. Chapter 5: How Testing Works © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 24 of 108

heading: SECTION 5.3
body: SECTION 5.3 Why screens are not final: cross-reactivity Antibodies grab shapes, and some legal medications have similar shapes. This cross-reactivity can cause a screen to show non-negative when the drug is not there. Examples that labs and MROs see: • Some cold medicines, ADHD medications and bupropion can trigger amphetamine screens. • Dextromethorphan (cough syrup) can trigger PCP screens. • Some antidepressants and antipsychotics can trigger benzodiazepine, methadone or tricyclic screens. • Poppy seeds contain real morphine and codeine. At the 300 ng/mL opiate cutoff many private programs use, poppy seeds can cause a non-negative screen and sometimes a confirmed result; the MRO sorts these out. DOT uses a 2,000 ng/mL cutoff largely for this reason (Chapter 18). Screens can also miss drugs, called false negatives, when the drug is below the cutoff, outside the window, not covered by the antibody (many benzodiazepine screens miss clonazepam and lorazepam), or masked by tampering. SECTION 5.4 Step 2: Confirmation (GC-MS and LC-MS/MS) Confirmation tests are done only in a laboratory and are the legal standard of proof. 1. Chromatography separates the specimen into its individual chemicals. In gas chromatography (GC) the sample is vaporized and carried through a column; in liquid chromatography (LC) it is carried by a liquid. Each chemical comes out at a characteristic time. 2. Mass spectrometry (MS) breaks each chemical into charged fragments and weighs them. The pattern of fragments is a molecular fingerprint unique to each drug. M ETHOD N OTES GC-MS The long-time gold standard. Often needs extra preparation steps. LC-MS/MS (tandem mass spectrometry) Now the most common. More sensitive, handles more drugs, including fentanyl and other low-level drugs, with less preparation. Confirmation identifies the exact drug, not just the class, and measures the amount using known reference standards. A confirmed result tells you, for example, that a positive amphetamine screen was actually methamphetamine, or was a prescribed drug the MRO can verify.

heading: DOT NOTE
body: A common, defensible model is rapid screening for speed, with every non-negative sent to an HHS-certified or CAP-FDTaccredited laboratory for confirmation and MRO review. DOT NOTE DOT drug tests must be laboratory tests; rapid drug tests are not allowed. See Chapter 18 (Drug testing under DOT). SECTION 5.6 What a number does and does not mean A confirmed concentration shows the drug was present above the cutoff. It does not show how much was taken, when, or whether the person was impaired. Urine concentration also changes with how much the person drank. Avoid statements like "the level was high, so they were high at work." SECTION 5.7 Laboratory credentials to look for • HHS-certified: certified through SAMHSA's National Laboratory Certification Program (formerly called NIDA-certified). The strongest credential for workplace testing, and required for DOT and federal testing. • CAP Forensic Drug Testing accreditation: a strong credential for non-federal testing. • CLIA certification: the basic federal lab license; required for many clinical tests, but by itself not a forensic credential. heading: PART II | TESTING SCIENCE
body: PART II | TESTING SCIENCE Collection and Chain of Custody Most drug test challenges are won or lost at the collection, not at the lab. A result is only as strong as the paperwork that proves the specimen came from the right person, was not tampered with, and reached the lab sealed. That paperwork is the chain of custody. 6.1 The custody and control form 6.2 A standard urine collection, step by step 6.3 Oral fluid and hair collections 6.4 Specimen validity and problem collections 6.5 Fatal flaws and correctable flaws 6.6 Choosing and auditing collectors 6.7 Cheating and specimen tampering Check your understanding SECTION 6.1 The custody and control form Every forensic test uses a custody and control form, on paper or electronic. It records: • The donor's identity and the reason for the test • The employer, collector, collection site, lab and MRO • A unique specimen ID number that also appears on the specimen seals • Specimen temperature and any problems or remarks • The signatures and dates of every person who handled the specimen Non-DOT tests must use a non-federal custody form. The federal Custody and Control Form (CCF) is reserved for federally regulated tests; never use it for a company test. DOT NOTE DOT tests must use the federal CCF. See Chapter 18 (DOT collection rules). SECTION 6.2 A standard urine collection, step by step 1. Before the donor arrives, secure the restroom: blue dye in the toilet, water sources taped or turned off, no soap or cleaners available. 2. Verify the donor's identity with photo ID. If the donor has no acceptable ID, the employer must identify them. 3. Explain the process. Have the donor remove outer clothing such as coats and hats, and empty their pockets. Chapter 6: Collection and Chain of Custody © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 28 of 108

heading: 4. Have the donor wash and dry their hands.
body: 4. Have the donor wash and dry their hands. 5. Give the donor a sealed collection cup and ask for at least 45 mL (enough for a split specimen). 6. Within 4 minutes, check the temperature. It must be 90-100°F (32-38°C). 7. Inspect for unusual color, odor or foreign objects. 8. In front of the donor, pour into bottles (for split specimens, 30 mL in A and 15 mL in B), seal with tamper-evident labels, and have the donor initial the seals. 9. Complete the form; collector and donor sign and date. 10. Package and ship to the lab, or run the rapid test according to the device instructions. A rapid test collection follows the same identity, security and documentation steps. Record the device name, lot number and expiration date, and keep any image or digital reading. SECTION 6.3 Oral fluid and hair collections • Oral fluid: the collector watches the donor for about 10 minutes with nothing in the mouth, then the donor places the swab as directed until the indicator shows enough sample. The collector seals the device in front of the donor. • Hair: the collector cuts a pencil-thick lock close to the scalp, usually from the back of the head, wraps it with the root end marked, and seals it in a foil and envelope set. SECTION 6.4 Specimen validity and problem collections • Temperature out of range, or signs of tampering, require an immediate second collection under direct observation. Both specimens are sent to the lab. • Directly observed collections are done by a same-sex observer. Best practice is to also observe return-to-duty and follow-up collections, and any collection the MRO directs. • Shy bladder: if the donor cannot provide enough urine, give them a reasonable amount of fluid over a set time; many programs follow the federal model of up to 40 ounces over up to 3 hours. If the donor still cannot provide a specimen, have a physician evaluate whether a medical condition explains it; if not, treat it as a refusal. Where your policy allows, an oral fluid test is a practical alternative.

heading: 4. Have the donor wash and dry their hands.
body: • Refusals at the site: leaving before the collection is finished, refusing to wash hands or empty pockets, or being caught with a cheating device must be documented on the form and reported to the employer. DOT NOTE DOT sets exact rules for observed collections, shy bladder and other problem collections. See Chapter 18 (DOT collection rules). SECTION 6.5 Fatal flaws and correctable flaws Some mistakes destroy a test; others can be fixed with a signed statement from the collector. A sound program treats these as follows: F LAW R ESULT Specimen ID on the bottle does not match the form Fatal; test cancelled Seal broken or missing when the lab receives it Fatal; test cancelled Collector's printed name and signature missing Fatal; test cancelled Chapter 6: Collection and Chain of Custody © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 29 of 108

heading: F LAW
body: F LAW R ESULT Not enough specimen for the lab to test Fatal; test cancelled Collector forgot to sign the certification Correctable with a signed memo These standards come from the federal rules, and every program should hold its collectors to them. A cancelled test protects no one. DOT NOTE DOT's list of fatal and correctable flaws is set by rule. See Chapter 18 (DOT collection rules). SECTION 6.6 Choosing and auditing collectors • Use collectors trained to the federal standard: qualification training, five error-free mock collections, and refresher training every five years. Ask for their training records. • Visit your collection sites, review a sample of completed forms each year, and track how often tests are cancelled for collection errors. DOT NOTE DOT collectors must meet these qualifications by rule. See Chapter 18 (DOT collection rules). SECTION 6.7 Cheating and specimen tampering Cheating products are cheap, easy to buy online and in stores, and marketed directly at people facing drug tests. Anyone running a program, and especially anyone collecting on site, needs to know what they look like.

heading: F LAW
body: M ETHOD H OW IT WORKS H OW TO CATCH IT Synthetic urine Lab-made liquid with urea, creatinine and a Temperature check; secure restroom; watch for normal pH, often sold with a heating pad and a belt heat packs or devices when pockets are emptied; or prosthetic device observed collection when indicated; lab tests that look for markers of real human urine Someone else's urine Clean urine carried in a bottle, condom or device Same as above; observed collection Adulterants Chemicals added to the cup (bleach, nitrite, Lab validity tests; unusual color, odor, foam or chromate, peroxide, glutaraldehyde, soap) to break bubbles; no soap or cleaners in the restroom down drugs or the test Dilution Water from the sink or toilet, or drinking large Blue dye in the toilet, water turned off; lab amounts beforehand creatinine and specific gravity; a dilute result triggers your policy's retest rule Masking products "Detox" drinks and pills sold to hide use Usually just dilution; caught the same way What the lab checks. Specimen validity testing measures creatinine, specific gravity and pH, and screens for oxidizers and other adulterants. HHS-certified labs follow federal criteria for calling a specimen dilute, adulterated, substituted or invalid. Rapid on-site devices check much less, often only temperature, and some cups include basic adulteration strips. That is one reason on-site programs need a secure restroom and strict temperature checks. Chapter 6: Collection and Chain of Custody © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 30 of 108

heading: Signs at the collection: a specimen too cold or too hot, no condensation, an unusual color
body: Signs at the collection: a specimen too cold or too hot, no condensation, an unusual color or no odor, a donor who takes too long or insists on keeping a bag, heat packs or tubing found when emptying pockets, or sounds of a container being opened in the stall. Document what you observe; do not accuse. Oral fluid and hair collections are always observed, so these methods largely remove substitution and adulteration. Employers with a cheating problem often switch some test reasons to oral fluid. State laws. At least 18 states make it a crime to sell, possess or use synthetic urine or products designed to defeat a drug test, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. Examples include Arkansas, Florida, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Texas and Virginia. Your policy should treat tampering as a refusal whether or not your state has such a law. Chapter 6: Collection and Chain of Custody © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: PART III | TESTING IN THE WORKPLACE
body: PART III | TESTING IN THE WORKPLACE Testing On Site With Rapid Tests Many employers can screen employees and applicants at their own workplace with rapid point-of-care (POCT) tests, getting negative results in minutes instead of days. Done right, on-site testing saves time, travel and lost work. Done wrong, it creates legal exposure fast. The rule to remember: an on-site rapid test is only a screen. Every non-negative goes to a laboratory for confirmation and to a Medical Review Officer before any final decision. Employers who choose to act on rapid screens alone should read the rapid-test-only section later in this chapter. 7.1 When on-site testing fits 7.2 The law for on-site testing ** 7.3 Setting up an on-site program 7.4 The on-site collection, step by step 7.5 Reading and talking about results 7.6 Sending a non-negative to the lab 7.7 The MRO's role in an on-site program 7.8 Risks and how to manage them 7.9 If you choose a rapid-test-only program ** 7.10 Alcohol testing on site Check your understanding SECTION 7.1 When on-site testing fits O N-SITE TESTING WORKS WELL WHEN U SE A COLLECTION SITE OR LAB INSTEAD WHEN You hire in volume and need fast negatives The test is a DOT-required drug test Employees work at remote sites far from clinics Your state bans or tightly restricts on-site testing You need post-accident or reasonable suspicion tests at odd You cannot provide a private, secure collection area hours You can train and dedicate reliable collectors No one on staff can collect without a conflict of interest Your policy and state allow acting on lab-confirmed results The result is likely to be disputed in court or arbitration from the only start Many employers use a hybrid: on-site rapid screens for pre-employment and post-accident testing, and a collection site for DOT tests and anything likely to be contested. Chapter 7: Testing On Site With Rapid Tests © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 33 of 108

heading: HOSPITALITY NOTE
body: HOSPITALITY NOTE Large hotels, resorts and casinos that hire in volume are good on-site candidates. Keep collections in a private HR or security office, never in guest areas, and keep line managers out of the collector role. SECTION 7.2 The law for on-site testing ** • DOT: rapid drug tests cannot be used for DOT drug tests, and DOT alcohol tests have their own device and technician rules. See Chapter 18. • State law: some states ban, restrict or license on-site testing. Examples: Oregon requires registration with the state health authority and lab confirmation before adverse action; Hawaii requires lab confirmation of rapid non-negatives; Maryland limits on-site testing; Vermont generally requires lab testing; some states apply laboratory licensing laws to on-site testing. Check the state law table in Chapter 2 and confirm your state before you buy a single device. • CLIA: the federal Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments regulate laboratory testing. Federal rules exempt forensic testing and employment drug testing done by HHS-certified labs, and some state agencies have said employment-only drug screening does not need a CLIA certificate. Others, and many device sellers, advise a CLIA Certificate of Waiver for any on-site testing. A Certificate of Waiver is obtained by filing CMS Form 116 with your state CLIA agency and paying a modest fee every two years. Ask your state CLIA agency in writing; many employers simply get the waiver to be safe. • Device labeling: rapid drug tests are sold under different labels: FDA-cleared (often CLIA-waived), "employment and insurance" (E&I) exempt, or "forensic use only." Some states require FDA-cleared devices. Match the device's intended use to your program and state, and keep the package insert. • Cutoffs: choose devices whose screening cutoffs match your lab's, so a non-negative screen has a fair chance of confirming. • Consent, notice and confidentiality apply exactly as they do for lab testing. On-site testing does not relax any rule in Chapters 2 and 14.

heading: HOSPITALITY NOTE
body: NEW AND DEVELOPING LAW ** Laws in these areas are new and developing. Please confirm any policy decisions regarding these issues that you may include in your program with your attorneys. SECTION 7.3 Setting up an on-site program People • Choose collectors who are reliable, discreet and not the direct supervisor or close coworker of the people they test. Train at least two, plus backups for nights and weekends. • Train every collector on your procedure and the device instructions, have them complete practice collections, and keep written proof of training and competency. • Use a same-sex observer for any observed collection. Place • A private, single-occupancy restroom you can secure: blue dye in the toilet, water turned off or taped, no soap or cleaners, nothing to hide a specimen in. • A clean, private table area for reading devices and completing forms, out of view of coworkers. • For oral fluid, any private space works. Chapter 7: Testing On Site With Rapid Tests © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 34 of 108

heading: Supplies
body: Supplies • Rapid devices (urine cups or oral fluid swabs) with temperature strips, gloves, tamper-evident seals, lab specimen bottles or kits, non-federal custody forms, lab shipping supplies, and a locked storage cabinet. • Store devices as the package insert directs (temperature, humidity), track lot numbers and expiration dates, and never use an expired device. Paperwork and partners • A written standard operating procedure that follows the device insert and your policy. • An account with a confirming laboratory and an MRO before the first test, with shipping or courier arranged. • A confidential on-site testing log (Form B-8 in Appendix B). SECTION 7.4 The on-site collection, step by step 1. Confirm the reason for the test and that the donor received your policy and signed consent (Form B-2). 2. Verify identity with photo ID. 3. Have the donor remove outer clothing and empty pockets, then wash and dry their hands. 4. Check the device: correct panel, sealed pouch, not expired. Record the lot number. 5. Give the donor the sealed cup; ask for enough urine to fill to the line (enough for lab confirmation). 6. Read the temperature strip within 4 minutes. Out of range (outside 90-100°F) means an immediate second collection under direct observation. 7. Keep the specimen in view of the donor at all times. 8. Start the test as the insert directs and read it at the time the insert specifies, not earlier and not later. Late readings can change. 9. Record every drug's result, the device, lot, time and collector, and capture an image or digital reading if you have one. 10. Have the donor initial and sign where your form requires. For oral fluid: watch the donor for about 10 minutes with nothing in the mouth, have them place the swab as directed until the indicator shows enough sample, then run and read the device the same way. SECTION 7.5 Reading and talking about results • A visible test line, even a faint one, means negative for that drug. No test line means non-negative. No control line means invalid: retest with a new device.

heading: Supplies
body: • Never call a rapid result "positive." Say: "This screen needs laboratory confirmation. Nothing is final until a doctor reviews the lab result." • Do not ask the donor what they took or what medications they use. That conversation belongs to the MRO. • Record the result only in the confidential log, never in a personnel file or email to a supervisor. SECTION 7.6 Sending a non-negative to the lab 1. Tell the donor the specimen will go to a laboratory for confirmation. 2. Prepare the specimen for the lab exactly as your lab instructs: some labs accept the sealed device, others require pouring into lab bottles. Do it in front of the donor. 3. Seal with tamper-evident labels and have the donor initial the seals. 4. Complete the lab's non-federal custody form, including the specimen ID number on both the form and the seals. 5. Package and ship the same day, or store securely as the lab directs until pickup. Chapter 7: Testing On Site With Rapid Tests © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 35 of 108

heading: SECTION 7.7
body: 6. If your policy and state law allow, remove a safety-sensitive employee from duty pending results. Take no final action. 7. Wait for the MRO's verified result. SECTION 7.7 The MRO's role in an on-site program The laboratory reports confirmed non-negative results to the MRO, not to you. The MRO reviews the chain of custody and lab report, interviews the donor about legitimate medical explanations, and only then reports a verified result to your program owner. Without an MRO, an employer would have to judge prescriptions and medical explanations itself, which creates ADA and privacy risk and weakens every result in a dispute. Some employers also have the MRO review on-site negatives for program oversight; ask your MRO what they recommend. SECTION 7.8 Risks and how to manage them R ISK H OW TO MANAGE IT Acting on an unconfirmed screen Written rule: no final action until MRO verification Reading errors, especially faint lines Train collectors, read at the exact time, use a digital reader Collector bias or conflicts Collectors do not test people they supervise or work closely with Privacy breaches Private collection area, confidential log, need-to-know only Cheating with substituted or adulterated urine Secure restroom, temperature check, observed recollection when indicated, or switch to oral fluid State law violations Confirm your state's on-site rules before buying devices Expired or mishandled devices Storage rules, lot and expiration tracking Broken chain of custody to the lab Seal in front of the donor, matching specimen IDs, same-day shipping SECTION 7.9 If you choose a rapid-test-only program ** This guidebook recommends lab confirmation and MRO review for every non-negative screen. Some employers, usually to save cost or time, act on rapid screens alone, most often for applicants. If you make that choice, understand what you give up and reduce the risk where you can. What you give up: • Defensibility. A rapid screen identifies a drug class, not the drug. Without confirmation you cannot rule out crossreactivity, and false positives are where most drug testing lawsuits come from.

heading: SECTION 7.7
body: • The medical explanation. Without an MRO, no one can verify a prescription privately. Asking the person yourself creates ADA and privacy risk. • State law compliance. Several states require lab confirmation before adverse action, and some restrict on-site testing altogether (Chapter 2). In those states a rapid-test-only program is not an option. • Legal protections. Drug-free workplace premium discounts, workers' compensation defenses and unemployment benefit denials usually depend on confirmed results. How to reduce the risk: • Use rapid-only results only where your state allows it, and generally only for pre-employment decisions, not for discipline or termination of current employees. • Use FDA-cleared devices with cutoffs at or below your lab's, and a digital reader that records the result. heading: • Before any decision, give the person a private chance to disclose prescriptions, ideally
body: • Before any decision, give the person a private chance to disclose prescriptions, ideally to a contracted MRO or other physician who reviews the screen, not to HR. • Offer lab confirmation on request. Keep the specimen sealed and stored so it can be sent to a lab if the person disputes the result. • Consider a second screen with a different device or method before acting. It raises confidence, but it is not a confirmation and should not be called one. • Write the rapid-test-only approach, its limits and the person's right to request confirmation into your policy, and apply it the same way every time. • Use full lab confirmation and MRO review for any current employee, any safety-sensitive decision, and any result likely to be disputed. NEW AND DEVELOPING LAW ** Laws in these areas are new and developing. Please confirm any policy decisions regarding these issues that you may include in your program with your attorneys. SECTION 7.10 Alcohol testing on site • Breath alcohol devices give immediate results. For non-DOT programs, use devices that meet your state's rules, and confirm any screen at or above your policy threshold on an evidential breath testing device if you will act on it. • Oral fluid alcohol screening devices are another option for screening. • Some states limit employer breath testing (Oregon, for example, requires consent or reasonable grounds). Check yours. DOT NOTE DOT alcohol tests require DOT-approved devices and qualified technicians. See Chapter 18 (Alcohol testing under DOT). heading: PART III | TESTING IN THE WORKPLACE
body: PART III | TESTING IN THE WORKPLACE Types of Testing Your policy must say exactly when testing happens. Each reason for testing has its own purpose, legal risks and procedures, and the most common mistakes happen in reasonable suspicion and post-accident testing. 8.1 Pre-employment 8.2 Random 8.3 Reasonable suspicion (for cause) 8.4 Post-accident 8.5 Return-to-duty and follow-up 8.6 Other reasons 8.7 Applicants and edge cases Check your understanding SECTION 8.1 Pre-employment Purpose: keep drug users from being hired. • Test every applicant for the same job category, never selected individuals. • Test after a conditional job offer. This is required for alcohol tests under the ADA, and it simplifies prescription questions, which should go to the MRO, not to HR. • State the offer is contingent on a negative result, and do not let the person start safety-sensitive work before the result. • Check state and local marijuana rules before testing applicants for marijuana (Chapter 2). HOSPITALITY NOTE Many hospitality employers have dropped pre-employment testing for most front-of-house and back-of-house jobs to keep hiring moving. If you do, keep it for safety-sensitive roles and keep reasonable suspicion and postaccident testing for everyone (Chapter 11). SECTION 8.2 Random Purpose: deterrence. Random testing is the strongest deterrent because employees cannot plan around it. • Use a scientifically valid method, usually a computer program run by a third party, so every person in the pool has an equal chance at every draw. • Spread tests through the year, on different days and shifts, and keep them unannounced. • Send selected employees for testing immediately once notified. Chapter 8: Types of Testing © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 39 of 108

heading: DOT NOTE
body: • A person may be picked more than once, or not at all, in a year. That is how true random selection works. • Some states allow random testing only for safety-sensitive jobs. Define who is in the pool in your policy. DOT NOTE DOT sets minimum yearly random testing rates. See Chapter 18 (2026 minimum random testing rates). SECTION 8.3 Reasonable suspicion (for cause) Purpose: remove and test an employee who shows signs of use or impairment now. You may see this called "probable cause." Probable cause is a criminal law standard for police. In employment, the standard is reasonable suspicion: specific, current, observable facts that a trained supervisor can describe. • Base the decision on what you see, hear and smell now: speech, balance, behavior, odor, appearance, or direct evidence of use or possession. Do not rely on rumor, past history or a hunch. • Have a trained supervisor make the call, ideally confirmed by a second person. • Write it down before the test, using the checklist in Appendix B (Form B-3). • Never let the employee drive to the collection site. Arrange transport. • Remove the employee from duty pending results. DOT NOTE DOT requires trained supervisors and sets time limits for reasonable suspicion tests. See Chapter 18 (Required tests). SECTION 8.4 Post-accident Purpose: determine whether drugs or alcohol may have contributed to an incident. • Define in the policy exactly which events trigger a test, such as a fatality, an injury needing medical treatment beyond first aid, property damage over a set dollar amount, or a citation. • Test the employees whose actions could have contributed, not everyone who reports an injury. OSHA prohibits using post-accident testing to discourage injury reporting. • Test fast. Best practice is an alcohol test within 2 hours and no later than 8, and a drug specimen within 32 hours. Record the reason for any delay on the post-accident decision record. • Medical care for the injured always comes first.

heading: DOT NOTE
body: • Use the post-accident decision record (Form B-4). DOT NOTE DOT defines which accidents require testing and sets firm deadlines. See Chapter 18 (Required tests). HOSPITALITY NOTE Common hospitality incidents include shuttle and valet crashes, kitchen burns and cuts, falls in engineering work and guest injuries involving staff. Test the employees whose actions could have contributed, never automatically after every employee injury report. Chapter 8: Types of Testing © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 40 of 108

heading: SECTION 8.5
body: SECTION 8.5 Return-to-duty and follow-up Purpose: confirm an employee who violated the policy is clean before returning, then keep confirming. • Return-to-duty: a negative test required before the employee goes back to work, after any required evaluation or treatment. • Follow-up: unannounced tests for a set period after return, commonly at least six in the first 12 months, over 12 to 24 months. Best practice is to observe these collections directly. • Put the terms in a written last chance or return-to-work agreement (Form B-7). DOT NOTE DOT's return-to-duty and follow-up rules, including the SAP process, are set by rule. See Chapter 18 (Violations and the SAP process). SECTION 8.6 Other reasons • Periodic or annual: scheduled tests, often with a physical. Weak deterrent because they are announced. • Blanket or company-wide: testing everyone at once, such as when a program starts. Check state law first. SECTION 8.7 Applicants and edge cases • Deadlines: give applicants a firm, written deadline to test, commonly 24 to 48 hours after the conditional offer, and say that missing it will be treated as withdrawing from the process or as a refusal. A long gap lets a drug clear the system. • No-shows: decide in advance whether a no-show is a refusal or a withdrawn application, apply the rule consistently, and document the deadline you gave. • Dilute or invalid results: say in the policy whether an applicant gets one recollection, and whether it will be observed. • Minors: check your state's rules before testing employees under 18; some states add consent or notice requirements, and federal child labor rules already bar minors from many hazardous, safety-sensitive jobs. • Language and literacy: give the policy, notices and consent forms in a language each employee can read, or explain them and document that you did. A consent the employee could not understand is weak evidence. • Disability accommodations at collection: an applicant who cannot provide urine for a medical reason, or needs help, should be offered another specimen type or an accommodation, not treated as a refusal. heading: PART III | TESTING IN THE WORKPLACE
body: PART III | TESTING IN THE WORKPLACE Recognizing Signs of Drug and Alcohol Use Reasonable suspicion testing depends on what a supervisor sees, hears and smells. Supervisors are not expected to diagnose anyone or name the drug. They are expected to notice specific, current signs, describe them accurately, and follow the policy. This chapter gives them the vocabulary. 9.1 Two kinds of signs 9.2 Signs by drug type 9.3 Medical emergencies come first 9.4 What to document 9.5 What not to do 9.6 Impairment and performance tests ** Check your understanding SECTION 9.1 Two kinds of signs • Acute signs happen now: slurred speech, stumbling, odor, pinpoint pupils, nodding off. These support a reasonable suspicion test today. • Pattern signs build over time: lateness, absences, missed deadlines, mood changes, accidents, money problems. On their own, they do not support a test today. They support a performance conversation and an EAP referral, and they help a supervisor know what to watch for. Many signs have innocent causes: illness, diabetes, fatigue, medication, stress or a disability. That is why the decision rests on documented observations, a second observer when possible, and a test, not on a supervisor's conclusion. HOSPITALITY NOTE In bars, restaurants and banquet areas, the smell of alcohol on clothing can come from spills and service. Do not rely on odor alone; look for other specific signs such as slurred speech, poor balance or service errors before making a reasonable suspicion referral (Chapter 12). Call 911 immediately if a person is unresponsive, has slow or stopped breathing, blue lips or fingertips (signs of an opioid overdose), a seizure, chest pain, or extreme agitation. Many employers keep naloxone (Narcan) on site and train staff to use it. Testing waits until the person is safe. SECTION 9.4 What to document • The date, time and place of each observation. • Exactly what you saw, heard and smelled, in plain words: "slurred speech when answering questions," not "he was high." • How long it lasted and who else observed it. • What the employee said, word for word if possible. • Any direct evidence, such as drugs or alcohol seen. Use the reasonable suspicion checklist (Form B-3) and complete it before the test. SECTION 9.5 What not to do • Do not accuse, diagnose or guess the drug.

body: • Do not argue, threaten or physically restrain the employee. • Do not search the employee's person or belongings unless your policy allows it and law enforcement is not a better choice. heading: SECTION 9.6
body: • Do not let the employee drive, return to safety-sensitive work, or leave alone. • Do not discuss the situation with coworkers. • Do not delay. Signs fade, and the test window closes. SECTION 9.6 Impairment and performance tests ** Because a marijuana test shows past use rather than impairment, employers in states that protect off-duty use are asking about tools that try to measure impairment directly: tablet-based reaction and attention tests, eye-tracking devices, and balance or coordination tasks. • What they can do: flag a worker who is performing below their own baseline right now, from any cause, including fatigue, illness, medication or drugs. • What they cannot do: identify which substance is involved, or prove legal impairment. Most have limited independent validation for marijuana. • How to use them: as a supplement to trained supervisor observation and, where allowed, testing, not as a replacement. A low score supports a fitness-for-duty conversation and possibly a reasonable suspicion test. • Watch the law: some states, such as New Jersey, have created or proposed formal impairment-recognition roles for workplaces. Check your state's current rules, and treat these tools as medical-type information under the ADA. NEW AND DEVELOPING LAW ** Laws in these areas are new and developing. Please confirm any policy decisions regarding these issues that you may include in your program with your attorneys. heading: PART III | TESTING IN THE WORKPLACE
body: PART III | TESTING IN THE WORKPLACE Handling Results The result you receive should already be MRO-verified, and your response should already be written in your policy. Decide consequences in advance, apply them the same way every time, and document every step. 10.1 The MRO process, step by step 10.2 Result types and what to do 10.3 Refusals to test 10.4 Prescriptions and the ADA 10.5 Prescriptions in safety-sensitive jobs: the ADA interactive process 10.6 Employees in medication-assisted treatment (MAT) ** 10.7 Giving employees a fair process 10.8 Licensed professionals and reporting duties Check your understanding SECTION 10.1 The MRO process, step by step What happens between the laboratory result and your phone call: 1. The lab reports to the MRO, not to you, along with the custody form. This includes positives, adulterated, substituted and invalid results. 2. The MRO reviews the paperwork for collection and lab errors. A fatal flaw cancels the test. 3. The MRO contacts the donor privately. If the MRO cannot reach them, the MRO may ask the employer's program contact to tell the employee, without giving any detail, to call the MRO. Your policy should give the employee a short deadline to call, commonly 72 hours. 4. The interview. The MRO confirms identity, explains the result, and asks whether there is a legitimate medical explanation, such as a prescription. The MRO verifies it with the pharmacy or prescriber. 5. The decision. Verified negative, verified positive, refusal (for adulterated or substituted specimens), cancelled, or negative with a safety concern. 6. The report. The MRO reports only the verified result to your program contact. Medical details stay with the MRO, except information needed to address a safety concern. 7. Split specimen window. The employee may ask the MRO to test the split specimen at another lab (commonly within 72 hours). If the employee refuses to talk to the MRO, or cannot be reached after reasonable efforts within the time the rules allow, the MRO may verify the result without an interview. Your policy should tell employees to keep their phone numbers current for this reason. Chapter 10: Handling Results © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 47 of 108

heading: DOT NOTE
body: DOT NOTE DOT sets the MRO's contact rules, deadlines and split specimen procedures. See Chapter 18 (DOT results, MRO and refusals). SECTION 10.2 Result types and what to do R ESULT W HAT IT MEANS E MPLOYER ACTION Negative No drugs found above cutoffs No action. File the result confidentially. Negative-dilute Negative, but the urine was watered down Follow your policy. Best practice is an immediate recollection, directly observed when the MRO reports very low creatinine. Non-negative (rapid Preliminary only screen) Send to the lab. Take no final action. Safetysensitive employees may be removed from duty pending results if the policy says so. Verified positive Lab-confirmed and MRO-verified, with no Apply the policy consequence: removal from legitimate medical explanation duty, then termination, last chance agreement or referral to treatment. Adulterated or The specimen was tampered with or is not substituted human urine Invalid The lab cannot get a valid result Treated as a refusal to test. The MRO decides the next step, usually a recollection, sometimes observed. Cancelled A procedural or lab problem voided the test Treat as neither positive nor negative. Retest only if required. Negative, safety concern The MRO verified negative due to a prescription Follow up through a fitness-for-duty evaluation, but believes the drug may make the person not discipline. unsafe DOT NOTE DOT sets exact rules for dilute, invalid and cancelled results. See Chapter 18 (DOT results, MRO and refusals). SECTION 10.3 Refusals to test A refusal is treated the same as a verified positive. Common refusals include failing to report for testing in a reasonable time, leaving before the test is finished, failing to give enough specimen without a valid medical reason, refusing an observed collection when required, and tampering. Spell out your own list of refusals in your policy. DOT NOTE DOT's list of refusals is set by rule and is longer. See Chapter 18 (DOT results, MRO and refusals). heading: SECTION 10.4
body: SECTION 10.4 Prescriptions and the ADA • Do not ask applicants or employees to list their medications as part of testing. Let the MRO handle prescription questions privately. • A lawfully prescribed medication taken as directed is a legitimate explanation, and the MRO will report the test as negative. • If a prescribed drug may make someone unsafe in a safety-sensitive job, handle it as a fitness-for-duty and reasonable accommodation question under the ADA, not as a policy violation. • Marijuana is different: under most non-DOT policies a medical marijuana card is not a legitimate medical explanation, but some states protect registered patients' off-duty use. Check state medical marijuana protections. DOT never accepts it (Chapter 18). SECTION 10.5 Prescriptions in safety-sensitive jobs: the ADA interactive process When a lawfully prescribed medication may make an employee unsafe, the ADA requires an individualized, good-faith process, not a blanket rule. 1. Start confidentially. The trigger is usually an MRO safety concern or an employee's own request. Only the people who need to know are involved. 2. Get medical facts, not guesses. With the employee's written release, ask the treating provider whether the employee can safely perform the essential functions of the job on this medication, and with what limits. 3. Consider accommodations, such as temporary reassignment to non-safety-sensitive work, schedule changes, leave, or time for the provider to adjust the medication. 4. Apply the "direct threat" standard before excluding anyone: a significant risk of substantial harm, based on objective medical evidence about this person, that cannot be reduced by reasonable accommodation. 5. Document each step and the reasons for the decision. 6. Keep medical information separate from the personnel file. Avoid rules such as "no one on opioids may work here." Blanket medication bans invite ADA claims. Post-offer, employers may ask applicants for a job category about medications only if they ask everyone in that category; for current employees, questions must be job-related and consistent with business necessity. Involve your attorney early.

heading: SECTION 10.4
body: SECTION 10.6 Employees in medication-assisted treatment (MAT) ** Medication-assisted treatment uses buprenorphine (Suboxone, Sublocade), methadone or naltrexone (Vivitrol), with counseling, to treat opioid use disorder. As more employers add buprenorphine and methadone to their panels, program owners will see these results, and handling them wrong is one of the clearest legal risks in testing today. The EEOC's 2020 guidance on opioids and the ADA (Use of Codeine, Oxycodone, and Other Opioids: Information for Employees) makes these points: • Opioid use disorder can be an ADA disability. People in recovery who are not currently using illegal drugs are protected. • MAT taken as prescribed is lawful use. An employer generally cannot refuse to hire or fire someone just because they are in a MAT program, unless they cannot do the job safely and effectively or federal law disqualifies them. • Testing: an employee should have the chance to explain lawful use that causes a result. In a properly run program, the MRO does this and reports the result as negative. • Safety concerns require an individualized assessment and the interactive process (above), not a blanket rule. • Accommodations may include schedule changes or time off for treatment, counseling or support meetings, or leave for treatment. Chapter 10: Handling Results © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 49 of 108

heading: In practice:
body: • What employers never have to do: excuse current illegal drug use, lower performance standards, or remove essential job functions. In practice: • Never write a policy that bans everyone on MAT, or everyone taking buprenorphine or methadone. • Let the MRO handle the medical explanation; do not ask employees whether they are in treatment. • If the MRO reports a safety concern, use the interactive process with the treating provider. • Train HR and supervisors that a verified negative means negative, whatever medication caused the screen. • DOT-regulated jobs have their own medical qualification rules; an MRO's DOT safety concern follows those rules (Chapter 18). NEW AND DEVELOPING LAW ** Laws in these areas are new and developing. Please confirm any policy decisions regarding these issues that you may include in your program with your attorneys. SECTION 10.7 Giving employees a fair process • Tell the employee the result privately, in writing (Form B-6 is a notice template). • Explain the right to have the split specimen or a retained portion tested at a second lab. Best practice is to offer it in your policy. • If you used a third-party screening company, follow FCRA adverse action steps before final action. • Keep everything confidential and limited to those who need to know. SECTION 10.8 Licensed professionals and reporting duties Some employees hold licenses that bring their own rules. Healthcare employers, for example, may have duties to report a nurse, pharmacist or physician's diversion or impairment to a state licensing board, and many boards run confidential peer assistance or alternative-to-discipline programs. Commercial drivers have FMCSA Clearinghouse reporting (Chapter 18). If your employees hold licenses, ask your attorney what reporting your state and their board require, and write it into your policy so the duty is known before it arises. Chapter 10: Handling Results © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 50 of 108

heading: CHAPTER 10 REVIEW
body: CHAPTER 10 REVIEW Check your understanding These are the same questions as in the online course. Choose the best answer. Answers are in Appendix D. heading: PART IV | HOSPITALITY FOCUS
body: PART IV | HOSPITALITY FOCUS Designing a Program for a Hospitality Workforce Hospitality employers face a combination few other industries do: high turnover, many part-time and seasonal workers, young employees, multilingual teams, franchise and management-company structures, and a workforce with high marijuana positivity in states that increasingly protect off-duty use. A program built for a factory or a trucking company does not fit. This chapter covers how to design one that does. 11.1 Decide where testing matters 11.2 Choosing your testing reasons 11.3 Turnover, part-time and seasonal staff 11.4 Workers under 18 ** 11.5 Franchises, management companies and brands ** 11.6 Unions 11.7 Second-chance and recovery-friendly hiring Check your understanding SECTION 11.1 Decide where testing matters Start with risk, not habit. Most hospitality programs focus on these roles: R OLE U SUALLY SAFETY-SENSITIVE? W HY Shuttle, van and courtesy drivers Yes Guests on public roads; some are DOT-covered (Chapter 13) Valet attendants Yes Drive guest vehicles Engineering and maintenance Yes Boilers, electrical, chemicals, work at height Security officers Yes Use of force, emergencies; may be state-licensed or armed Lifeguards and pool staff Yes Guest lives; pool chemicals Childcare and kids' club staff Yes Responsible for children Cooks and kitchen staff Often Knives, slicers, fryers and burns; decide by duties Bartenders and servers Depends Alcohol service duties and laws (Chapter 12) Housekeeping, front desk, reservations Usually no Unless duties include the work above Chapter 11: Designing a Program for a Hospitality Workforce © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 52 of 108

heading: R OLE
body: R OLE U SUALLY SAFETY-SENSITIVE? W HY Casino gaming employees Depends Gaming regulators may set their own requirements Write your list into the policy (Attachment 1) before relying on it, especially in states that protect off-duty marijuana use or allow random testing only for safety-sensitive jobs. NEW AND DEVELOPING LAW ** Laws in these areas are new and developing. Please confirm any policy decisions regarding these issues that you may include in your program with your attorneys. SECTION 11.2 Choosing your testing reasons • Pre-employment: keep it for safety-sensitive roles. Many employers drop it for other roles, or drop marijuana from it, to keep hiring moving. • Reasonable suspicion and post-accident: keep for every employee. These are the most defensible tests and protect guests. • Random: usually limited to safety-sensitive roles. • Return-to-duty and follow-up: use with last chance agreements to keep experienced staff. SECTION 11.3 Turnover, part-time and seasonal staff • Use fast methods for pre-employment testing, such as on-site oral fluid with lab confirmation of non-negatives, and give firm deadlines after conditional offers. • Apply the same rules to seasonal and year-round employees in the same job. • Keep your random pool current; remove departed employees and add new hires each selection period. • Train supervisors at every location and on every shift, including new supervisors promoted from the line. SECTION 11.4 Workers under 18 ** • Check state law before testing minors; some states add consent or notice requirements, including parental consent. • Federal child labor rules already bar workers under 18 from many hazardous jobs, such as operating power-driven meat slicers and many driving jobs, so minors are kept out of many safety-sensitive jobs, though not all; lifeguards, for example, are often under 18. • Never file a minor's result in the general personnel file, and limit who sees it even more strictly than for adults. LAWS VARY BY STATE ** This section states the general rule. Rules vary by state; check with your attorneys if you have any questions about the specific rules in your state.

heading: R OLE
body: SECTION 11.5 Franchises, management companies and brands ** In many hotels the brand (franchisor), the owner, the management company and the operator are different companies. The testing program belongs to the employer of record. Keep the brand out of individual testing decisions and results: a franchisor that controls hiring, discipline or testing of a franchisee's workers increases joint-employer risk. Brands may set standards and receive certifications or aggregate data, not individual results. body: LAWS VARY BY STATE ** This section states the general rule. Rules vary by state; check with your attorneys if you have any questions about the specific rules in your state. SECTION 11.6 Unions Many hotels, casinos and food service operations are unionized, and testing terms are often set in the collective bargaining agreement. Bargain before changing testing, follow the contract's procedures exactly, and have the union sign last chance agreements. SECTION 11.7 Second-chance and recovery-friendly hiring Hospitality depends on people who may have struggled in the past. Last chance agreements, EAP access and recoveryfriendly policies help keep good employees, as long as they are offered consistently and safety-sensitive standards stay intact. heading: PART IV | HOSPITALITY FOCUS
body: PART IV | HOSPITALITY FOCUS Alcohol on the Job: Service, Tasting and Events In hospitality, alcohol is part of the job. Bartenders pour it, servers sell it, sommeliers taste it, and employees attend events where it flows. Your policy has to separate serving alcohol from drinking it, and handle reasonable suspicion in places that smell of alcohol all day. 12.1 On-duty drinking rules 12.2 Company events 12.3 Responsible beverage service and dram shop exposure 12.4 Reasonable suspicion around alcohol 12.5 THC drinks and edibles ** 12.6 Casinos Check your understanding SECTION 12.1 On-duty drinking rules • Prohibit drinking alcohol while on duty, including on breaks, except for written exceptions. • Allow tasting only where the job requires it (for example, a sommelier or a manager approving a new cocktail), in small amounts, with spitting where practical, and never for employees who drive or perform other safety-sensitive work that shift. • Set a rule for drinking at your own outlets after a shift: many employers ban it in uniform or for a set time after clocking out. • Set an alcohol threshold for violations, such as 0.04, and require removal from duty at a lower level, such as 0.02. SECTION 12.2 Company events Holiday parties and staff events can create liability. Limit drinks, provide food and transportation, keep alcohol away from employees under the legal drinking age, and remind supervisors that the policy and reasonable suspicion procedures still apply to employees who are scheduled to work. SECTION 12.3 Responsible beverage service and dram shop exposure Many states have dram shop laws that make a business liable for harm caused by guests it over-served, and some require responsible beverage service training for servers and bartenders. An impaired bartender is more likely to overserve. Keep your service training records with your policy records, and treat an impaired server as both a policy violation and a liability risk. Chapter 12: Alcohol on the Job: Service, Tasting and Events © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 12.4
body: SECTION 12.4 Reasonable suspicion around alcohol • Do not rely on odor alone in bars, restaurants and banquet areas; spills and service put alcohol on clothing. • Look for specific signs: slurred speech, poor balance, glassy eyes, service errors, incorrect cash handling, and behavior changes. • Have a second manager observe when possible, and document on the reasonable suspicion checklist (Form B-3). • Use an on-site breath screen with confirmation on an evidential device if you will act on the result (Chapter 7). SECTION 12.5 THC drinks and edibles ** Many bars, restaurants and venues now sell hemp-derived THC drinks or edibles, and some employees will sample them. These products cause marijuana positives. Treat them like alcohol in your policy: no use on duty, and no tasting unless approved in writing. Federal limits on hemp-derived THC products are DUE TO TAKE EFFECT on December 11, 2026, which may change what your venues can sell (Chapter 2). LAWS VARY BY STATE ** This section states the general rule. Rules vary by state; check with your attorneys if you have any questions about the specific rules in your state. SECTION 12.6 Casinos Gaming employees may need licenses from state gaming regulators or tribal gaming commissions, which can impose their own background and testing requirements. Check your regulator's rules and make sure your policy meets them; regulators may also require reporting of certain violations. Chapter 12: Alcohol on the Job: Service, Tasting and Events © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: PART IV | HOSPITALITY FOCUS
body: PART IV | HOSPITALITY FOCUS Drivers, Security and Other Special Roles A few hospitality roles carry most of the safety risk. This chapter covers drivers, including the DOT trap many hotels miss, and other special roles. 13.1 The shuttle driver DOT trap 13.2 Valets and other drivers 13.3 Security officers 13.4 Engineering and maintenance 13.5 Lifeguards, pools and childcare 13.6 Kitchens Check your understanding SECTION 13.1 The shuttle driver DOT trap Many hotels treat the airport shuttle as a guest amenity and never ask whether it is a commercial vehicle. If the vehicle is designed to carry 16 or more passengers, including the driver, the driver needs a commercial driver's license (CDL), and FMCSA drug and alcohol testing rules apply, whether the shuttle crosses state lines or not. That means DOT preemployment testing, a DOT random pool, Clearinghouse queries, trained supervisors and the rest of Chapter 18. V EHICLE C DL REQUIRED? D OT TESTING? Designed for 16 or more passengers, including the Yes Yes (FMCSA) No No; company program Yes Yes (FMCSA) No No; company program driver Designed for 15 or fewer passengers, including the driver Truck over 26,000 pounds (for example, a laundry or commissary truck) Cars, SUVs and vans used by valets and staff Count the seats the vehicle was designed for, not how many guests usually ride. Use the vehicle checklist (Form B-9) for every vehicle you own, lease or contract. HOSPITALITY NOTE If a contractor runs your shuttle, require written proof that its drivers are in a compliant DOT program, and keep it on file. heading: SECTION 13.2
body: SECTION 13.2 Valets and other drivers Valets and staff who drive cars, SUVs or small vans are not DOT-covered, but they drive guests or guest property on public roads. Treat them as safety-sensitive in your company policy, test them under it, and check driving records regularly. SECTION 13.3 Security officers Security officers make use-of-force decisions and respond to emergencies. Many states license security officers, and armed officers face additional requirements. Treat security as safety-sensitive, check state licensing rules, and coordinate with any contract security company's program. SECTION 13.4 Engineering and maintenance Engineers work on boilers, electrical systems, elevators, pool chemicals and roofs. OSHA rules such as lockout/tagout apply. Treat these roles as safety-sensitive, suspend work authorizations during any removal from duty, and include serious near misses in post-incident triggers. SECTION 13.5 Lifeguards, pools and childcare Lifeguards and kids' club staff are responsible for guests' lives and for children. Treat them as safety-sensitive, apply reasonable suspicion procedures without hesitation, and check state rules if these roles are filled by workers under 18. SECTION 13.6 Kitchens Commercial kitchens have knives, slicers, fryers, hot surfaces and constant motion. Decide by duties whether cooks are safety-sensitive in your policy, and remember that federal child labor rules bar workers under 18 from operating many kitchen machines, such as power-driven meat slicers. heading: PART V | BUILDING YOUR PROGRAM
body: PART V | BUILDING YOUR PROGRAM Writing Your Policy Your written policy is the foundation of the program. Courts, arbitrators and state agencies judge a program first by whether the employer wrote clear rules, told employees in advance, and then followed its own rules. Appendix A is a draft you can adapt. 14.1 Decisions to make before you write 14.2 Required elements of a policy 14.3 Policy pitfalls 14.4 Executives and supervisors under the same rules Check your understanding SECTION 14.1 Decisions to make before you write D ECISION Q UESTIONS TO ANSWER Who is covered All employees? Applicants? Contractors and temps? Which jobs are safety-sensitive? DOT or not Do any employees fall under DOT? If so, separate pools and rules for them. Reasons for testing Which of pre-employment, random, reasonable suspicion, post-accident, return-to-duty, follow-up and periodic will you use? Specimens and panel Urine, oral fluid, hair or breath? Which drugs, at what cutoffs? Marijuana Test for it in all jobs, only safety-sensitive jobs, or not pre-employment? What do your states allow? Rapid or lab On-site rapid screens with lab confirmation, or lab-only? Alcohol threshold What level is a violation? Consequences Termination, last chance agreement, or treatment for a first positive? Same for a refusal? Second chances Will you offer an Employee Assistance Program (EAP) referral or a last chance agreement? Self-referral Can an employee who asks for help before being tested keep their job? Vendors Who is your collector, lab, MRO, and (if used) third-party administrator? SECTION 14.2 Required elements of a policy 1. Purpose and scope, including who is covered. Chapter 14: Writing Your Policy © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 62 of 108

heading: 2. Prohibited conduct: use, possession, sale or being under the influence at work, and ref
body: 2. Prohibited conduct: use, possession, sale or being under the influence at work, and refusal to test. 3. Definitions of key terms (safety-sensitive, reasonable suspicion, refusal and others). 4. The circumstances for each type of test. 5. Drugs tested and the testing process, including MRO review. 6. Consequences for violations and refusals. 7. Assistance available, such as an EAP. 8. Confidentiality of results. 9. Employee rights, such as split specimen testing and explaining a result to the MRO. 10. A signed acknowledgment of receipt. 11. A reservation of the right to change the policy, with notice. SECTION 14.3 Policy pitfalls • Copying a template without changing it. A policy that does not match what you actually do is worse than no policy. • Promising something you won't do, such as "every positive will be offered treatment." • Ignoring state law where employees work, especially for marijuana and random testing. • Mixing DOT and non-DOT rules in a way that applies company rules to DOT tests. • Skipping notice. Many states require advance written notice, sometimes a set number of days, before testing starts. SECTION 14.4 Executives and supervisors under the same rules Decide in writing whether owners, executives and managers are covered, and cover them on the same terms as everyone else in the same kind of job. Leaders in safety-sensitive roles belong in the random pool. Exempting leadership tells employees the program is about control, not safety, and it weakens the employer's defense that the policy is applied consistently. If an executive tests positive, follow the policy exactly as written, with counsel involved, and keep it as confidential as any other result. heading: PART V | BUILDING YOUR PROGRAM
body: PART V | BUILDING YOUR PROGRAM Running the Program A good policy fails without good execution. Most program failures come from poorly chosen vendors, untrained supervisors, sloppy records and inconsistent follow-through. 15.1 Building your vendor team 15.2 Setting up collection sites 15.3 Training 15.4 Recordkeeping 15.5 Confidentiality 15.6 Helping employees: EAPs and second chances 15.7 Auditing your program 15.8 Budgeting and cost 15.9 Contractors, temps and staffing agencies ** 15.10 Privacy and data security Check your understanding SECTION 15.1 Building your vendor team R OLE W HAT THEY DO W HAT TO CHECK Collection site Collects specimens and runs rapid tests or Trained, certified collectors; hours and breath alcohol tests locations that fit your shifts; after-hours and on-site options for post-accident tests Laboratory Screens and confirms specimens HHS-certified preferred, or at least CAP-FDT accredited; turnaround time; panel options Medical Review Officer Reviews non-negative results and talks to Certified MRO; how fast they reach donors; how donors they report safety concerns Third-party administrator Runs the program for you: random selections, Experience with your industry and states; FCRA (TPA) scheduling, recordkeeping, reporting compliance if reporting results; a secure online portal Consortium Pools small employers into one random pool Useful for small employers; check selection method and records. DOT owner-operators: see Chapter 18 Substance Abuse Evaluates and refers employees who violate DOT-qualified SAP for DOT employees; EAP Professional / EAP the policy coverage and cost for others Chapter 15: Running the Program © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 65 of 108

heading: SECTION 15.2
body: Get every vendor agreement in writing, including turnaround times, confidentiality, data security and who owns the records. SECTION 15.2 Setting up collection sites Collection sites are your partners in the field, and most testing problems start with unclear instructions. Before the first test: • Set up a written account with each site: your company name and account number, authorized contacts, payment terms and hours, including after-hours and weekend post-accident options. • Tell them exactly which tests to run for each reason: specimen, panel, DOT or non-DOT, and whether to use rapid tests. • Send donors with a written authorization or electronic order, never just a phone call from a supervisor. • Confirm where results go: to the MRO and then your DER, never to the supervisor who sent the employee. • Agree how the site will tell you about refusals, shy bladders, temperature problems and no-shows, and how fast. • Visit at least once a year. Check privacy, cleanliness, restroom security and wait times, and review a few completed forms. SECTION 15.3 Training • Supervisors: recognizing signs of impairment, documenting observations, making a reasonable suspicion decision, and handling the employee safely and respectfully. Best practice is at least 60 minutes on drugs and 60 minutes on alcohol, before a supervisor makes a reasonable suspicion decision, with periodic refreshers. • Employees: the policy, the dangers of drug and alcohol use, how testing works, and where to get help. Repeat at hiring and at least yearly. • HR and program staff: the policy, result handling, confidentiality and recordkeeping. DOT NOTE DOT requires this supervisor training for anyone supervising DOT employees. See Chapter 18 (What the employer must do). SECTION 15.4 Recordkeeping Keep testing records apart from personnel files, in a locked or access-controlled system. Use these retention periods, which match DOT's, as a minimum: R ECORD R ECOMMENDED RETENTION Positive results, refusals, SAP reports, follow-up schedules 5 years Collection process and supervisor training records 2 years Negative and cancelled results 1 year Check state law, which can require longer retention or specific handling.

heading: SECTION 15.2
body: DOT NOTE For DOT records these periods are mandatory. See Chapter 18 (DOT recordkeeping). Chapter 15: Running the Program © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 66 of 108

heading: SECTION 15.5
body: SECTION 15.5 Confidentiality • Share results only with people who need to know: the designated program contact, the employee's decision-maker, and legal counsel. • Never discuss a result with coworkers. • Release results to outside parties only with the employee's written consent or as law requires. SECTION 15.6 Helping employees: EAPs and second chances • An Employee Assistance Program offers confidential counseling and referral. Many employers encourage selfreferral before a test by promising no discipline for coming forward first. • A last chance agreement lets an employee keep their job after a violation if they complete treatment, pass a returnto-duty test, and accept follow-up testing. Any later violation ends employment. • Second chances can help retention in tight labor markets, but they must be offered consistently. HOSPITALITY NOTE Hospitality has high rates of substance use and depends on keeping experienced staff. Recovery-friendly policies, EAP access and last chance agreements are especially valuable here, as long as they are offered consistently. SECTION 15.7 Auditing your program Once a year, review: positivity and refusal rates by test reason, whether random selections were completed on schedule, supervisor training records, vendor performance, policy changes needed for new laws, and any complaints or claims. SECTION 15.8 Budgeting and cost Testing costs vary widely by region, volume, specimen and vendor, so get written quotes. Published figures give a starting point: lab-based tests often start around $50 and hair tests around $125 (Checkr), and published fee schedules for a DOT urine test including collection, lab analysis and MRO review cluster around $65 to $80. What goes into the cost of a lab-based test: • Collection fee (higher for observed, after-hours or on-site mobile collections) • Laboratory screen, plus confirmation for non-negatives • MRO review • TPA or consortium fees: annual membership, random selection, reporting • Travel time and lost work while employees go to a collection site What goes into the cost of an on-site rapid program:

heading: SECTION 15.5
body: • Rapid devices, temperature strips and collection supplies • Collector time and training • Lab confirmation and MRO fees for each non-negative (usually a small share of tests) • Shipping or courier to the lab • Any state registration or CLIA certificate fees • Less travel and lost work, which is often the biggest saving Building an annual budget. Estimate the number of tests by reason, then multiply by the cost per test: Chapter 15: Running the Program © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 67 of 108

heading: T EST REASON
body: T EST REASON H OW TO ESTIMATE THE COUNT Pre-employment Expected hires for the year, including turnover Random Pool size × your random rate (for example, 100 employees × 50% = 50 tests) Post-accident and reasonable suspicion Last year's incidents, plus a cushion Return-to-duty and follow-up Number of employees on last chance agreements × required tests Add confirmation and MRO fees for the share of tests you expect to be non-negative, plus fixed costs such as TPA fees, training and supplies. Comparing vendor quotes. Ask every vendor for the all-in price for the same test, and check: • What is included: collection, lab screen, confirmation, MRO, reporting • Fees for after-hours, observed, shy bladder and cancelled collections • Turnaround time for negatives and for MRO-verified results • Minimums, contract length and price changes • Who owns the records, and what it costs to get them if you leave The cheapest price per test is rarely the cheapest program. A cancelled test, a lost specimen or a slow result that delays a hire costs more than a few dollars per test. SECTION 15.9 Contractors, temps and staffing agencies ** People who work at your site but are not your employees create two risks: an impaired contractor can hurt your people, and testing someone else's employee directly can make you look like their employer. • Put testing in the contract. Require contractors and staffing agencies to run a program that meets your standards: which tests, which panel, an MRO and who is excluded from your site after a positive or refusal. • Let the contractor test its own people and certify compliance to you, rather than testing them yourself. Testing, disciplining and controlling another company's workers is one factor in finding joint employment. • Ask for proof: a written policy, a certificate of compliance, or aggregate results. Do not ask for individual results unless the contract and law clearly allow it and the worker has consented. • Site access rules can still apply to everyone: "No one may work on site while impaired, and anyone involved in an incident may be required to test under the contractor's program." • Customer requirements flow down. If your customer requires your workers to be tested, write the same requirement into your subcontracts and staffing agreements.

heading: T EST REASON
body: • DOT contractors must be in a compliant DOT program, often through a consortium. Verify before they drive or work under your DOT authority. NEW AND DEVELOPING LAW ** Laws in these areas are new and developing. Please confirm any policy decisions regarding these issues that you may include in your program with your attorneys. HOSPITALITY NOTE Banquet and event staffing agencies, franchise structures and management companies are common in hospitality. Be clear about who the employer is for each worker, and keep a franchisor or brand out of individual testing decisions and results (Chapter 11). heading: SECTION 15.10
body: SECTION 15.10 Privacy and data security Drug test results are some of the most sensitive records an employer holds, and they increasingly live in software systems. • Who can see results: limit system access to the program owner and named backups. Check that your HR system, TPA portal and email do not quietly give supervisors or IT staff access. • Separate storage: keep results out of the general personnel file and general HR system, as the ADA requires for medical information. • HIPAA: usually does not apply to an employer acting as an employer. It may apply to your MRO, clinic or health plan. Do not assume either way; ask your counsel. • State privacy laws may cover employee data, such as California's privacy law for employee information, and some states regulate biometric data if your systems use fingerprints or facial images. • Vendors: require confidentiality, data security, breach notice and return or destruction of records in every vendor contract. • Email and texts: never send results or names of donors by unencrypted email or text. • Retention and destruction: keep records for the required periods (above), then destroy them securely, unless a lawsuit or claim is pending. • Litigation hold: once a claim or lawsuit is likely, stop routine destruction of every related record, including emails, logs and images. Use the vendor and privacy rules above together: most data problems in testing programs come from vendor systems and email, not from paper files. heading: PART V | BUILDING YOUR PROGRAM
body: PART V | BUILDING YOUR PROGRAM Communicating the Program A program succeeds when everyone involved understands it and trusts it. As the program owner, you are its spokesperson: you explain why the company tests, how it works and what happens next, to people with very different concerns. Prescriptions are discussed privately with the doctor, not with your supervisor." • Help: "If you have a problem, ask for help before you are tested. We have an EAP, and asking for help early is protected under our policy." HOSPITALITY NOTE Hospitality workforces are often multilingual. Deliver the policy, talking points and FAQ in the languages your employees read, and use bilingual managers or interpreters for reasonable suspicion and results conversations. SECTION 16.3 Reporting to leadership Executives want to know whether the program is working, what it costs and whether the company is exposed. Report quarterly, with no names: M EASURE W HY IT MATTERS Tests completed by reason (pre-employment, random, reasonable Shows the program is running as written suspicion, post-accident, follow-up) Positive and refusal rates by reason, compared with industry benchmarks Shows where risk is concentrated such as the Quest Drug Testing Index Random testing completed vs. the required or planned rate Chapter 16: Communicating the Program © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb.
