heading: M EASURE
body: M EASURE W HY IT MATTERS Cancelled tests and collection errors Shows vendor quality Turnaround from collection to result Affects hiring speed Cost per test and total cost Budget Workplace incidents and workers' comp claims Shows impact over time Policy changes needed for new laws Legal risk SECTION 16.4 Scripts for hard conversations Adapt these to your policy. Keep conversations private, calm and short, and have a second manager present for anything involving discipline. Announcing a new program: "Starting [DATE], we are launching a drug and alcohol testing program for [WHO]. Here is why we are doing it, how it works, and what your rights are. Everyone will get a copy of the policy and a chance to ask questions before any testing starts." Notifying a random selection: "You've been randomly selected for a test today. This is computer-generated, not based on anything you've done. Please go to [LOCATION] now; [NAME] will go with you." Reasonable suspicion: "I've noticed [SPECIFIC OBSERVATIONS] today. Because of what I've seen, our policy requires a test. I'm not accusing you of anything. We will take you to the collection site, and you will not be able to work until we have the result." Do not argue, diagnose or ask what they took. Post-accident: "Our policy requires testing after incidents like this one, for everyone whose actions could have contributed. It isn't a judgment about what happened. Once you've received any medical care you need, [NAME] will take you to the collection site." Delivering a verified positive: "The doctor who reviews our tests has verified your test as positive for [SUBSTANCE]. Under our policy, [CONSEQUENCE]. Here is a written notice, including how to request a test of your split specimen and how to reach our EAP." Do not debate the science; refer questions to the MRO. A coworker asks about someone's test: "I can't discuss anyone's personal information, just as I wouldn't discuss yours." An employee asks for help: "Thank you for coming to me. Under our policy, asking for help before you're selected for a test is protected. Let's get you connected with [EAP]." Then follow the self-referral section of your policy.

heading: M EASURE
body: SECTION 16.5 Answering common employee questions • "Marijuana is legal in my state. Why can you test for it?" State law may protect some off-duty use, and our policy follows the law where you work. No state protects use or impairment at work, and DOT rules prohibit marijuana for covered jobs regardless of state law. • "Can CBD make me test positive?" It can. Many CBD products contain THC, even when labeled otherwise, and hempderived THC products such as delta-8 test positive for marijuana. Neither is a legitimate medical explanation. Federal limits on hemp-derived THC products are due to take effect on December 11, 2026 (Chapter 2). • "What about my prescriptions?" Discuss them privately with the MRO if your test is non-negative. A valid prescription taken as directed is reported as negative. • "Can poppy seeds or secondhand smoke make me fail?" Poppy seeds can cause an opiate screen to show nonnegative, especially at the lower cutoffs many private programs use. That is why every non-negative goes to the lab and the MRO, who considers poppy seeds before verifying a result. Normal secondhand marijuana smoke exposure is very unlikely to reach the cutoff. heading: SECTION 16.6
body: • "Who sees my results?" Only the people listed in the policy who need to know. • "What if I refuse?" A refusal is treated the same as a positive result. SECTION 16.6 Employee FAQ handout Give this one-page summary to every employee with the policy, filled in with your details: NOTE Our Drug and Alcohol Testing Program: What You Need to Know • Why we test: To keep every employee, our customers and the public safe. • Who is tested: [WHO], under the same rules for everyone in the same job. • When: [Before hire / random / reasonable suspicion / after accidents / return-to-duty and follow-up]. • How: A [urine / oral fluid / hair / breath] sample collected privately by a trained collector. Any non-negative screen is confirmed by a certified lab and reviewed by a physician (MRO) before any decision. • Prescriptions: Discussed only with the MRO, privately. • Your results: Confidential and kept separate from your personnel file. • Refusing or tampering: Treated the same as a positive result. • Getting help: Contact [EAP NAME, PHONE] any time. Asking for help before you are selected for a test is protected under our policy. • Questions: Contact [PROGRAM CONTACT, PHONE, EMAIL]. heading: PART VI DOT AND PRACTICE
body: PART VI DOT AND PRACTICE DOT Testing Requirements If any of your employees perform DOT safety-sensitive work, federal rules decide almost everything about their testing: who is tested, when, how, by whom and what happens after a violation. You cannot opt out of, add to or relax these rules. The rest of this guidebook describes best practice for non-DOT programs; wherever DOT differs, a DOT note points here. Always check the current rules at the DOT Office of Drug and Alcohol Policy and Compliance (ODAPC), transportation.gov/ odapc. 18.1 How the rules fit together 18.2 Where DOT differs from this guidebook 18.3 What the employer must do 18.4 Required tests 18.5 2026 minimum random testing rates 18.6 Drug testing under DOT 18.7 DOT drug panel and cutoffs 18.8 DOT collection rules 18.9 DOT results, MRO and refusals 18.10 Alcohol testing under DOT 18.11 Violations and the SAP process 18.12 The FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse 18.13 DOT recordkeeping 18.14 Common DOT audit findings Check your understanding SECTION 18.1 How the rules fit together • 49 CFR Part 40 sets the testing procedures for every DOT agency: collection, labs, MROs, alcohol testing, SAPs and records. • Each DOT agency's own rule decides who is covered, which tests are required, and specific duties. A GENCY A GENCY RULE W HO IS COVERED FMCSA 49 CFR Part 382 CDL drivers of commercial motor vehicles FAA 14 CFR Part 120 Flight crew, flight attendants, mechanics, dispatchers, air traffic controllers and other aviation safety jobs Chapter 18: DOT Testing Requirements © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: • Name a Designated Employer Representative (DER) to receive results and remove employees
body: • Name a Designated Employer Representative (DER) to receive results and remove employees from duty. • Contract with qualified service agents: collectors, an HHS-certified lab, an MRO, a SAP and optionally a consortium/ third-party administrator (C/TPA). • Check every new hire's drug and alcohol violation history with previous DOT-regulated employers: the past two years under Part 40, and three years for CDL drivers. For FMCSA drivers, a full Clearinghouse pre-employment query now satisfies this check for prior FMCSA employers; ask employers regulated by other DOT agencies directly. • Run a limited Clearinghouse query on every CDL driver at least once a year. • Train supervisors: at least 60 minutes on drugs and 60 minutes on alcohol for reasonable suspicion. • Give employees the required education materials. • Keep records for the required periods and file annual testing data (MIS) reports when your agency requires them. • Keep DOT and non-DOT testing completely separate. SECTION 18.4 Required tests T EST D OT REQUIREMENT Pre-employment A negative drug test before first safety-sensitive work. Pre-employment alcohol testing is optional for most agencies. Random Unannounced, spread through the year, at least the agency's minimum rate. Reasonable suspicion Based on a trained supervisor's specific, current observations made just before, during or just after duty. Alcohol test within 2 hours if possible, and never after 8. Post-accident Required when the agency's accident criteria are met. For FMCSA, for example: any fatality, or an injury treated away from the scene or a vehicle towed away, when the driver receives a citation. Alcohol within 8 hours (ideally 2), drugs within 32 hours. Return-to-duty Directly observed, after the SAP process, before returning to safety-sensitive work. Follow-up Directly observed, unannounced, at least 6 in the first 12 months, for up to 5 years, as the SAP directs. SECTION 18.5 2026 minimum random testing rates Rates are set each year by each agency and posted by ODAPC. These apply to calendar year 2026: A GENCY R ANDOM DRUG RATE R ANDOM ALCOHOL RATE FMCSA 50% 10% FAA 25% 10% FRA (covered service and maintenance-of-way)

heading: SECTION 18.6
body: The rate is a percentage of your average number of covered positions. With 100 FMCSA drivers, you must complete at least 50 random drug tests and 10 random alcohol tests during the year. SECTION 18.6 Drug testing under DOT • Urine only, for now. DOT has authorized oral fluid testing, but employers cannot use it until HHS certifies at least two oral fluid laboratories; none had been certified when DOT last addressed this in May 2026. Under a rule effective June 10, 2026, in the limited situations where DOT would otherwise require an oral fluid test, a directly observed urine collection is required instead. Check transportation.gov/odapc for current status. • The fixed DOT panel: marijuana, cocaine, amphetamines (including methamphetamine, MDMA and MDA), opioids (codeine, morphine, 6-AM, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, oxycodone, oxymorphone) and PCP. Fentanyl was proposed in September 2025 but is not yet part of the panel. Employers may not add drugs to a DOT test or apply company cutoffs. • An HHS-certified lab tests the specimen; every non-negative goes to the MRO. SECTION 18.7 DOT drug panel and cutoffs DOT laboratories must use these urine cutoffs, in ng/mL (49 CFR 40.85): C OMPARED WITH TYPICAL NON-DOT D RUG (TARGET ANALYTE) D OT SCREEN D OT CONFIRM Marijuana metabolite (THC-COOH) Same Cocaine metabolite (benzoylecgonine) Same Codeine / morphine 2,000 2,000 each Different: many non-DOT programs screen P RACTICE at 300 6-acetylmorphine (heroin) Same Hydrocodone / hydromorphone 100 each Same Oxycodone / oxymorphone 100 each Same Phencyclidine (PCP) Same Amphetamine / methamphetamine 250 each Same MDMA / MDA 250 each Same Fentanyl Not tested Not tested Different: many non-DOT programs test for it The opiate difference. DOT screens and confirms codeine and morphine at 2,000 ng/mL, mainly so that poppy seeds do not cause positives. Many private programs screen at 300 ng/mL to detect more use. The same specimen can be negative on a DOT test and non-negative on a company test. Never apply company cutoffs or company drugs to a DOT test; if you want broader testing for a DOT employee, it must be a separate non-DOT test under your company policy, on a non-federal form, where law allows.

heading: SECTION 18.6
body: Federal agencies are different again. Federal agency programs (not DOT) follow the HHS panel, which since July 2025 includes fentanyl and norfentanyl at 1 ng/mL and uses a 4,000 ng/mL morphine confirmation cutoff. DOT has not adopted those changes. Chapter 18: DOT Testing Requirements © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 18.8
body: SECTION 18.8 DOT collection rules • Federal form. Every DOT collection uses the federal Custody and Control Form, on paper or an approved electronic version. • Collector qualifications. Collectors must complete qualification training, pass five error-free mock collections, and take refresher training every five years. • Direct observation by a same-sex observer is required for return-to-duty and follow-up tests, when the temperature is out of range or tampering is suspected, when the MRO orders it, and in the other situations listed in 49 CFR 40.67. • Shy bladder. The donor may drink up to 40 ounces of fluid over up to 3 hours. If they still cannot provide 45 mL, the employer must arrange a medical evaluation within 5 days. If no medical condition explains it, it is a refusal. • Dilute specimens. If the MRO reports a dilute negative with creatinine of 2 to 5 mg/dL, the employee must be recollected immediately under direct observation. DOT treats these collection errors as follows: F LAW R ESULT UNDER DOT Specimen ID on the bottle does not match the form Fatal; test cancelled Seal broken or missing when the lab receives it Fatal; test cancelled Collector's printed name and signature missing Fatal; test cancelled Not enough specimen for the lab to test Fatal; test cancelled Collector forgot to sign the certification Correctable with a signed memo Non-federal form used for a DOT test Correctable with a signed memo SECTION 18.9 DOT results, MRO and refusals • MRO interview. The MRO interviews the employee before verifying a positive. A state medical marijuana card or a Schedule III marijuana product is not a legitimate medical explanation. • Reaching the employee. If the MRO cannot reach the employee, the DER tells the employee to call the MRO, without giving details. The employee then has 72 hours to call. If the employee does not, the MRO may verify the result without an interview.

heading: SECTION 18.8
body: • Split specimen. The employee may ask the MRO, within 72 hours, to have the split specimen tested at a second HHScertified lab. The employer may not delay action while waiting. • Refusals are defined in 49 CFR 40.191. They include failing to appear in a reasonable time, leaving before the test is complete, failing to provide enough specimen without a medical explanation, refusing an observed collection or failing to follow the observer, refusing to empty pockets, carrying or wearing a device to tamper, an adulterated or substituted result, admitting adulteration or substitution, and failing to cooperate. • Invalid and cancelled results. The MRO directs any required recollection, which may be observed. • Safety concerns. When the MRO believes a prescribed medication makes the employee medically unqualified or a safety risk, the MRO reports it, and the DOT agency's medical qualification rules govern what happens next. SECTION 18.10 Alcohol testing under DOT • Trained breath alcohol technicians or screening test technicians use DOT-approved devices. • A screening result of 0.02 or higher must be confirmed on an evidential breath testing device, after a waiting period of at least 15 minutes, starting within 30 minutes of the screen. Chapter 18: DOT Testing Requirements © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 84 of 108

heading: SECTION 18.11
body: • 0.04 or higher: a violation. Removal from safety-sensitive duty and the SAP process. • 0.02 to 0.039: not a violation, but the employee must be removed from safety-sensitive duty for a period set by the agency (24 hours for FMCSA). • Agencies also bar alcohol use within set hours before duty (for example, 4 hours for FMCSA drivers, 8 hours for FAA flight crew) and after an accident until tested. SECTION 18.11 Violations and the SAP process A DOT violation is a verified positive, an alcohol result of 0.04 or higher, a refusal, or alcohol or drug use on or before duty in violation of agency rules. After any violation: 1. Remove the employee from safety-sensitive duty immediately. 2. Give the employee a list of qualified Substance Abuse Professionals. This is required even if you terminate the employee. 3. The SAP evaluates the employee and requires education or treatment. 4. The SAP re-evaluates and, if the employee complied, sets a follow-up testing plan. 5. The employee passes a directly observed return-to-duty test. 6. The employee completes the follow-up testing plan, which travels with them to any new DOT employer. DOT does not require you to rehire or keep the employee. That is your company's decision, but if you do return them to safety-sensitive work, they must complete this process first. SECTION 18.12 The FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse For CDL drivers, employers, MROs and SAPs must report violations, refusals and return-to-duty steps to the Clearinghouse. Since November 2024, state licensing agencies downgrade the CDL of a driver in "prohibited" status until the return-toduty process is complete. Driving with a prohibited status is a serious violation for the driver and the carrier.

heading: SECTION 18.11
body: SECTION 18.13 DOT recordkeeping DOT records must be kept confidential, apart from personnel files, and released only as 49 CFR Part 40 allows. heading: PART VI DOT AND PRACTICE
body: PART VI DOT AND PRACTICE Case Scenarios These scenarios apply the guidebook to situations program owners face. Each is an example only; the right answer in your company depends on your policy and the law where the employee works. 19.1 Scenario 1: A non-negative on-site screen for an applicant 19.2 Scenario 2: A forklift accident 19.3 Scenario 3: The smell of alcohol after lunch 19.4 Scenario 4: A prescription and a crane 19.5 Scenario 5: "Why do I keep getting picked?" 19.6 Scenario 6: A cold specimen 19.7 Scenario 7: "It was only CBD" 19.8 Scenario 8: A DOT driver at 0.03 19.9 Scenario 9: A union representative 19.10 Scenario 10: Asking for help before a test 19.11 Scenario 11: Two shuttles 19.12 Scenario 12: The bartender's shift drink 19.13 Scenario 13: A 17-year-old host 19.14 Scenario 14: A cook in Nevada 19.15 Scenario 15: The brand asks for names 19.16 Scenario 16: An impaired banquet server Check your understanding SECTION 19.1 Scenario 1: A non-negative on-site screen for an applicant An applicant for an office job in New Jersey gives a urine specimen on site after a conditional offer. The rapid cup shows no test line for THC. What to do: Tell the applicant the screen needs lab confirmation, seal and send the specimen to the lab, and take no action. When the MRO reports the result, check New Jersey law before acting: New Jersey allows the test, but bars withdrawing the offer based only on a positive cannabis result without documented evidence of impairment, and a recent appellate decision lets applicants sue over offers withdrawn for a positive alone. For an office job, a positive THC result by itself is unlikely to support withdrawing the offer. Your policy should already say how marijuana is handled for this job in this state. Lesson: The screen is never final, and marijuana results must be read against state law where the person works. Chapter 19: Case Scenarios © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 88 of 108

heading: SECTION 19.2
body: SECTION 19.2 Scenario 2: A forklift accident A forklift strikes a rack, causing $8,000 in damage. A coworker standing nearby twisted an ankle stepping away. Your policy requires testing for property damage over $5,000. What to do: Get the injured worker medical care first. Test the forklift operator, whose actions could have contributed. Do not test the coworker just because they were injured; that risks an OSHA violation for discouraging injury reporting. Complete the post-accident decision record (Form B-4) and test promptly, ideally alcohol within 2 hours and drugs within 32. Lesson: Test the people whose actions could have contributed, not the people who got hurt. SECTION 19.3 Scenario 3: The smell of alcohol after lunch A supervisor notices an employee returning from lunch with a strong odor of alcohol, flushed face and loud, slurred speech. The employee drove back to work. What to do: Remove the employee from duty, have a second supervisor observe if possible, and complete the reasonable suspicion checklist (Form B-3). Arrange transport to the collection site, or test on site with an approved breath device. Do not let the employee drive. If the employee insists on driving away, do not restrain them; consider calling law enforcement for public safety. Lesson: Specific, current observations, documented before the test, are what make reasonable suspicion defensible. SECTION 19.4 Scenario 4: A prescription and a crane A crane operator's random test is reported by the MRO as negative because of a valid opioid prescription, with a safety concern noted. What to do: This is not a policy violation. Begin the ADA interactive process: confidentially, with the employee's release, ask the treating provider whether the employee can safely operate a crane on this medication, consider temporary reassignment or leave, and document the decision. Lesson: A safety concern is a fitness-for-duty question, not discipline. SECTION 19.5 Scenario 5: "Why do I keep getting picked?" An employee has been selected for random testing three times this year and complains that they are being targeted. What to do: Explain that selections are computer-generated by your TPA, that everyone has an equal chance at every draw, and that being picked several times, or not at all, is normal. Offer to show documentation that the selection method is scientifically valid, without revealing anyone else's selections.

heading: SECTION 19.2
body: Lesson: True random selection does not even out over a year, and your records should prove the method. SECTION 19.6 Scenario 6: A cold specimen During an on-site collection, the cup's temperature strip shows no reading in the 90-100°F range. What to do: Note the temperature, keep the first specimen, and immediately conduct a second collection under direct observation by a same-sex observer. Send both specimens to the lab. If the employee refuses the observed collection, document it as a refusal. Lesson: Temperature is the first line of defense against substituted urine. Chapter 19: Case Scenarios © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 89 of 108

heading: SECTION 19.7
body: SECTION 19.7 Scenario 7: "It was only CBD" An employee's MRO-verified result is positive for marijuana. The employee says they only use a CBD product. What to do: Follow the policy. CBD products can contain THC even when labeled otherwise, and CBD use is not a legitimate medical explanation. The MRO has already considered any explanation offered. Check whether state law protects off-duty cannabis use for this job before deciding the consequence. Lesson: The MRO process, not the employer, weighs explanations. SECTION 19.8 Scenario 8: A DOT driver at 0.03 A CDL driver's random breath alcohol confirmation is 0.03. What to do: This is not a DOT violation, but the driver must be removed from safety-sensitive duty for 24 hours under FMCSA rules. Your company policy may set its own consequence for non-DOT purposes, as long as it is applied consistently and labeled as a company rule. Lesson: Know the difference between a DOT violation and a DOT removal (Chapter 18). SECTION 19.9 Scenario 9: A union representative During a reasonable suspicion meeting, a union employee asks for a union representative. What to do: Honor the request for an investigatory interview that could lead to discipline. Follow your contract and counsel's guidance on proceeding with the test itself, which should not be delayed beyond the testing window. Lesson: Union rights and testing deadlines both apply; plan for both in advance. SECTION 19.10 Scenario 10: Asking for help before a test An employee tells HR they have a drinking problem and want help. The next morning, they are selected for random testing. What to do: If your policy protects self-referral before selection, honor it: refer the employee to the EAP and follow the selfreferral terms. The random test still happens; how a result is handled depends on what your policy says about selfreferral. Lesson: Write the self-referral rule clearly, and apply it exactly as written. SECTION 19.11 Scenario 11: Two shuttles Your resort runs a 14-passenger van and a 24-passenger bus to the airport, both within one state. Neither driver is in a DOT program.

heading: SECTION 19.7
body: What to do: The bus is designed for 16 or more passengers including the driver, so its drivers need a CDL and must be in an FMCSA DOT program now: pre-employment test, Clearinghouse query, random pool. The van driver is not DOTcovered; test under your company policy as a safety-sensitive driver. Lesson: Designed capacity, not route, decides DOT coverage. Chapter 19: Case Scenarios © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Employer’s Guidebook: Hospitality Edition Version 1.2.1 / Updated Nov 2026 | Page 90 of 108

heading: SECTION 19.12
body: SECTION 19.12 Scenario 12: The bartender's shift drink A bartender is seen drinking a shot with guests during a busy Saturday shift. Her speech is normal. What to do: Drinking on duty violates your policy whether or not she seems impaired. Remove her from service, document what was seen, and, if your policy calls for it, conduct a breath test. Apply the consequence your policy sets for on-duty use. Lesson: The rule is about drinking on duty, not only about impairment. SECTION 19.13 Scenario 13: A 17-year-old host You offer a host position to a 17-year-old applicant, and your policy requires pre-employment testing for all hires. What to do: Check your state's rules on testing minors and any parental consent requirement before testing. A host is usually not safety-sensitive; consider whether pre-employment testing is needed for the role at all. Lesson: Minors need extra legal checks, and testing should follow risk. SECTION 19.14 Scenario 14: A cook in Nevada An applicant for a line cook job in Las Vegas tests positive for marijuana on a pre-employment test. What to do: Nevada bars refusing to hire most applicants for a pre-employment marijuana positive, with exceptions that include jobs that, in the employer's determination, could adversely affect the safety of others. Unless your policy already designated line cooks as safety-sensitive before testing, do not withdraw the offer based on the result; consult counsel. If you test the cook within the first 30 days of employment, Nevada also lets the employee rebut the result with a second test at their own expense, which you must accept and consider. Lesson: Designate safety-sensitive roles before testing, and know your state's marijuana law. SECTION 19.15 Scenario 15: The brand asks for names Your franchise brand's quality auditor asks for the names and results of employees who failed drug tests this year. What to do: Decline to share individual results. Provide a certification that your program meets the brand's standard, or aggregate data if the franchise agreement requires it, after checking with counsel. Lesson: Keeping the brand out of individual testing decisions limits joint-employer risk and protects privacy. SECTION 19.16 Scenario 16: An impaired banquet server During a wedding, a server from your event staffing agency is slurring and stumbling.

heading: SECTION 19.12
body: What to do: Remove the server from guest service and the event, arrange safe transport home, document your observations, and notify the agency, which handles any test under its program and the contract. Lesson: Protect guests first; contracts decide who tests whom. Chapter 19: Case Scenarios © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: APPENDIX
body: APPENDIX Appendix A: Draft Drug and Alcohol Testing Policy This is a starting draft for a non-DOT company program. Replace every item in [brackets], delete options you do not use, and have an employment attorney review it for every state and city where you have employees before you adopt it. DOT-regulated employees need a separate policy that follows 49 CFR Part 40 and the rules of their DOT agency. [COMPANY NAME] Drug and Alcohol Testing Policy Effective date: [DATE] 1. Purpose. [COMPANY NAME] is committed to a safe, healthy and productive workplace. Drug and alcohol use can endanger employees, customers and the public. This policy sets the rules for a drug- and alcohol-free workplace and explains when and how testing will be done. 2. Who is covered. This policy applies to all employees and to applicants who receive a conditional offer of employment [, and to temporary workers and contractors working on company premises]. Employees covered by U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) rules are also subject to the company's separate DOT policy, which controls for DOT testing. 3. Prohibited conduct. While on duty, on company premises, in company vehicles, or while conducting company business, employees may not: • Use, possess, sell, distribute, or be under the influence of illegal drugs or controlled substances not lawfully prescribed to them; • Use or be under the influence of marijuana, regardless of state legality [modify where state law protects off-duty use]; • Use or possess alcohol, or be under the influence of alcohol (an alcohol concentration of [0.04] or higher), except at company-approved events where the employee is not on duty; • Misuse prescription or over-the-counter medications; • Refuse to submit to a test or tamper with a test. 4. Definitions. • Safety-sensitive position: a job in which impairment could cause injury to the employee or others, including [list positions or job categories]. • Reasonable suspicion: a belief, based on specific, current, observable facts about an employee's appearance, behavior, speech or odor, that the employee has violated this policy. • Refusal to test: any conduct listed in Section 9. • Verified positive: a result confirmed by a laboratory and verified by a Medical Review Officer (MRO). 5. When testing will be done. The company will test:

heading: APPENDIX
body: • Pre-employment: all applicants for [all positions / safety-sensitive positions] after a conditional offer of employment. The offer depends on a negative result. • Random: employees in [safety-sensitive positions / all positions], selected by a scientifically valid random method. Each employee in the pool has an equal chance of selection at each draw. Tests are unannounced, and selected employees must report immediately. • Reasonable suspicion: when a trained supervisor has reasonable suspicion, documented on the company's reasonable suspicion checklist and [confirmed by a second supervisor or manager when available]. • Post-accident: after any work-related incident involving [a fatality; an injury requiring medical treatment beyond first aid; property damage over $[AMOUNT]; or a moving traffic citation], for each employee whose actions could have contributed. Testing will not be used to discourage the reporting of injuries. • Return-to-duty and follow-up: before an employee returns after a violation, and unannounced for up to [24] months afterward, as set out in a written agreement. • [Periodic: as part of scheduled physical examinations for [positions].] Appendix A: Draft Drug and Alcohol Testing Policy © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. body: 6. Testing procedures. Tests will be performed by qualified collectors using [urine / oral fluid / hair / breath] specimens under chain-of-custody procedures. The panel tests for [list drugs or panel]. [Rapid on-site screens may be used; every non-negative screen will be confirmed by an [HHS-certified / CAP-FDT-accredited] laboratory.] Every non-negative laboratory result will be reviewed by an MRO, who will give the employee an opportunity to provide a legitimate medical explanation before reporting the result to the company. 7. Prescription medications. Employees do not need to report prescriptions to their supervisor as part of testing. Prescriptions are discussed privately with the MRO. Employees in safety-sensitive positions who take a medication that may affect safe performance should [notify the company's designated health and safety contact], who will handle the matter confidentially and consider reasonable accommodation. 8. Consequences. An applicant with a verified positive result or a refusal will not be hired [and may reapply after [6] months]. An employee with a verified positive result or a refusal will be removed from duty immediately and [will be terminated / may, at the company's discretion, be offered one last chance agreement requiring evaluation, completion of any recommended treatment, a negative return-to-duty test and follow-up testing]. A second violation will result in termination. 9. Refusal to test. Each of the following is a refusal: failing to report for a test as directed without delay; leaving the collection site before the test is complete; failing to provide a sufficient specimen without a valid medical reason; refusing a required observed collection; failing to cooperate with the testing process; and providing an adulterated or substituted specimen. 10. Removal from duty pending results. An employee tested for reasonable suspicion or after an accident [or with a nonnegative rapid screen] will be removed from duty pending results. [Pay status during removal: specify.] An employee whose final result is negative will be returned to work [with back pay for scheduled time missed].

heading: BEFORE YOU BEGIN
body: BEFORE YOU BEGIN How to use this workbook Read each section, then complete the exercise that follows it. Write your answers directly in the workbook. The chapter review and answer key are at the end. Complete the review before checking the key. LEARNING OBJECTIVES When you finish this chapter you will be able to: 1. Explain what a rapid drug test is and what it is not. 2. Name the parts of a test strip, including multi-line strips, and what each one does. 3. Describe how antibodies recognize a drug, and what cross-reactivity means. 4. Explain why a visible test line means negative on a competitive drug test. 5. Identify the common device formats and specimen types, and the trade-offs of each. 6. Describe the basic FDA and CLIA rules that apply to rapid test use. 7. Store and handle devices so they perform as the manufacturer intended. 8. List the built-in limitations of any rapid screening test. Chapter contents 1.1 What a rapid test is 1.2 Anatomy of a test strip: single-line and multi-line 1.3 Antibodies, antigens, and cross-reactivity 1.4 The competitive format: why a line means negative 1.5 Device formats 1.6 Specimen types: urine and oral fluid 1.7 The rules: FDA clearance and CLIA 1.8 Storage and handling 1.9 Built-in limitations Chapter review Answer key (trainer use) A NOTE ON WORDS This workbook uses non-negative (also called preliminary positive) for a rapid test that detected a drug at or above its cut-off. A rapid test result is a screen, not a final answer, so we do not call it "positive." Only a laboratory confirmation can do that. Laboratories sometimes call the same result "presumptive positive." With clients and donors, say non-negative. Program means the employer, court, agency, or treatment program that ordered the test. heading: SECTION 1.1
body: SECTION 1.1 What a rapid test is A rapid drug test is a single-use screening device that tells you, in minutes, whether a specimen contains a drug or drug class at or above a set concentration. It answers a yes-or-no question. It does not tell you how much drug is present, exactly which drug it was, or when it was used. Technically, a rapid drug test is a lateral flow immunoassay. "Lateral flow" means the liquid specimen travels sideways along a strip of absorbent material. "Immunoassay" means the test uses antibodies, the same kind of recognition proteins the immune system makes, to detect the drug. Screening versus confirmation RAPID TEST (SCREEN) LABORATORY CONFIRMATION Method Immunoassay on a test strip GC-MS or LC-MS/MS (mass spectrometry) Result type Qualitative: negative or non-negative Quantitative: names each compound and its concentration in ng/mL What it detects Anything the antibody recognizes, including Specific named compounds (analytes) related compounds Time to result About 5 minutes Typically days, including transport Where At the point of collection In a certified laboratory Role Fast sorting: clear negatives, flag the rest Definitive identification GOVERNING RULE A rapid test is a screen. Every non-negative result is preliminary until a laboratory confirms it. EXERCISE 1.1 1. In your own words, what does "lateral flow immunoassay" mean? 2. Name two things a rapid test cannot tell you about a specimen. Chapter 1: Understanding Rapid Test Kit Technology © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 7 of 217

heading: SECTION 1.2
body: SECTION 1.2 Anatomy of a test strip Every strip has the same five parts, whether it tests for one drug or several. The specimen enters at one end and is pulled toward the other by the absorbent pad. Figure 1.1 shows the simplest design, a single-line strip. Multi-line strips are covered on the next page. DIRECTION OF FLOW T C Sample pad Conjugate pad Membrane Test and control lines Absorbent (wick) pad Plastic backing card runs the full length underneath Figure 1.1 Cross-section of a single-drug lateral flow test strip (simplified, not to scale) # PART WHAT IT DOES Sample pad Receives the specimen, filters particles, and buffers it (adjusts its pH and salt balance) so it flows evenly and the antibodies react as designed. Conjugate pad Holds dried antibodies attached to colored particles (usually colloidal gold, which looks red to purple). The specimen dissolves them and carries them forward. Membrane A nitrocellulose strip where the reaction is read. Liquid moves along it by capillary action. Test line(s) and control Each T line is a band of one drug fixed to the membrane. The C line captures the colored line antibodies whether or not drug is present. A strip has one C line, however many T lines it carries. Absorbent pad Soaks up the liquid and keeps it moving in one direction so the strip does not back-flow. Chapter 1: Understanding Rapid Test Kit Technology © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 8 of 217

heading: SECTION 1.2 CONTINUED
body: SECTION 1.2 CONTINUED Multi-line strips Many devices, including many Labb test kits, use multi-line strips: several test lines on one strip, each for a different drug, sharing a single control line. One strip can screen three or more drugs from the same flow of specimen. DIRECTION OF FLOW Conjugate pad holds antibodies for A, B, and C T1 Drug A T2 Drug B T3 Drug C C Control Line count, order, and drug assignment vary by product. Always read against the device label and package insert. Figure 1.2 A multi-line strip: three test lines and one shared control line (simplified, not to scale) How a multi-line strip works The conjugate pad holds a separate colored antibody for each drug, and each T line carries a different drug, so each line reacts only to its own antibody. Read each T line on its own: one drug can be non-negative while the others on the same strip are negative. The single C line confirms flow and reagent function for every T line on that strip. SINGLE-LINE STRIP MULTI-LINE STRIP Drugs per strip One Two or more Control line One, for that drug One, shared by every drug on the strip If the C line fails That one drug is invalid Every drug on that strip is invalid Identifying each line Strip is labeled with one drug Line position identifies the drug. Match each line to the label. GOVERNING RULE On a multi-line strip, no control line means every drug on that strip is invalid, even if some test lines appear. EXERCISE 1.2 1. Which part stores the colored antibodies before the test is run? 2. What gives a test line its visible color? 3. A three-drug strip shows T1 and T3 but no T2, and no C line. What do you report for each drug? 4. Why must you match each line to the device label before reading a multi-line strip? Chapter 1: Understanding Rapid Test Kit Technology © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 9 of 217

heading: SECTION 1.3
body: SECTION 1.3 Antibodies, antigens, and cross-reactivity An antibody recognizes a drug by its shape. Molecules that share part of that shape can also be recognized. That single fact explains most of the "unexpected" rapid test results you will ever see. The molecule being recognized is the antigen. On a drug test, that is the drug or its metabolite. The antibody is a Yshaped protein with binding sites shaped to fit the antigen. Manufacturers produce antibodies against a chosen target drug. Monoclonal and polyclonal antibodies MONOCLONAL POLYCLONAL Source Identical copies of one antibody A mixture of many antibodies Recognizes One specific part of the molecule Several parts of the molecule Effect on the test Narrower, more specific detection Broader detection across related compounds Either type can be used, and manufacturers choose different antibodies for the same drug class. This is one reason two brands of test can read the same specimen differently. Target drug and cross-reactivity Each test is built around one target drug (also called the calibrator). The printed cut-off, for example "BZO 200 ng/mL," is the concentration of that target drug the test is designed to detect. Other compounds with a similar shape may also bind the antibody. This is cross-reactivity. • Some related compounds react more strongly than the target, so less of them is needed to turn the test nonnegative. • Some react weakly, so much more is needed. • Some unrelated medications can react because part of their structure is similar. The package insert lists the compounds tested and the concentration of each needed to produce a non-negative. Reading that table is covered in Chapter 6. WHY IT MATTERS Class tests such as THC, BZO (benzodiazepines), BAR (barbiturates), OPI (opiates), AMP, and MET detect whole families of drugs, and each family member reacts differently. The cut-off on the label applies only to the manufacturer's target drug. EXERCISE 1.3 1. Define cross-reactivity in one sentence. 2. A BZO test is labeled 200 ng/mL. Does that mean every benzodiazepine is detected at 200 ng/mL? Explain. Chapter 1: Understanding Rapid Test Kit Technology © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 10 of 217

heading: SECTION 1.4
body: SECTION 1.4 The competitive format: why a line means negative Drug molecules are too small to be "sandwiched" between two antibodies, so drug tests use a competitive design. The drug in the specimen and the drug fixed on the test line compete for the same colored antibodies. A. Drug absent or below cut-off B. Drug at or above cut-off Antibodies are free when they reach the T line Specimen drug fills the antibodies first T C T C Free antibodies bind the drug fixed on the T line. Antibodies are already occupied and cannot bind Color builds up and a T line appears. the T line. No color builds up, so no T line forms. T line visible = NEGATIVE No T line = NON-NEGATIVE Figure 1.3 Competitive immunoassay. Y shapes are colored antibodies, and triangles are drug molecules. The C line forms in both cases. GOVERNING RULE On a rapid drug test, a visible T line means negative. A missing T line, with a valid C line, means non-negative. This is the opposite of a pregnancy test. Why lines can be faint Drug near the cut-off occupies some antibodies but not all. Fewer free antibodies reach the T line, so it forms but looks lighter. A faint line is still a line and is read as negative unless the package insert says otherwise. Do not compare line darkness between strips or devices. Chapter 1: Understanding Rapid Test Kit Technology © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 11 of 217

heading: SECTION 1.6
body: SECTION 1.6 Specimen types: urine and oral fluid Urine and oral fluid show different things. Urine mostly shows what the body has already processed. Oral fluid mostly shows what is circulating now. Tests are built for one specimen type only and cannot be swapped. URINE ORAL FLUID Metabolites (for example THC-COOH, Parent drugs (for example THC, benzoylecgonine) cocaine) Longer: commonly about 1 to 3 days for many drugs, Shorter: commonly minutes after and longer with frequent cannabis use use to about 1 to 2 days Best at showing Use over the past few days Recent use Collection Unobserved or observed Observed by default Needs temperature and validity checks Harder to substitute or dilute Set for urine concentrations Much lower, set for oral fluid Mainly detects General detection window Cut-offs concentrations Detection windows are general ranges. They vary with the drug, dose, frequency of use, individual metabolism, hydration, and the device cut-off. NEVER Never run a urine device on oral fluid, or an oral fluid device on urine, and never compare a urine cut-off to an oral fluid cut-off. The numbers measure different things. There is no conversion between them: drugs enter oral fluid and urine at different concentrations and at different times, so an oral fluid result of 4 ng/mL does not equal any particular urine value. Each specimen has its own cut-offs. EXERCISE 1.6 1. A donor used a drug two hours before collection. Which specimen is more likely to show it, and why? 2. Why are oral fluid cut-offs so much lower than urine cut-offs? Chapter 1: Understanding Rapid Test Kit Technology © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 1.7
body: SECTION 1.7 The rules: FDA clearance and CLIA Two federal frameworks shape how rapid tests are sold and used in the US. The FDA decides whether a device can be marketed and for what use. CLIA governs the facilities that test human specimens for health purposes. FDA • Rapid drug tests are medical devices. Most reach the market through FDA 510(k) clearance, which covers a specific intended use, specimen type, drug panel, and cut-offs. • The intended use statement in the package insert describes what the FDA cleared. Using the device outside that statement is off-label use. Some kits are not FDA cleared and are labeled for forensic or employment use only (Chapter 3, Section 3.10). CLIA TEST CATEGORY WHAT IT MEANS Waived Simple tests with low risk of error. The facility needs a CLIA Certificate of Waiver and must follow the manufacturer's instructions exactly. Moderate complexity More involved tests with personnel, quality control, and proficiency testing requirements. High complexity The strictest requirements. Any change to a waived test's instructions moves it into this category. GOVERNING RULE Follow the package insert exactly. Changing the specimen volume, dip time, read window, or reading method of a waived test takes it out of waived status. CHECK WITH YOUR COMPLIANCE ADVISOR Whether CLIA applies depends on how results are used. Testing used for clinical care generally requires CLIA certification. CLIA generally does not apply to testing done only for legal purposes, and may not apply to some workplace testing. State laws may add licensing, collector training, or confirmation requirements. Confirm the rules for your clinic's specific testing programs. EXERCISE 1.7 1. Where on your clinic's wall or files is your CLIA certificate kept, and when does it expire? 2. A coworker reads cups at 10 minutes because it is "easier to see." What is the problem? Chapter 1: Understanding Rapid Test Kit Technology © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 15 of 217

heading: SECTION 1.8
body: SECTION 1.8 Storage and handling Antibodies and membranes are sensitive to heat and moisture. A device stored or handled outside its limits may fail silently, reading negative when it should not, or showing an invalid control line. STORAGE Store within the temperature range printed on the insert and box (commonly room temperature or refrigerated). Do not freeze unless the insert allows it. AT THE TIME OF USE Check the expiration date on the pouch. Never use an expired device. If refrigerated, let the pouch reach room temperature before opening. Keep devices in the sealed foil pouch until use. Keep out of direct sunlight and away from heaters, vehicles, and damp areas. Open the pouch only when ready to test, and use promptly. Record the lot number with the result. Rotate stock: first expiring, first used. KEEP THE INSERT Keep a copy of the package insert for every lot you use, dated by when that lot was in service. Inserts are revised, and any later review of a result must use the insert that matched the device actually used. EXPIRED DEVICES The manufacturer guarantees performance only through the expiration date. There is no grace period: a device one day past expiry is treated the same as one a year past. Using an expired device takes the test outside its labeling, removes waived status for a CLIA-waived test, and makes any result easy to challenge. A supply shortage does not change this. Use another approved device or send the specimen to the laboratory, and quarantine expired stock and record its disposal. EXERCISE 1.8 1. Check your supply room today. Record the storage range on the box and the actual room condition. 2. Why does the lot number matter if a result is questioned months later? heading: SECTION 1.9
body: SECTION 1.9 Built-in limitations Every rapid test has limits that no amount of care can remove. Knowing them is what separates a correct report from an overstated one. LIMITATION WHAT IT MEANS IN PRACTICE Qualitative only The test says above or below the cut-off. It cannot tell how much drug is present. Cut-off dependent A negative means below the cut-off, not zero drug. A different cut-off can give a different result on the same specimen. Cross-reactivity Related drugs and some medications can trigger a non-negative. Some drugs in a class are detected poorly or not at all. Preliminary Non-negative results require laboratory confirmation before any decision is based on them. Adulteration and dilution Added chemicals or dilute specimens can lower or disrupt results. Validity checks reduce but do not remove this risk. Timing Reading outside the window, or a specimen collected outside the detection window, can produce a result that does not reflect use. Human reading Faint lines, lighting, and eyesight affect visual reads. Digital readers reduce this variation. Does not show impairment A result shows presence of a drug, not whether a person was impaired or when use occurred. GOVERNING RULE Report exactly what the device shows, in the device's terms. Never report more than the test can tell you. EXERCISE 1.9 1. A donor asks, "Does negative mean the test proves I never used?" Write how you would answer. heading: SECTION 2.1
body: SECTION 2.1 Drug classes and schedules Drugs are grouped by their effects (stimulants, opioids, sedatives, and so on) and by their legal control under the federal Controlled Substances Act. Both matter in testing: the class tells you which assay may detect a drug, and the schedule tells you whether a legitimate prescription can exist. SCHEDULE DEFINITION EXAMPLES I High potential for abuse Heroin, LSD, MDMA, most synthetic cannabinoids, nitazenes, non- No currently accepted medical use medical marijuana High potential for abuse, accepted Fentanyl, oxycodone, hydrocodone, methadone, morphine, medical use, and severe dependence amphetamine, methamphetamine (Desoxyn), cocaine, risk methylphenidate Moderate to low dependence risk Buprenorphine, ketamine, anabolic steroids, dronabinol (Marinol), II III state-licensed medical marijuana (since April 2026) IV V Low potential for abuse relative to Benzodiazepines, zolpidem, tramadol, carisoprodol, phenobarbital, Schedule III phentermine Lowest potential for abuse Pregabalin, low-dose codeine cough preparations Key ideas for testing • Parent drug and metabolite. The body converts most drugs into metabolites. Urine tests often detect the metabolite (benzoylecgonine for cocaine). Oral fluid tests often detect the parent drug. • Class assays. One test line may detect many drugs in a class, each at a different level (Chapter 6, Section 6.5). • Prescription status. A Schedule II to V drug may be lawfully prescribed. The MRO decides whether a prescription explains a result (Chapter 7, Section 7.5). A Schedule I drug has no prescription explanation. • States can differ. States may control substances the federal government does not (for example gabapentin, xylazine, or kratom), and may treat marijuana differently. EXERCISE 2.1 1. Why can a laboratory positive for oxycodone become a verified negative, but a positive for heroin (6-AM) cannot? heading: SECTION 2.2
body: SECTION 2.2 Panels and abbreviations A panel is the set of drugs a test covers. Panels are described by number (5-panel, 10-panel, 12-panel), but the number tells you little: two "12-panel" cups can test different drugs. Always read the actual drug list. Common panels PANEL TYPICALLY INCLUDES Federal workplace (HHS) Marijuana, cocaine, amphetamines (including methamphetamine, MDMA, and MDA), opioids (codeine, morphine, 6-AM, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, oxycodone, oxymorphone), PCP, and fentanyl (added by HHS in July 2025). Check DOT's current panel for DOT programs. 5-panel (non-regulated) Often THC, COC, AMP, OPI, PCP. Varies by product. 10-panel Often adds BZO, BAR, MTD, OXY, and MDMA or PPX to a 5-panel base 12- to 14-panel Adds items such as MET, BUP, FYL, TCA, TRA. Common in treatment and courts. Expanded / specialty Fentanyl analogs, nitazenes, xylazine, designer benzodiazepines, synthetic cannabinoids, cathinones, kratom, gabapentin, EtG. Usually laboratory-only. THE PANEL SETS THE LIMIT A negative result only covers drugs on the panel, detected at the panel's cut-offs. A donor using a drug that is not on the panel will test negative. Match panels to the client's real concerns, especially in treatment and court programs. Chapter 2: Drug Classes and Emerging Substances © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 2.4 CONTINUED
body: SECTION 2.4 CONTINUED How opioids convert Several opioids turn into other opioids in the body. Knowing these pathways explains many laboratory results that look confusing at first. Heroin 6-AM Minor: small amount of hydromorphone possible Morphine Codeine (codeine also yields a little hydrocodone) Hydrocodone Hydromorphone Oxycodone Oxymorphone Figure 2.1 Common opioid conversions. Blue boxes are metabolites that also exist as prescription drugs. What the pathways mean • Hydromorphone alone can come from a hydromorphone prescription. Hydromorphone with hydrocodone suggests hydrocodone was taken. • Oxymorphone with oxycodone is expected after oxycodone use. • Morphine with codeine is expected after codeine. The ratio helps the MRO interpret it. • 6-AM can only come from heroin. Without 6-AM, morphine alone cannot prove heroin use. • Poppy seeds can produce real morphine and codeine. DOT MROs require clinical evidence of illicit use for morphine or codeine below 15,000 ng/mL without 6-AM (Chapter 7, Section 7.5). EXERCISE 2.4 1. A donor with a Percocet prescription has oxycodone and oxymorphone on the lab report. Is the oxymorphone suspicious? 2. An OPI 2000 rapid test is negative, but the lab later finds oxycodone. Why? heading: SECTION 2.5
body: SECTION 2.5 Fentanyl, nitazenes, and new synthetic opioids Illicit fentanyl has largely replaced heroin in much of the US drug supply. It is often pressed into counterfeit pills made to look like oxycodone, alprazolam, or other prescription drugs, and it is mixed into other drugs, so many people are exposed without knowing it. Fentanyl and analogs • Fentanyl is detected by FYL tests, which target fentanyl, norfentanyl, or both. Choose devices that detect norfentanyl, which lasts longer in urine. • Fentanyl analogs (for example acetylfentanyl, para-fluorofentanyl, carfentanil) cross-react with FYL tests at widely varying levels. Some, especially carfentanil, are detected poorly. • Fentanyl in a stimulant or benzodiazepine user's specimen may reflect contamination of the supply rather than intended use. Report results neutrally. Nitazenes Nitazenes (benzimidazole opioids such as isotonitazene, metonitazene, protonitazene, and N-pyrrolidino etonitazene) are synthetic opioids, many more potent than fentanyl. They are found in counterfeit pills and mixed with other drugs. FACT TESTING IMPACT Not chemically related to fentanyl Not detected by fentanyl or opiate immunoassays Very potent Requires sensitive laboratory LC-MS/MS testing with specific nitazene analytes Present at very low levels New nitazenes appear regularly Laboratory panels must be updated continually. Ask your lab which are covered. Many are in Schedule I No prescription explanation Other new synthetic opioids Other novel opioids continue to appear, including brorphine and, more recently, cychlorphine and related "orphine" compounds reported by state health departments in 2026. Like nitazenes, they are not detected by standard opioid tests. GOVERNING RULE A negative opioid panel does not rule out nitazenes or other novel synthetic opioids. Only a targeted laboratory test can. EXERCISE 2.5 1. A treatment client overdosed last week, but all rapid tests including FYL were negative. What should the program ask its laboratory about? heading: SECTION 2.6
body: SECTION 2.6 Adulterants: xylazine, medetomidine, and others Many illicit drugs contain other substances added by suppliers, called adulterants or cutting agents. Some are inactive fillers. Others are dangerous drugs in their own right, and people are usually unaware they are there. ADULTERANT WHAT IT IS WHY IT MATTERS TESTING Xylazine ("tranq") Veterinary sedative (alpha-2 agonist), not approved for humans. Mixed with fentanyl. Deep sedation and severe skin wounds. Not reversed by naloxone. Laboratory. Drug-checking test strips for drug samples. Controlled in some states. Medetomidine Veterinary sedative in the same class as xylazine but far more potent. Spreading rapidly since 2024. Prolonged sedation, slow heart rate, low blood pressure. Severe withdrawal that may need intensive care. Not reversed by naloxone. Laboratory Emerging drug-checking strips Levamisole Veterinary deworming drug Common in cocaine Can damage white blood cells and skin Laboratory Local anesthetics Lidocaine, procaine, benzocaine in cocaine and fentanyl Mimic numbing effect of cocaine Laboratory Usually not reported Industrial chemicals For example BTMPS, a plastics additive found in the fentanyl supply since 2024 Unknown long-term effects Specialized laboratory Other drugs Fentanyl in stimulants Designer benzodiazepines in opioid supply Unexpected combinations raise overdose risk Standard or expanded panels depending on the drug WHAT THIS MEANS FOR TESTING PROGRAMS • An unexpected finding may be an adulterant the donor did not know about. Report neutrally. Interpretation belongs to the MRO or program. • Treatment programs should consider periodic expanded testing that includes xylazine and medetomidine where they are present in the local supply. • Drug-checking strips, such as fentanyl or xylazine test strips, are harm-reduction tools used to test a sample of a drug (a powder or pill dissolved in water), not a person's urine. They are not urine dip cards or forensic tests, and their legal status varies by state. EXERCISE 2.6 1. Why does naloxone not fully reverse an overdose involving xylazine or medetomidine, and should it still be given? heading: SECTION 2.8
body: SECTION 2.8 Cannabinoids Cannabinoids are the most complicated class in testing today. Natural marijuana, hemp-derived products, prescription cannabinoids, and synthetic cannabinoids all behave differently, and their legal status has been changing. SUBSTANCE SOURCE THC TEST RESULT NOTES Delta-9 THC Marijuana Detected (THC-COOH) Urine: 1 to 3 days single use, up to 30 days heavy use. Oral fluid: hours to about 1 day. Delta-8 THC Made from hemp CBD Usually detected (crossreacts) Lab may confirm only delta-9 THC-COOH. Ask for delta-8 testing (Chapter 6, Section 6.5) Delta-10, THC-O, HHC, THCP Hemp-derived, semi-synthetic Variable Metabolites differ Lab-specific analytes needed THCA flower Hemp sold as "legal" flower Detected THCA converts to delta-9 THC when smoked. Results look like marijuana use. CBD Hemp Epidiolex (prescription) CBD itself not detected Many CBD products contain enough THC to cause a positive. Not a legitimate explanation in DOT programs. Dronabinol / nabilone Marinol, Syndros / Cesamet Dronabinol detected Nabilone not Prescription MRO reviews Synthetic cannabinoids "K2," "Spice" For example MDMB-4en-PINACA, ADB-BUTINACA Not detected Hundreds of compounds. Rapid K2 tests target specific older ones, so lab NPS panels are needed. Can be far more toxic than marijuana. Legal status, September 2026 • Marijuana: Since April 2026, FDA-approved marijuana products and marijuana under a state medical marijuana license are in Schedule III. All other marijuana, including recreational marijuana, remains in Schedule I. A DEA hearing on rescheduling the rest of marijuana ended in July 2026, and a decision is pending. • DOT: DOT testing for marijuana continues unchanged. State medical cards are still not a legitimate medical explanation in DOT programs (Chapter 7, Section 7.5). • Hemp: A 2025 federal law redefines hemp by total THC, including THCA, delta-8, and similar cannabinoids. It is scheduled to take effect in November 2026, which will make most intoxicating hemp products federally illegal unless Congress changes it. • States: Most states allow medical marijuana and many allow recreational use. Many protect off-duty use for some employees. Non-regulated programs must follow state law (check current state law with counsel). heading: SECTION 2.12
body: SECTION 2.12 Why emerging substances evade testing New psychoactive substances are made to imitate known drugs while differing enough in structure to escape both drug laws and drug tests. As soon as one is scheduled or detected, replacements appear. Why standard tests miss them • Antibodies recognize specific shapes. Immunoassays are designed around known drugs. A new structure may not bind at all (Chapter 1, Section 1.3). • Test development lags behind. Designing, validating, and clearing a new rapid test takes far longer than it takes for a new substance to appear. • Very high potency means very low levels. Drugs such as nitazenes and some synthetic cannabinoids are active at amounts below what many methods can detect. • Laboratories must know what to look for. Even mass spectrometry only reports compounds the laboratory has added to its method. How programs respond STRATEGY HOW Know the local supply Follow state health alerts, CDC reports, DEA's National Forensic Laboratory Information System, and NPS Discovery trend reports Use expanded lab panels when indicated Order novel psychoactive substance panels when behavior, overdose, or program concerns don't match standard results Ask the laboratory what it covers Get a current list of analytes for each expanded panel and how often it is updated Document observations Factual notes on presentation help the program and MRO decide on further testing Don't over-trust a negative A negative means "not detected on this panel," nothing more GOVERNING RULE When what you observe and what the test shows don't match, the test may be looking for the wrong drug. Record what you observed and tell the program, following its policy. The program decides whether to order expanded laboratory testing. This does not mean calling the MRO. EXERCISE 2.12 1. Name two sources your clinic could follow to learn which substances are appearing in your area. Chapter 2: Drug Classes and Emerging Substances © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 2.13
body: SECTION 2.13 Staff safety and overdose response Clinics that test people who use drugs should be ready for an overdose on site, and should understand the real, not imagined, risks of handling specimens and devices. Fentanyl exposure: facts • Brief skin contact with fentanyl is very unlikely to cause overdose. Toxicology experts have found incidental exposure to be low risk. • Use standard precautions: gloves, no touching your face, and wash hands with soap and water (not alcohol sanitizer) after handling specimens. • If a donor brings powder or pills into the clinic, do not handle it. Follow your clinic's procedure. Recognizing an overdose OPIOID OVERDOSE SIGNS SEDATIVE ADULTERANTS • Unresponsive or cannot be woken • Deep sedation that persists after breathing • Slow, shallow, or no breathing. Gurgling or improves snoring. • Very slow heart rate, low blood pressure • Pinpoint pupils • Suspect xylazine or medetomidine when • Blue or gray lips and fingertips naloxone restores breathing but not alertness Responding 1. Call 911 and follow the dispatcher's instructions while you wait for emergency services. 2. Give naloxone (nasal spray) as directed. Repeat if no response after the time on the package. 3. Be ready to assist with breathing and start CPR as needed. The dispatcher can coach you. 4. Place in the recovery position once breathing: on their side, top knee bent, head tilted slightly back so the airway stays open and vomit can drain. Stay with the person. 5. Hand over to emergency services. Document the event and report it internally. CLINIC READINESS Keep naloxone in date and visible. Have every staff member complete naloxone training before relying on them to give it. Many free and low-cost online courses are available. Naloxone can cause sudden withdrawal: the person may wake confused, sick, or agitated, and occasionally combative, so keep a safe distance. Post the response steps, and review them after any event. Naloxone should still be given when xylazine or medetomidine is suspected, because opioids are almost always present too. EXERCISE 2.13 1. Where is naloxone kept in your clinic, and when does it expire? Chapter 2: Drug Classes and Emerging Substances © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: BEFORE YOU BEGIN
body: BEFORE YOU BEGIN How to use this chapter Chapter 1 explained how a rapid test strip works. This chapter covers the devices that hold those strips, the specimens they test, and the collection practices that decide whether a result can be trusted. Read each section, complete its exercise, then finish the chapter review. LEARNING OBJECTIVES When you finish this chapter you will be able to: 1. Compare urine, oral fluid, and hair as specimens, including detection windows. 2. Explain the difference between cassettes, dip cards, and integrated cups, and rank them by sample control. 3. Explain one-step (instant activation) and two-step (delayed activation) cups and when to use each. 4. Recognize the signs of a substituted or tampered urine specimen and respond correctly. 5. Compare oral fluid cassettes, integrated wands, and independent wands, and explain their regulatory status and THC limitations. 6. Run an oral fluid collection that avoids dry strips, including the primer sample. 7. Describe how rapid hair tests work and where they fit. 8. Explain the IVD, OTC, FUO, and EUO designations and how each limits a kit's use. 9. Choose the right kit for a given testing situation. heading: SECTION 3.4
body: SECTION 3.4 Cassettes and dip cards Cassette (pipette) kits The donor provides a specimen in a collection cup. The collector draws specimen into the supplied pipette and places the exact number of drops the insert specifies, commonly 3, into the sample well. ADVANTAGES WATCH FOR • Precise, repeatable sample volume • Too many or too few drops • Flat, easy-to-read result window • Bubbles in the pipette changing the volume • Low cost per drug. Good for a single-drug check • Moving the cassette while it runs. Keep it flat. or retest. Dip cards The collector removes the cap and dips the absorbent ends of the card into the specimen, no deeper than the max line, for the time stated in the insert (often 10 to 15 seconds), then lays the card flat to run. ADVANTAGES WATCH FOR • Timed, temporary contact with the specimen • Dipping past the max line, which floods the strips • Strips are not sitting over warm specimen, so • Dipping too briefly, which starves them humidity and condensation do not build up • Handling an open specimen. Wear gloves. around them • Many panel options. Easy to read. USING BOTH A clinic that screens with cups can keep cassettes or dip cards on hand to rescreen a questionable result from the same specimen before sending it to the laboratory. EXERCISE 3.4 1. heading: SECTION 3.5
body: SECTION 3.5 Integrated cups: one-step and two-step An integrated cup combines the collection cup and the test strips. The donor voids into the cup, the lid is sealed, and the strips run inside. Cups come in two activation styles. ONE-STEP (INSTANT ACTIVATION) TWO-STEP (DELAYED ACTIVATION) The strips contact the specimen as soon as it is in The specimen is sealed in the cup first. Testing starts the cup. Testing starts immediately, and the result is only when the collector activates the cup, for read at the time in the insert. example by pushing a key, pressing a plunger, or Advantages: Fastest workflow, no extra step to forget, and simplest to train. turning or tilting the device. Advantages: Collection and screening can happen at different times. Custody can be established before testing. The collector controls when the test starts. When to use delayed activation • Collect now, test later. A specimen collected in the field or after hours can be sealed, labeled, and signed for, then screened hours later by trained staff. • Chain of custody first. The seal and custody paperwork are completed before any result exists, so no one can claim the result influenced the handling. • Controlled timing. The collector starts the timer when ready, rather than the moment the donor hands over the cup. • Donor privacy. The donor does not watch the result develop in front of them. CHECK THE INSERT Confirm how long, and at what temperature, a sealed specimen may wait before activation. Specimen temperature must still be read within the time limit after collection, even if the test is activated later. Integrated cup cautions • Fill between the minimum and maximum lines. Overfilling can flood the strips: more liquid reaches the pads than they can absorb, washing reagents past the test zone and causing invalid results or lines that cannot be read. Underfilling can starve them: too little liquid reaches the strips, so lines may not form. • Tighten the lid fully and keep the cup upright on a flat surface while it runs. • Peel the label only as the insert directs, and read inside the read window.

heading: SECTION 3.6
body: SECTION 3.6 Urine collection integrity Urine is the easiest specimen to defeat because the donor is usually alone in the restroom. Substituted urine, dilution, and adulterants are all possible. Strong collection practice is the clinic's main defense. Check every specimen CHECK NORMAL SUSPICIOUS Temperature 90 to 100 °F (32 to 38 °C), read within 4 Outside the range, or a temperature strip that does not minutes of collection register Pale yellow to amber Clear like water. Unusual colors such as blue, green, or Color bright orange. Clarity Clear to slightly cloudy Excessive foam or bubbles, particles, oily film, and separated layers Smell Typical urine odor Bleach, ammonia, cleaning products, soap, or no odor at all Volume At or above the minimum line Well below the minimum without explanation Validity strips Creatinine, specific gravity, pH, and oxidant Any pad out of range pads in range When a specimen looks off 1. Document exactly what you observed: temperature reading, color, clarity, odor, and donor behavior. 2. Screen the specimen as normal and record the result. 3. Perform a second collection and screen right away, following your program's rules (under direct observation where required). 4. Keep and send both specimens to the laboratory if your program calls for it, clearly labeled. GOVERNING RULE Any specimen that looks off gets documented, screened, and followed by a second collection and screen. Never simply discard it. REGULATED PROGRAMS DOT and other federally regulated programs do not use rapid tests and have their own required steps, such as an immediate second collection under direct observation when temperature is out of range. Follow those rules exactly for regulated collections. Chapter 3: Rapid Test Kit Types and Specimens © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 3.6 CONTINUED
body: SECTION 3.6 CONTINUED Securing the collection site Most substitution happens because the restroom gives the donor privacy and the tools to tamper. Remove the tools and watch for the signs. BEFORE THE DONOR ENTERS Add bluing agent to the toilet tank and bowl. Secure or tape faucets and other water sources. Remove soap and cleaning products. Inspect the restroom for hidden containers or products. Keep the collection cup sealed until it is handed to the donor. DONOR PREPARATION Ask the donor to remove outer clothing (coats, jackets, hats) and leave bags outside. Ask the donor to empty pockets and show the contents. Have the donor wash and dry hands, then not wash again until the specimen is handed over. Tell the donor not to flush and to return the specimen promptly. Warning signs • Unusual bulges in clothing, or heat packs, straps, or tubing • Sounds of a container opening, or water running • A long delay, or reluctance to empty pockets or remove outer clothing • A specimen that arrives at the edge of the temperature range, or very quickly • Knowledge of the process that seems rehearsed, or requests to use a specific restroom OBSERVED COLLECTIONS Where the program allows or requires it, a direct observed collection by a same-gender observer is the strongest defense against substitution. Follow your program's written observed collection procedure. EXERCISE 3.6 1. A specimen reads 88 °F, is completely clear, and has no odor. List the steps you take. heading: SECTION 3.7 CONTINUED
body: SECTION 3.7 CONTINUED Oral fluid: regulatory status and THC performance Two facts separate oral fluid rapid tests from urine rapid tests, and clinics must disclose both to clients: most oral fluid devices are not FDA cleared, and many detect THC poorly. FDA clearance and CLIA status A rapid test must first have FDA 510(k) clearance before it can be CLIA waived. Most rapid oral fluid tests do not have 510(k) clearance, so they are not CLIA waived. At the time of writing, only one rapid oral fluid device has 510(k) clearance. Devices without clearance are typically labeled Forensic Use Only (FUO) or Employment Use Only (EUO), for legal or workplace testing (Section 3.10). WHAT TO DO WHY Check every oral fluid device's labeling Clearance and permitted uses differ by product and intended use Do not use an uncleared device for Clinical testing on human specimens falls under CLIA clinical diagnosis or treatment decisions Send every non-negative for laboratory The screen is preliminary regardless of format confirmation THC detection THC is the parent drug detected in oral fluid, and it is present at low concentrations. It is also sticky: THC binds to the collection swab and to the plastic of the device housing, so much of it never reaches the test strip. As a result, many rapid oral fluid tests detect THC poorly and can read negative even after recent marijuana use. NOT ALL DEVICES ARE EQUAL Some products use special, patented technology that keeps THC available to the strip, giving strong THC performance. OraFlo (ORF:31C) is one example. Check state law as well: some states limit oral fluid workplace testing. Ask manufacturers for THC performance data at and below the cut-off, tell clients plainly when a device has limited THC detection, and where marijuana use matters most, use a device with proven THC performance, urine, or laboratory testing. GOVERNING RULE A THC negative on an oral fluid device with poor THC performance is not evidence of no marijuana use. EXERCISE 3.7 CONTINUED 2. Why do many oral fluid rapid tests miss THC, and what should you tell a client? Chapter 3: Rapid Test Kit Types and Specimens © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 3.8
body: SECTION 3.8 Oral fluid collection practices The most common oral fluid failure is a dry strip: not enough specimen reached the strips for them to run. Most dry strips are caused by the donor, and most are preventable by the collector. Before collection • Wait period. Nothing in the donor's mouth for 10 to 12 minutes before collection: no food, drink, gum, candy, tobacco, vaping, mouthwash, or breath strips. • Mouth check. Ask the donor to open their mouth and show that it is empty. Remove anything found and restart the wait period. • Instructions. Explain that the donor must not chew, suck on, or squeeze the swab, and must not swallow oral fluid during the collection. During collection • Watch the donor the entire time. Donors may try to squeeze the specimen back out of the collector with their teeth, tongue, or cheeks, which leaves the swab dry. • Placement. Keep the swab between the cheek and gum or under the tongue as the insert directs, and let saliva pool naturally. • No swallowing. Remind the donor to hold oral fluid in the mouth rather than swallow it. • Saturation indicator. Wait for the indicator to change, or for the time in the insert. Do not remove the swab early. LABB RECOMMENDATION: THE PRIMER SAMPLE After the collector swab is removed, ask the donor to deposit all oral fluid remaining in their mouth directly into the oral fluid device. This primer sample adds volume and greatly reduces dry strips. Use the primer sample with devices whose instructions allow oral fluid to be added directly. Where a device's insert does not allow it, follow the insert. After collection • Keep the device upright and flat as the insert directs, and start the timer. • Confirm the control line and that fluid has moved across every strip before reading. • If a strip does not run: add more specimen (cassette, integrated wand), use a second swab (removable wand), or recollect with a new device (locking wand). Document what happened.
