heading: SECTION 3.9
body: SECTION 3.9 Rapid hair tests Rapid hair tests bring the long hair detection window to the point of collection. Unlike urine and oral fluid devices, most rapid hair test kits work the same way: the drug is extracted from the hair first, then the extract is run on a strip. How a rapid hair test works 1. Collect. The collector cuts a sample of hair as close to the scalp as possible from the back of the head, in the amount and length the kit specifies. The first 1.5 inches from the scalp represent roughly 90 days. 2. Extract. The hair is placed in the kit's extraction vial with its reagent and mixed, ground, or incubated for the time stated, which releases drug from the hair. 3. Test. The extract is added to a cassette or strip, which runs like any other rapid test. 4. Read. Results are read at the time stated in the insert. ADVANTAGES LIMITATIONS • Longest detection window, about 90 days • Does not show use in roughly the past 7 to 10 • Observed, non-invasive collection days • Very difficult to substitute or adulterate • Bleaching, dyeing, and relaxers can lower drug • Shows a pattern of use, not just a single event levels • Longer time to result because of extraction • Not all donors have enough head hair. Body hair covers a different, less defined period. • External contamination. Drugs in the environment, such as smoke or residue, can reach the hair surface. Laboratories wash hair and test for metabolites to separate use from contact. Rapid kits do not, so non-negative results need laboratory confirmation. PAIRING SPECIMENS Because hair misses the most recent days and oral fluid only covers the most recent days, some programs pair hair with urine or oral fluid for complete coverage. EXERCISE 3.9 1. A donor used a drug three days ago for the first time. Would a hair test show it? Which specimen would? Chapter 3: Rapid Test Kit Types and Specimens © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 3.10
body: SECTION 3.10 Regulatory status of rapid test kits Every rapid test kit carries a regulatory designation on its label and package insert. The designation tells you whether the FDA has reviewed the device, and it limits how and by whom the kit may be used. Using a kit outside its designation can create regulatory risk for the clinic and make results easy to challenge. DESIGNATION LABEL WORDING FDA STATUS CLIA STATUS INTENDED FOR NOT INTENDED FOR IVD In vitro diagnostic "For in vitro diagnostic use". Often "Rx only" or "for professional use" Requires FDA clearance (510(k)) for the stated Categorized as waived or moderate complexity Clinical diagnosis, treatment, and health assessment by professionals. Also commonly used for workplace and legal testing. Use outside the cleared intended use, specimen type, or user (for example a prescription-use device sold to the public) OTC Over the counter "Over the counter" or "for home use" Cleared for use by lay users without a prescription Waived Personal and home testing. Also usable by clinics as a waived test. Use without the confirmation step the insert describes. Treating a home result as final. FUO Forensic Use Only "For forensic use only" Not FDA cleared Not categorized. Cannot be performed as a CLIA waived test. Legal and criminal justice settings: law enforcement, courts, probation, parole, corrections Diagnosis, treatment, or health assessment, including clinical decisions in treatment programs EUO Employment Use Only "For employment use only" (sometimes "employment and insurance") Not FDA cleared Not categorized. Cannot be performed as a CLIA waived test. Non-regulated workplace testing, such as preemployment and random testing, where state law allows Diagnosis, treatment, or health assessment. DOT and other federally regulated testing. States that require FDA-cleared devices. intended use1 GOVERNING RULE Match the kit's designation to the purpose of the test. An FUO or EUO kit is never used to make a medical, diagnostic, or treatment decision.

heading: SECTION 3.10
body: CLEARANCE DECIDES THE STATUS, NOT THE WORDING FDA requires 510(k) clearance for a device to be an IVD. Some manufacturers still print "in vitro diagnostic" on inserts for workplace products, a practice left over from when all rapid tests were described that way. Regardless of what an insert says, treat a kit as IVD only if its clearance appears in the FDA 510(k) database. A kit without clearance is a workplace (EUO) or forensic (FUO) product, and is never used for clinical decisions. 1. A kit is an IVD only if it holds FDA clearance. Some package inserts for workplace or forensic products use "in vitro diagnostic" wording, a holdover from when rapid tests were routinely described that way. body: TRAINER USE Answer key Suggested answers. Accept answers that show the same understanding in the participant's own words. Section exercises EXERCISE KEY POINTS 3.1 (1) Oral fluid. It detects recent use of parent drug within hours. (2) Urine. Collection is usually unobserved, allowing substitution, dilution, or adulteration. 3.2 Hair. Drug does not appear in hair until about 7 to 10 days after use. 3.3 The strip receives exactly the volume it was designed for, every time. A cup's strips wick an uncontrolled amount from pooled specimen. 3.4 (1) The strips flood and may not run properly. The result may be invalid. (2) Discard the cassette, document it, and run a new cassette with the correct 3 drops. 3.5 Two-step (delayed activation) cup: seal and custody at collection, activate and screen later at the clinic, within the insert's time limits. 3.6 Document temperature, color, clarity, odor, and behavior. Screen the specimen. Perform a second collection and screen right away (observed where required). Send both to the laboratory per program rules. 3.7 (1) A second swab can be inserted into the same device if the first was insufficient. A locking wand cannot be removed, so a new device is needed. (2) THC is present at low levels and sticks to the swab and plastic housing, so little reaches the strip. heading: READ BEFORE YOU BEGIN
body: READ BEFORE YOU BEGIN Important notice LEGAL DISCLAIMER This chapter is not a certified DOT training. It is general educational material. It is not a DOT collector qualification course, breath alcohol technician (BAT) course, or screening test technician (STT) course, and completing it does not qualify or certify anyone to perform a regulated collection or alcohol test. All collectors must be certified before collecting any regulated sample. Anyone who collects a specimen or conducts an alcohol test under U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) or other federally regulated programs must first complete the qualification training and proficiency demonstration required by 49 CFR Part 40 and the applicable agency rules, and must keep that qualification current. The regulations control. Regulated collections must follow 49 CFR Part 40, the applicable DOT agency rules, and the HHS Mandatory Guidelines as currently in effect. Where this workbook differs from, or does not address, a regulatory requirement, the regulation governs. Regulations change. Always confirm the current rules. Non-regulated collections must follow the employer's or program's written policy, the laboratory's and device manufacturer's instructions, and applicable state and local law, which vary by jurisdiction. Not legal advice. This material does not provide legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel and your compliance advisor about the requirements that apply to your clinic and your clients' programs. HOW TO USE THIS CHAPTER Use this chapter to understand how collections work and to build good habits. For regulated collections, it is a companion to your certified training, not a substitute for it. heading: SECTION 4.2
body: SECTION 4.2 Collector qualification For regulated collections, qualification is a legal requirement, not a courtesy. A specimen collected by an unqualified collector can be challenged and the test cancelled. DOT urine collectors REQUIREMENT WHAT IT INVOLVES Basic information Knowledge of Part 40, the DOT collection guidelines, and agency rules Qualification training Training on collection procedures, completing the CCF, problem collections, fatal and correctable flaws, and collector responsibilities Proficiency demonstration Five consecutive error-free mock collections, including problem scenarios, monitored and evaluated by a qualified person Refresher training Repeat qualification training and proficiency demonstration at least every five years Error correction training Required after a collection error causes a test to be cancelled DOT alcohol testing personnel ROLE WHAT THEY MAY DO Screening Test Technician (STT) Conduct alcohol screening tests on approved alcohol screening devices (breath or saliva) Breath Alcohol Technician (BAT) Conduct screening and confirmation tests on evidential breath testing devices (EBTs) STTs and BATs must be trained on the specific devices they use, demonstrate proficiency, and complete refresher training on schedule. GOVERNING RULE No qualification, no regulated collection. Keep proof of every collector's current qualification on file. Non-regulated collectors Programs and some states set their own requirements. Labb recommends training every collector to the regulated standard, which produces more defensible specimens for every program. EXERCISE 4.2 1. heading: SECTION 4.3
body: SECTION 4.3 Steps common to every collection Whatever the specimen or program, every collection has the same backbone: the right donor, the right paperwork, an unbroken chain of custody, and a clear record of anything unusual. 1. Prepare the site. Private, secure area. Supplies in date and sealed. Unauthorized people kept out. 2. Verify identity. Check photo identification, or identification by an employer representative as the program allows. If identity cannot be verified, do not proceed. Contact the employer or program. 3. Explain the process. Tell the donor what will happen. Do not discuss results, medications, or likely outcomes. 4. Select the correct form and kit. Regulated or non-regulated. Correct laboratory. Correct panel. 5. Let the donor see sealed supplies. The donor watches kits and containers opened. 6. Collect under the specimen's procedure. Sections 5.5 to 5.9. 7. Seal in front of the donor. Tamper-evident seals applied, dated, and initialed by the donor as required. 8. Complete the form. Every required field. Signatures from collector and donor. 9. Document anything unusual in the remarks section. 10. Package and ship the same day where possible (Section 4.10). Refusals The collector documents what happened. The employer (and in some cases the MRO) decides whether it is a refusal. Common refusal situations include: SITUATION COLLECTOR ACTION Donor fails to appear, or leaves before the collection is Record the facts and times complete Notify the employer Donor refuses a required step (emptying pockets, observed Explain the consequence once, record the refusal, and notify collection, signing) the employer Donor admits adulterating or substituting, or is found with a Stop, document, notify the employer, and follow program tampering device rules Donor is abusive, or the collector feels unsafe End the collection, document, and notify the employer EXERCISE 4.3 1. heading: SECTION 4.5
body: SECTION 4.5 Laboratory-based urine collection Urine remains the most common laboratory specimen and the one most exposed to tampering. The steps below follow the regulated procedure. Non-regulated collections should follow the same steps unless the program's policy says otherwise. Collection steps 1. Secure the restroom: Bluing agent in toilet and tank, water sources secured, soap and cleaners removed, area inspected. 2. Prepare the donor: Outer clothing and bags left outside. Pockets emptied and shown. Hands washed and dried. 3. Hand over an individually wrapped collection container, unwrapped in front of the donor, and instruct the donor: provide at least the required volume, do not flush, return promptly. 4. Check temperature within 4 minutes: 90 to 100 °F (32 to 38 °C). 5. Inspect the specimen: Volume, color, clarity, odor, and any signs of tampering. 6. Split in front of the donor (regulated collections are always split): pour at least 30 mL into Bottle A and at least 15 mL into Bottle B. 45 mL total minimum. 7. Seal and label: Apply bottle seals, date them, and have the donor initial them. 8. Complete the form: Collector and donor sections. Remarks for anything unusual. 9. Package the bottles and the laboratory copy in the sealed specimen bag in the donor's presence. NON-REGULATED DIFFERENCES Programs may use a single bottle rather than a split, different minimum volumes, or on-site rapid screening before laboratory submission. Where a rapid test is used, the laboratory specimen must still be collected, sealed, and documented to the same standard. EXERCISE 4.5 1. The donor returns with 35 mL. What is the problem for a regulated collection, and what happens next? (See Section 4.5 continued.) Chapter 4: Specimen Collections and Procedures © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 4.6
body: SECTION 4.6 Laboratory-based oral fluid collection Laboratory oral fluid uses a collection device paired with a specific laboratory. Every collection is observed from start to finish, which makes substitution very difficult. Collection steps 1. Confirm the device is the one the laboratory accepts for the program, in date and sealed. 2. Wait period: Nothing in the donor's mouth for at least 10 minutes before collection (Labb recommends 10 to 12 minutes). Inspect the mouth. If anything is found, remove it and restart the wait. 3. Instruct: Do not chew, suck, or squeeze the collector. Do not swallow oral fluid. 4. Collect with the collector placed as the device directs, until the volume adequacy indicator shows enough specimen. 5. Observe the donor continuously. Watch for attempts to squeeze the specimen out or tamper with the device. 6. Transfer and seal the collector into its transport tube in front of the donor. For split specimens, both A and B as the device directs. 7. Label, initial, and complete the form. Record the collection time and any difficulties. DRY MOUTH VOLUME INDICATOR If the donor cannot produce enough specimen Never remove the collector before the indicator within the allowed time, follow the program's shows adequate volume. An underfilled device may procedure. In non-regulated programs, switching to be rejected, or may not allow the laboratory to a urine collection is often allowed. REGULATED ORAL FLUID When DOT oral fluid becomes available, collectors will need specific oral fluid qualification training and must use a device approved for the certified laboratory. Do not perform regulated oral fluid collections until both are in place. EXERCISE 4.6 1. The donor was chewing gum in the lobby. What do you do before collecting? heading: SECTION 4.7
body: SECTION 4.7 Hair collection Hair collection is observed, fast, and non-invasive, but technique matters: the laboratory needs enough hair, cut close enough to the scalp, with the root end clearly identified. Collection steps 1. Check the donor's hair. Head hair should be at least the length the laboratory requires (commonly 1.5 inches for a 90-day window). Hair extensions, weaves, and wigs cannot be used. 2. Clean the scissors with an alcohol wipe in front of the donor, and wear new gloves. 3. Select the area. The back of the head at the crown is preferred. Take hair from several spots if needed to reduce any visible gap. 4. Cut close to the scalp. Collect the amount the laboratory requires, commonly about the thickness of a pencil (roughly 100 mg). 5. Keep the root ends aligned and place the hair in the foil or collection card with the root end marked as the kit directs. 6. Seal, label, and initial the envelope in front of the donor, and complete the form. BODY HAIR DOCUMENT If head hair is too short or absent, many laboratories Record hair color, any visible bleaching or dyeing, accept body hair (for example chest, underarm, or the collection site on the body, and anything the leg). Body hair grows differently and covers a longer, donor reports about cosmetic treatments. less precise period. Record the body site on the form. REGULATED STATUS Hair testing is not authorized for DOT or other federally regulated drug testing. It may be used alongside a regulated urine test, never in place of one. Congress directed HHS in 2015 to issue hair guidelines. HHS proposed them in 2020 but never finalized them, and in 2026 SAMHSA said it will issue a new proposal, citing unresolved concerns about external contamination. DOT must then write its own rules. COMPANY AUTHORITY HAIR TESTING Many motor carriers add a hair test under company policy alongside the required DOT urine test. Use a separate non-DOT custody form and consent, never the federal CCF. The employer may act on the result under its own policy, but it cannot report it to the FMCSA Clearinghouse or treat it as a DOT violation in previous employer checks.

heading: SECTION 4.8
body: SECTION 4.8 Breath alcohol testing Alcohol testing measures current impairment risk rather than past use. In DOT programs it follows a two-step process much like drug testing: a screening test and, if needed, a confirmation test on an evidential device. The DOT two-step process STEP WHAT HAPPENS Screening An STT or BAT tests with an approved alcohol screening device (breath or saliva) or an EBT. A result below 0.02 is negative and the test ends. Waiting period If the screen is 0.02 or higher, a confirmation test follows after at least 15 minutes and must begin no later than 30 minutes after the screening result. During the wait the employee must not eat, drink, belch, or put anything in the mouth. Confirmation A BAT performs the test on an EBT: air blank reading zero, new individually sealed mouthpiece, result printed or recorded. CONFIRMED RESULT (DOT) CONSEQUENCE Below 0.02 Negative 0.02 to 0.039 Not a rule violation, but the employee may not perform safety-sensitive duties for a set period (typically 24 hours) under agency rules 0.04 or higher Rule violation. Removal from safety-sensitive duty and the return-to-duty process. Best practices for every alcohol test • Use devices on the NHTSA conforming products lists, and follow the manufacturer's quality assurance plan for calibration checks and maintenance. • Keep calibration and maintenance logs. An out-of-calibration device can invalidate results. • Test in a private area. Show the employee the sealed mouthpiece and the displayed result. • Record every step on the ATF (regulated) or the program's alcohol form (non-regulated). • Non-regulated programs set their own thresholds and follow-up, within state law. EXERCISE 4.8 1. An employee screens at 0.03. What happens next, and what must the employee avoid during the wait? heading: SECTION 4.9
body: SECTION 4.9 Fingernail collection Fingernail testing is a laboratory-based, non-regulated option that covers a long window, commonly several months. It is useful when hair is unavailable or too short. Collection steps 1. Check the nails. Only natural nails can be collected. Artificial nails, gels, and tips cannot be used. Follow the laboratory's instructions on nail polish. 2. Have the donor wash and dry hands to remove surface contamination. 3. Use clean clippers, new or cleaned with an alcohol wipe in front of the donor, and wear new gloves. 4. Clip from all ten fingers where possible, taking the amount the laboratory requires (commonly around 100 mg in total). 5. Place the clippings in the collection foil or envelope. Seal, label, and initial in front of the donor. Complete the form. Typical window FINGERNAIL HAIR Several months (fingernails) About 90 days (1.5 inches of head hair) Longer for toenails Cosmetic effects Less affected by hair Bleaching, dyeing, and relaxers can lower levels treatments Availability Needs enough nail length Needs enough hair. Not possible with extensions or shaved Not possible with artificial heads. nails Regulated use No No TOENAILS If fingernails are too short, many laboratories accept toenail clippings. Toenails grow more slowly and cover a longer period. Record which nails were collected. EXERCISE 4.9 1. A donor has a shaved head and acrylic fingernails. What options could you offer the program? heading: SECTION 4.10
body: SECTION 4.10 Packaging, shipping, and records A perfect collection can still fail in transit. Package correctly, ship promptly, and keep a record that proves what you did. Packaging • Place each specimen and the laboratory copy of the form in the specimen bag and seal it in the donor's presence. • Use the laboratory's shipping container. Include absorbent material for liquid specimens. • Keep the MRO copy and collector copy separate from the specimen, and send the MRO copy as the program requires. Shipping • Ship the same day where possible. If a specimen cannot ship immediately, keep it in a secure, locked area and document who had access. • Protect liquid specimens from heat. Refrigerate if the laboratory directs. • Follow shipping regulations for biological specimens, and the courier's labeling requirements. • Record the courier, tracking number, and ship time for every package. Records to keep RECORD WHY Collector copy of each custody form Proof of the collection and chain of custody Rapid test results, device lot numbers, package Needed for any later discrepancy review inserts Collector qualification and refresher records Required for regulated collections Defends every collection Alcohol device calibration and maintenance Supports the validity of alcohol results logs Shipping and tracking records Shows the specimen was secure in transit Keep records for at least as long as the regulations, your contracts, and your laboratory require. Ask your compliance advisor for your clinic's retention schedule. GOVERNING RULE If it is not documented, it did not happen. Every collection should be defensible from its paperwork alone. body: BEFORE YOU BEGIN How to use this chapter Chapter 1 covered the rapid test at your clinic. This chapter follows the specimen to the laboratory. heading: SECTION 5.1
body: SECTION 5.1 The two-step process Laboratories test in two steps. A fast, inexpensive screen sorts every specimen. Only specimens that screen non-negative go on to a slower, specific confirmation test. Most specimens are negative and are reported after step 1. Negative Reported negative Usually within 24 hours STEP 1 Specimen Screening received and accessioned Immunoassay on an automated chemistry analyzer plus specimen validity tests STEP 2 Non-negative Confirmation GC-MS or LC-MS/MS on a fresh aliquot Positive or negative with ng/mL Figure 5.1 The laboratory two-step process Question answered Technology STEP 1: SCREENING STEP 2: CONFIRMATION Is anything in this drug class above the screening Which specific compound is present, and cut-off? how much? heading: SECTION 5.2
body: SECTION 5.2 Step 1: Laboratory screening Laboratory screening uses the same antibody principle as your rapid test, run on an automated analyzer that measures the reaction with a light detector instead of your eyes. The analyzer compares each specimen's signal to a calibrator made at the cut-off concentration. The equipment Screening runs on high-volume clinical chemistry analyzers. Common platforms include the Beckman Coulter AU series, Roche cobas, Siemens Atellica, and Abbott Alinity and Architect systems. Specimens are loaded in racks, barcodes are read automatically, and the analyzer pipettes a small volume of each specimen into reagent cuvettes for every drug on the panel. Common immunoassay types ASSAY TYPE HOW IT SIGNALS EIA / EMIT (enzyme Drug in the specimen frees an enzyme to react. The analyzer reads the change in absorbance. immunoassay) CEDIA (cloned enzyme Drug in the specimen allows two enzyme fragments to join and react. donor) KIMS (kinetic interaction of Drug in the specimen prevents microparticles from clumping. The analyzer reads the change microparticles) in cloudiness. Like rapid tests, each laboratory assay has a target drug, a cut-off, and a cross-reactivity profile. A laboratory screen and a rapid test can disagree simply because they use different antibodies. Specimen validity testing (SVT) At the same time as the drug screen, the analyzer checks whether the specimen is consistent with normal human urine: TEST WHAT IT DETECTS Creatinine and specific Dilution or substitution (very low values). Specific gravity is often measured with a gravity refractometer. pH, oxidants, nitrites Added acids, bases, or chemical adulterants that can destroy drugs or disrupt the assay EXERCISE 5.2 1. Your rapid test read COC non-negative, but the laboratory screen was negative. Give one reason, other than error, this can happen. 2. What two validity tests identify a dilute specimen? heading: SECTION 5.3
body: SECTION 5.3 Step 2: Confirmation Confirmation separates the specimen into its individual compounds, then identifies and measures each one by its molecular fingerprint. It is performed on a fresh aliquot (portion) of the specimen, never on the material used for the screen. The equipment GC-MS LC-MS/MS Gas chromatography with mass spectrometry. Liquid chromatography with tandem mass The prepared specimen is vaporized and carried spectrometry. Compounds are separated in a through a long, thin column. Compounds leave the liquid stream, then filtered through two mass column at different times. The mass spectrometer analyzers in series. It is faster to prepare, very breaks each compound into fragments and sensitive, and can measure many drugs in one run. identifies it by their pattern. Many drugs must first It is now the most common confirmation method. be chemically modified (derivatized) to travel through the column. What happens during confirmation 1. Aliquot. A measured portion of the original specimen is taken. 2. Internal standard added. A known amount of a labeled version of each drug (often deuterated) is added to correct for losses during preparation. 3. Hydrolysis (when needed). Enzymes or chemicals free drugs that the body has bound to glucuronide, so the total drug can be measured. 4. Extraction. Solid-phase or liquid extraction removes salts, proteins, and other urine components. 5. Analysis. The extract runs with calibrators and controls in the same batch. 6. Identification. The compound must appear at the expected retention time with the correct ratio of ion fragments. 7. Quantitation. The concentration is calculated against the calibration curve and compared with the confirmation cut-off. 8. Review. A certifying scientist reviews the data, controls, and chain of custody before release. WHY CONFIRMATION IS MORE SPECIFIC A screen responds to anything the antibody recognizes. Confirmation measures named compounds. That is why a screen non-negative can confirm as a different compound (MDMA rather than methamphetamine), or as nothing above the confirmation cut-off. EXERCISE 5.3 1. What two pieces of evidence does the mass spectrometer use to identify a compound? Chapter 5: Understanding Laboratory Testing © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 5.4
body: SECTION 5.4 Accessioning Accessioning is the laboratory's front door. Every specimen is received, inspected, matched to its paperwork, and entered into the laboratory information system (LIS) before any testing starts. Most problems found here trace back to collection. Accessioning steps 1. Receipt. The shipping container is logged and opened. The date and time are recorded. 2. Seal inspection. Tamper-evident seals on each bottle are checked for breaks or signs of tampering. 3. Paperwork match. The specimen ID on the bottle label must match the custody and control form (CCF) or requisition. 4. Form review. Required fields are checked: donor ID, collector name and signature, collection date, test panel, and chain of custody entries. 5. Specimen check. Volume, leakage, and condition are inspected. 6. LIS entry and barcoding. The specimen gets an internal accession number and barcode that follows it through every step. 7. Aliquoting. A portion is poured or pipetted for screening. The primary bottle is retained for confirmation, and any split bottle (Bottle B) stays sealed. Problems found at accessioning TYPE EXAMPLES OUTCOME Fatal flaw Specimen ID on the bottle does not match the form. Specimen rejected, test cancelled, Broken or missing seal. No specimen or insufficient and recollection needed volume. No CCF. Correctable flaw Condition issue Missing collector signature. Missing or wrong fields on Specimen held until the collector the form. supplies a signed correction Leakage, heat exposure, delayed shipping Tested with notation, or rejected per laboratory policy GOVERNING RULE Most accessioning delays and rejections start at collection. A complete form and an intact seal are the fastest route to a result. EXERCISE 5.4 1. The specimen ID on the bottle ends in 4417. The form says 4471. What happens? 2. The collector forgot to sign the form. What will the laboratory need from your clinic? Chapter 5: Understanding Laboratory Testing © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 5.5
body: SECTION 5.5 How a specimen moves through the laboratory From courier pickup to final report, a specimen passes through a fixed sequence. A routine negative can clear in about a day after receipt. A confirmed result typically adds one to three more business days. 1. Collection 2. Transport 3. Accessioning 4. Aliquot 5. Screen + SVT Clinic, sealed, and shipped Courier or overnight Inspect, match, barcode Screening portion Chemistry analyzer Negative Non-negative or validity flag Negative review Released to report 9. Final report 8. MRO review 7. Data review 6. Confirmation Released to client If the program uses one Certifying scientist GC-MS or LC-MS/MS Negatives go straight to the report. Every specimen goes to storage after testing (Section 5.9). Figure 5.2 A specimen's path through the laboratory Chain of custody inside the laboratory Every time a specimen or aliquot changes hands or location, the laboratory records who, when, and why. This internal chain of custody is what allows a result to stand up to challenge. Breaks in it can invalidate a result. THE MRO STEP In federally regulated programs, and in many non-regulated programs, a Medical Review Officer (a licensed physician) reviews confirmed positives and contacts the donor about legitimate prescriptions before the result is final. This adds time but protects the donor and the employer. EXERCISE 5.5 1. List, in order, the steps a non-negative specimen passes through after the screen. heading: SECTION 5.6
body: SECTION 5.6 Laboratory cut-off levels Laboratories use two cut-offs for most drugs: a screening cut-off for the immunoassay and a lower confirmation cut-off for the specific analyte. Neither has to match your rapid test's cut-off. DRUG CLASS SCREEN CUT-OFF CONFIRMATION ANALYTE CONFIRM CUT-OFF Marijuana metabolite 50 ng/mL THC-COOH (Δ9THCC) 15 ng/mL Cocaine metabolite 150 ng/mL Benzoylecgonine 100 ng/mL Amphetamine / 500 ng/mL Amphetamine 250 ng/mL each methamphetamine MDMA / MDA Methamphetamine 500 ng/mL MDMA 250 ng/mL each MDA Hydrocodone / hydromorphone 300 ng/mL Hydrocodone 100 ng/mL each Hydromorphone Oxycodone / oxymorphone 100 ng/mL Oxycodone 100 ng/mL each Oxymorphone 6-Acetylmorphine (heroin) 10 ng/mL 6-AM 10 ng/mL Phencyclidine 25 ng/mL PCP 25 ng/mL Fentanyl 1 ng/mL Fentanyl 1 ng/mL each Norfentanyl Source: HHS federal workplace urine drug testing panel (Federal Register notice, 2026). Selected classes shown. Non-regulated laboratories may use different cut-offs and add classes such as benzodiazepines, barbiturates, buprenorphine, and methadone. Points to teach • Screen cut-offs apply to a class. Confirmation cut-offs apply to one compound. A specimen can screen nonnegative because several related compounds added together, yet each one confirms below its own cut-off. • Methamphetamine has an extra rule. In federal testing, methamphetamine is reported positive only if amphetamine, its metabolite, is also present at 100 ng/mL or more. • Below the cut-off is not zero. Laboratories can often detect drug well below the reporting cut-off. The limit of detection (LOD) is the lowest amount reliably detected. The limit of quantitation (LOQ) is the lowest amount reliably measured. • Know your laboratory's menu. Ask for the laboratory's cut-off list for every panel your clinic orders, and keep it with your rapid test package inserts. EXERCISE 5.6 1. A specimen confirms benzoylecgonine at 120 ng/mL. Is it positive under the federal panel? Would a 300 ng/mL rapid test likely have caught it? Chapter 5: Understanding Laboratory Testing © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 89 of 217

heading: SECTION 5.7
body: SECTION 5.7 What causes reporting delays A negative usually reports quickly. Anything that sends a specimen back through a step adds time. Knowing the common causes helps your clinic set expectations and prevent the avoidable ones. TYPICAL ADDED CAUSE WHAT HAPPENS Confirmation required Non-negative screen goes to GC-MS or LC-MS/MS in the next TIME 1 to 3 business days batch High concentration specimen Result is above the calibration range. Specimen is diluted and 1 to 2 business days reanalyzed (Section 5.7 continued) d/l isomer analysis Methamphetamine positive is separated into its two forms by a 2 to 5 business chiral method (Section 5.7 continued) days, more if sent to another laboratory Specimen validity result Dilute, adulterated, substituted, or invalid specimens need 1 to 3 business days confirmatory validity tests Paperwork flaw Correctable flaw held until the collector's signed correction arrives Until the correction is received Quality control failure A control in the batch is out of range. The whole batch is rerun. 1 business day or more Analytical interference Interfering peak or failed ion ratio. Reinjection or an alternate 1 to 3 business days method. Carryover check A specimen run right after a very high one is retested to rule out 1 business day contamination Add-on or send-out test MRO review Test not on the laboratory's own menu goes to a reference Several business laboratory days MRO must reach the donor for a prescription interview Depends on donor contact Transport and calendar Courier delays, weekends, holidays, instrument maintenance Varies Added times are general ranges for training. Your laboratory's turnaround times govern. DELAYS YOUR CLINIC CAN PREVENT Complete, signed forms, matching specimen IDs, intact seals, enough volume, correct temperature checks, and same-day shipping. Clinic-caused delays are the only delays that add no value to the result. Chapter 5: Understanding Laboratory Testing © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 5.7 CONTINUED
body: SECTION 5.7 CONTINUED High concentration specimens: dilute and retest A confirmation instrument is calibrated to measure accurately only within a set range. When a specimen's result is above the top of that range, the laboratory cannot report the number as measured. It must dilute the specimen and run it again. CALIBRATED (LINEAR) RANGE: reportable as measured Instrument response Specimen above range Measured x 10 = reported After 1:10 dilution LOQ / cut-off Upper limit of linearity Concentration in specimen (ng/mL) Figure 5.3 Above the upper limit of linearity the response flattens, so the specimen is diluted into the range and the result is multiplied back What the laboratory does 1. Flags the result as above the upper limit of linearity (ULOL). 2. Takes a new aliquot and dilutes it by a set factor, for example 1 part specimen to 9 parts diluent (1:10). 3. Adds internal standard, prepares, and runs it in the next batch with controls. 4. Multiplies the measured value by the dilution factor, or reports it as "greater than" the upper limit, per laboratory policy. 5. Checks the next specimen that ran after the high one for carryover, and retests it if needed. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOUR CLINIC A delayed result is not a sign of a problem with your collection. A very high concentration specimen simply needs a second analysis. Some laboratories report "greater than" the upper limit instead of an exact number. Ask how yours reports. Chapter 5: Understanding Laboratory Testing © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 91 of 217

heading: SECTION 5.7 CONTINUED
body: SECTION 5.7 CONTINUED d/l isomer analysis for methamphetamine Methamphetamine exists in two mirror-image forms, called isomers. Routine confirmation measures them together. When a methamphetamine positive needs to be explained, the laboratory runs a separate chiral test to find out how much of each form is present. ISOMER ALSO CALLED COMMON SOURCES d-methamphetamine Dextro, (S)-methamphetamine Illicit methamphetamine Prescription Desoxyn l-methamphetamine Levo, (R)-methamphetamine, Over-the-counter nasal decongestant inhalers (for example levmetamfetamine Vicks VapoInhaler). Metabolite of the prescription drug selegiline. Why it takes longer • It is a separate test with its own preparation, a chiral derivatizing agent or chiral column, and its own calibrators and controls. • Many laboratories batch chiral tests less often than routine confirmations, or send them to a reference laboratory. • It is usually ordered after the methamphetamine positive is reported, often at the request of an MRO, which adds another turnaround cycle. How results are read Results are reported as the percentage of each isomer. A result that is predominantly l-methamphetamine (a commonly used interpretive guideline is more than 80 percent) is consistent with an over-the-counter or prescription source. A significant d-methamphetamine percentage is consistent with illicit or prescription d-methamphetamine use. Interpretation is the MRO's or ordering provider's role, not the collector's. COLLECTOR NOTE Collectors should never tell a donor that a nasal inhaler "explains" a result. Record any medications the donor volunteers on the appropriate form or as your procedure directs, and let the review process decide. EXERCISE 5.7 1. Name three causes of delay your clinic can prevent. 2. Why can't the laboratory simply report a result above the upper limit of linearity as measured? 3. A donor uses a Vicks VapoInhaler. Which isomer would you expect a chiral test to show? Chapter 5: Understanding Laboratory Testing © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 5.8
body: SECTION 5.8 Split specimens (Bottle B) and retesting A split specimen collection divides one void into two sealed bottles. Bottle A is tested. Bottle B stays sealed and stored so the donor has an independent way to challenge a positive result. BOTTLE A (PRIMARY) BOTTLE B (SPLIT) About 30 mL in federal collections. Opened at About 15 mL in federal collections. Stays sealed and accessioning. Used for the screen and confirmation. frozen at the first laboratory until a split test is requested. How a split specimen test works (federal / DOT) 1. The MRO verifies a positive, adulterated, or substituted result and notifies the donor. 2. The donor has 72 hours from that notification to request a test of Bottle B. 3. Bottle B is sent, still sealed and under chain of custody, to a second, independent certified laboratory. 4. The second laboratory tests only for the drug or condition reported in Bottle A. 5. For drugs, it tests to reconfirm the presence of the drug. It does not apply the usual cut-off. Any reliably detected amount (at or above the limit of detection) reconfirms. 6. If Bottle B reconfirms, the result stands. If it fails to reconfirm, the test is cancelled. Retesting compared with split testing RETEST OF THE PRIMARY SPECIMEN SPLIT SPECIMEN (BOTTLE B) TEST Specimen New aliquot from Bottle A Sealed Bottle B Laboratory Usually the same laboratory A different laboratory Common use Non-regulated programs Federal and DOT programs Legal or client requests Some non-regulated programs Per the laboratory's policy Limit of detection (federal) Cut-off applied NON-REGULATED PROGRAMS Split collection, who may request a retest, the time limit, and who pays are set by the program and the laboratory. Make sure your clinic's policy states these before a dispute arises. EXERCISE 5.8 1. Why does a Bottle B test not use the normal confirmation cut-off? Chapter 5: Understanding Laboratory Testing © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 93 of 217

heading: SECTION 5.9
body: SECTION 5.9 Specimen storage and retains After testing, specimens are stored so results can be checked, retested, or defended. Negatives are kept briefly. Positives and other non-negative results are kept frozen for at least a year. SPECIMEN TYPE FEDERAL REQUIREMENT NON-REGULATED PRACTICE Negative No long-term retention required Commonly kept a few days to a Discarded after reporting few weeks Positive, adulterated, substituted, Kept frozen (-4 °F (-20 °C) or colder) for at least 1 Set by laboratory policy and state or invalid (Bottle A) year law. Often 1 year. Bottle B Kept frozen with the primary for at least 1 year Per program and laboratory policy Legal hold Kept longer when a written request is received Same during the retention period Request in writing Why storage matters • Stability. Some drugs break down at room temperature or with repeated freezing and thawing. Frozen storage protects what was measured. • Defensibility. A retained specimen allows a retest if a result is challenged, including in litigation or arbitration. • Deadlines. Once the retention period ends, the specimen may be destroyed. A request made after that date cannot be honored. GOVERNING RULE If a result may be challenged, send a written retention request to the laboratory right away. Do not wait for the retention period to run out. YOUR CLINIC'S OWN RECORDS Keep your copy of the custody form, rapid test result, device lot number, and package insert version for every specimen sent to the laboratory, for at least as long as the laboratory keeps the specimen. Federal programs require laboratories to keep records for at least two years. EXERCISE 5.9 1. A donor disputes a positive result 14 months after collection. What is the likely problem? Chapter 5: Understanding Laboratory Testing © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 94 of 217

heading: SECTION 5.10
body: SECTION 5.10 Laboratory hair testing Laboratory hair testing follows the same two steps as urine testing, screening and confirmation, but hair needs extra preparation first. Drug is locked inside the hair shaft and must be released, and drug sitting on the surface of the hair must be removed so it is not mistaken for use. How a laboratory tests hair 1. Wash. The hair is washed with solvents or buffers to remove surface residue, oils, and hair products. Some laboratories also test the wash itself to judge how much drug was on the surface. 2. Cut or grind and extract. The washed hair is cut or ground and incubated to release drug from inside the shaft. 3. Screen. The extract is screened by immunoassay. Results are reported in picograms of drug per milligram of hair (pg/mg). 4. Confirm. Non-negative screens are confirmed by GC-MS or LC-MS/MS. Telling use from contamination APPROACH HOW IT WORKS Wash procedures Remove drug deposited on the outside of the hair before testing Metabolite testing Metabolites are formed in the body, so finding them supports use. For marijuana, laboratories confirm THC-COOH, which smoke alone does not deposit. Metabolite criteria For cocaine, a positive commonly requires a metabolite, such as benzoylecgonine, above a set level and in a minimum ratio to the parent drug These methods reduce the risk from contamination, but they do not settle every case. HHS still lists external contamination as an unresolved issue for federal hair testing. Donors who handle drugs in their work, such as some first responders and laboratory staff, are the most likely to raise it. Quality and accreditation • Hair testing laboratories may hold CLIA certification, College of American Pathologists (CAP) forensic accreditation, New York State Department of Health approval, or ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation. • Proficiency testing programs, such as those of the Society of Hair Testing (SoHT), send blind samples to compare laboratories. • Some laboratories hold FDA 510(k) clearance for their hair screening assays.

heading: SECTION 5.10
body: Because hair is not federally certified, there is no HHS-certified hair laboratory list. Ask a hair laboratory which accreditations and clearances it holds before you send it specimens. heading: SECTION 6.1
body: SECTION 6.1 Why the package insert matters The package insert is the manufacturer's official description of what a test detects, at what level, and how well. It is the only standard a rapid test can be judged against. A result that matches the insert is a test that performed as designed, even when the laboratory disagrees. GOVERNING RULE The only way to know whether a rapid test performed as expected is to compare the laboratory confirmation report against the package insert for the exact device and lot used. Keep the right insert • Manufacturers revise inserts. Cut-offs, cross-reactivity data, and instructions can change between versions. • Keep a copy of the insert for every lot you use, dated by when that lot was in service. • Record the device name and lot number with every result (Chapter 1, Section 1.8). • When a result is reviewed months later, use the insert that shipped with that lot, not the current one. Key terms TERM MEANING Target drug (calibrator) The specific compound the manufacturer used to set the cut-off Cut-off The concentration of the target drug, in ng/mL, the test is designed to detect Cross-reactivity How strongly the test responds to compounds other than the target drug Class assay A test that detects a family of related drugs, each at a different level Analyte The specific compound a laboratory measures and reports Interfering substance A compound, often a medication, that can change a test result without being the drug the test is meant to detect EXERCISE 6.1 1. Where does your clinic keep package inserts today? Can you find the insert for a device used six months ago? heading: SECTION 6.2
body: SECTION 6.2 Anatomy of a package insert Inserts follow a similar structure. You do not need to read every word, but you do need to know where each answer lives. INSERT SECTION WHAT TO PULL FROM IT WHY IT MATTERS Intended use Specimen type, qualitative or semi- Confirms the device is being used as quantitative, and regulatory designation (IVD, intended OTC, FUO, or EUO, as described in Chapter 3, Section 3.10) Summary and principle Assay format (competitive immunoassay) Explains how lines are read Test panel and cut-offs Each drug abbreviation, its target drug, and Defines negative and non-negative for this its cut-off in ng/mL device Temperature range Explains failures from improper storage Storage and stability Time after opening Directions for use Sample volume, dip time, read window Reads outside these limits are invalid Interpretation of results How to read C and T lines, including faint lines Governs how results are reported Limitations Known interferences, adulteration effects, the Lists predictable failure modes preliminary-result statement Analytical specificity Every compound tested and the (cross-reactivity) concentration that produces a non-negative Interfering substances Common compounds tested that did not The key table in any discrepancy Rules out common medications affect results, usually at a stated concentration Precision near the cut-off Results at levels such as 25%, 50%, 75%, 125%, Shows how the test behaves close to the line and 150% of cut-off Method comparison Agreement with GC-MS or LC-MS/MS Shows expected disagreements near the cut-off NEAR THE CUT-OFF No immunoassay switches perfectly at its cut-off. The precision data usually shows mostly negatives at 75% of cut-off, mostly non-negatives at 125%, and mixed results in between. A specimen close to the cut-off can read either way on two devices from the same box, and both are performing as designed. EXERCISE 6.2 1. Which section would you check to see whether sertraline was tested as an interfering substance? Chapter 6: Reading Package Inserts and Resolving Discrepancies © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 102 of 217

heading: SECTION 6.3
body: SECTION 6.3 Reading the cross-reactivity table The cross-reactivity table lists compounds and the concentration of each needed to turn the test nonnegative. The lower the number, the more sensitive the test is to that compound. The target drug appears at exactly the cut-off. Percent cross-reactivity Some inserts also give a percent. It compares each compound with the target drug: % cross-reactivity = (cut-off ÷ concentration needed for that compound) × 100 PERCENT MEANING 100% Reacts like the target drug Above 100% (for example 200%) More sensitive: needs less than the cut-off (half, at 200%) Below 100% (for example 20%) Less sensitive: needs more than the cut-off (five times, at 20%) Not listed The insert makes no claim. Do not assume detection or non-detection. Worked example (illustrative values) A BZO test has a 200 ng/mL cut-off with oxazepam as target. The insert lists lorazepam at 1,000 ng/mL. % cross-reactivity = (200 ÷ 1,000) × 100 = 20%. Lorazepam must be present at five times the cut-off to trigger this device. EXERCISE 6.3 1. An AMP test has a 1,000 ng/mL cut-off (d-amphetamine). MDA is listed at 2,000 ng/mL. What is the percent cross-reactivity? 2. The same insert lists a compound at 500 ng/mL. Is the test more or less sensitive to it than to the target? 3. The lab reports a compound that is not in the cross-reactivity table. What can you conclude? Chapter 6: Reading Package Inserts and Resolving Discrepancies © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 103 of 217

heading: SECTION 6.4
body: SECTION 6.4 Cut-off levels: a negative is not zero A negative rapid test means the drug was below that test's cut-off, not that the donor did not use. Drug concentration is a continuous number. The cut-off is a line the manufacturer drew on it, and manufacturers draw it in different places. Example: cocaine Cocaine (COC) tests target benzoylecgonine and are commonly sold at 150 ng/mL and 300 ng/mL cut-offs. A donor specimen contains 201 ng/mL of benzoylecgonine. COC TEST USED CUT-OFF SPECIMEN AT 201 NG/ML READS 150 ng/mL assay 150 ng/mL Non-negative 300 ng/mL assay 300 ng/mL Negative Same donor, same specimen, same drug use, opposite results. Calling this donor negative on the 300 ng/mL test is correct reporting of that test. It is not evidence of no cocaine use. What moves a specimen across the cut-off • Time since use. Concentration rises, then falls. A late collection can read negative. • Amount and frequency of use. • Hydration. Dilute urine lowers concentration without changing use. • Individual metabolism. Know three numbers 1. The rapid test's cut-off for its target drug (from the insert) 2. The laboratory's confirmation cut-off for the analyte (from the lab report or menu) 3. The concentration the laboratory actually measured Laboratories usually confirm at lower cut-offs than rapid tests screen at. The federal benzoylecgonine confirmation cut-off is 100 ng/mL (Chapter 5, Section 5.6). A specimen can screen negative on a rapid test and still contain a reportable amount of drug. EXERCISE 6.4 1. A donor screens negative on a 300 ng/mL COC test. The lab reports benzoylecgonine at 240 ng/mL. Did the rapid test fail? Chapter 6: Reading Package Inserts and Resolving Discrepancies © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 104 of 217

heading: SECTION 6.5
body: SECTION 6.5 Class assays: THC, BZO, and BAR A cut-off printed on a class assay applies to one compound only: the manufacturer's target drug. Every other drug in the class has its own detection level, found in the cross-reactivity table. This matters most on THC, BZO, and BAR tests, where the class is large and manufacturers choose different targets. Benzodiazepines (BZO) A "BZO 200" test detects 200 ng/mL of its target drug. Common targets include oxazepam and nordiazepam, and the choice differs by manufacturer. The table shows the format of a BZO cross-reactivity table. The values are illustrative only. NEEDED FOR NON-NEGATIVE % CROSS- COMPARED WITH THE 200 NG/ML (ILLUSTRATIVE) REACTIVITY TARGET Oxazepam (target) 200 ng/mL 100% Equal to cut-off Diazepam 150 ng/mL 133% More sensitive Alprazolam 100 ng/mL 200% More sensitive Lorazepam 1,500 ng/mL 13% Much less sensitive 7- 5,000 ng/mL 4% Much less sensitive COMPOUND aminoclonazepam In this example, a donor taking prescribed lorazepam could have lorazepam at 1,000 ng/mL and still screen negative. That is the test performing as designed. GLUCURONIDES SPECIFIC ANALYTES Many benzodiazepines leave the body mainly as The lab may report a metabolite, such as alpha- glucuronide conjugates, which many hydroxyalprazolam, rather than the parent drug. immunoassays detect poorly. Laboratories often Look up that exact analyte in the insert's table. hydrolyze before confirmation, so the lab can measure drug the rapid test was never able to see. heading: SECTION 6.5 CONTINUED
body: SECTION 6.5 CONTINUED THC and barbiturates Cannabinoids (THC) Urine THC tests usually target 11-nor-9-carboxy-THC (THC-COOH), commonly at 50 ng/mL, with other cut-offs available. Other cannabinoid metabolites cross-react at different levels, including delta-8 THC metabolites from hemp-derived products, which many THC immunoassays detect. A COMMON THC DISCREPANCY A donor using delta-8 THC products screens THC non-negative. The laboratory confirms only delta-9 THC-COOH and reports negative. The rapid test reacted to a real cannabinoid the laboratory did not look for. Ask your laboratory which cannabinoid analytes it reports, and whether delta-8 testing is available. Several cannabinoid metabolites below their individual confirmation cut-offs can also add up to a non-negative screen. For oral fluid THC, see Chapter 3, Section 3.7: many devices detect THC poorly because THC sticks to the swab and housing. Barbiturates (BAR) BAR tests commonly target secobarbital or butalbital, often at 300 ng/mL. Barbiturates vary widely in cross-reactivity. Some, such as phenobarbital, may need concentrations well above the stated cut-off on some devices. Check the insert for the specific barbiturate the laboratory reports. GOVERNING RULE The cut-off on a class assay applies only to the manufacturer's target drug. Every other drug is judged by its own line in the cross-reactivity table. EXERCISE 6.5 1. A BZO 200 test reads negative. The lab confirms lorazepam at 900 ng/mL. The insert lists lorazepam at 1,500 ng/mL. Did the test perform as expected? 2. Why might a THC non-negative fail to confirm when the donor uses hemp products? Chapter 6: Reading Package Inserts and Resolving Discrepancies © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 106 of 217

heading: SECTION 6.6
body: SECTION 6.6 MDMA and MDA: the MET and AMP lines MDMA can make the methamphetamine (MET) line disappear, and MDA can make the amphetamine (AMP) line disappear. This happens through cross-reactivity, not because the body turns them into methamphetamine or amphetamine. The laboratory then confirms MDMA or MDA and reports methamphetamine and amphetamine not detected. Why it happens • MDMA is methamphetamine with an added ring structure (3,4-methylenedioxy-methamphetamine). MET antibodies recognize the shared structure. • MDA is the matching amphetamine derivative (3,4-methylenedioxy-amphetamine) and cross-reacts with many AMP assays. • The body converts part of an MDMA dose into MDA, so MDMA use can affect both lines. • MDMA and MDA are not metabolized into methamphetamine or amphetamine. If a lab finds methamphetamine with MDMA, the likely cause is that the product contained methamphetamine, which is common in street ecstasy. What to expect SUBSTANCE MET LINE AMP LINE LAB TYPICALLY REPORTS MDMA Often missing (non-negative) or faint, May be faint or missing, MDMA, often MDA depending on the assay's MDMA cross- from the MDA metabolite Methamphetamine and reactivity MDA Usually unaffected amphetamine not detected Often missing (non- MDA negative) or faint Amphetamine not detected A faint line is still read as negative. The table shows what a collector may see, not a new way to report it. What to do • Check the MET and AMP cross-reactivity tables for MDMA and MDA on the device in use. The degree of reaction varies widely by manufacturer. • If the device has a separate MDMA (XTC) strip, compare it with the MET and AMP lines. • Make sure the laboratory confirmation panel includes MDMA and MDA whenever MET or AMP is non-negative. If it does not, the result will look like an unexplained false positive. EXERCISE 6.6 1. MET non-negative. The lab reports methamphetamine not detected, MDMA 1,800 ng/mL. False positive? What do you check? Chapter 6: Reading Package Inserts and Resolving Discrepancies © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 107 of 217

heading: SECTION 6.7
body: SECTION 6.7 Other discrepancy patterns Beyond class assays and MDMA, a handful of patterns explain most of the remaining disagreements between rapid tests and laboratories. Opioid tests are not one test • OPI and MOP tests target morphine, commonly at 2,000 or 300 ng/mL. They detect codeine and morphine well, but most detect oxycodone poorly. That is why OXY is a separate test. • Poppy seeds can produce real morphine and codeine, which is a true detection, not a device failure. • Fentanyl tests target fentanyl or norfentanyl. Fentanyl analogs cross-react at widely varying levels. Medications reported to interfere with some immunoassays TEST MEDICATIONS REPORTED IN PUBLISHED LITERATURE AMP / MET Pseudoephedrine, bupropion, labetalol, trazodone, selegiline (which produces true l-methamphetamine) BZO Sertraline, efavirenz, oxaprozin THC Efavirenz. Some older assays with certain NSAIDs. OPI Some fluoroquinolone antibiotics, rifampin PCP Dextromethorphan, venlafaxine, diphenhydramine, tramadol TCA Quetiapine, cyclobenzaprine, carbamazepine Whether a medication affects your device depends on its antibody. Check the insert's interfering substances and cross-reactivity tables. Never tell a donor a medication "explains" a result. That is the MRO's role (Chapter 7, Section 7.9). Process and specimen causes • Read outside the read window, or a faint line misread as missing • Expired or improperly stored device • Too much or too little specimen (flooded or starved strip) • Dilute or adulterated specimen • Rapid test and lab testing different specimens, such as a rapid urine screen and a lab oral fluid test EXERCISE 6.7 1. An OPI 300 test reads negative. The lab confirms oxycodone at 800 ng/mL. What is the most likely explanation? Chapter 6: Reading Package Inserts and Resolving Discrepancies © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 108 of 217

heading: SECTION 6.8
body: SECTION 6.8 The discrepancy review A laboratory "negative" on a rapid-test non-negative is not automatically a false positive. A rapid-test negative that the laboratory finds drug in is not automatically a false negative. Follow the same steps every time, and write down the answer. Review steps 1. Get the full laboratory report, not just the summary: each analyte tested, the concentration found, and the laboratory's confirmation cut-off for each. 2. Pull the package insert for the exact device and lot used. 3. Note the target drug and cut-off for each drug line in question. 4. Look up each analyte the lab found in the cross-reactivity table. Note the concentration needed to trigger a nonnegative. 5. Compare. At or above its cross-reactivity level: a non-negative was expected. Below: a negative was expected. Near the level: either result is within normal performance. 6. Look for what the lab did not test. Compounds the insert lists as cross-reactive but the lab did not measure (MDMA on a MET line, delta-8 on a THC line). 7. Rule out process causes: Read time, faint lines, device condition, specimen volume, dilution, transport time. 8. Document the conclusion on the worksheet and keep it with the lab report, insert, and device record. GOVERNING RULE Judge the device by its insert, not by the laboratory's positive or negative call. WHEN TO CONTACT THE MANUFACTURER If the review finds no explanation, no process error, and a laboratory result clearly outside what the insert predicts, report it to the manufacturer with the lot number, and keep remaining devices from that lot for their investigation. Chapter 6: Reading Package Inserts and Resolving Discrepancies © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 109 of 217

heading: SECTION 6.9
body: SECTION 6.9 Worked cases Each case uses illustrative insert values. Work through them with the review steps before reading the conclusion. CASE A MET NON-NEGATIVE, LAB NEGATIVE Lab: Methamphetamine not detected. MDMA 1,800 ng/mL. MDA 300 ng/mL. Insert: MET cut-off 1,000 ng/mL (dmethamphetamine). MDMA listed at 1,500 ng/mL. Conclusion: MDMA at 1,800 ng/mL is above the 1,500 ng/mL needed. Performed as expected. CASE B BZO NEGATIVE, LAB POSITIVE Lab: Lorazepam 900 ng/mL after hydrolysis. Insert: BZO cut-off 200 ng/mL (oxazepam). Lorazepam listed at 1,500 ng/mL. Conclusion: 900 ng/mL is below the 1,500 ng/mL needed, and hydrolysis measured conjugated drug the device detects poorly. Performed as expected. CASE C THC NON-NEGATIVE, LAB NEGATIVE Lab: Delta-9 THC-COOH 8 ng/mL (confirmation cut-off 15 ng/mL). Delta-8 not tested. Insert: THC cut-off 50 ng/ mL. Delta-8 THC-COOH listed at 60 ng/mL. Conclusion: Cannabinoids were present but below the lab's cut-off, and the likely cross-reactant was not tested. Unable to determine. Request delta-8 testing. CASE D COC NEGATIVE, LAB POSITIVE Lab: Benzoylecgonine 201 ng/mL (confirmation cut-off 100 ng/mL). Insert: COC cut-off 300 ng/mL. Conclusion: 201 ng/mL is below the device's 300 ng/mL cut-off but above the lab's 100 ng/mL cut-off. Performed as expected. A 150 ng/mL device would likely have flagged it. heading: SECTION 7.1
body: SECTION 7.1 What an MRO is A Medical Review Officer is a licensed physician who reviews drug test results before they become final. The MRO is the one person in the process with both the medical training and the authority to decide whether a laboratory result means drug misuse. Qualifications (DOT) REQUIREMENT WHAT IT MEANS Licensed physician An MD or DO licensed to practice medicine Knowledge Clinical knowledge of substance use disorders, drug testing, and the federal rules Qualification training and exam Completes MRO training and passes an examination from a recognized MRO certification organization Continuing education Ongoing continuing education and periodic requalification to keep the credential current Independence The MRO must be independent and impartial. The MRO is not an advocate for the employer or the donor. The MRO is an advocate for the accuracy and integrity of the testing process. In federally regulated testing, an MRO may not have a financial relationship with the laboratory that could create a conflict of interest. GOVERNING RULE A laboratory result is not a final result. In an MRO program, only the MRO's verified result is reported to the employer. What the MRO does and does not do THE MRO DOES THE MRO DOES NOT Review custody paperwork. Interview donors. Act for the employer against the donor. Make Evaluate prescriptions and medical explanations. employment decisions. Accept a result that fails Verify, downgrade, or cancel results. Report safety custody review. Share a donor's medical information concerns. Keep medical information confidential. without a legal basis. EXERCISE 7.1 1. In one sentence, whose side is the MRO on? Chapter 7: Understanding the MRO Process © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 118 of 217

heading: SECTION 7.2
body: SECTION 7.2 Where the MRO fits The MRO sits between the laboratory and the employer. The laboratory reports to the MRO, not to the employer. The employer receives only the MRO's verified result. Clinic / collector Laboratory Collects, completes custody form Screens and confirms MRO Employer (DER) Administrative review Receives verified result only Medical review Verified result MRO copy of the custody form (sent directly) Donor Verification interview Figure 7.1 Results flow through the MRO. DER = Designated Employer Representative. What the MRO receives • From the laboratory: The laboratory result and the laboratory's copy of the custody and control form, including quantitative values for confirmed drugs. • From the collector: The MRO copy of the custody form, sent directly by the collection site. • From the donor: Information given during the verification interview, and prescription or medical records the donor or the prescriber provides. NEGATIVE RESULTS MROs review negatives too. Negatives receive an administrative review of the paperwork, which trained MRO staff may perform under the MRO's supervision. Non-negative results always receive the MRO's personal medical review. EXERCISE 7.2 1. Why does the laboratory send results to the MRO rather than to the employer? Chapter 7: Understanding the MRO Process © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 119 of 217

heading: SECTION 7.3
body: SECTION 7.3 How the MRO reviews a result Every MRO review has two parts. The administrative review asks whether the test was done correctly. The medical review asks what the result means for this donor. A result must pass the first before the second matters. heading: SECTION 7.5 CONTINUED
body: SECTION 7.5 CONTINUED Verified negative with a safety concern A verified negative protects the donor's privacy, but it does not ignore safety. If the prescribed medication, or the underlying condition, makes the donor medically unqualified or a significant safety risk in a safetysensitive job, the MRO has a duty to act. 1. The MRO reports the result as negative. 2. The MRO tells the donor about the safety concern and gives a short period (typically 5 days) for the prescribing physician to contact the MRO, for example to confirm a change of medication. 3. If the concern is not resolved, the MRO reports the safety concern to the employer or the appropriate authority (for example, the employer's designated representative, or a licensing body or regulator where a rule requires reporting), sharing only the information needed to address it. WHY THIS MATTERS TO CLINICS AND EMPLOYERS The employer learns about a genuine safety risk without learning the donor's diagnosis or full medical history. That balance is one of the main legal protections the MRO provides (Section 7.8). GOVERNING RULE A laboratory positive plus a legitimate medical explanation equals a verified negative. The explanation must be verified, not just claimed. EXERCISE 7.5 1. A donor's specimen confirms oxycodone. The donor has a current oxycodone prescription. What does the employer receive? 2. heading: SECTION 7.7
body: SECTION 7.7 How donors interact with the MRO The verification interview is the donor's opportunity to be heard before a result becomes final. It is a private conversation between a physician and the donor. The verification interview 1. Identification. The MRO identifies themselves and confirms the donor's identity. 2. Disclosure. The MRO explains the laboratory result and the donor's right to explain it. 3. Questions. The MRO asks about prescriptions, recent medical or dental care, and anything else that could explain the result. 4. Records. If needed, the donor provides prescription records, or the MRO contacts the prescriber or pharmacy. The MRO may allow a short period (typically up to 5 days) for records to arrive. 5. Split specimen notice. For a verified positive, adulterated, or substituted result, the MRO tells the donor about the 72-hour right to request a Bottle B test. 6. Decision. The MRO verifies the result and reports it. DONOR RIGHTS DONOR RESPONSIBILITIES • Be told the result and speak with the MRO before • Respond promptly to the MRO or DER it is verified • Provide truthful information • Offer a legitimate medical explanation • Supply records or prescriber contact when asked • Request a split specimen test within 72 hours • Carry the burden of proving a medical • Have medical information kept confidential explanation Medications at collection In DOT collections, collectors do not ask about or record medications on the custody form. Donors may make private notes on their own copy to help them during the MRO interview. The MRO, not the collector, is the right person to hear about medications. EXERCISE 7.7 1. A donor at your front desk wants to show you their prescription bottle before collection. What do you say? Chapter 7: Understanding the MRO Process © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 7.8
body: SECTION 7.8 How the MRO protects everyone The MRO is the process's legal safeguard. By checking that every rule was followed, that the chain of custody is intact, and that medical explanations are handled by a physician, the MRO keeps a flawed or misunderstood result from ever reaching the employer. WHO RISK WITHOUT AN MRO HOW THE MRO PROTECTS THEM Clinic Staff interpret results or give medical opinions. A A physician makes the determination, not clinic paperwork error leads to a wrongful action staff. Administrative review catches collection errors traced back to the clinic. and cancels flawed tests before they cause harm. Labeled a drug user for lawful medication use. Verification interview and legitimate medical Private medical information exposed to the explanation review. Medical details stay employer. confidential. Split specimen rights preserved. Acts on an unverified result. Faces wrongful Receives only a verified, defensible result. Avoids termination, disability discrimination, or privacy receiving medical information. Safety concerns are claims. Learns medical information it should not reported in a controlled way. Donor Employer hold. The chain of custody check A drug test is only as strong as its documentation. Opposing counsel in a dispute will look first at the custody form: signatures, times, seals, specimen IDs, and every hand-off. The MRO's administrative review is the last point where a broken chain is caught and the test cancelled, rather than defended later in a hearing or lawsuit. PROTECTIONS THE MRO PROCESS SUPPORTS • Regulatory compliance: Results reported in the form and time the rules require. • Privacy: Medical information shared only where the rules allow, such as a safety concern. • Disability and medication laws: Lawful prescription use is not reported as a positive. • Due process: The donor is heard before the result is final. • Documentation: A complete record of the review that can be produced if challenged. GOVERNING RULE It is better for a flawed test to be cancelled by the MRO than defended by the employer. EXERCISE 7.8 1. Name one way the MRO process protects the clinic, and one way it protects the employer. Chapter 7: Understanding the MRO Process © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 7.9
body: SECTION 7.9 The clinic's role in the MRO process The MRO can only review what the clinic documents. Most MRO cancellations trace back to collection. Every item below protects the result and the clinic. CLINIC CHECKLIST Complete every required field on the custody form, including collector signature and printed name. Confirm the specimen ID on the bottle label matches the form before the donor leaves. Record temperature, observed collections, and any unusual events in the remarks. Send the MRO copy of the form to the MRO promptly, as the program requires. Respond quickly to any request for a signed correction of a flaw. Keep the MRO's name and phone number available for donors who call. Never discuss results, medications, or likely outcomes with donors. Be ready to perform recollections under direct observation when the MRO directs. Non-regulated programs TOPIC WHAT CAN DIFFER MRO use MRO review is not federally required, but it is strongly recommended and some states require it for workplace testing. Marijuana State laws on medical or recreational marijuana may affect how results are handled and reported. Timelines and retests Response windows and split testing are set by the program and the MRO service. Rapid test results An MRO verifies laboratory-confirmed results. A rapid test non-negative is a screen and should be sent for confirmation before any MRO decision. EXERCISE 7.9 1. heading: BEFORE YOU BEGIN
body: BEFORE YOU BEGIN How to use this chapter Alcohol is legal, widely used, and leaves the body quickly. That makes alcohol testing different from drug testing: the question is often not "was alcohol used?" but "how recently, and how much?" Different tests answer different versions of that question. LEARNING OBJECTIVES When you finish this chapter you will be able to: 1. Explain how the body absorbs and eliminates alcohol. 2. Compare the detection windows of breath, urine, blood, and hair alcohol tests. 3. Explain what EtG, EtS, and PEth are and what each shows. 4. Recognize incidental exposure and why low-level results need caution. 5. Choose the right alcohol test for a program's purpose. 6. Collect dried blood spot specimens for PEth correctly. 7. Give donors clear instructions about alcohol-containing products. Chapter contents 8.1 How alcohol moves through the body 8.2 Detection windows 8.3 Breath and saliva alcohol 8.4 Urine ethanol 8.5 EtG and EtS 8.6 PEth 8.7 Hair alcohol markers 8.8 Indirect clinical markers 8.9 Choosing the right alcohol test 8.10 Incidental exposure Tools: donor product advisory, test selection card Chapter review Answer key (trainer use) REGULATED ALCOHOL TESTING DOT alcohol testing uses breath or saliva screening and evidential breath confirmation only, performed by qualified STTs and BATs (Chapter 4, Section 4.8). The biomarkers in this chapter are used in non-regulated programs such as treatment, courts, monitoring programs, and some employers. heading: SECTION 8.1
body: SECTION 8.1 How alcohol moves through the body Alcohol (ethanol) is absorbed within minutes, reaches every part of the body, and is eliminated at a fairly steady rate. The body clears most of it within hours, which is why direct alcohol tests have short windows. STAGE WHAT HAPPENS Absorption Mostly from the stomach and small intestine. Blood levels usually peak within 30 to 90 minutes, later with food. Distribution Alcohol spreads through body water, which is why breath, saliva, and blood levels track each other Metabolism Most alcohol is broken down in the liver, first to acetaldehyde and then to acetate Elimination rate On average about 0.015 g/dL of blood alcohol per hour, roughly one standard drink per hour. Varies by person. Minor pathways A very small fraction, well under 1 percent, is converted into EtG, EtS, and PEth, which last much longer than alcohol itself Direct and indirect markers DIRECT MARKERS INDIRECT MARKERS Alcohol itself, or compounds formed only when Changes in the body caused by heavy drinking over alcohol is present: ethanol, EtG, EtS, PEth, and fatty time, such as liver enzymes. They can be raised by acid ethyl esters (FAEE). A direct marker is specific to other conditions, so they are less specific (Section drinking. 8.8). GOVERNING RULE Alcohol tests measure presence and time frame, not impairment, except breath and blood alcohol tests taken at the time in question. EXERCISE 8.1 1. A donor's breath alcohol is 0.060 at 8 a.m. At the average elimination rate, roughly when would it reach zero? Chapter 8: Alcohol Testing and Biomarkers © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 134 of 217

heading: SECTION 8.2
body: SECTION 8.2 Detection windows Each alcohol test looks through a different window. Breath and blood alcohol show the last several hours. EtG and EtS in urine show the last one to three days. PEth shows the last several weeks. Hair shows the last three months. Breath / saliva / blood ethanol Urine ethanol Urine EtG and EtS Blood (dried spot) PEth Hair not yet in hair (about 1 week) EtG 1 hr 6 hr 1 day 3 days 1 wk 2 wks 4 wks 90 days Time since drinking (log scale) Figure 8.1 General alcohol detection windows. Solid bars show the common range. Light bars show longer detection after heavy drinking. TEST SPECIMEN TYPICAL WINDOW Ethanol Breath, saliva, blood While alcohol is in the body: hours, depending on the amount consumed Ethanol Urine Up to about 12 hours EtG and EtS Urine Up to about 1 to 3 days. Up to about 80 hours after heavy drinking. PEth Blood (dried blood About 2 to 4 weeks, depending on how much and how often spot) EtG, FAEE Hair Up to about 3 months (3 cm of head hair), after about a one-week lag General approximate ranges for training. Actual windows depend on amount and pattern of drinking, individual metabolism, hydration, cut-off, and laboratory method. EXERCISE 8.2 1. A court wants to know whether a person drank at all during a 30-day supervision period. Which single test covers most of that period?
