heading: SECTION 8.3
body: SECTION 8.3 Breath and saliva alcohol Breath and saliva tests measure alcohol in the body right now. Of the tests clinics perform, they are the only alcohol tests that relate to current impairment, which is why DOT and most workplace programs use them for reasonable suspicion and post-accident testing. DEVICE HOW IT WORKS TYPICAL USE Evidential breath tester (EBT) Fuel cell or infrared analysis of deep lung air. Prints DOT confirmation. Any result results. Built-in checks. that may be challenged. Handheld fuel cell or semiconductor sensor Screening Breath screening device Non-regulated programs Saliva screening device Pad or strip changes color in proportion to saliva Screening where breath devices alcohol are not practical Best practices • Use approved devices. For DOT, devices must be on NHTSA's conforming products lists. Non-regulated programs are more defensible using the same devices. • Wait out mouth alcohol. Mouthwash, breath spray, and recent drinks leave alcohol in the mouth that can raise a reading. Observe at least 15 minutes, and no more than 30 minutes, with nothing in the mouth before a confirmation test. • Follow the device's quality plan: Calibration checks, air blanks, and maintenance logs (Chapter 11, Section 11.1). • Confirm screens of 0.02 or higher on an evidential device in DOT programs (Chapter 4, Section 4.8). • Read saliva devices on time and store them as labeled. Color development changes after the read time. SEMICONDUCTOR SENSORS Low-cost semiconductor breath devices can react to substances other than alcohol and drift over time. Fuel cell devices are more specific and stable. For any result a client may act on, use a fuel cell or evidential device. EXERCISE 8.3 1. A donor used mouthwash five minutes before a breath test. What should you do? Chapter 8: Alcohol Testing and Biomarkers © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 136 of 217

heading: SECTION 8.4
body: SECTION 8.4 Urine ethanol Laboratories can measure alcohol itself in urine, but it is one of the weakest alcohol tests. Its window is short, it does not match blood alcohol at any moment, and in some specimens alcohol can be created after collection. Limitations • Short window: Up to about 12 hours, similar to breath. • Poor timing: Urine collects over hours in the bladder, so the level does not reflect alcohol in the blood at collection time. • Formation after collection: In urine containing sugar (for example from uncontrolled diabetes) and yeast or bacteria, fermentation can produce alcohol in the container after collection, especially if the specimen sits warm. WHEN A URINE ETHANOL RESULT IS QUESTIONED A positive urine ethanol result with negative EtG and EtS points to alcohol formed after collection rather than drinking. This is why EtG and EtS, rather than ethanol alone, are preferred for urine alcohol monitoring. Handling urine specimens for alcohol testing • Seal tightly. Alcohol can evaporate from loosely capped containers. • Refrigerate if shipping is delayed, and ship promptly. • Note on the form if the donor reports diabetes only if the program's procedure allows. Otherwise the laboratory or MRO handles medical explanations. EXERCISE 8.4 1. A urine specimen is positive for ethanol but negative for EtG and EtS. What is the most likely explanation? Chapter 8: Alcohol Testing and Biomarkers © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 137 of 217

heading: SECTION 8.5
body: SECTION 8.5 EtG and EtS Ethyl glucuronide (EtG) and ethyl sulfate (EtS) are formed from a tiny fraction of alcohol and stay in urine far longer than alcohol itself. They are the standard urine tests for abstinence monitoring. Formed by ETG ETS The body attaching glucuronic acid to alcohol The body attaching sulfate to alcohol Window About 1 to 3 days Similar, often slightly shorter Longer after heavy drinking Stability Testing Can be formed or broken down by bacteria, for example in Not affected by bacteria a urinary tract infection More stable Rapid EtG tests and laboratory immunoassay screens. LC- Laboratory LC-MS/MS, usually MS/MS confirmation. together with EtG Cut-offs EtG results are reported against cut-offs that vary by laboratory and device, commonly 100, 250, 500, or 1,000 ng/mL. Lower cut-offs detect drinking further back but are more likely to detect incidental exposure. A widely used general interpretation is shown below. ETG LEVEL GENERAL INTERPRETATION Above 1,000 ng/mL Consistent with heavy drinking the same or previous day, or lighter drinking within about the last day 500 to 1,000 ng/mL Consistent with drinking within the past few days, or recent intense incidental exposure 100 to 500 ng/mL May reflect earlier heavy drinking, recent light drinking, or recent incidental exposure Adapted from SAMHSA's advisory on alcohol biomarkers. Interpretation belongs to the MRO, treating clinician, or program, not the collector. Chapter 8: Alcohol Testing and Biomarkers © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 138 of 217

heading: SECTION 8.5 CONTINUED
body: SECTION 8.5 CONTINUED Using EtG and EtS responsibly Why test both Because bacteria can create or destroy EtG after collection, a laboratory result with both EtG and EtS positive is much stronger evidence of drinking than EtG alone. An EtG positive with EtS negative should be treated with caution and may call for retesting or another biomarker. Rapid EtG tests • Rapid EtG cups and dip cards, commonly at a 500 ng/mL cut-off, screen for recent drinking at the point of collection. • Like every rapid test, a non-negative is preliminary. Send it for laboratory EtG and EtS confirmation before any action is taken. • Read the insert's cross-reactivity and cut-off data (Chapter 6, Section 6.3). Rapid EtG devices differ. GOVERNING RULE A low-level EtG result on its own should not be the sole basis for a serious consequence. Confirm with EtS, consider incidental exposure, and use other evidence or biomarkers. WHERE THIS COMES FROM SAMHSA's advisory on alcohol biomarkers cautions against using EtG or EtS alone as the basis for legal or disciplinary action, because incidental exposure can produce low positive results. Programs should build this into their policies. EXERCISE 8.5 1. A treatment program donor has EtG 180 ng/mL and EtS negative. The donor reports heavy use of hand sanitizer at work. What would you recommend the program consider? 2. Why is a lower EtG cut-off not always better? Chapter 8: Alcohol Testing and Biomarkers © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 8.6
body: SECTION 8.6 PEth Phosphatidylethanol (PEth) forms in the membranes of red blood cells only when alcohol is present. It builds up with repeated drinking and lasts for weeks, which makes it the best current marker for drinking over the past several weeks. PETH Specimen Blood, usually a dried blood spot from a fingerstick Window About 2 to 4 weeks Longer after sustained heavy drinking Specificity Forms only from alcohol. Ordinary incidental exposure is very unlikely to produce a meaningful level. Shows How much has been consumed over recent weeks, not a single moment PETH LEVEL (COMMONLY USED RANGES) GENERAL INTERPRETATION Below 20 ng/mL Abstinence or light drinking 20 to 200 ng/mL Significant drinking Above 200 ng/mL Heavy drinking Ranges vary by laboratory. Interpretation belongs to the MRO, clinician, or program. Collecting a dried blood spot 1. Wash and dry the donor's hands. Warm the hand if needed for blood flow. 2. Clean the finger as the kit directs and let it dry completely. 3. Use the kit's single-use lancet on the side of the fingertip. Wipe away the first drop if the kit says to. 4. Let drops fall onto each circle until filled. Do not touch the card to the finger or smear the blood. 5. Air-dry the card flat for the time the kit requires, away from heat and sunlight. 6. Seal in the supplied bag with desiccant. Label, initial, and complete the custody form. 7. Dispose of the lancet in a sharps container (Chapter 11, Section 11.9). EXERCISE 8.6 1. Why is PEth less affected by hand sanitizer than EtG? Chapter 8: Alcohol Testing and Biomarkers © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 140 of 217

heading: SECTION 8.7
body: SECTION 8.7 Hair alcohol markers Hair can show a pattern of drinking over about three months. Two markers are used: EtG and fatty acid ethyl esters (FAEE). MARKER WHAT IT SHOWS COMMON INTERPRETATION (HAIR) Hair EtG Repeated drinking over the period covered by the Levels at or above 5 pg/mg suggest hair segment repeated drinking. At or above 30 pg/mg suggest chronic excessive drinking. Hair FAEE Supports EtG in identifying heavy drinking Used alongside EtG More affected by hair products Interpretive values reflect Society of Hair Testing consensus as commonly applied. Laboratories may use different values. Limitations • Bleaching, dyeing, perming, and relaxers can lower hair EtG levels. • Hair products containing alcohol can raise FAEE. • Hair does not show the most recent week or so of drinking. • Hair shows a pattern over months, not a single drinking event. COLLECTION Hair for alcohol testing is collected the same way as hair for drug testing (Chapter 4, Section 4.7). Check the laboratory's required length: alcohol testing commonly uses 3 cm of head hair for a three-month window. Document visible cosmetic treatments. EXERCISE 8.7 1. A donor with recently bleached hair has a low hair EtG. What should the program consider? Chapter 8: Alcohol Testing and Biomarkers © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 141 of 217

heading: SECTION 8.8
body: SECTION 8.8 Indirect clinical markers Clinicians sometimes use standard blood tests that change with heavy drinking over time. They are useful for medical care but are not specific enough to prove drinking on their own. MARKER WHAT RAISES IT LIMITATION GGT (gamma-glutamyl Heavy drinking over weeks Also raised by liver disease, transferase) Liver strain obesity, some medications CDT (carbohydrate-deficient Sustained heavy drinking, commonly several Less sensitive in some groups transferrin) drinks a day for about two weeks Certain conditions affect it AST and ALT (liver enzymes) Liver damage, including from alcohol Many non-alcohol causes MCV (red blood cell size) Long-term heavy drinking Changes slowly Many other causes ROLE IN MONITORING Indirect markers are ordered and interpreted by clinicians, usually alongside a direct marker such as PEth. They are not used as stand-alone evidence of drinking in workplace or legal programs. EXERCISE 8.8 1. Why shouldn't a raised GGT alone be used to show someone has been drinking? heading: SECTION 8.9
body: SECTION 8.9 Choosing the right alcohol test Start with the question the program needs answered. The right test depends on the time frame and whether the program needs to know about impairment, recent use, or a pattern. PROGRAM QUESTION BEST TEST WHY Is this person under the influence right Breath (evidential), or saliva Measures current alcohol now? screen Relates to impairment Did they drink in the past 1 to 3 days? Urine EtG and EtS Covers recent days Standard for abstinence checks Have they been drinking over the past PEth few weeks? What is their drinking pattern over Covers weeks, reflects amount, and is little affected by incidental exposure Hair EtG Covers about three months Frequent EtG/EtS, periodic Overlapping windows leave few gaps months? Continuous abstinence monitoring PEth A low EtG result is disputed EtS confirmation, then PEth EtS rules out bacterial effects. PEth is rarely affected by incidental exposure. COMBINING TESTS Many monitoring programs combine a short-window test with a long-window test, for example weekly EtG/EtS with monthly PEth. Agreement between them strengthens a result. Disagreement signals a need to look closer. EXERCISE 8.9 1. A client in a treatment program is tested only once a month. Which test gives the most complete picture? Why? heading: SECTION 8.10
body: SECTION 8.10 Incidental exposure Alcohol is in many everyday products. Heavy or repeated use of some of them can produce low EtG results in a person who has not been drinking. Programs that use low EtG cut-offs must warn donors in advance. PRODUCT TYPE EXAMPLES Hygiene Alcohol-based hand sanitizer (especially frequent use), mouthwash, some body sprays and aftershaves Food and drink "Non-alcoholic" beer and wine (may contain small amounts), kombucha, foods cooked with alcohol, some desserts and sauces Medicines Some cough syrups and liquid medicines, some herbal tinctures and extracts Household and workplace Cleaning products and solvents used in poorly ventilated areas What the clinic should do • Give donors in EtG programs a written product advisory at enrollment, and have them sign that they received it. • Do not interpret results or accept explanations at collection. Route them to the MRO, clinician, or program. • Record donor-volunteered information only as the program's procedure directs. • Make sure the program understands that low-level EtG results need caution (Section 8.5). GOVERNING RULE Warn donors about incidental exposure before testing begins, not after a positive result. EXERCISE 8.10 1. A new donor in an EtG program asks what they need to avoid. What do you give them, and what do you tell them? Chapter 8: Alcohol Testing and Biomarkers © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: TRAINER USE
body: TRAINER USE Answer key Suggested answers. Accept answers that show the same understanding in the participant's own words. Section exercises EXERCISE KEY POINTS 8.1 About 4 hours (0.060 ÷ 0.015), so around noon. Individual rates vary. 8.2 PEth (about 2 to 4 weeks), ideally with periodic EtG/EtS. 8.3 Wait at least 15 minutes with nothing in the mouth before testing. Document it. 8.4 Alcohol formed in the specimen after collection (fermentation), not drinking. 8.5 (1) Treat with caution: EtS negative and a low EtG are consistent with incidental exposure or bacterial effects. Consider retesting, PEth, and the donor's disclosure. Do not rely on this result alone. (2) Lower cut-offs are more likely to detect incidental exposure, producing results that are hard to interpret. 8.6 PEth forms only with significant alcohol in the blood over time. Small incidental amounts are very unlikely to produce a meaningful level. 8.7 Bleaching can lower hair EtG. The result may understate drinking. Consider PEth or EtG/EtS for recent weeks. 8.8 GGT rises with liver disease, obesity, and some medications. It is not specific to alcohol. 8.9 PEth, because its window covers most of the month. Add EtG/EtS if more frequent testing is possible. 8.10 Give the product advisory, have them sign it, and tell them to check labels and ask their program about any product. Do not interpret future results. Chapter review PART ANSWERS A 1 T, 2 F, 3 T, 4 T, 5 F, 6 T, 7 T, 8 F B 1 C, 2 D, 3 B, 4 A C (1) 0.015. (2) 15. (3) Red blood. (4) 200. D1 Report as a preliminary non-negative. Send for laboratory EtG and EtS confirmation. Do not interpret the mouthwash explanation. Tell the donor the result is preliminary and the program will review it. D2 PEth reflects drinking over recent weeks. Employers must consider disability, privacy, and state law issues before testing applicants for alcohol use, so counsel review is essential. D3 Follow the kit's instructions. A smeared or overlapping card is usually unacceptable. Collect a new card from a fresh fingerstick, document, and discard the failed card properly. heading: BEFORE YOU BEGIN
body: BEFORE YOU BEGIN How to use this chapter A correct result reported with the wrong words can do as much harm as a wrong result. This chapter gives staff the language, scripts, and boundaries to communicate results accurately, calmly, and within their role. LEARNING OBJECTIVES When you finish this chapter you will be able to: 1. Use the correct term for every rapid, laboratory, and MRO result. 2. Explain what collectors may and may not say to donors. 3. Report a rapid test result to a client without overstating it. 4. Explain delays and discrepancies to clients in plain language. 5. De-escalate an upset donor and respond to a donor in crisis. 6. Hold firm when a client pressures you to change, rush, or skip steps. 7. Communicate fairly with every donor, including those who need accommodations. 8. Document every result communication. heading: SECTION 9.1
body: SECTION 9.1 Principles of result communication Every result communication, to a donor or a client, in person, by phone, or in writing, should pass four tests. ACCURATE AUTHORIZED Uses the correct term for what the result actually is. A Goes only to someone entitled to it, through a secure screen is never described as a confirmed result. channel (Chapter 10, Section 10.7). NEUTRAL DOCUMENTED States facts without judgment, opinion, or speculation Recorded: who, when, how, and what was said. about drug use or medications. Stay within your role ROLE COMMUNICATES DOES NOT Collector Collection steps, the rapid result where the Interpret results, discuss medications, program allows, and next steps predict outcomes Results and status to authorized client contacts Make employment or legal decisions for Clinic manager / reporting staff the client Laboratory Confirmed results to the MRO or ordering party Contact donors MRO Verified results, medical explanations, and safety Make employment decisions concerns GOVERNING RULE Report what the test shows, in the test's terms, to the person entitled to it. Never add your opinion. EXERCISE 9.1 1. A donor asks the collector, "Will my blood pressure medicine make this positive?" Which principle applies, and whose question is it to answer? heading: SECTION 9.2
body: SECTION 9.2 The language of results Each stage of testing has its own result words. Using a later stage's words for an earlier stage's result, such as calling a rapid screen "positive," is the most common and most damaging communication error. STAGE CORRECT TERMS MEANING Rapid test Negative, non-negative (preliminary A screen only positive), and invalid Non-negatives need confirmation Negative, positive (confirmed), dilute, Confirmed by mass spectrometry adulterated, substituted, invalid, and rejected Not yet medically reviewed Negative, negative-dilute, positive, refusal to The final, verified result in MRO programs Laboratory MRO test, and test cancelled Words to avoid AVOID SAY INSTEAD "Positive" for a rapid screen "Non-negative" or "preliminary positive, sent for confirmation" "Failed," "dirty," "hot" "Non-negative for [drug class]" or "positive for [drug]" "Passed," "clean" "Negative" "You're on [drug]" "The screen was non-negative for [drug class]" "The test is broken" or "it's a false positive" "It's being sent to the laboratory for confirmation" "It's probably your medication" "The medical review officer will discuss any medications with you" Drug slang or street names The drug class name on the device or report WHY WORDS MATTER Language that implies guilt can expose the clinic and client to defamation, discrimination, or wrongful termination claims. Neutral, accurate words protect everyone, and reflect Labb's approach: compliance, not intimidation. EXERCISE 9.2 1. Rewrite this sentence correctly: "Joe failed his drug test, he's dirty for meth." Chapter 9: Communicating Results © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 153 of 217

heading: SECTION 9.3
body: SECTION 9.3 Talking with donors Donors are often nervous, and some are frightened. Clear explanations and calm, consistent language make collections smoother and reduce complaints. Before and during collection • Introduce yourself and explain each step before it happens. • Explain the rules (emptying pockets, not flushing, wait periods) as standard for everyone, not as suspicion of this donor. • Answer process questions. Do not answer questions about results, medications, or consequences. "This is the same process for everyone. I'll walk you through each step before we do it." When the donor asks about medications "I'm not able to discuss medications. If anything on your test needs an explanation, a medical review officer, who is a physician, will contact you privately. You're welcome to make notes on your copy of the form." "Oh, that won't cause a problem." / "That might make it show up." Should the donor be told the rapid result? DOT drug tests do not use rapid tests. For non-regulated programs, the program's written policy decides whether the collector tells the donor the rapid result. Follow it consistently for every donor. Chapter 9: Communicating Results © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 154 of 217

heading: SECTION 9.3 CONTINUED
body: SECTION 9.3 CONTINUED Scripts for rapid results Where the program allows collectors to share rapid results, use consistent wording. Deliver it privately, calmly, and without commentary. NEGATIVE "Your screen today was negative. Your results will be sent to [program or employer] as usual." NON-NEGATIVE "Your screen showed a non-negative result for [drug class]. That is a preliminary result, not a final one. The specimen is being sent to the laboratory for confirmation. If there's anything that needs explaining, a medical review officer will contact you. Here is what happens next and how long it usually takes." "You tested positive for [drug]." / "What did you take?" INVALID "The device didn't run correctly, so there's no result from it. That happens occasionally and isn't a reflection on you. We need to [repeat the screen / collect again] per the procedure." DONOR DISPUTES THE RESULT "I understand. The screen is only preliminary, and that's exactly why the specimen goes to a laboratory for confirmation. You'll have the chance to talk with the medical review officer if it's confirmed." EXERCISE 9.3 1. A donor's rapid test is non-negative for THC. They say, "I only used CBD." Write your response. Chapter 9: Communicating Results © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 155 of 217

heading: SECTION 9.4
body: SECTION 9.4 Reporting to clients Clients act on what you tell them. Every report must make clear what the result is, what it is not, and what happens next. RESULT HOW TO REPORT IT Rapid negative "Negative on rapid screen for the [panel] panel." Note any specimen that will also go to the laboratory. Rapid non-negative "Preliminary non-negative for [drug class] on rapid screen. Specimen sent to [laboratory] for confirmation on [date]. Expected result by [date]. This is not a confirmed result." Invalid "Device invalid. No result. [Rescreened / recollected] per procedure." Never report an invalid as a refusal. Collection event State facts only: "Specimen temperature out of range, second specimen collected under direct observation, and both sent to laboratory." Possible refusal State facts: what happened, when, and what the donor said. The client, and in some cases the MRO, determines whether it is a refusal. Laboratory or MRO Report exactly as issued. In MRO programs, report only the MRO's verified result. result ACTING ON A PRELIMINARY RESULT Whether a client takes any action on a rapid non-negative is the client's decision under its own policy and applicable law. The clinic's job is to make sure the client clearly understands the result is preliminary. Some states restrict adverse action based on unconfirmed results. Clients should check with their counsel. GOVERNING RULE Every rapid non-negative report says "preliminary," names the laboratory, and gives an expected confirmation date. EXERCISE 9.4 1. Write a report for a rapid screen non-negative for AMP, sent to the laboratory today. Chapter 9: Communicating Results © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 156 of 217

heading: SECTION 9.5
body: SECTION 9.5 Explaining delays and discrepancies When results take longer than expected, or the laboratory disagrees with the rapid test, clients want a clear answer. Explain the process in plain language, give facts you actually have, and never guess. Delays (Chapter 5, Section 5.7) "The specimen screened non-negative at the laboratory, so it's going through confirmation testing. [If known: It needed an additional step, such as dilution and retest, which adds a day or two.] I'll update you by [date/time]." "The lab is slow." / "It's probably positive if it's taking this long." Rapid non-negative, laboratory negative (Chapter 6, Section 6.7) "The rapid test is a screen designed to flag specimens for confirmation. The laboratory's confirmation measured the specific compounds and reported negative. That's the final result. If you'd like, we can review the laboratory report against the device's package insert and document why the screen reacted." "Our cups must be bad." / "The lab missed it." Laboratory positive, MRO negative (Chapter 7, Section 7.5) "The medical review officer reviewed the result and verified it as negative. That's the final result. The MRO keeps any medical details confidential." "They had a prescription for it." / "Between us, the lab found something." FOLLOW UP ON YOUR PROMISES If you tell a client you will update them by a certain time, do it, even if the update is "no change yet." Unkept promises create more calls than delays do. EXERCISE 9.5 1. An employer asks, "Why was it positive at the lab but the MRO says negative? What did they find?" Write your response. Chapter 9: Communicating Results © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 157 of 217

heading: SECTION 9.6
body: SECTION 9.6 Difficult conversations with donors A donor who is angry, frightened, or in tears is usually reacting to what the result could mean, not to you. Staying calm and consistent protects the donor, the collection, and you. De-escalation steps 1. Stay calm and lower your voice. Match their calm, not their volume. 2. Listen without interrupting. 3. Acknowledge feelings without agreeing or judging: "I can see this is stressful." 4. Explain what you can do and what happens next. 5. Set limits clearly and respectfully: "I want to help, and I need you to lower your voice so we can continue." 6. Know when to stop. If the donor becomes threatening, end the conversation, move to safety, and get help. HELPFUL HARMFUL • Open body language. Stay at a safe distance. • Arguing about the result • Use the donor's name • Threats: "You'll lose your job" • Offer water and a chance to sit • Sarcasm or visible frustration • Repeat the next steps simply • Blocking the door or touching the donor A DONOR IN CRISIS If a donor talks about harming themselves or others, take it seriously. Do not leave them alone if it is safe to stay. Follow your clinic's emergency procedure. Call 911 for immediate danger. The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988) is available 24 hours a day. Document what happened and notify your manager. EXERCISE 9.6 1. A donor slams the cup on the counter and shouts that the test is rigged. Write your first two sentences. Chapter 9: Communicating Results © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 158 of 217

heading: SECTION 9.7
body: SECTION 9.7 Pressure from clients Clients sometimes push clinics to do things they should not: change a result, skip confirmation, share more than allowed, or hurry a collection. Holding firm protects the client as much as the clinic. PRESSURE RESPONSE "Just tell me if he's positive, I don't need "The screen is preliminary. I'll report it as a preliminary non-negative now and the lab." send the confirmed result when it's back." "Change it to negative, he's our best "I can't change a result. I can explain the confirmation and review process if that driver." helps." "Skip the observed collection, it's "The procedure requires it in this situation. Skipping it would make the result awkward." challengeable." "What medications is she on?" "We don't collect or share medication information. Any safety concern would come directly from the MRO." "Don't send it to the MRO, just give us the "The program requires MRO review. Results go to you once verified." lab report." "Can you just email me everyone's "I'll send them through the secure portal to your authorized contacts." results?" GOVERNING RULE Results are never altered, withheld from the proper recipient, or reported before they are ready. Escalate any request to do so to your manager and document it. EXERCISE 9.7 1. A long-standing client says they'll move their account if you don't release a result before the MRO finishes. What do you do? Chapter 9: Communicating Results © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 159 of 217

heading: SECTION 9.8
body: SECTION 9.8 Fair and accessible communication Every donor must receive the same process, the same explanations, and the same respect. Consistency is fairness, and it is also the clinic's best defense against discrimination claims. SITUATION GOOD PRACTICE Limited English Use a qualified interpreter or language line, not a family member or the employer's representative. Use translated forms where available. Hearing impairment Written instructions, visual aids, or a sign language interpreter as needed. Vision or reading difficulty Read forms aloud. Confirm understanding before the donor signs. Mobility or medical needs Accessible restroom and collection area. Reasonable adjustments within the procedure's requirements. Minors Follow the program's and state's rules on parental or guardian consent and on who receives results. Gender identity Treat every donor with respect. For observed collections, follow the program's current rules on observer assignment. CONSISTENCY CHECK Would you explain the process, apply the rules, and choose your words the same way for every donor? If not, change the practice, not just the wording. EXERCISE 9.8 1. A donor's supervisor offers to translate for a Spanish-speaking donor. Why should you decline, and what should you use instead? Chapter 9: Communicating Results © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 160 of 217

heading: SECTION 9.9
body: SECTION 9.9 Documenting communications If a result is ever disputed, the record of who was told what, and when, is often as important as the result itself. Record every result communication • Date and time • Who was contacted, and how their identity and authority were verified • Channel used (portal, phone, fax, encrypted email, in person) • What was communicated, in the exact result terms used • Any questions, disputes, or requests, and your response • Staff member's name or initials Also record • Requests to change, rush, or withhold results, and how they were handled • Donor disputes, complaints, and incidents • Promised follow-ups and when they were completed WRITE FACTS, NOT OPINIONS "Donor stated the result was wrong and asked for a retest. Explained specimen sent for laboratory confirmation. Donor left at 10:42." "Donor was obviously guilty and got defensive." ELECTRONIC RECORDS Result portals and electronic systems automatically record when results were released and viewed. They do not record phone calls or conversations. Log those separately. EXERCISE 9.9 1. Rewrite as a factual note: "Guy freaked out about his results and was super rude." Chapter 9: Communicating Results © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 161 of 217

body: TOOL Result communication phrase guide Post this at the front desk and collection area. SITUATION SAY NEVER SAY Rapid negative "The screen was negative." "You passed." "You're clean." heading: BEFORE YOU BEGIN
body: BEFORE YOU BEGIN How to use this chapter A drug test result can cost someone a job, custody of a child, or their freedom. The information must reach exactly the people entitled to it and no one else. This chapter explains the rules and the daily habits that keep a clinic on the right side of them. LEARNING OBJECTIVES When you finish this chapter you will be able to: 1. Identify the main laws that protect drug testing information. 2. Explain what information is confidential, beyond the result itself. 3. Determine who may receive results in each type of program. 4. Recognize a valid written authorization. 5. Protect privacy at the front desk, during collection, and when sharing results. 6. Secure paper and electronic records, and destroy them properly. 7. Respond correctly to subpoenas, court orders, and records requests. 8. Recognize a privacy breach and respond to it. Chapter contents 10.1 Why privacy matters 10.2 The laws that apply 10.3 What is confidential 10.4 Who may receive results 10.5 Consent and authorization 10.6 Privacy at the front desk and collection site 10.7 Sharing results securely 10.8 Securing and destroying records 10.9 Subpoenas, court orders, and records requests 10.10 Privacy breaches Tools: privacy walk-through, breach report form Chapter review Answer key (trainer use) NOT LEGAL ADVICE Privacy law depends on the type of clinic, the program, and the state. This chapter gives a general overview and best practices. Your clinic should have privacy policies reviewed by qualified legal counsel, and should route legal requests to counsel. heading: SECTION 10.1
body: SECTION 10.1 Why privacy matters Every donor trusts the clinic with information that could change their life. Protecting it is a legal duty, a business necessity, and the basis of the clinic's reputation. WHO IS AFFECTED WHAT A PRIVACY FAILURE CAN CAUSE The donor Loss of a job or opportunity, embarrassment, discrimination, exposure of medications or medical conditions The client Legal claims from the donor, damaged employee relations, regulatory violations in their own program The clinic Lawsuits, regulatory penalties, loss of clients and laboratory or MRO relationships, reputational damage The minimum necessary principle Share only the information a person needs for their role, and only with people who have a right to it. An employer needs to know whether an applicant passed. It does not need to know the donor's medications. A front desk worker needs the donor's name and appointment. They do not need the result. GOVERNING RULE If you are not sure someone is entitled to information, do not share it. Verify first, or ask your privacy lead. NAME A PRIVACY LEAD Every clinic should name one person responsible for privacy policies, training, requests, and breach response. Staff should know who that person is and how to reach them. EXERCISE 10.1 1. Who is your clinic's privacy lead? If there is none, who should it be? 2. Give one example of the minimum necessary principle in your daily work. Chapter 10: Privacy and Confidentiality © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 170 of 217

heading: SECTION 10.2
body: SECTION 10.2 The laws that apply No single law governs all drug testing privacy. Which rules apply depends on who the clinic is, who ordered the test, and why. LAW APPLIES TO KEY POINTS FOR CLINICS HIPAA Health care providers that conduct certain Protects health information. Limits electronic transactions (such as billing health disclosures. Requires safeguards and breach plans), health plans, clearinghouses, and notification. A covered provider generally their business associates needs the donor's written authorization to release results to an employer. 49 CFR Part 40, Subpart P DOT-regulated testing Service agents may not release individual results without the employee's specific written consent, except as Part 40 allows. Disclosures Part 40 requires are permitted without further consent. 42 CFR Part 2 Federally assisted substance use disorder Stricter protection for records that identify treatment programs someone as a patient in treatment. Recent rule changes aligned it more closely with HIPAA, with compliance required by February 2026, but important limits remain, especially for legal proceedings. ADA Employers with 15 or more employees A test for illegal drug use is not a medical exam, but information about prescribed medications and medical conditions is medical information that must be kept confidential and separate. State laws Varies Drug testing statutes, medical privacy laws, and data breach notification laws (every state has one). Some are stricter than federal law. Chapter 10: Privacy and Confidentiality © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 171 of 217

heading: SECTION 10.2 CONTINUED
body: SECTION 10.2 CONTINUED Which rules apply to your clinic? Ask these questions for each testing program your clinic runs. The answers determine which rules govern it. QUESTION IF YES Does the clinic bill health plans electronically or otherwise HIPAA applies to the clinic's health information meet HIPAA's definition of a covered health care provider? Does the clinic perform services for a HIPAA covered entity? The clinic may be a business associate and need a business associate agreement Is the test DOT-regulated? Part 40 confidentiality rules apply Is the clinic, or its client, a federally assisted substance use 42 CFR Part 2 may apply to treatment records disorder treatment program? Does the state have a drug testing or medical privacy State rules apply, and may be stricter statute? WHEN MORE THAN ONE LAW APPLIES Several laws can apply to the same record. The general approach is to follow the strictest applicable rule. For DOT tests, disclosures required by Part 40 are treated as required by law and are permitted under HIPAA. BEST PRACTICE FOR EVERY CLINIC Even where HIPAA does not technically apply, treat every drug test record as confidential health information. Following HIPAA-level safeguards everywhere is simpler to train, protects donors, and reduces legal exposure. EXERCISE 10.2 1. List each testing program your clinic runs (for example DOT, non-DOT employer, court, treatment) and the laws you believe apply to each. Review your list with your privacy lead. heading: SECTION 10.3
body: SECTION 10.3 What is confidential Confidentiality covers far more than a positive result. The fact that someone was tested at all can be sensitive. body: SECTION 10.4 Who may receive results Results go only to the people the program, the law, or the donor's valid authorization names. Everyone else gets nothing, including family members, coworkers, and supervisors who are not the designated contact. PROGRAM AUTHORIZED RECIPIENTS NOTES DOT-regulated MRO (from the laboratory), employer's Designated Laboratory reports go to the MRO, not the Employer Representative (from the MRO), and the employer. Other releases need the employee on request employee's specific written consent or a Part 40 exception. Non-DOT employer The employer's designated contact, and the MRO Based on the donor's signed authorization where one is used and the employer's policy Court, probation, or The supervising officer or court named in the order Confirm the authority in writing. Outside DOT, the answer depends on the program, who ordered and paid for the test, HIPAA (where it applies), and state law. Some states treat an employer-ordered test as an employment record that the donor gets from the employer, not the clinic. Have a written procedure for donor requests: verify identity, record the request, follow the ordering party's instructions, and check with counsel when unsure. EXERCISE 10.4 1. heading: SECTION 10.5
body: SECTION 10.5 Consent and authorization For most non-regulated testing, the donor's written authorization is what allows the clinic to send a result to the employer or program. A vague or incomplete form may not protect the clinic. Elements of a valid written authorization A specific description of the information to be released (for example, "drug test results for this collection") Who is releasing it (the clinic, and the laboratory and MRO if applicable) Who will receive it (the named employer or program) The purpose of the release An expiration date or event The donor's right to revoke in writing, and how A statement about re-disclosure by the recipient Whether testing or employment depends on signing The donor's signature and date, and a copy offered to the donor These elements reflect HIPAA authorization requirements. 42 CFR Part 2 consent has its own required elements. Have counsel approve your forms. PROGRAM CONSENT IN PRACTICE DOT-regulated No separate consent is needed for disclosures Part 40 requires. The donor signs the certification on the custody form. Other releases need specific written consent. Non-regulated Donor signs a consent and release authorization before collection, naming the recipient Treatment (Part 2) Part 2-compliant written consent before disclosure, with limited exceptions EXERCISE 10.5 1. A donor signs a release naming "ABC Trucking" but the result request comes from ABC's parent company. Can you release it? Why? heading: SECTION 10.6
body: SECTION 10.6 Privacy at the front desk and collection site Most privacy failures happen in plain sight: in the lobby, at the counter, and on the phone. Small habits prevent them. LOBBY AND FRONT DESK COLLECTION AREA • Sign-in sheets that do not show other donors' • Collections in a private room with the door names, or electronic check-in closed • Call donors by first name only. Never announce • One donor's paperwork and specimens out at a the test type or program. time • Screens turned away from the public. Privacy • Devices and results out of view of other donors filters where needed. • No discussion of results or medications with the • Forms and IDs never left face up on the counter donor (Chapter 7, Section 7.7) • Sensitive conversations moved to a private area • Observed collections handled with dignity and explained step by step PHONES, PRINTERS, AND FAX • Never confirm whether a person was tested to an unverified caller. • Leave voicemails with a name and callback number only. Never mention results or the reason for the call. • Collect printouts immediately. Do not leave results on shared printers or fax machines. • Double-check fax numbers and email addresses before sending. Use cover sheets with a confidentiality notice. EXERCISE 10.6 1. Walk your lobby and counter. List two things another visitor could see or hear that they should not. Chapter 10: Privacy and Confidentiality © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 176 of 217

heading: SECTION 10.7
body: SECTION 10.7 Sharing results securely Before a result leaves the clinic, confirm two things: the recipient is authorized, and the channel is secure. Verify the recipient • Keep a current list of each client's authorized contacts, with how to reach them. • For phone requests, call back at the number on file rather than trusting an incoming number. • Use a client PIN or password for phone releases where your procedure provides one. • When a client changes contacts, get the change in writing from an authorized person. Choose a secure channel CHANNEL GUIDANCE Secure portal Preferred. Results delivered to authorized logins with access tracking, such as the LabbHR platform. Encrypted email Acceptable when encrypted. Never send results by ordinary email or text message. Fax Only to verified numbers, with a confidentiality cover sheet. Confirm receipt for sensitive results. Phone Only to a verified, authorized person after identity check. Document the call. In person Verify identity with photo ID. Deliver in a sealed envelope or private setting. GOVERNING RULE Right person, right channel, documented. If any of the three is missing, stop. EXERCISE 10.7 1. A client emails from a personal Gmail address asking for today's results. What do you do? Chapter 10: Privacy and Confidentiality © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 177 of 217

heading: SECTION 10.8
body: SECTION 10.8 Securing and destroying records Records must be protected for as long as they are kept and destroyed so they cannot be read afterward. PAPER RECORDS ELECTRONIC RECORDS • Locked cabinets in a locked room • Unique login for every user. No shared passwords. • Keys limited to authorized staff. Key log kept. • Strong passwords and multi-factor • Records never taken home authentication • Clean desk at the end of each day • Screens that lock automatically • Medical and medication information filed • Encryption on laptops, phones, and backups separately from general records • Access limited by role. Access logs reviewed. • Access removed the day an employee leaves Retention and destruction • Keep records for the period required by regulations, contracts, and state law (Chapter 11, Section 11.10), and no longer than necessary. • Shred paper with a cross-cut shredder or a bonded shredding service that provides a certificate of destruction. • Wipe or destroy electronic media securely before disposal or reuse. Deleting files is not enough. • Keep a destruction log: what was destroyed, when, how, and by whom. • Suspend destruction of any record subject to a legal hold or pending request. EXERCISE 10.8 1. A staff member resigns on Friday. What access and property must be removed or returned that day? Chapter 10: Privacy and Confidentiality © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 178 of 217

heading: SECTION 10.9
body: SECTION 10.9 Subpoenas, court orders, and records requests Legal requests for records are common in drug testing. Never ignore them, and never answer them on the spot. Route every one to your privacy lead and counsel. REQUEST WHAT IT IS KEY POINT Court order Signed by a judge Generally must be followed, within its Directs release scope Often issued by an attorney or clerk, not a judge May not be enough on its own to release Subpoena health or treatment records. Counsel must review. Law enforcement request Request from police or an investigator Release only as the law allows. Ask for it in writing and route to counsel. Attorney letter Request from a donor's or employer's attorney Requires a valid authorization or legal process Steps for every legal request 1. Date-stamp it and send it to the privacy lead the same day. 2. Do not release anything, and do not destroy anything. 3. Counsel reviews validity, scope, and which laws apply. 4. Release only what is required, to the named recipient, by a secure method. 5. Document exactly what was released, when, and to whom. SPECIAL CASES Treatment records under 42 CFR Part 2 generally cannot be released for legal proceedings on a subpoena alone. A court order meeting Part 2's requirements is usually needed. DOT records may be released in certain legal proceedings as Part 40 allows. Counsel should decide both. EXERCISE 10.9 1. A process server hands the front desk a subpoena for a donor's records. What does the front desk do? Chapter 10: Privacy and Confidentiality © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 179 of 217

heading: SECTION 10.10
body: SECTION 10.10 Privacy breaches A breach is any access, use, or disclosure of confidential information that is not permitted. Most are accidents. What matters is reporting them immediately so the clinic can respond within legal deadlines. Common breaches • Result emailed or faxed to the wrong recipient • Lost or stolen laptop, phone, or paper files • Staff looking up records they have no work reason to view • Results discussed with or disclosed to an unauthorized person • Hacked email account or ransomware attack • Records thrown away without shredding Response steps 1. Contain it. Recall the email, ask the wrong recipient to destroy the information and confirm in writing, lock accounts, recover devices. 2. Report internally at once to the privacy lead, using the breach report form. 3. Assess what information was involved, how many people, and the risk of harm. 4. Notify as required. HIPAA, state breach laws, and client contracts set who must be told and by when. Under HIPAA, affected individuals must be notified without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery. Counsel should guide notification. 5. Correct the cause through the corrective action process (Chapter 11, Section 11.8) and document everything. GOVERNING RULE Report every suspected breach immediately. Hiding a breach turns a mistake into a violation. Staff who report in good faith must never face retaliation. EXERCISE 10.10 1. You realize you faxed a positive result to the wrong employer an hour ago. List your first three actions. Chapter 10: Privacy and Confidentiality © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. The donor must provide written authorization naming her, or come in personally with photo ID. Do not confirm the donor was tested. D2 Do not release. Ask for the request in writing with the legal authority for it, and route it to the privacy lead. Release only to recipients named in the program agreement or a valid order. D3 Remove the post immediately. Report as a breach on the incident form. Privacy lead assesses and handles notification. Corrective action (clean-desk rule, social media policy, retraining). heading: Chapter 11: Quality Control and Compliance
body: Chapter 11: Quality Control and Compliance Quality Control and Compliance How a clinic proves its testing is reliable: the CLIA Certificate of Waiver, external quality control, lot verification, storage monitoring, staff competency, written procedures, corrective action, and the records an inspector will ask to see. Includes ready-to-use logs and a self-audit checklist. 11.1 Quality control and quality assurance 11.2 The CLIA Certificate of Waiver 11.3 External quality control 11.4 Receiving and verifying new lots 11.5 Storage and temperature monitoring 11.6 Staff training and competency 11.7 Written procedures 11.8 Errors and corrective action 11.9 Other compliance areas 11.10 Records and inspections Tools Chapter review Answer key (trainer use) Chapter 11: Quality Control and Compliance © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: BEFORE YOU BEGIN
body: BEFORE YOU BEGIN How to use this chapter Earlier chapters taught how to run and interpret tests. This chapter covers how a clinic proves, on paper, that every test was run correctly. When a result is challenged or an inspector visits, the clinic's records are its defense. LEARNING OBJECTIVES When you finish this chapter you will be able to: 1. Explain the difference between quality control and quality assurance. 2. Describe what a CLIA Certificate of Waiver requires of a clinic. 3. Run and record external quality control, and respond to a QC failure. 4. Receive and verify a new lot of test devices. 5. Monitor and record storage temperatures. 6. Train and assess staff competency, and keep the records. 7. Maintain written procedures and a corrective action log. 8. Conduct a self-audit before an inspection. Chapter contents 11.1 Quality control and quality assurance 11.2 The CLIA Certificate of Waiver 11.3 External quality control 11.4 Receiving and verifying new lots 11.5 Storage and temperature monitoring 11.6 Staff training and competency 11.7 Written procedures 11.8 Errors and corrective action 11.9 Other compliance areas 11.10 Records and inspections Tools: QC log, temperature log, self-audit checklist Chapter review Answer key (trainer use) NOT LEGAL ADVICE Requirements differ by state and by how test results are used. This chapter describes common requirements and best practices. Confirm the rules that apply to your clinic with your compliance advisor or legal counsel. Chapter 11: Quality Control and Compliance © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 187 of 217

heading: SECTION 11.1
body: SECTION 11.1 Quality control and quality assurance Quality control checks that a test works today. Quality assurance checks that the whole testing operation works every day. A clinic needs both. QUALITY CONTROL (QC) QUALITY ASSURANCE (QA) Specific checks that a test system is performing The system that makes good results routine and correctly at a point in time. provable. • Control line on every strip (internal control) • Written procedures and training • Known negative and positive controls (external • Storage monitoring and supply management control) • Competency checks, audits, and corrective • New lot and new shipment checks action • Complete, retrievable records Where errors really happen Most testing errors do not come from the device. They come from the steps around it. PHASE EXAMPLES Before testing Wrong donor identified, wrong device or panel, expired or heat-damaged device, and poor specimen collection During testing Wrong volume or dip time, read outside the window, faint line misread, and wrong strip matched to a drug After testing Result recorded against the wrong donor, transcription errors, non-negative not sent for confirmation, and records lost GOVERNING RULE Quality is proven by records. A step that was done but not documented cannot be defended. EXERCISE 11.1 1. Name one error from each phase that has happened, or could happen, at your clinic. Chapter 11: Quality Control and Compliance © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 188 of 217

heading: SECTION 11.2
body: SECTION 11.2 The CLIA Certificate of Waiver The Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA) apply to facilities that test human specimens for health assessment, diagnosis, or treatment. A site that performs only waived tests for those purposes needs a CLIA Certificate of Waiver. What the certificate requires REQUIREMENT WHAT IT MEANS FOR THE CLINIC Enroll and pay fees Apply through CMS (Form CMS-116) and pay the certificate fee. The certificate must be renewed on schedule, typically every two years. Perform only waived tests Use only tests cleared and categorized as waived. Check each device's status. FUO and EUO kits are not FDA cleared and cannot be run as waived tests (Chapter 3, Section 3.10) Follow the manufacturer's Any change to a waived test's procedure makes it a high-complexity test the clinic instructions exactly is not certified to perform Report changes Notify the state agency of changes such as address, ownership, or director, within the required time Allow inspections CMS or the state may visit to check compliance or investigate a complaint DOES CLIA APPLY TO YOUR TESTING? It depends on how results are used. Clinical testing (treatment programs, health assessment) generally requires CLIA certification. CLIA generally does not apply to testing done only for legal purposes, and may not apply to some workplace testing. Some states (for example, New York and Washington) run their own laboratory programs in place of CLIA. Confirm with your compliance advisor for each testing program your clinic runs. YOUR LABORATORY'S CERTIFICATE DOES NOT COVER YOUR CLINIC A CLIA certificate covers only the facility named on it. Collecting a specimen and sending it to a CLIA-certified laboratory does not require a CLIA certificate at your clinic. But if your clinic runs rapid tests whose results are used by a treatment program or for any health purpose, your clinic needs its own Certificate of Waiver (or your state's equivalent), and it must use FDA-cleared waived devices for those clients. FUO and EUO kits cannot be used for them.

heading: SECTION 11.2
body: Best practice beyond the minimum The Certificate of Waiver requires few formal quality steps. CMS and CDC nonetheless recommend good laboratory practices for waived sites, and those practices are what protect a clinic when a result is challenged. The rest of this chapter follows them. CMS's free booklet Ready? Set? Test! is a good companion reference. EXERCISE 11.2 1. Where is your clinic's CLIA certificate posted, what is its expiration date, and who is listed as director? Chapter 11: Quality Control and Compliance © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 189 of 217

heading: SECTION 11.3
body: SECTION 11.3 External quality control The control line proves the strip flowed. It does not prove the strip detects drug correctly. External controls, specimens with a known result, test that. CONTROL TYPE WHAT IT IS WHAT IT PROVES Internal (procedural) The C line built into every strip The specimen flowed and reagents reacted Negative control Drug-free control material The device does not give false nonnegatives Positive control Control material with drug above the cut-off The device detects drug at the level it (commonly about 25 to 50 percent above) should Use commercially prepared controls made for drug-of-abuse testing, within their expiration dates and stored as labeled. Run controls exactly as you would run a donor specimen, by the same staff who test donors. When to run external controls As often as the package insert requires, and at least as often as your written procedure states With every new lot, before donor testing begins With every new shipment, even of a lot already in use When a new staff member begins testing After a storage temperature excursion When results seem unusual, such as an unexpected run of non-negatives or invalids Many clinics also run controls on a fixed schedule, such as monthly, even when no lot changes. Set the frequency in your written procedure and follow it. Chapter 11: Quality Control and Compliance © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 190 of 217

heading: SECTION 11.3 CONTINUED
body: SECTION 11.3 CONTINUED When QC fails A failed control means donor results from that device type cannot be trusted until the cause is found and fixed. Do not test donors with a lot that failed QC. 1. Stop donor testing with that lot. 2. Check the obvious: Control expiration, control storage, device expiration, procedure followed, read time. 3. Repeat with fresh control material and a new device from the same lot. 4. If it fails again, quarantine the lot. Label it "Do not use," separate it from stock, and contact the manufacturer with the lot number. 5. Look back. Review donor results since the last passing QC on that lot. Decide, with your director, whether any need follow-up or retesting. 6. Document the failure, the investigation, the corrective action, and the date testing resumed. FAILURE COMMON CAUSES Negative control reads non-negative Contaminated control, expired device, read too late, and device damaged by heat or humidity Positive control reads negative Degraded control, wrong control level, flooded strip, and faulty lot No control line Insufficient volume, damaged device, and expired device GOVERNING RULE No passing QC, no donor testing. Every failure needs a documented investigation and corrective action. EXERCISE 11.3 1. A new lot's positive control reads negative on the COC line twice. List your next four actions. Chapter 11: Quality Control and Compliance © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 191 of 217

heading: SECTION 11.4
body: SECTION 11.4 Receiving and verifying new lots Every shipment should be inspected and logged before a single device reaches the testing area. Heat in transit is invisible, and it is one of the most common causes of poor device performance. Receiving inspection Shipping box intact. No crushing, water damage, or signs of extreme heat. Product, panel, and quantity match the order Every pouch sealed. No punctures. Expiration date allows enough time to use the stock Lot number and insert version recorded in the receiving log Insert filed and dated for the new lot (Chapter 6, Section 6.1) Moved promptly to storage within the labeled temperature range Before first use 1. Run negative and positive external controls on the new lot (Section 11.3). 2. Record the results in the QC log with the lot number. 3. Release the lot for donor testing only after QC passes. 4. Use older lots first (first expiring, first used). WHY THE INSERT VERSION MATTERS If a new lot ships with a revised insert, cut-offs or cross-reactivity data may have changed. Review the changes with staff before the lot goes into use, and keep both versions on file. EXERCISE 11.4 1. A shipment arrives after sitting on a loading dock in July heat for an afternoon. What do you do? Chapter 11: Quality Control and Compliance © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 192 of 217

heading: SECTION 11.5
body: SECTION 11.5 Storage and temperature monitoring Devices, controls, and stored specimens each have a storage range. If you cannot show they stayed in range, you cannot show the results they produced are reliable. ITEM WHERE THE RANGE COMES FROM MONITOR Test devices Package insert and box label (commonly room Storage room or cabinet temperature) QC controls Control manufacturer's label (often refrigerated) Refrigerator Specimens awaiting shipment Laboratory instructions Secure refrigerator or locked area Monitoring practice • Use a thermometer that records minimum and maximum temperatures, or a digital data logger. • Record the current, minimum, and maximum readings every day the clinic is open, then reset. • Keep the thermometer's calibration or accuracy certificate on file. • Do not store devices near windows, heaters, vents, or exterior doors, or in vehicles. • Keep food and drink out of any refrigerator used for specimens or controls. When a reading is out of range 1. Record the reading and how long it was out of range, if known. 2. Correct the condition and move stock if needed. 3. Quarantine affected devices or controls until assessed. 4. Run external QC on affected lots before returning them to use. Contact the manufacturer if the excursion was large. 5. Document the corrective action in the log. EXERCISE 11.5 1. Monday's log shows a weekend maximum of 97 °F in the supply room. The insert allows up to 86 °F. What do you do? Chapter 11: Quality Control and Compliance © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 193 of 217

heading: SECTION 11.6
body: SECTION 11.6 Staff training and competency Training shows a person was taught. Competency shows they can do it correctly. Keep records of both for every person who collects or tests. Training record for each staff member Orientation to clinic procedures and these workbook chapters Training on each device and specimen type they use Regulated collector, BAT, or STT qualification and refresher dates, where applicable (Chapter 4, Section 4.2) Safety training, including bloodborne pathogens (Section 11.9) Signed and dated by the trainee and the trainer Assessing competency Assess competency when a person starts testing, again after about six months, and at least once a year after that. Use more than one method: METHOD EXAMPLE Direct observation Watch a complete collection and test from start to finish Record review Check a sample of the person's forms, results, and logs for completeness Blind or known specimens Have the person test a control or previously tested specimen without knowing the result Problem solving Ask how they would handle a scenario, such as a cold specimen or failed QC WHEN COMPETENCY IS NOT MET Remove the person from independent testing, retrain, reassess, and document each step. Do not let someone test donors alone until they pass. EXERCISE 11.6 1. When was each of your testing staff last assessed for competency? Where are those records? Chapter 11: Quality Control and Compliance © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 194 of 217

heading: SECTION 11.7
body: SECTION 11.7 Written procedures A written procedure makes every collector do the same thing the same way, and it shows an inspector or a court what the clinic's standard is. If the written procedure and daily practice differ, fix one of them. Procedures every clinic should have PROCEDURE COVERS Donor identification and collection Each specimen type and program (Chapter 4, Section 4.3) Rapid testing Each device: volume, timing, reading, reporting (from the insert) Quality control Control types, frequency, acceptance, failure response Receiving and storage Inspection, lot release, temperature monitoring Result reporting Who receives results, how, and what staff may say Laboratory submission Forms, packaging, shipping Problem collections and refusals Suspect specimens, shy bladder, dry mouth, refusals Corrective action How errors are reported, investigated, and closed Safety and waste PPE, spills, exposure, biohazard disposal Keeping procedures current • Base each testing procedure on the current package insert. Never contradict it. • Put a version number, effective date, and approval signature on every procedure. • Review all procedures at least once a year, and whenever a device, insert, or rule changes. • Keep retired versions on file with the dates they were in use. • Have staff sign that they have read each new or revised procedure. EXERCISE 11.7 1. Which procedure in the table does your clinic not yet have in writing? Chapter 11: Quality Control and Compliance © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 195 of 217

heading: SECTION 11.8
body: SECTION 11.8 Errors and corrective action Errors will happen. What matters is that each one is recorded, understood, and prevented from happening again. A clinic with a well-kept corrective action log looks stronger to an inspector than one that claims it never makes mistakes. The corrective action cycle 1. Record the event: what happened, when, who, which donor, or lot. 2. Contain it: stop testing, quarantine stock, notify the client or laboratory if a result is affected. 3. Find the root cause. Ask "why" until you reach something the clinic can change: a procedure, training, supply, or layout. 4. Correct the cause, not just the single event. 5. Verify the fix worked after a set period. 6. Close the entry with a date and signature. Example STEP ENTRY Event Laboratory rejected specimen: bottle ID did not match the form Containment Client notified Donor recollected the same day Root cause Two donors' kits open on the counter at the same time Correction Procedure changed: one donor's kit open at a time. Two-minute form check added before donor leaves. Verification No ID mismatches in the following 60 days of collections GOVERNING RULE Fix the cause, not just the event. Retraining alone rarely fixes a process problem. EXERCISE 11.8 1. Three results in a month were recorded under the wrong donor. Write a likely root cause and a correction. Chapter 11: Quality Control and Compliance © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 196 of 217

heading: SECTION 11.9
body: SECTION 11.9 Other compliance areas Testing quality is only one part of compliance. These areas are regularly checked by regulators and raised in disputes. AREA WHAT CLINICS TYPICALLY NEED Bloodborne pathogens A written exposure control plan, annual training for exposed staff, gloves and other PPE, (OSHA) hepatitis B vaccination offered to exposed staff, and exposure incident procedure Biohazard waste Disposal of used devices, specimens, and contaminated materials under state and local medical waste rules Privacy and confidentiality Results shared only with authorized recipients. Records secured. HIPAA and, for substance use treatment programs, 42 CFR Part 2 where they apply. Device intended use Devices used as labeled, including FUO and EUO designations and specimen-type limits (Chapter 3, Section 3.10) State testing laws Rules on on-site testing, confirmation, collector qualifications, marijuana, and specimen types, which vary by state Regulated programs Collector and technician qualification records Part 40 procedures (Chapter 4, Section 4.4) Instruments Maintenance and calibration logs for digital readers and breath alcohol devices, following each manufacturer's schedule DIGITAL READERS A digital reader, such as the Labb Station, removes visual reading errors and keeps a time-stamped image of each result. It still needs its own quality steps: follow the manufacturer's maintenance and verification schedule, keep software current, and record any reader errors in the corrective action log. EXERCISE 11.9 1. Does your clinic have a written bloodborne pathogen exposure control plan? When was staff last trained on it? Chapter 11: Quality Control and Compliance © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 197 of 217

heading: SECTION 11.10
body: SECTION 11.10 Records and inspections An inspector, auditor, or opposing attorney will ask for records, not explanations. Keep them organized so any record can be produced within minutes. Records to keep RECORD CONTENTS CLIA certificate and state licenses Current certificate, renewal notices, change notifications QC log Date, lot, control lot, results, pass or fail, initials, action taken Receiving log and insert file Lots received, dates, condition, insert versions Temperature logs Daily current, minimum, and maximum readings. Excursion actions. Training and competency files Per staff member, including regulated qualifications Written procedures Current and retired versions with dates Corrective action log Every event through closure Testing records Results, custody forms, device lots, reader images Instrument logs Maintenance, calibration, repairs Keep records for at least two years, and longer where state law, regulated program rules, or client contracts require. Confirm your retention schedule with your compliance advisor. During an inspection • Be courteous. Ask for identification and the purpose of the visit. • Have one person coordinate and retrieve records. • Answer what is asked, accurately. Do not guess. Offer to find the answer. • Take notes on any findings and ask for them in writing. • Respond to any deficiencies by the deadline with a documented corrective action. EXERCISE 11.10 1. Time yourself: how long does it take to find last March's QC log and temperature log? Chapter 11: Quality Control and Compliance © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. body: TRAINER USE Answer key Suggested answers. Accept answers that show the same understanding in the participant's own words. Section exercises EXERCISE KEY POINTS 11.1, 11.2 Clinic specific. 11.3 Stop donor testing with the lot. Check control and device expiration, storage, and procedure. Repeat with fresh control and a new device. If it fails again, quarantine the lot, contact the manufacturer, look back at recent results, and document. 11.4 Inspect and log the shipment. Quarantine it. Run external QC before use. Contact the supplier if QC fails or heat damage is suspected. Document. 11.5 Record the excursion. Correct the condition. Quarantine affected devices. Run QC on affected lots before use. Contact the manufacturer given the size of the excursion. Document the action. 11.6, 11.7, 11.9, Clinic specific. 11.10 11.8 Example: results entered from memory after several donors, or similar names. heading: CROSS-REACTIVITY
body: CROSS-REACTIVITY Cases 1 to 4 CASE 1 POPPY SEEDS A donor is non-negative on the OPI line and says she ate two poppy seed muffins that morning. The laboratory reports morphine at 1,400 ng/mL and codeine at 90 ng/mL. What explains the screen, and who decides whether the poppy seed explanation is accepted? CASE 2 OXYCODONE AND THE OPI LINE A donor with an oxycodone prescription is negative on the OPI line but non-negative on the OXY line. A supervisor asks why the opiate test "missed" the oxycodone. What do you tell them? CASE 3 AN ANTIDEPRESSANT AND THE TCA LINE A donor is non-negative on the TCA line and says she takes no tricyclic antidepressants. The package insert lists quetiapine as cross-reacting with the TCA line at 10,000 ng/mL. She takes quetiapine. What does this mean, and what happens next? CASE 4 FENTANYL ON AN OPIATE-ONLY CUP A treatment program client's cup shows negative on every line, including OPI. The laboratory later reports fentanyl and norfentanyl. Did the cup fail? heading: TRAINER USE
body: TRAINER USE Practice cases answer key CASE KEY POINTS SEE Poppy seeds contain morphine and codeine, and the OPI line detects them. The collector and clinic do not judge the explanation. The MRO reviews the laboratory result and the donor's explanation and reports the verified result. 2.4, 7.5 Nothing was missed. Standard OPI tests are designed for morphine and codeine and detect oxycodone poorly, which is why oxycodone has its own OXY line. Check the insert's cross-reactivity table for each line. 2.4, 6.3 If her quetiapine level reached the concentration listed in the insert, the TCA line can turn non-negative without any tricyclic present. Do not discuss medications with her. Send the specimen for laboratory confirmation, and the MRO will review any prescription. 6.3, 6.7 The cup performed as designed. Fentanyl is not detected by OPI tests, so it needs its own FYL line. The program should review whether its panel matches the drugs its clients use. 2.5, 6.3 Do not interpret it. A read after the interpretation window is not valid. Record what happened and rescreen with a new device, or follow the program's procedure. Read every device at the stated time. 1.9, 6.2 No. The cups were stored outside the insert's range, and heat can damage the reagents even when the device looks normal. Quarantine and replace them, and record it on the storage log. 1.8, 11.5 Wait until the full 10 minutes have passed since the coffee, observing the donor, then collect. Record the wait and the reason. Collecting early can affect the result and takes the test outside its instructions. 3.8, 4.6 "The screen was non-negative for amphetamines. It's a preliminary result, not a confirmed one, and the specimen has gone to the laboratory. I'll send the confirmed result as soon as we have it." Never say passed or failed.

heading: TRAINER USE
body: 9.2, 9.4 "Actually, on this test any line in that spot, even a faint one, means negative for that drug." Faint lines are the most common reading error. A reader removes the guesswork. 1.4 Share only what the client is entitled to receive under the program and the donor's authorization.
