heading: Appendix B: Glossary
body: Appendix B: Glossary APPENDICES B Glossary Definitions of the terms and abbreviations used in this handbook. Chapter and section references point to where each term is explained in depth. # B 6-AM (6-acetylmorphine). A metabolite produced only by heroin. Its presence confirms heroin use (2.4). Barbiturates (BAR). Sedative drugs such as butalbital and phenobarbital, detected by a class assay (2.7, 6.5). 7-OH (7-hydroxymitragynine). An active kratom alkaloid sold in concentrated products. Not detected by standard opioid tests (2.10). BAT (Breath Alcohol Technician). A person qualified to conduct DOT alcohol screening and confirmation tests on an EBT (4.2). 42 CFR Part 2. Federal rule protecting records of federally assisted substance use disorder treatment programs (10.2). Benzodiazepines (BZO). Sedatives such as alprazolam, clonazepam, and diazepam. Rapid tests detect some much better than others (2.7, 6.5). 49 CFR Part 40. DOT rule setting procedures for regulated workplace drug and alcohol testing (4.1). Benzoylecgonine. The main cocaine metabolite detected in urine (2.3). 510(k). FDA premarket notification process through which most rapid drug tests are cleared (3.10). Bottle B. The sealed split specimen held for independent retesting at the donor's request (5.8). A Breach. Access, use, or disclosure of confidential information that is not permitted (10.10). Accessioning. The laboratory process of receiving, inspecting, matching, and logging a specimen before testing (5.4). Administrative review. The MRO's check that paperwork and chain of custody are correct (7.3). Adulterant. A substance added to a specimen to defeat a test, or added to street drugs by suppliers (3.6, 2.6). Adulterated specimen. A specimen containing a substance not expected in urine, or at an unexpected level (7.6). Aliquot. A measured portion of a specimen taken for testing (5.3). Amphetamines (AMP). Stimulants including amphetamine and its derivatives. Prescription amphetamine can explain a positive result (2.3, 2.11). Analyte. The specific compound a laboratory measures and reports (5.3, 6.1). Antibody. A protein that recognizes and binds a specific molecular shape. The detection element of an immunoassay (1.3). Antigen. The molecule an antibody recognizes. In drug testing, the drug or metabolite (1.3). ASD (alcohol screening device). A breath or saliva device approved for DOT alcohol screening (4.8). ATF (Alcohol Testing Form). The form used for DOT alcohol tests (4.4). Appendix B: Glossary © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved.

heading: Appendix B: Glossary
body: Bromazolam. A designer benzodiazepine common in the illicit supply, often sold as fake Xanax and mixed with fentanyl. Requires a laboratory designer panel (2.7). Buprenorphine (BUP). A Schedule III opioid used to treat opioid use disorder. Not detected by standard opiate tests (2.4, 2.11). C Calibrator (target drug). The compound a manufacturer uses to set a test's cut-off (6.1). Cannabinoids (THC). Compounds from marijuana and hemp. Tests detect the THC metabolite THC-COOH (2.8). Cassette. A rapid test in a plastic housing. The collector applies the specimen to a sample well with a dropper (3.4). CBD (cannabidiol). A non-intoxicating cannabinoid. Pure CBD is not detected by THC tests, but products may contain THC (2.8). CCF (Custody and Control Form). The federal chain of custody form for regulated drug tests (4.4). CDT (carbohydrate-deficient transferrin). An indirect blood marker raised by sustained heavy drinking (8.8). Certificate of Waiver. The CLIA certificate that allows a site to perform waived tests (11.2). Chain of custody. The documented record of every person who handled a specimen, and when (4.3, 7.8). LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 210 of 217

heading: Class assay. A test that detects a family of related drugs, each at
body: Class assay. A test that detects a family of related drugs, each at its own level (6.5). CLIA. Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments. Federal rules for facilities testing human specimens for health purposes (1.7, 11.2). Cocaine (COC). A stimulant detected through its metabolite benzoylecgonine (2.3). Collection site. The place where specimens are collected, including the restroom, the collection area, and records storage (3.6, 10.6). Donor. The person who provides the specimen (4.3). DOT. U.S. Department of Transportation. Its agencies require regulated testing under Part 40 (4.1). Dried blood spot. A fingerstick blood specimen dried on a card, used for PEth testing (8.6). Dry strip. A rapid test strip that does not run because too little specimen reached it (3.8). E Collector. A trained person who instructs and assists donors and handles specimens during collection (4.2). EBT (evidential breath tester). A breath alcohol device approved for DOT confirmation tests (4.8, 8.3). Company authority testing. A test an employer orders under its own policy instead of a federal rule, such as a hair test added to a required DOT urine test. Results cannot be reported as DOT violations (4.7). EDDP. The main methadone metabolite. Shows methadone was metabolized (2.4). Competency assessment. Documented evaluation that a person can perform a test correctly (11.6). EUO (Employment Use Only). Designation for kits not FDA cleared, intended for non-regulated workplace testing (3.10). Competitive immunoassay. The rapid test format in which a visible test line means negative (1.4). External control. A specimen with a known result used to check that a test detects drug correctly (11.3). Confirmation. A specific laboratory test, usually GC-MS or LC-MS/ MS, that identifies and measures drugs (5.3). F Control line (C line). The line that proves the specimen flowed and reagents worked (1.2). Correctable flaw. A paperwork error that can be fixed with a signed correction (5.4). Corrective action. The documented steps taken to fix an error and prevent it from happening again (11.8). Cross-reactivity. A test's response to compounds other than its target drug (1.3, 6.3). Cut-off. The concentration of target drug at which a test is designed to change from negative to non-negative (6.4). EtG / EtS. Ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate. Urine alcohol biomarkers detectable for about 1 to 3 days (8.5).

heading: Class assay. A test that detects a family of related drugs, each at
body: FAEE (fatty acid ethyl esters). Direct alcohol markers that can be measured in hair (8.1, 8.7). Fatal flaw. A collection or paperwork error that cancels a test, such as a specimen ID mismatch (5.4). Fentanyl (FYL). A potent synthetic opioid not detected by standard opiate tests. Requires a specific fentanyl test (2.5). Fingernail testing. Testing of nail clippings for a long detection window, usually several months (4.9). Follow-up test. An unannounced DOT test after return to duty, collected under direct observation (4.5). D FUO (Forensic Use Only). Designation for kits not FDA cleared, intended for legal and criminal justice testing (3.10). Delayed activation. A two-step cup design in which the collector starts the test after the cup is sealed (3.5). G Delta-8 THC. A hemp-derived THC that usually cross-reacts with THC tests. The laboratory may confirm only delta-9 THC-COOH (2.8). DER (Designated Employer Representative). The employer's authorized contact for receiving test results (7.2). Designer benzodiazepine. An unapproved benzodiazepine, such as bromazolam, sold in the illicit supply (2.7). Detection window. The period after use during which a test can detect a drug (3.2, 8.2). Dilute specimen. A specimen with creatinine and specific gravity below normal but consistent with human urine (7.6). Dip card. A rapid test dipped into a collected specimen for a timed period (3.4). Direct marker. A compound formed only when alcohol is present, such as EtG, EtS, PEth, or FAEE (8.1). Direct observation. A collection in which a same-gender observer watches urine leave the body (4.5). d/l isomer analysis. A laboratory test separating the two mirrorimage forms of methamphetamine (5.7). Appendix B: Glossary © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. Gabapentin. A prescription nerve pain medication increasingly misused, often with opioids. Not on standard panels (2.7). GC-MS. Gas chromatography with mass spectrometry. A confirmation method (5.3). GGT (gamma-glutamyl transferase). A liver enzyme raised by heavy drinking over weeks and by other conditions (8.8). Glucuronide. A water-soluble form of a drug made by the body, often poorly detected by immunoassays (6.5). H Hair testing. Testing of a hair sample for a detection window of about 90 days (3.9, 4.7). HHS-certified laboratory. A laboratory certified by HHS to test federally regulated specimens (4.1). HHS Mandatory Guidelines. Federal standards for workplace drug testing laboratories and procedures (5.6).

body: HIPAA. Federal law protecting health information held by covered entities and their business associates (10.2). Hydrolysis. A laboratory step that frees drugs from glucuronides so total drug can be measured (5.3). LabbHR Clinic Owners Handbook | Q4 2026 Page 211 of 217

heading: Multi-line strip. A strip with several test lines and one shared
body: I Multi-line strip. A strip with several test lines and one shared control line (1.2). Immunoassay. A test that uses antibodies to detect a substance (1.1, 5.2). N Incidental exposure. Non-drinking contact with alcohol, such as hand sanitizer, that can produce low EtG results (8.10). Indirect marker. A change in the body caused by heavy drinking over time, such as raised liver enzymes. Less specific than direct markers (8.8). Integrated cup. A collection cup with built-in test strips (3.5). Interfering substance. A compound that can change a test result without being the target drug (6.7). Invalid result. A rapid test without a control line, or a laboratory result that cannot be obtained (1.4, 7.6). IVD (in vitro diagnostic). A device cleared by FDA, usually through 510(k), for testing specimens taken from the body. A kit is an IVD only if it holds FDA clearance, whatever its insert says (3.10). K Ketamine. A dissociative anesthetic, Schedule III, not on most standard panels (2.9). Kratom. A plant product with opioid-like effects. Its alkaloids are not detected by standard opioid tests (2.10). L Lateral flow. The movement of a liquid specimen along a test strip by capillary action (1.1). LC-MS/MS. Liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry. The most common confirmation method (5.3). Legitimate medical explanation. A lawful, medically appropriate reason for a laboratory result, verified by the MRO (7.3). Naloxone. An opioid overdose reversal medication (2.13). Negative-dilute. An MRO-verified negative in a dilute specimen (7.4). Nitazenes. Potent synthetic opioids not detected by fentanyl or opiate immunoassays (2.5). Non-negative (preliminary positive). A screening result at or above the cut-off that requires confirmation (1.1, 9.2). Non-regulated testing. Testing not governed by federal rules, following program policy and state law (4.1). NPS (novel psychoactive substances). New drugs designed to imitate known drugs and evade testing (2.12). O Observed collection. See direct observation. One-step cup. An integrated cup that begins testing as soon as urine enters it (3.5). Opiates (OPI). Drugs derived from the poppy, such as morphine and codeine. Standard opiate tests do not detect most synthetic opioids (2.4). Oral fluid. Saliva and other fluids collected from the mouth. Shows recent use (1.6, 3.7).

heading: Multi-line strip. A strip with several test lines and one shared
body: OTC (over the counter). A test cleared by FDA for lay use without a prescription. CLIA waived (3.10). Oxycodone (OXY). A semi-synthetic opioid that needs its own test because opiate tests detect it poorly (2.4). P LOD / LOQ. Limit of detection and limit of quantitation: the lowest amounts reliably detected and measured (5.6). Package insert. The manufacturer's instructions and performance data for a device (6.1). Lot number. The manufacturer's batch code. Links a result to its package insert and QC (1.8, 11.4). Panel. The set of drugs a test covers (2.2). M Passive exposure. Being near marijuana smoke. Rarely produces a urine result above standard cut-offs. Evaluated by the MRO or program, not the collector (2.8). MDMA (ecstasy). A stimulant and hallucinogen that may show on the MDMA line and sometimes the MET or AMP line (2.3, 6.6). Medetomidine. A veterinary sedative found as an adulterant in the illicit opioid supply (2.6). Metabolite. A compound the body produces from a drug (2.1). Methadone (MTD). A synthetic opioid used for pain and opioid use disorder. Detected by a methadone or EDDP test (2.4). Methamphetamine (MET). A stimulant. Laboratory d/l isomer analysis can separate illicit use from some over-the-counter products (2.3, 5.3). Minimum necessary. The principle of sharing only the information a person needs for their role (10.1). Monoclonal antibody. Identical copies of one antibody, giving narrower and more specific detection than polyclonal antibodies (1.3). MRO (Medical Review Officer). A licensed physician who reviews and verifies laboratory results (7.1). Appendix B: Glossary © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. Parent drug. The drug as taken, before the body changes it (2.1). PCP (phencyclidine). A dissociative drug on many panels (2.9). PEth (phosphatidylethanol). A blood alcohol biomarker reflecting drinking over about 2 to 4 weeks (8.6). Poppy seeds. A food that can produce morphine or codeine in urine (2.4, 7.5). Positive (confirmed). A laboratory result above the confirmation cut-off. In MRO programs, verified by the MRO (9.2). Post-accident test. A test after a workplace accident that meets the employer's or regulator's criteria (10.3). Presumptive positive. A laboratory term for a screening result above the cut-off, before confirmation. Clinics should say nonnegative or preliminary positive when talking with clients and donors (9.2).

heading: Primer sample. Labb's practice of depositing remaining oral fluid
body: Primer sample. Labb's practice of depositing remaining oral fluid into the device after the swab is removed, where the insert allows (3.8). STT (Screening Test Technician). A person qualified to conduct DOT alcohol screening tests (4.2). Privacy lead. The person responsible for a clinic's privacy policies and breach response (10.1). Subpoena. A legal demand for records or testimony. Clinics respond only through their documented records-request process (10.9). Program. The employer, court, probation agency, or treatment program that orders testing and decides how results are used (1.1). Substituted specimen. A specimen inconsistent with human urine (7.6). Proficiency demonstration. Error-free mock collections required for DOT collector qualification (4.2). SVT (specimen validity testing). Tests for dilution, substitution, and adulteration (5.2). Q Synthetic cannabinoids (K2, spice). Lab-made compounds that act like THC but are not detected by THC tests (2.8, 2.12). Quality assurance (QA). The system that makes reliable results routine and provable (11.1). Quality control (QC). Checks that a test system is working correctly at a point in time (11.1). R Random test. An unannounced test of employees selected at random from a pool (10.3). Read window. The period stated in the insert during which a result may be read (1.7, 6.2). Reasonable suspicion test. A test based on specific, observed signs of possible drug or alcohol use (8.3, 10.3). Refusal to test. A result reported when a donor tampers with or refuses a required step (4.3, 7.4). Retain. A specimen kept by the laboratory after testing (5.9). Return-to-duty test. A DOT test after a violation, before the employee resumes safety-sensitive duties. Collected under direct observation (4.5). S Safety concern. An MRO's report that a donor's lawful medication may make safety-sensitive work unsafe (7.4). Saliva alcohol test. An alcohol screen using an approved saliva device (8.3). Schedule (I to V). Federal controlled substance categories (2.1). Screening. A fast, preliminary test that sorts negatives from specimens needing confirmation (5.1). Shy bladder. A donor's inability to provide enough urine within the allowed time (4.5). SoHT (Society of Hair Testing). An international scientific society that publishes hair testing guidance and runs proficiency testing (5.10, 8.7).

heading: Primer sample. Labb's practice of depositing remaining oral fluid
body: Specific gravity. A measure of urine concentration used to detect dilution (5.2). Split specimen. One void divided into Bottle A and Bottle B (5.8). Appendix B: Glossary © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. Synthetic cathinones. Lab-made stimulants sometimes called bath salts, not detected by standard panels (2.3). T Temperature check. A reading of a urine specimen's temperature within four minutes of collection. The acceptable range is 90 to 100°F (32 to 38°C) (3.6, 4.5). Test line (T line). The band where a drug-specific result appears. Visible means negative (1.2). THC-COOH. The main THC metabolite detected in urine (2.8). Tramadol. A Schedule IV synthetic opioid with its own test, not detected by standard opiate tests (2.4). Two-step cup. A delayed-activation cup that seals the specimen before the test starts (3.5). U ULOL (upper limit of linearity). The highest concentration an instrument measures accurately. Above it, specimens are diluted and retested (5.7). V Verification interview. The MRO's private conversation with a donor before verifying a result (7.7). W Waived test. A simple test categorized under CLIA as low risk. Requires following the instructions exactly (1.7, 11.2). Wash procedure. The laboratory step that removes drug, oils, and products from the outside of hair before testing (5.10). X Xylazine. A veterinary sedative found in the fentanyl supply. Not reversed by naloxone (2.6). Z Z-drugs. Sleep medications such as zolpidem (Ambien), eszopiclone, and zaleplon. Not detected by benzodiazepine tests (2.7). heading: SECTION 1.1
body: SECTION 1.1 What a background check is An employment background check is a report about a person, assembled from public records and other sources, that an employer uses to make a hiring, retention, promotion, or reassignment decision. In the United States, most of these reports are regulated as consumer reports under the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA). A background check does not tell an employer whether to hire someone. It tells the employer what records exist about a person, from specific sources, within specific time frames. The employer decides what those records mean for a specific job, and the law tightly limits how that decision is made and communicated. A BACKGROUND CHECK IS A BACKGROUND CHECK IS NOT A report of records found in the A complete history of everything a person has ever done sources searched Limited to the jurisdictions, A "national" search of every court in the country databases, and dates actually searched Regulated when it is prepared by a Something an employer can order without the applicant's written permission third party for an employment purpose Accurate only to the extent the A guarantee that a person is safe, honest, or qualified records and matching were accurate GOVERNING RULE A background check reports records. It does not make the hiring decision, and it never replaces the employer's judgment about the job. Why employers screen • Safety. Protecting coworkers, customers, patients, and the public. • Negligent hiring. An employer can be liable for harm caused by an employee if a reasonable check would have revealed a relevant risk. • Legal and contract requirements. Many industries, such as transportation, healthcare, finance, and education, are required to screen. • Honesty and qualifications. Confirming that employment history, education, and licenses are what the applicant claims. EXERCISE 1.1 1. An employer asks you for "a full national background check that shows everything." What is wrong with that request? Chapter 1: The Background Screening Industry © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 1.2
body: SECTION 1.2 The parties in every screening transaction Every employment background check involves at least four parties. Each one has legal duties. Has the right to see the report, dispute errors, and receive required notices. Consumer reporting The company that assembles and delivers Verifies users, follows reasonable procedures agency (CRA) the report for maximum possible accuracy, observes reporting limits, and handles disputes. heading: SECTION 1.3
body: SECTION 1.3 How a clinic fits in Clinics that already serve employers with drug testing are natural partners for background screening. The same customers need both, and many prefer a single provider. But the clinic's role in the transaction decides which laws apply to the clinic itself. MODEL HOW IT WORKS WHAT IT MEANS FOR THE CLINIC Referral partner The clinic introduces the employer, and the Lowest legal exposure. The clinic does not employer contracts directly with the CRA or handle reports or consumer data. platform. Agent or sales The clinic sells the service on behalf of the CRA The clinic must market accurately and follow representative or platform, which delivers the reports. the CRA's procedures for onboarding employers. It usually does not see report contents. Reseller The clinic buys reports and sells them to The clinic may be treated as a CRA, with full employers under its own name. FCRA duties, possible state licensing or registration, and direct liability to consumers. Collection site only The clinic collects fingerprints, identity The clinic follows the program's collection documents, or drug test specimens for a procedures and protects the personal data it screening program. handles. KNOW YOUR ROLE BEFORE YOU SELL Your written agreement with Labb or any screening provider defines your role. Read it, and have your attorney confirm what that role means for you under the FCRA and your state's laws, before you solicit customers. Do not describe yourself to employers as a consumer reporting agency unless you are one. Why the law comes first Background screening is one of the most heavily litigated areas of employment law. The FCRA lets consumers sue for actual damages, and for willful violations, statutory damages of $100 to $1,000 per person, plus punitive damages and attorney fees. Because a single flawed form is often used for every applicant, one mistake can become a class action covering thousands of people. Employers know this, and they choose screening partners who understand it. EXERCISE 1.3 1. Under your current or planned agreement, which model describes your clinic? Who will confirm that with your attorney? Chapter 1: The Background Screening Industry © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 1.4
body: SECTION 1.4 The industry and its standards Background screening is a large, competitive industry. Providers range from national firms that screen millions of people a year to small regional companies. Employers increasingly expect their screening partners to show evidence of compliance, security, and accuracy. Accreditation The Professional Background Screening Association (PBSA) runs an accreditation program, administered by the Background Screening Credentialing Council. Accredited screening firms have passed an independent audit against standards covering consumer protection, legal compliance, client education, product standards, service standards, and general business practices. Accreditation is voluntary, but many large employers require it of their screening providers. QUESTIONS EMPLOYERS ASK PROVIDERS ANSWERS A CLINIC SHOULD HAVE READY • Are you accredited, and by whom? • The name and accreditation of the CRA that • Where do your criminal records come from? prepares the reports • How do you verify database results? • How the platform delivers disclosures and • How do you protect applicant data? • How do you handle disputes? • What are your typical turnaround times? adverse action notices • Who handles applicant disputes, and how • Where data is stored and who can access it • What each search covers, and what it does not How the industry is changing • Faster, more automated screening, with growing scrutiny of accuracy when records are matched by name and date of birth alone. • Fair chance laws limiting when and how criminal history can be considered (Chapter 5). • Clean Slate laws automatically sealing older records in a growing number of states. • AI hiring laws regulating automated tools that score or rank candidates (Chapter 6). • Shifting federal enforcement, with more activity coming from private lawsuits and state agencies (Chapter 2). body: Chapter 2: The Fair Credit Reporting Act The Fair Credit Reporting Act The federal law that governs employment background checks: definitions, permissible purpose, employer duties, agency and reseller duties, accuracy, and liability. 2.1 What the FCRA covers 2.2 Permissible purpose and employer certification 2.3 Disclosure and authorization 2.4 Duties of consumer reporting agencies 2.5 Resellers and agents 2.6 Enforcement and liability Chapter review Answer key (trainer use) LEARNING OBJECTIVES 1. heading: SECTION 2.1
body: SECTION 2.1 What the FCRA covers The Fair Credit Reporting Act (15 U.S.C. 1681 and following) is the federal law that governs consumer reports, including most employment background checks. Its goals are accuracy, fairness, and privacy. It applies to the agencies that prepare reports, the employers that use them, and the companies that furnish or resell the information. Key definitions TERM MEANING IN PLAIN LANGUAGE Consumer The individual the report is about. In employment, the applicant or employee. Consumer report Any communication by a consumer reporting agency about a person's character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living that is used, or expected to be used, for a purpose such as employment. Criminal records, driving records, and verifications prepared by a screening company are consumer reports. Consumer reporting agency Anyone who, for a fee, regularly assembles or evaluates information on consumers to (CRA) furnish consumer reports to third parties. Screening companies are CRAs. Investigative consumer A report based on personal interviews with people who know the consumer, such as report reference checks that ask about character. Additional notice rules apply. Employment purposes Evaluating a person for employment, promotion, reassignment, or retention. User The person or business that obtains and uses a consumer report. In employment, the employer. Adverse action In employment, any decision that adversely affects a current or prospective employee, such as not hiring, firing, or denying a promotion. WHEN THE FCRA DOES NOT APPLY An employer that searches public court websites itself, with its own staff, is not using a consumer report, because no CRA is involved. That employer still must follow anti-discrimination and fair chance laws, and some state laws regulate in-house checks too. The FCRA applies the moment a third party prepares the report. EXERCISE 2.1 1. A screening company calls an applicant's former supervisor and asks about the applicant's honesty and work habits. What kind of report is this, and why does it matter? heading: SECTION 2.2
body: SECTION 2.2 Permissible purpose and employer certification A CRA may furnish a consumer report only to someone with a permissible purpose listed in the law. Employment is a permissible purpose only when the employer follows the FCRA's employment rules and certifies that it will. The employer's certification Before a CRA may provide reports for employment purposes, the employer must certify to the CRA that it: 1. Has given, or will give, the required disclosure to the consumer and obtained written authorization. 2. Will not use the information in violation of any federal or state equal employment opportunity law or regulation. 3. Will follow the adverse action procedures if it takes adverse action based in whole or in part on the report. Verifying the employer CRAs must maintain reasonable procedures to verify the identity of each new user and the purposes for which it will use reports. In practice, this means credentialing every new employer client before the first order is placed: Confirm the business is real: legal name, address, phone, and tax or registration information. Confirm the person ordering works for the business and is authorized to sign. Obtain the signed certification and service agreement. For credit reports and some other products, complete any site inspection or extra verification the data supplier requires. Be alert to red flags: residential address only, no web presence, pressure to skip steps, or requests to screen people who are not applicants or employees. GOVERNING RULE No certification, no report. Curiosity, personal disputes, and checking on a neighbor, ex-spouse, or competitor are never permissible purposes. Knowingly obtaining a consumer report under false pretenses is a federal crime under the FCRA, in addition to civil liability. EXERCISE 2.2 1. A business owner asks you to screen his daughter's new boyfriend "as a favor." What do you say? Chapter 2: The Fair Credit Reporting Act © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Background Screening Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 13 of 83

heading: SECTION 2.3
body: SECTION 2.3 Disclosure and authorization Before ordering a report for employment purposes, the employer must give the applicant a clear and conspicuous written disclosure that a report may be obtained, in a document that consists solely of the disclosure, and must obtain the applicant's written authorization. The standalone disclosure "Consists solely of the disclosure" is the most litigated phrase in the FCRA. Courts have found willful violations where employers added extra content to the disclosure form. Keep it clean. GENERALLY ACCEPTABLE DO NOT INCLUDE • A brief statement that a consumer report may • Liability waivers or releases be obtained for employment purposes • Extra state law notices crowded onto the federal • The authorization signature line, which the FTC disclosure has said may appear on the same form • Employment application questions • Brief identifying information, such as the CRA's • Acknowledgments, policies, or at-will statements name Electronic disclosures and e-signatures are widely used and are acceptable when they meet the same standalone and clear-and-conspicuous requirements. State notices usually belong on separate pages or screens. Investigative consumer reports If the employer orders an investigative consumer report, such as reference interviews about character, it must also disclose that fact to the applicant in writing within three days after the report is first requested, and tell the applicant they may request a complete description of the nature and scope of the investigation. If the applicant asks, that description must be provided within five days. Current employees Screening current employees, including periodic rescreening and continuous monitoring, also requires disclosure and authorization. Authorization forms can state that consent covers the period of employment, where state law allows (Chapter 6). EXERCISE 2.3 1. A client's disclosure form includes a sentence releasing the employer and screening company from all liability. What is the risk, and what should change? Chapter 2: The Fair Credit Reporting Act © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Background Screening Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 14 of 83

heading: SECTION 2.4
body: SECTION 2.4 Duties of consumer reporting agencies The CRA that prepares the report has its own duties, separate from the employer's. Clinics that act as agents should understand them, because employers will ask, and clinics that resell reports may share them. DUTY WHAT IT REQUIRES Maximum possible accuracy Follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of the information reported. Matching records to the right person is the most common accuracy failure. Public record notice (Section When reporting public records likely to have an adverse effect on employment, either 613) notify the consumer at the time the information is reported, with the user's name and address, or maintain strict procedures to make sure the information is complete and up to date. Most screening firms verify database hits at the original court source. Reporting time limits (Section Do not report arrests that did not lead to conviction, civil suits, civil judgments, paid tax 605) liens, accounts in collection, or other adverse items older than seven years. Criminal convictions have no federal time limit. These limits do not apply to jobs with an annual salary of $75,000 or more. State laws can be stricter (Chapter 7). Disputes (Section 611) Reinvestigate disputed information free of charge, generally within 30 days, and correct or delete information that is inaccurate, incomplete, or cannot be verified. File disclosure On request and with proper identification, give the consumer the information in their file and the sources. User notices Provide users with the required notice of their FCRA obligations, and provide consumers' Summary of Rights where required. NAME-ONLY MATCHING Reporting a record because the name matches, without confirming identifiers such as full date of birth, is a leading cause of lawsuits against screening companies. A common name can produce dozens of false matches. Employers should prefer providers that match on at least two strong identifiers and verify at the source. EXERCISE 2.4 1. A report shows a 9-year-old arrest with no conviction for a $45,000 per year warehouse job. Should it have been reported under federal law? Why? heading: SECTION 2.5
body: SECTION 2.5 Resellers and agents A reseller is a company that obtains consumer reports from a CRA and sells them to employers. Under the FCRA, a reseller that assembles and merges information from other CRAs can itself be treated as a CRA. Resellers have specific added duties. Reseller duties • Identify the end user. When buying a report for resale, disclose to the supplying CRA the identity of the end user and each permissible purpose. • Verify and certify. Establish and follow reasonable procedures to make sure reports are resold only for permissible purposes, including identifying each end user and obtaining its certification. • Accuracy and disputes. Take part in dispute handling, and pass disputes to the supplying CRA when the error lies there. • Contract flow-down. Pass the supplying CRA's required terms and notices down to each employer client. Agents and referral partners If your clinic sells on behalf of a CRA or platform and the employer contracts directly with that CRA, the CRA carries the CRA and reseller duties. Your duties come from your agreement and from general law: market honestly, follow the onboarding process, protect any personal data you touch, and never handle reports outside the platform. QUESTION WHY IT MATTERS Whose name is on the employer's service That company is generally the CRA or reseller of record. agreement? Who sends the invoice? Billing in your name can suggest you are reselling. Do you see or store reports? Handling reports brings data security and confidentiality duties. Who answers applicant disputes? Dispute handling is a CRA duty. Know who owns it. Does your state license screening firms or Some states regulate or license screening or investigative work. investigators? EXERCISE 2.5 1. heading: SECTION 2.6
body: SECTION 2.6 Enforcement and liability The FCRA is enforced by federal agencies, state attorneys general, and, most actively, by consumers and their attorneys through private lawsuits. ENFORCER ROLE Federal Trade Commission Enforces the FCRA against most non-bank companies, including employers and screening (FTC) firms. Consumer Financial Writes FCRA rules and supervises larger consumer reporting agencies. In May 2025, the CFPB Protection Bureau (CFPB) withdrew a large body of its prior FCRA guidance, including a 2024 advisory opinion on background screening and a 2024 circular on background dossiers and algorithmic scores used in employment. The statute itself did not change. State attorneys general May enforce the FCRA and their own state consumer reporting laws. Consumers May sue for actual damages for negligent violations. For willful violations, statutory damages of $100 to $1,000 per consumer, punitive damages, and attorney fees. WHY CLASS ACTIONS ARE COMMON Employers use the same disclosure form and process for every applicant. If the form or process is defective, every applicant who went through it may be part of a class. Statutory damages of $100 to $1,000 multiplied by thousands of applicants can reach millions of dollars, even when no one suffered a concrete loss. Common claims involve disclosure forms with extra content, skipped pre-adverse action notices, and inaccurate criminal records. GOVERNING RULE Withdrawn federal guidance does not mean relaxed law. The statute, the courts, state agencies, and private plaintiffs still enforce every requirement in this chapter. EXERCISE 2.6 1. heading: SECTION 3.1
body: SECTION 3.1 Identity and address history Most screening packages begin with an identity and address history search, often called an SSN trace. It uses the applicant's Social Security number to find names and addresses associated with that number in commercial data, so the screening company knows where to search for records. AN ADDRESS HISTORY SEARCH DETAILS Is used to Find counties where the applicant has lived, and other names (such as maiden names) to search under. Is not Proof of identity, verification that the SSN is valid or belongs to the applicant, or evidence of work authorization. Comes from Credit header and other commercial data. It can be incomplete for young people, recent immigrants, and people with little credit history. Should never be The basis for an employment decision. Unexpected names or addresses are research leads, not findings. VERIFYING IDENTITY AND WORK AUTHORIZATION Identity verification and employment eligibility are separate processes. Work authorization is handled through Form I-9 and, where used, E-Verify, which have their own rules against discrimination and premature use. Never use a background check address search to decide whether someone may legally work. EXERCISE 3.1 1. An address history shows an applicant has used a different last name. Should the employer treat this as dishonesty? What is it actually for? Chapter 3: Workplace Screening Searches © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 3.2
body: SECTION 3.2 Criminal record searches There is no single national source of criminal records available for private employment screening. Records live in thousands of county courts, state repositories, and federal courts, each with its own access rules, formats, and identifiers. A sound criminal search combines sources. TYPICAL TURNAROUND SEARCH SOURCE STRENGTHS LIMITS County criminal Felony and misdemeanor records at the county courthouse, searched in person, by court runner, or through an official court system Primary source, most current, most complete for that county Covers only the counties searched. Some courts redact dates of birth, which slows matching. 1 to 3 business days, longer for some courts Statewide criminal State court system or state repository Covers many counties at once in states with good systems Quality varies widely by state. Some repositories are incomplete or omit misdemeanors. Same day to several days Federal criminal U.S. district courts, through PACER Covers federal crimes such as fraud, tax, and federal drug charges Limited identifiers in federal records, which makes matching harder 1 to 3 business days Multi-jurisdictional database Commercial compilation of records from many states, often sold as a "national" search Broad, fast, inexpensive way to find counties to search Incomplete, often out of date, and not real time. Hits should be verified at the original court before reporting. Minutes Sex offender registry State registries and the national public registry Important for jobs with access to children or vulnerable people Registry rules vary by state. Matching must be confirmed. Same day Watchlists and sanctions Government lists such as the OFAC sanctions list Required or expected for some financial and security roles Name-based lists produce false matches. Confirm with identifiers. Same day GOVERNING RULE A database search finds leads. The original court record confirms them. Never sell a database search as a complete national criminal check. What criminal records contain A typical court record shows the charge, the level (felony or misdemeanor), the filing date, the disposition (for example, convicted, dismissed, or deferred), the disposition date, and the sentence. Pending cases, dismissed charges, and deferred adjudications are treated very differently by state and local law, so the disposition matters as much as the charge (Chapter 5).

heading: SECTION 3.3
body: SECTION 3.3 Verifications Verifications confirm what the applicant has claimed. Resume fraud is common, and verifications often matter more to job performance than criminal records do. VERIFICATION WHAT IS CONFIRMED NOTES Employment Employer name, dates of employment, and title. Many employers confirm only dates and title. Sometimes eligibility for rehire and reason for Some use third-party verification services, leaving. which may charge a fee. Delays are common when employers are slow to respond. Education School, degree, major, and graduation date Usually confirmed through the school's registrar or a clearinghouse. Watch for diploma mills and unaccredited schools. Professional license License type, number, status, expiration, and Verify with the issuing state board. Essential disciplinary actions for nurses, drivers, pharmacists, and other licensed roles. References Opinions about the applicant's work and Questions about character or reputation can character make the report an investigative consumer report (Chapter 2). SALARY HISTORY Many states and cities prohibit employers from asking about or verifying an applicant's salary history. Employment verifications should not collect pay information unless the client confirms it is lawful where the applicant is located and for the role. EXERCISE 3.3 1. A client wants to know why a former employer would only confirm dates of employment. How do you explain it? Chapter 3: Workplace Screening Searches © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 3.4
body: SECTION 3.4 Turnaround and delays Employers want fast results. Most clear checks finish within one to three business days, but some always take longer. Setting expectations honestly prevents frustration and protects the clinic's credibility. CAUSE OF DELAY WHY IT HAPPENS Court access Some courts require in-person searches, limit public terminals, or have clerks process requests by hand. Missing identifiers Courts that redact dates of birth force extra steps to confirm a record belongs to the applicant. Record found A possible match must be verified at the source, with the full disposition, before it is reported. Verifications pending Past employers and schools respond on their own schedules. Closed businesses take longest. Applicant information Incomplete or mistyped names, dates of birth, or previous addresses send searches to the wrong places. International searches Foreign sources vary widely in access and speed (Chapter 6). Holidays and closures Court closures, weather, and holidays stop research. WHAT YOU CAN CONTROL Most avoidable delays start with incomplete applicant information. Make sure clients use the platform's applicant invitation, so applicants enter their own information, sign electronically, and correct errors before the order is placed. EXERCISE 3.4 1. A client complains that one check has taken five days while others took one. Name two likely reasons. Chapter 3: Workplace Screening Searches © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Background Screening Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 24 of 83

heading: SECTION 3.5
body: SECTION 3.5 Matching searches to the job Good screening is relevant screening. Searches should relate to the duties of the job. Over-screening costs the employer money, increases legal risk, and can screen out qualified people for reasons that have nothing to do with the work. JOB TYPE COMMON PACKAGE General warehouse or retail Address history, county criminal for counties of residence (often seven years), multi-jurisdictional database with source verification, sex offender registry, drug test Driver (non-DOT) The general package plus motor vehicle record and employment verification Commercial driver (DOT) DOT-required checks (Chapter 8), motor vehicle records, previous employer safety history, DOT drug and alcohol testing, plus any additional employer searches Healthcare The general package plus license verification, healthcare sanctions and exclusion checks, and any staterequired fingerprint checks (Chapter 8) Finance or cash handling The general package plus federal criminal, employment and education verification, and credit report where lawful (Chapter 6) Work with children or vulnerable adults The general package plus sex offender registry, state-required checks, and abuse registries where available Management or executive The general package plus federal criminal, employment and education verification, professional licenses, and civil records Packages are examples for discussion. The employer decides what to order, based on the job, its industry rules, and applicable law. CONSISTENCY Employers should apply the same package to everyone applying for the same job. Screening some applicants more deeply than others for the same role invites discrimination claims. EXERCISE 3.5 1. A client wants a credit report on every warehouse applicant. What questions do you ask before setting up that package? Chapter 3: Workplace Screening Searches © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: Chapter 4: The Screening Process Step by Step
body: Chapter 4: The Screening Process Step by Step PART II WORKPLACE SCREENING IN PRACTICE The Screening Process Step by Step From onboarding an employer to the final adverse action notice: every step, who is responsible, and the documents involved. 4.1 The process at a glance 4.2 Onboarding an employer 4.3 Applicant consent and information 4.4 The adverse action process 4.5 Disputes, corrections, and records Tools Chapter review Answer key (trainer use) LEARNING OBJECTIVES 1. heading: SECTION 4.2
body: SECTION 4.2 Onboarding an employer Onboarding is where compliance starts. It is also where a clinic adds the most value, by helping the employer set up correctly the first time. 1. Verify the business and the person who will order (Chapter 2, Section 2.2). 2. Sign the agreements. The service agreement and the employer's FCRA certification, plus any supplier terms for products such as credit or driving records. 3. Deliver the required notices to users, including the notice of their FCRA responsibilities. 4. Confirm where the employer hires. Applicant and job locations decide which state and local rules apply (Chapter 7). 5. Build packages by job, so the same searches apply to everyone in the same role (Chapter 3, Section 3.5). 6. Set up users and access, limited to people who need it, with individual logins. 7. Train the employer's users on ordering, reading reports, and the adverse action process. THE EMPLOYER OWNS THE DECISION Employers sometimes ask the clinic or CRA to tell them whom to hire. Do not. The CRA may apply criteria the employer has set, but the employer must make the decision and is responsible for it. Never give legal advice about a client's hiring policy. Recommend that they review it with their counsel. EXERCISE 4.2 1. A new client hires in three states. Why must you know that before setting up their account? heading: SECTION 4.3
body: SECTION 4.3 Applicant consent and information Most screening today is ordered through an applicant invitation. The applicant receives a secure link, reads the disclosure and any state notices, signs electronically, and enters their own information. What a compliant consent flow includes The standalone FCRA disclosure, on its own screen or page The written authorization, with electronic signature and date Any required state or local notices, on separate screens or pages The Summary of Your Rights Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, where required, and an option for the applicant to request a copy of the report where state law requires one Collection of only the information needed: legal name, other names, date of birth, Social Security number, address history, and the employment, education, or license details to be verified Secure transmission and storage of that information When the applicant does not complete the invitation An employer may not order the report until consent is complete. Reminders through the platform are fine. Pressuring an applicant, or having someone else sign for them, is not. If an applicant needs help because of a disability, language, or lack of internet access, the employer should provide an accessible alternative. EXERCISE 4.3 1. Before deciding, send a Give a reasonable time to Review disputes, If the decision stands, send copy of the report and the respond. Some places require more. dispute is open. Pre-adverse action notice Waiting period Consider the response Adverse action notice The final adverse action notice must state • The name, address, and phone number of the CRA that furnished the report, including a toll-free number for nationwide agencies. • That the CRA did not make the decision and cannot explain why it was made. • The applicant's right to a free copy of the report from the CRA if requested within 60 days. • The applicant's right to dispute the accuracy or completeness of the report with the CRA. GOVERNING RULE Never take adverse action first and notify later. The pre-adverse notice must reach the applicant before the decision is final. heading: SECTION 4.5
body: SECTION 4.5 Disputes, corrections, and records Mistakes happen in records and in matching. How quickly and fairly they are corrected determines whether an error becomes a lawsuit. When an applicant disputes a report 1. Direct the applicant to the CRA's dispute process, and tell the employer a dispute is open. 2. The CRA reinvestigates, free of charge, generally within 30 days, and contacts the source as needed. 3. The CRA corrects or deletes information that is inaccurate, incomplete, or cannot be verified, and sends results to the applicant. 4. The employer receives the corrected report and reconsiders its decision. Employers should hold the position open, or at least avoid finalizing a decision, while a timely dispute is pending, where practical. Keeping and destroying records RECORD GUIDANCE Disclosures and authorizations Keep for as long as FCRA claims could be brought: generally two years from discovery of a violation, up to five years from the violation. Reports and adverse action notices Same as above. Federal equal employment rules generally also require keeping hiring records for at least one year. Proof of notices sent Keep delivery records for every pre-adverse and adverse action notice. Disposal The FTC Disposal Rule requires reasonable measures to destroy consumer report information, such as shredding paper and securely wiping electronic files. Retention periods vary with state law, contracts, and pending claims. Confirm the clinic's schedule with counsel. EXERCISE 4.5 1. An applicant calls the clinic saying their report is wrong. heading: SECTION 5.1
body: SECTION 5.1 Why criminal records are different A criminal search is the core of most workplace screens. It is also the search most likely to produce a lawsuit, a regulatory complaint, or a lost customer when it is done badly. Three things make criminal records sensitive: • Accuracy. Records are matched to people by name and date of birth, often without a Social Security number. Common names, missing identifiers, and court data errors cause mismatches. Reporting the wrong person's record is one of the most common FCRA claims against CRAs. • Fairness. Arrest and conviction rates differ across racial and ethnic groups. A blanket policy that excludes everyone with a record can have a disparate impact that violates Title VII. • Layered rules. Federal, state, and local laws all limit what may be reported, when an employer may ask, and how a decision must be made. RECORD TYPE WHAT IT MEANS REPORTING NOTE Arrest A person was taken into custody. No finding of guilt. Non-convictions are limited to seven years under the FCRA and further limited by many states. Pending case Charges filed, no final outcome. Generally reportable as pending. Some states limit how employers may use it. Dismissed or not guilty Case ended without conviction. Non-conviction. Many states bar employers from considering it. Conviction Guilty plea or finding of guilt. No FCRA time limit, but some states limit reporting to seven years. Diversion or deferred Case resolved through a program, often dismissed Treatment varies by state and adjudication on completion. outcome. Sealed or expunged Record removed from public access by court order Should not be reported. or law. heading: SECTION 5.2
body: SECTION 5.2 Title VII and the individualized assessment Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 bars employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, and national origin. It applies to employers with 15 or more employees. A criminal record policy can violate Title VII in two ways: • Disparate treatment: applying the policy differently to people of different races or national origins. For example, overlooking a record for one applicant and rejecting another for the same record. • Disparate impact: a neutral policy, such as "no one with a conviction," that disproportionately excludes a protected group and is not job related and consistent with business necessity. The Green factors Courts and the EEOC have long looked at three factors, from Green v. Missouri Pacific Railroad (1975), to decide whether a criminal record exclusion is job related: Nature and gravity Time elapsed Nature of the job of the offense or conduct since the offense or completion of the its duties, setting, and access to sentence people or property An individualized assessment applies these factors to the person. It gives the applicant a chance to show that the exclusion should not apply, for example through evidence of rehabilitation, employment history, or the circumstances of the offense. STATUS OF EEOC GUIDANCE, OCTOBER 2026 The EEOC's 2012 enforcement guidance on arrest and conviction records has been the main federal reference since its release. In early October 2026, the EEOC sent a final rule rescinding that guidance to the White House for review. Until it is published, the guidance remains on the books. Even after rescission, Title VII itself and its disparate impact standard still apply, private lawsuits remain possible, and many state and local laws require an individualized assessment. Check the current status before relying on either position. Chapter 5: Criminal Records and Fair Chance Hiring © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Background Screening Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 40 of 83

heading: SECTION 5.3
body: SECTION 5.3 Fair chance and ban-the-box laws Fair chance laws control when an employer may ask about criminal history and how it must decide. About 17 states plus the District of Columbia apply them to private employers, along with many cities and counties. Common requirements REQUIREMENT WHAT IT USUALLY MEANS Remove the box No criminal history question on the job application. Delay the check No criminal background check until after an interview or a conditional offer. Individualized assessment A written review of the specific record against the job, often using the Green factors and evidence of rehabilitation. Specific notices A preliminary decision notice that names the records relied on, followed by a final notice. Longer response time Some laws require more than five business days for the applicant to respond. Excluded records Some records may never be considered, such as arrests without conviction, sealed records, or certain old or minor offenses. Two examples of detailed laws CALIFORNIA FAIR CHANCE ACT NEW YORK CITY FAIR CHANCE ACT Applies to employers with five or more employees. No Applies to employers with four or more employees. No criminal history inquiry before a conditional offer. A written criminal history check until after a conditional offer. The individualized assessment is required, then a preliminary employer must perform an analysis under New York Article notice with a response period of at least five business days, 23-A, provide a Fair Chance Notice with the analysis and the with more time if the applicant is gathering evidence. report, and allow at least five business days to respond. Updated regulations took effect in October 2023. Los Angeles Amendments added protections for pending cases and and San Francisco add their own rules. current employees. GOVERNING RULE Configure each client's process for every place it hires. The strictest applicable law sets the timing and the notices. heading: SECTION 5.4
body: SECTION 5.4 Clean Slate, sealing, and expungement Records can disappear from public view. A CRA must not report what the law has sealed, and employers in many states may not consider it even if they learn of it. • Expungement generally destroys or legally erases a record. • Sealing keeps the record but closes it to the public and most employers. • Clean Slate laws seal eligible records automatically after a waiting period, without the person having to apply. About 13 states had enacted them as of March 2026. Virginia's automatic sealing began July 1, 2026. Why this matters to a screening business Sealing happens on a schedule, and court databases update at different speeds. A record found in a commercial database may already be sealed at the court. Accurate CRAs check the current court record before reporting, a practice the FCRA's accuracy standard effectively requires for employment reports. REPORTING THE OUTCOME, NOT JUST THE CHARGE A report that shows a felony charge but omits that it was reduced to a misdemeanor or dismissed is inaccurate and incomplete. The final disposition must be reported along with the charge. EXERCISE 5.4 1. A database hit shows a 2019 conviction in Virginia. The applicant says it was sealed this summer. What should happen before it is reported? Chapter 5: Criminal Records and Fair Chance Hiring © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 6.1
body: SECTION 6.1 Employment credit reports An employment credit report is a modified version of a consumer credit file. It shows accounts, payment history, collections, and public records, but no credit score and no birth year. It is ordered from a nationwide credit bureau through the CRA. Extra hurdles • Supplier approval. Credit bureaus require their own end user agreement and often a site inspection before an employer may order credit. • State and local limits. Eleven states (California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Maryland, Nevada, New York, Oregon, Vermont, and Washington) restrict employment credit checks. So do the District of Columbia, Chicago, New York City, and Philadelphia. • Adverse action. The same FCRA two-step process applies. Some state laws add notice content. WHERE CREDIT IS OFTEN STILL ALLOWED TYPICAL EXAMPLES, WHICH VARY BY LAW Required by law Positions where federal or state law requires a credit check Financial responsibility Access to cash, accounts, or financial information above a set level Security and trust Law enforcement, security clearances, confidential trade secrets Managerial Some laws allow credit checks for executive or managerial roles SALES CAUTION Do not include credit in a default package. Offer it only for roles where the client can name the financial duty and the location's law permits it. heading: SECTION 6.2
body: SECTION 6.2 Motor vehicle records A motor vehicle record (MVR) lists a driver's license status, class, endorsements, restrictions, violations, accidents, and suspensions. It is the right search for any job that involves driving. • Source. MVRs come from each state's department of motor vehicles. Look-back periods and content vary by state. • Driver's Privacy Protection Act (DPPA). This federal law limits who may obtain personal information from DMV records and for what purpose. Employment verification of a driver's license is a permitted purpose, but the employer must certify it, and records must be protected. • State consent forms. Some states require their own release form for MVR access. • Ongoing monitoring. Many fleet employers check MVRs annually or continuously. Each check needs a permissible purpose and valid authorization. Commercial drivers regulated by the Department of Transportation have additional federal requirements (Chapter 8). EXERCISE 6.2 1. A client wants an MVR on every applicant, including office staff. What do you recommend? Chapter 6: Other Workplace Searches and Special Rules © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 6.3
body: SECTION 6.3 Social media and online searches Online searches can find real risks, such as threats or harassment. They also expose protected information that an employer should never consider, such as religion, pregnancy, disability, or political activity. • When a CRA performs the search, it is a consumer report and the FCRA applies in full, including accuracy and adverse action. • Reputable vendors filter out protected-class information and report only defined categories of job-relevant conduct. • Many states bar employers from requesting an applicant's passwords or private account access. • Employers who search on their own, instead of using a CRA, take on discrimination and privacy risks without the CRA's controls. SECTION 6.4 International screening Applicants who have lived, worked, or studied abroad may need international searches. • Availability, cost, and turnaround vary widely by country. Some countries provide no criminal record access to private parties. • Foreign data protection laws, such as the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, can apply to collecting and transferring data. • Education and employment verifications abroad may need translation and extra time. • The FCRA still applies when a U.S. employer uses the report. heading: SECTION 6.5
body: SECTION 6.5 Rescreening and continuous monitoring Screening does not have to end at hire. Employers increasingly rescreen at set intervals or subscribe to monitoring that alerts them to new records. TYPE HOW IT WORKS Periodic rescreening A new report at a set interval, such as annually or at promotion Continuous criminal monitoring Ongoing alerts when new records appear for an enrolled employee MVR monitoring Alerts for violations, suspensions, or license changes License and exclusion monitoring Recurring checks of professional licenses and exclusion lists, common in healthcare Compliance points • The authorization must clearly cover ongoing checks during employment. Some states require a new authorization for each report. • An alert that leads to discipline or termination triggers the same adverse action process as a pre-hire report. • Fair chance and state laws often apply to current employees, not only applicants. • Monitoring alerts must be verified at the source before they are used. heading: SECTION 6.6
body: SECTION 6.6 AI and automated hiring tools Software that scores, ranks, or filters applicants, including tools that read background check results, is now regulated in several places. Disparate impact law applies to these tools whether or not a specific AI law exists. LAW STATUS MAIN REQUIREMENTS New York City Local Law 144 Enforced since July 5, 2023 Independent bias audit within the past year, public summary of results, and notice to candidates before using an automated employment decision tool Illinois HB 3773 Effective January 1, 2026 Bars AI use that discriminates on protected classes, including the use of ZIP codes as a proxy, and requires notice when AI is used in employment decisions California FEHA automateddecision regulations Effective October 1, 2025 Treats discriminatory automated decision systems as violations, applies fair chance rules to automated criminal history screening, and requires keeping records for four years Colorado AI Act Applies January 1, 2027, with enforcement currently held by court order Risk management and impact assessments for high-risk AI systems, including those used in hiring AUTOMATED ADJUDICATION Many platforms let employers set criteria that automatically label results as "meets" or "does not meet." These are useful but risky. The criteria must be the employer's own, must be job related, and must not skip the individualized assessment or notices required by fair chance laws. A "does not meet" label that leads directly to rejection, with no human review, is the kind of practice regulators and plaintiffs target. heading: SECTION 7.1
body: SECTION 7.1 How state law fits with the FCRA The FCRA sets a national floor. States may generally add stricter rules, except in a few areas the FCRA reserves to federal law. The result is that a single national employer may face dozens of different requirements. State and local laws commonly add: • Their own disclosure forms or notices, and a box for the applicant to request a free copy of the report. • Shorter look-back periods for convictions or other records. • Fair chance timing and assessment rules (Chapter 5). • Limits on credit checks (Chapter 6). • Limits on salary history, arrest records, juvenile records, or marijuana offenses. • Licensing or registration for CRAs or investigators in some states. GOVERNING RULE Which law applies depends on where the applicant lives, where the job is, and where the employer is located. When more than one law applies, follow the strictest. heading: SECTION 7.2
body: SECTION 7.2 State consumer reporting laws Several states have their own versions of the FCRA, often called "mini-FCRAs." These are the ones clinics will see most. STATE LAW KEY DIFFERENCES FROM THE FCRA California Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act (ICRAA) and Consumer Credit Reporting Agencies Act Separate disclosure requirements, a box to request a free copy of the report, seven-year limit on convictions with no salary exception, and higher damages. Courts have applied ICRAA to most employment background checks. New York Fair Credit Reporting Act (General Business Law Article 25) and Correction Law Article 23-A Copy of Article 23-A must be given to the applicant. Article 23-A sets eight factors for evaluating convictions. Seven-year conviction limit with a salary exception. Massachusetts Consumer reporting law and CORI rules Seven-year limits apply to convictions, with a salary exception. Specific rules for use of the state criminal record system (CORI). Washington Fair Credit Reporting Act (RCW 19.182) and Fair Chance Act Seven-year limit on convictions, with a salary exception. Statewide fair chance rules. Minnesota Consumer reporting statute A box to request a free copy, and a requirement that the CRA send the report within a set time if requested. Oklahoma Consumer reporting statute A box to request a free copy of the report. Other states Varies Colorado, Kansas, Maryland, Montana, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, and others limit the reporting of certain records or add notice duties. This table summarizes selected rules and is not complete. Laws change often. Confirm current requirements before configuring a client. heading: SECTION 7.3
body: SECTION 7.3 Look-back limits Under the FCRA, convictions can be reported regardless of age, and most other negative items are limited to seven years. Several states are stricter. RULE WHERE IT APPLIES (SELECTED) Convictions limited to seven years California, Kansas, Maryland, Massachusetts, Montana, New Hampshire, New Mexico, New York, Washington, and Colorado, often with a salary exception and specific details Non-convictions not reportable or not Many states, including California, Illinois, Massachusetts, and New York considered Certain marijuana offenses not considered Several states and cities where recreational marijuana is legal Juvenile records not considered Most states, as juvenile records are often sealed by law How the seven years is measured The FCRA measures seven years for non-conviction records from the date of entry, such as the arrest or filing. Some state laws measure from the date of disposition, release, or parole. Good CRAs apply each state's rule automatically. Clinic staff should know the rules exist and send questions to the CRA. EXERCISE 7.3 1. An applicant for a $50,000-a-year job in California has a 2015 conviction. May it be reported? Chapter 7: State and Local Laws © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 8.1
body: SECTION 8.1 The sectors at a glance Workplace screening is the core market for clinics, but customers in regulated industries have extra requirements. Knowing the basics helps you spot an opportunity, and know when a request is outside your offering. SECTOR MAIN EXTRA REQUIREMENTS KEY SOURCES Transportation (DOT) Previous employer safety history, Clearinghouse queries, MVRs, and medical certification FMCSA, FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse, PSP Healthcare Federal and state exclusion checks, license verification, and fingerprinting in many states OIG LEIE, SAM, state Medicaid exclusion lists, licensing boards Education and youth Fingerprint checks, sex offender registry, and child abuse registry checks State repositories, FBI, state registries Financial services Fingerprinting and statutory bars for certain offenses FINRA, FDIC Section 19, NMLS Tenant screening FCRA plus fair housing law Eviction records, credit, criminal records Gig and contract work FCRA applies to independent contractors in most courts' view Same as employment, often with monitoring Volunteers Often state-required checks for youth programs State repositories, registries Government and security Federal investigations and clearances, conducted by the government Federal agencies Chapter 8: Other Screening Sectors at a Glance © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 8.2
body: SECTION 8.2 DOT-regulated transportation Clinics already know DOT drug and alcohol testing. Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) rules also require background-type checks for commercial drivers. REQUIREMENT WHAT IT INVOLVES Safety performance history Employers must investigate the driver's previous three years of DOT-regulated employment, including accidents and drug and alcohol testing history (49 CFR 391.23 and 40.25). Clearinghouse queries A full query of the FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse before hire, and limited queries at least annually for current drivers. The driver must consent in the Clearinghouse. MVRs An MVR from each state where the driver held a license in the past three years, and an annual review. Pre-Employment Screening Optional FMCSA report of five years of crash data and three years of inspections. It has Program (PSP) its own disclosure and authorization. Driver qualification file The employer must keep a file containing the application, MVRs, medical certificate, and investigation results. CLINIC OPPORTUNITY Clinics that already serve DOT clients can bundle screening with testing. When a third party, such as a CRA, gathers the previous employer information, the FCRA may also apply. Check the provider's process before selling it. Chapter 8: Other Screening Sectors at a Glance © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Background Screening Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 64 of 83

heading: SECTION 8.3
body: SECTION 8.3 Healthcare Healthcare employers face federal penalties for employing or contracting with excluded individuals, and many states require fingerprint checks for workers who care for patients. • OIG List of Excluded Individuals and Entities (LEIE). The HHS Office of Inspector General lists people barred from federal health programs. Employers that bill Medicare or Medicaid can face civil penalties for employing them. Most check at hire and monthly. • System for Award Management (SAM). The federal list of debarred and excluded parties. • State Medicaid exclusion lists. Many states keep their own lists. • License verification. Primary source checks with the licensing board, plus disciplinary actions. • Fingerprint-based checks. Many states require them for long-term care, home health, and other patient-facing roles, often under programs run by the state. SECTION 8.4 Education, youth, and volunteers • Schools, child care providers, and youth programs usually must run state-mandated fingerprint checks through the state repository and the FBI. These are generally run through the state, not commercial CRAs. • Sex offender registries and child abuse or neglect registries are commonly required. • Volunteer screening by a CRA is usually still a consumer report, and the FCRA protections apply when the organization uses the report for a decision. Chapter 8: Other Screening Sectors at a Glance © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Background Screening Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 65 of 83

heading: SECTION 8.5
body: SECTION 8.5 Financial services • FINRA. Member broker-dealer firms must fingerprint most associated persons, and certain offenses disqualify them. • FDIC Section 19. Federal law bars people convicted of certain offenses involving dishonesty, breach of trust, or money laundering from working at insured banks without FDIC consent. Recent rule changes narrowed what is covered. • NMLS. Mortgage loan originators go through fingerprinting and credit checks as part of licensing. SECTION 8.6 Tenant screening Tenant screening is consumer reporting for housing. The FCRA applies, along with the federal Fair Housing Act and state and local housing laws. Key differences from employment: • No standalone disclosure and authorization requirement as in employment, but an adverse action notice is required. • Eviction records and rental history are central and carry their own accuracy problems. • Many cities restrict criminal history use in housing decisions. Tenant screening is a separate business with different customers and rules. Most clinics should not offer it without a provider and process built for it. SECTION 8.7 Gig work and government • Gig and contract platforms screen large volumes of independent workers. Courts and regulators generally treat this as employment purpose under the FCRA. • Government clearances are conducted by federal agencies, not private CRAs. Clinics may support related drug testing, but not the investigation. Chapter 8: Other Screening Sectors at a Glance © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 8.8
body: SECTION 8.8 When to refer A clinic builds trust by knowing what it does well. Refer the customer, or bring in the provider's specialist team, when a request falls outside your standard offering. REQUEST RESPONSE Standard pre-employment screen for a private Core offering. Proceed. employer DOT driver qualification Proceed if your provider offers the DOT products. Coordinate with your testing services. Healthcare exclusion monitoring Proceed if your provider offers it. State-mandated fingerprint checks Usually through the state's approved channel. Refer, or offer fingerprint capture only if you are an approved site. Tenant screening Refer unless you have a tenant screening product and process. Private investigation, surveillance, or locating a Refer. This often requires a private investigator license and is outside person employment screening. Checking a spouse, neighbor, or date Decline. There is no permissible purpose.
