heading: SECTION 9.1
body: SECTION 9.1 Know your role, in writing Everything a clinic may say and do depends on its role: referral partner, agent, or reseller (Chapter 1, Section 1.3). Confirm it in writing before you sell. QUESTION WHY IT MATTERS Who is the CRA on the report? That name goes on the adverse action notice and handles disputes. Who signs the client It determines who verifies and credentials the employer. agreement? Who sets prices and invoices? Resellers carry their own FCRA duties. What may the clinic see? Access to report contents brings data security duties. Who handles applicant calls? Disputes go to the CRA. Staff need a script. SECTION 9.2 Protecting applicant data Background screening involves Social Security numbers, dates of birth, and criminal records. A breach harms applicants and ends customer relationships. • Collect data through the platform, not by email, fax, or paper, wherever possible. • Use individual logins with strong passwords and multi-factor authentication. Never share accounts. • Give access only to staff who need it, and remove it as soon as they leave. • Do not download or print reports unless necessary, and dispose of them securely. • Report any suspected breach immediately to your provider and follow state breach notification laws. Chapter 9: Running a Compliant Screening Business © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Background Screening Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 71 of 83

heading: SECTION 9.3
body: SECTION 9.3 Honest marketing Misleading claims about background checks have drawn FTC enforcement and lawsuits. Describe what the product does, accurately. AVOID SAY INSTEAD "Instant national criminal check" "A multi-jurisdiction database search, with records verified at the source before reporting" "Complete criminal history" "Searches of the jurisdictions in your package" "FCRA compliant guaranteed" "Built to support your FCRA compliance, with forms and adverse action tools" "Results in minutes" "Many results within one to three business days, depending on courts and verifications" "We'll tell you who to hire" "You set the criteria and make the decision" "Legal advice included" "We explain the process. Your counsel advises on your policy." GOVERNING RULE Never promise speed, completeness, or legal compliance that the product and the law cannot deliver. Chapter 9: Running a Compliant Screening Business © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Background Screening Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 72 of 83

heading: SECTION 9.4
body: SECTION 9.4 Common customer questions Use these answers as a starting point. When a question is about the customer's own hiring policy, recommend they ask their counsel. QUESTION ANSWER Can I run a check before the interview? It depends on where you hire. Many states and cities require waiting until after an interview or a conditional offer. We set up your account for each location. Can I reject someone for any conviction? Blanket policies carry legal risk. Most laws expect you to consider the offense, how long ago it was, and the job. Review your policy with your counsel. Why does it take more than a day? Some courts require a clerk search, and verifications depend on schools and employers responding. Can I check current employees? Yes, with permissible purpose and proper authorization. The same adverse action rules apply. Do I need consent for a check? Yes. Federal law requires a standalone disclosure and the applicant's written authorization. The platform handles both. Can you check credit? For some roles and locations. Several states and cities restrict it. Tell us the job and location. The applicant says the report is wrong. What now? Pause your decision. The applicant should file a dispute with the CRA, which will reinvestigate and correct any errors. Can I see the applicant's social media? A filtered social media search through a CRA is available. Searching on your own risks seeing information you may not legally consider. Chapter 9: Running a Compliant Screening Business © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Background Screening Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 73 of 83

heading: SECTION 9.5
body: SECTION 9.5 Pairing screening with testing Clinic customers often need drug testing and background checks at the same point in hiring. Offering both can save the employer time and coordination. • Coordinate timing. Many employers order both after a conditional offer. • Keep the two processes legally separate. Drug test results and background reports have different rules, notices, and records. • Do not combine the background check disclosure with drug testing consent forms. The FCRA disclosure must stand alone. • For DOT clients, coordinate Clearinghouse, previous employer, and MVR requirements with testing services (Chapter 8). EXAMPLE OPENING "You already send new hires to us for drug testing. We can now run their background checks through the same account, with consent, state notices, and adverse action tools built in. Where do you hire, and which positions do you screen?" EXERCISE 9.5 1. A client asks to put the background check consent on the bottom of the drug testing form to save paperwork. What do you say? heading: Appendix A: Glossary
body: Appendix A: Glossary APPENDICES A Glossary Definitions of the terms and abbreviations used in this guidebook. Chapter and section references point to where each term is explained in depth. A Address history trace. A search of credit header and other data that lists names and addresses linked to a Social Security number. Used to decide where to search, not reported as a finding (3.1). Adjudication. Applying an employer's criteria to a report to label it, such as "meets" or "review." The employer sets the criteria and makes the decision (6.6). Adverse action. A denial of employment or any other decision for employment purposes that adversely affects a current or prospective employee (2.1, 4.4). Consumer report. Information from a CRA bearing on a person's character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living, used for employment or another permissible purpose (2.1). Continuous monitoring. Ongoing alerts of new records for enrolled employees (6.5). CORI. Criminal Offender Record Information, the Massachusetts criminal record system (7.2). County criminal search. A search of a county court's records, by a court researcher or electronic access. The most reliable criminal source (3.2). Adverse action notice. The final FCRA notice sent after an employer decides against an applicant based on a report (4.4). CRA (consumer reporting agency). A business that assembles or evaluates consumer information to furnish consumer reports to third parties (1.2, 2.1). Agent. A clinic or other party that sells or supports a CRA's services under the CRA's name and contracts (1.3). D Article 23-A. New York Correction Law article that sets factors for evaluating criminal convictions in employment (5.3, 7.2). Disclosure. The standalone document telling an applicant a consumer report may be obtained for employment purposes (2.3). Authorization. The applicant's written permission for an employer to obtain a consumer report (2.3). Disparate impact. Discrimination that results from a neutral policy that disproportionately excludes a protected group and is not job related (5.2). Automated employment decision tool. Software that substantially assists or replaces discretionary hiring decisions. Regulated in New York City and elsewhere (6.6). Disposition. The final outcome of a criminal case, such as conviction, dismissal, or acquittal (5.1, 5.4). B Dispute. A consumer's challenge to the accuracy or completeness of a report. The CRA must reinvestigate (4.5).

heading: Appendix A: Glossary
body: Ban-the-box. A fair chance law that removes criminal history questions from job applications (5.3). DPPA (Driver's Privacy Protection Act). Federal law limiting access to personal information in DMV records (6.2). Bias audit. An independent review of an automated tool's impact on protected groups (6.6). E C EEOC (Equal Employment Opportunity Commission). The federal agency that enforces Title VII (5.2). Certification (employer). The employer's written promise to a CRA that it will meet its FCRA duties (2.2). Expungement. Legal erasure or destruction of a criminal record (5.4). CFPB (Consumer Financial Protection Bureau). The federal agency with FCRA rulemaking authority (2.6). F Clean Slate law. A state law that automatically seals eligible criminal records after a waiting period (5.4). Fair chance law. A state or local law limiting when and how employers consider criminal history (5.3). Clearinghouse. The FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse, a database of CDL drivers' drug and alcohol program violations (8.2). FCRA (Fair Credit Reporting Act). The federal law governing consumer reports, 15 U.S.C. 1681 and following (Chapter 2). Federal criminal search. A search of U.S. district court records for federal crimes (3.2). Appendix A: Glossary © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Background Screening Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 78 of 83

heading: FTC (Federal Trade Commission). Shares FCRA enforcement
body: FMCSA. Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (8.2). FTC (Federal Trade Commission). Shares FCRA enforcement authority with the CFPB (2.6). Pre-adverse action notice. Notice sent before a final decision, with a copy of the report and the Summary of Rights (4.4). PSP. FMCSA's Pre-Employment Screening Program (8.2). G R Green factors. The nature and gravity of the offense, the time elapsed, and the nature of the job (5.2). Reinvestigation. The CRA's review of a disputed item, generally within 30 days (4.5). I Reseller. A CRA that assembles and merges information from other CRAs and resells it without maintaining its own database (1.3, 2.5). ICRAA. California's Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act (7.2). Individualized assessment. A review of a specific person's record against the job, with a chance for the person to respond (5.2). Investigative consumer report. A report based on personal interviews about a person's character or reputation. Requires extra disclosure (2.1). L LEIE. The HHS Office of Inspector General's List of Excluded Individuals and Entities (8.3). Look-back period. How far back a record may be reported or considered (2.4, 7.3). M Mini-FCRA. A state consumer reporting law (7.2). S SAM. The federal System for Award Management, which includes exclusion records (8.3). Sealing. Closing a record to public access by court order or law (5.4). Section 613. FCRA provision on public record information reported for employment purposes (2.4). Summary of Rights. The CFPB form "A Summary of Your Rights Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act" (4.4). T Title VII. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which bars employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, and national origin (5.2). Multi-jurisdiction database. A commercial database compiled from many court, corrections, and registry sources. Must be verified at the source (3.2). Turnaround time. The time from order to completed report (3.4). MVR (motor vehicle record). A state driving record (6.2). User. A person or business that obtains and uses a consumer report, such as an employer (1.2). P PBSA. The Professional Background Screening Association, the industry trade association (1.4).

heading: FTC (Federal Trade Commission). Shares FCRA enforcement
body: Permissible purpose. A reason the FCRA allows a consumer report to be obtained, such as employment (2.2). Appendix A: Glossary © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. heading: SECTION 1.1
body: SECTION 1.1 What you are paying for A drug test is not one price. It is a chain of services, and only some links in the chain apply to every test. Which links apply depends on whether the program screens in-house with rapid tests or sends every specimen straight to the laboratory. Finance teams that budget on the "price per test" alone are usually surprised by the invoice. COST WHAT IT IS APPLIES TO Collection Staff time, supplies, and the space to collect a specimen, in- Every test house or at a collection site Screen The first test: a rapid device read in-house, or a laboratory Every test (in the screen laboratory fee when testing straight to the laboratory) Laboratory confirmation Medical review Shipping and handling A second, more specific laboratory test on a specimen that Non-negative screens did not screen negative only A Medical Review Officer (MRO), a licensed physician, reviews Laboratory positives the laboratory result and interviews the donor (both models) Packaging and courier costs to send specimens to the Non-negatives only (in- laboratory house rapid) or every specimen (straight to laboratory) Administration Scheduling, records, reporting, and software Every test Lost time Hours a worker or applicant spends traveling and waiting Mostly when workers travel to an outside collection site GOVERNING RULE Every test pays for collection and a screen. Every positive pays for medical review. Where the screen happens decides what else every test pays for. Chapter 1: What Drug Testing Really Costs © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Drug Testing Cost Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 5 of 57

heading: SECTION 1.2
body: SECTION 1.2 Fixed costs and variable costs Think of each test as two parts: a fixed part every test carries, and a variable part that only applies when the screen is not negative. FIXED PER TEST VARIABLE PER TEST • Collection • Laboratory confirmation • Screen device or laboratory screen • MRO review and interview • Administration • Shipping Predictable. Multiply by the number of tests. • Follow-up such as recollections Depends on how many results are not negative. The basic formula Cost per test = fixed cost + (positive rate × cost to confirm and review one positive) With in-house rapid testing, the positive rate drives both confirmation and medical review. With straight-to-laboratory testing, confirmation is usually inside the laboratory fee, so the positive rate mainly drives medical review. Chapter 4 works through examples of both. EXERCISE 1.2 1. Your fixed cost is $10 per test and it costs $70 to confirm and review one positive. What is the cost per test at a 5% positive rate? At a 15% positive rate? Chapter 1: What Drug Testing Really Costs © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Drug Testing Cost Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 6 of 57

heading: SECTION 1.3
body: SECTION 1.3 Two ways to test: in-house rapid and straight to laboratory Every program uses one of two delivery models, or a mix of both. Each model is priced differently, so this guide prices them separately: in-house rapid testing in Chapter 4, straight-to-laboratory testing in Chapter 5, and the two side by side in Chapter 6. 100 tests collected Every test carries collection and a screen 94 negative screens 6 non-negative screens Stop on site. No laboratory, no MRO. Laboratory confirmation Fixed cost: paid on all 100 tests. 6 laboratory positives Variable cost: paid only on the 6. MRO review and donor interview Figure 1.1 In-house rapid testing: 100 urine tests at a 6% positive rate. Negatives stop on site. Only the 6 non-negatives carry laboratory and MRO costs. 100 tests collected and shipped Every specimen goes to the laboratory Laboratory screen and confirmation Usually one fee per specimen, whatever the result 94 negatives 6 laboratory positives Reported by the laboratory. No MRO interview. MRO review and donor interview Figure 1.2 Straight-to-laboratory testing: the same 100 tests. Every specimen carries the laboratory fee. Only the 6 positives carry MRO cost. heading: SECTION 2.1
body: SECTION 2.1 National positive rates by specimen The most widely cited national source is the Quest Diagnostics Drug Testing Index, built from millions of workplace tests each year. Its 2025 results for the general U.S. workforce show how much the specimen matters. SPECIMEN (GENERAL U.S. 2024 2025 WHAT IT REFLECTS Urine 5.6% 5.5% Use over the previous several days Oral fluid, all tests 5.4% 5.2% Very recent use, within hours to a day or two Oral fluid, marijuana, among tests 10.4% 11.1% Recent marijuana use 17.2% 19.1% Repeated use over about 90 days WORKFORCE) that include it Hair Urine Oral fluid, all tests 5.5% 5.2% Oral fluid, marijuana* 11.1% Hair 19.1% Figure 2.1 Positive rates by specimen, general U.S. workforce, 2025 (Quest Diagnostics Drug Testing Index). *Marijuana alone, among oral fluid tests that include it. Source: Quest Diagnostics Drug Testing Index, 2026 Annual Report (2025 data). For comparison, federally mandated safety-sensitive (DOT) urine tests were 2.2% positive in 2025. READING THE ORAL FLUID NUMBERS Quest's overall oral fluid rate is close to urine, but its marijuana rate alone is 11.1% among oral fluid tests that include marijuana. The two rates use different bases, and many oral fluid programs leave marijuana off the panel. When marijuana is on the panel, expect oral fluid positivity well above urine. That is the situation most employers budgeting for oral fluid will face. Chapter 2: Positive Rates by Specimen © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Drug Testing Cost Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 11 of 57

heading: SECTION 2.2
body: SECTION 2.2 Why the specimen changes the rate Different specimens look at different windows of time and catch different drugs better. A higher positive rate does not mean a worse test. It usually means the test sees more. SPECIMEN WHY ITS RATE IS WHERE IT IS Urine Detects most drugs for several days. It is the specimen people most often try to dilute, substitute, or adulterate, which can lower the positive rate. Oral fluid Collected in plain view, so it is very hard to cheat. Detects THC itself rather than only its metabolite, and catches recent marijuana use well. Hair Looks back about 90 days, so it finds repeated use that a short-window test misses. A worker cannot "wait it out" for a hair test. Oral fluid Hours to about 2 days Urine About 1 to 5 days, longer for heavy use Hair About 7 to 90 days 0d 1d 3d 7d 30d 90d Days after use (scale compressed) Figure 2.2 General detection windows by specimen. Longer windows find more use, which raises the positive rate. GOVERNING RULE Choosing a specimen is choosing a positive rate. Choosing a positive rate is choosing a budget. Chapter 2: Positive Rates by Specimen © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Drug Testing Cost Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 12 of 57

heading: SECTION 2.3
body: SECTION 2.3 Choosing a planning rate Budgets need a single number. National data is a starting point. Your own program's history is better once you have it. SPECIMEN NATIONAL REFERENCE (2025) PLANNING RANGE USED IN THIS GUIDE Urine 5.5% 5 to 7% Oral fluid, marijuana not on the 5.2% for all oral fluid tests 5 to 7%, the same as urine Oral fluid, marijuana on the panel 11.1% for marijuana alone 10 to 15% Hair 19.1% 20 to 25% panel Planning ranges reflect national data and typical results in programs Labb supports. Rates vary by industry, region, panel, and testing reason. Pre-employment and reasonable suspicion tests usually run higher than random tests. What moves your rate • Panel. Adding marijuana, fentanyl, or other drugs adds positives. • Testing reason. Reasonable suspicion and post-incident tests run higher than random tests. • Location. Regional drug use and state marijuana laws matter. • Reading accuracy. With in-house rapid testing, misread screens send negatives to the laboratory and add cost (Chapter 4, Section 4.4). EXERCISE 2.3 1. Your company is switching from urine to oral fluid with marijuana on the panel. What happens to the planning positive rate, and why? heading: SECTION 3.1
body: SECTION 3.1 Laboratory confirmation A screen is designed to sort specimens quickly. A non-negative screen is not proof of drug use. Before anyone acts on it, a laboratory confirms it with a second, more specific method, such as mass spectrometry. Rapid device or laboratory Non-negatives go to the Laboratory positives go to The MRO reports the verified screen. Most results are laboratory for confirmation. the MRO. result. Screen Confirm Review Report negative and stop here. • In-house rapid screening keeps negatives on site. Only non-negatives are packaged and shipped, so laboratory costs scale with the positive rate. • Laboratory-based testing sends every specimen to the laboratory. Many laboratory prices bundle the screen and confirmation into one fee, so laboratory cost scales with the number of tests instead. • Some non-negative screens do not confirm. The confirmation still has to be paid for. Chapter 3: Confirmation and Medical Review © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Drug Testing Cost Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 17 of 57

heading: SECTION 3.2
body: SECTION 3.2 Medical review: who the MRO is A Medical Review Officer is a licensed physician (an MD or DO) with specialized training in drug testing. The MRO is the last step before a result is reported, and the step that protects the employer and the donor. FOR A LABORATORY POSITIVE, THE MRO Reviews the laboratory report and WHY IT MATTERS TO COST Physician time on every positive the custody form Contacts and interviews the donor Phone calls, often several attempts, sometimes across several days Verifies prescriptions with More calls and records review pharmacies or prescribers Decides whether a legitimate A medical judgment only a physician can make medical explanation exists Reports the verified result and any Documentation that has to hold up if challenged safety concern HOW MROS BILL MRO services are commonly billed per positive reviewed, per test, or under a program fee. Read the contract: a per-test fee hides positive-rate risk inside the vendor's price, and a per-positive fee moves it to you. Chapter 3: Confirmation and Medical Review © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Drug Testing Cost Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 18 of 57

heading: SECTION 3.3
body: SECTION 3.3 Negatives and positives at the MRO This is where positive rates hit hardest. A negative result never needs a physician interview. A positive result always does. Laboratory result Negative Positive No donor interview Physician reviews the file No prescription checks Donor interview, often several calls Administrative review at most Prescription verification Little or no MRO cost Full MRO fee, every specimen type Figure 3.1 What happens at the MRO. Negatives cost little or nothing to review. Every positive needs a physician. GOVERNING RULE Every laboratory positive goes to an MRO, whatever the specimen. Never act on a positive the MRO has not verified. Skipping medical review to save money is a false economy. A positive caused by a legitimate prescription, reported without review, exposes the employer to discrimination, privacy, and wrongful termination claims that cost far more than the review. Chapter 3: Confirmation and Medical Review © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Drug Testing Cost Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 19 of 57

heading: SECTION 4.1
body: SECTION 4.1 How in-house rapid testing is priced With in-house rapid testing, the employer or clinic collects and screens on site. Negatives are final on the spot. Only non-negatives are packaged and sent to the laboratory, so most of the laboratory and medical review cost follows the positive rate. COST LINE HOW IT IS PAID Rapid device One per test, bought in advance Collection Staff time on site for every test Laboratory confirmation Per non-negative sent to the laboratory Shipping and supplies Per non-negative sent, often included in the confirmation price MRO review Per laboratory positive Reading and records Software, reader, or staff time for every test Rapid cost per test = device + collection + positive rate × (confirmation + shipping + MRO review) Example assumptions ILLUSTRATIVE ASSUMPTION URINE ORAL FLUID Rapid device per test $8 $12 Confirmation per non-negative, shipping included $35 $45 MRO review per positive $35 $35 Planning positive rate 6% 12% Illustrative prices, not Labb prices or quotes. The examples assume every non-negative confirms positive and leave out collection labor, which Chapter 6 adds back. Hair is not tested with rapid devices and is priced in Chapter 5. Chapter 4: Pricing In-House Rapid Testing © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Drug Testing Cost Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 23 of 57

heading: SECTION 4.2
body: SECTION 4.2 Rapid testing: cost per 100 tests PER 100 TESTS URINE (6%) ORAL FLUID (12%) Rapid devices 100 × $8 = $800 100 × $12 = $1,200 Confirmations 6 × $35 = $210 12 × $45 = $540 MRO reviews 6 × $35 = $210 12 × $35 = $420 Specimens shipped Total $1,220 $2,160 Cost per test $12.20 $21.60 Share spent on confirmation and MRO 34% 44% Cost per positive found $203 $180 Urine (6%) $12.20 Oral fluid (12%) $21.60 Rapid device Confirmation MRO review Figure 4.1 In-house rapid testing: cost per test split into device, confirmation, and MRO review. Illustrative prices. WHAT THE TABLE SHOWS Rapid oral fluid costs more per test than rapid urine, and most of the difference is not the device, though the device does cost more. A urine cup is simple. An oral fluid test needs a collection swab or pad built into the device. It is the doubled positive rate, which doubles the confirmations and MRO reviews. Because oral fluid finds twice as many positives, it costs less per positive found. Chapter 4: Pricing In-House Rapid Testing © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Drug Testing Cost Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 24 of 57

heading: SECTION 4.3
body: SECTION 4.3 Rapid testing: when the rate moves With rapid testing, a large share of the cost is variable. Small changes in the positive rate move the cost per test more than small changes in device price. ORAL FLUID POSITIVE RATE CONFIRMATIONS AND MRO PER 100 TESTS COST PER TEST 8% 8 × $80 = $640 $18.40 10% 10 × $80 = $800 $20.00 12% 12 × $80 = $960 $21.60 15% 15 × $80 = $1,200 $24.00 $80 is the illustrative confirmation ($45) plus MRO review ($35) for one oral fluid positive, added to the $12 device. $26 $24.00 $24 $21.60 $22 $20.00 $20 $18.40 $18 Planning range $16 6% 8% 10% 12% 14% 16% Oral fluid positive rate Figure 4.2 In-house rapid testing: oral fluid cost per test as the positive rate rises. Illustrative prices. BUDGET FOR THE HIGH END Going from 8% to 15% raises rapid oral fluid cost by $5.60 per test, about 30%. A hiring push, a new site in a highuse region, or adding marijuana to the panel can move the rate that much. Budget at the top of the planning range and track the actual rate monthly. EXERCISE 4.3 1. Using the rapid urine assumptions, what is the cost per test at a 9% positive rate? Chapter 4: Pricing In-House Rapid Testing © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: SECTION 4.4
body: SECTION 4.4 What adds cost to rapid testing Every rapid screen called non-negative when it is actually negative sends a specimen to the laboratory for nothing. Every one called negative when it is not lets a risk through. COST DRIVER COST TO THE PROGRAM A faint line called non-negative An unnecessary confirmation, shipping, and a delayed hire or return to work A reader who expects a positive after a The same unnecessary costs, plus a donor who feels judged donor mentions a medication A non-negative called negative No laboratory cost today, and an undetected risk on the job Non-negatives that do not confirm A confirmation paid for with no positive found Expired or damaged devices Inventory written off and tests repeated Collector turnover Training time for new collectors Objective, digital reading with LabbHR applies the same criteria to every test, so laboratory spend reflects real nonnegatives, not reading habits. EXERCISE 4.4 1. Your collectors send 9% of rapid urine screens to the laboratory, but only 5% confirm positive. What does the gap cost you, and what could cause it? heading: SECTION 7.1
body: SECTION 7.1 Building the annual budget Start with how many tests you will run, by reason and specimen. Then apply the cost per test from Chapter 4 for rapid testing or Chapter 5 for laboratory testing, collection included (Chapter 6). TESTING REASON HOW TO ESTIMATE THE COUNT Pre-employment Planned hires, plus applicants who test but are not hired Random Average covered headcount × annual random rate in your policy Post-incident Last year's qualifying incidents, adjusted for growth Reasonable suspicion Last year's count, or a small allowance Return-to-duty and follow-up Workers on last-chance agreements × follow-up tests each EXAMPLE A company plans 300 hires and has 500 covered employees with a 25% random rate. That is 300 + 125 = 425 tests, plus about 25 post-incident and reasonable suspicion tests, for 450 oral fluid tests. 450 ORAL FLUID TESTS, TESTING COST ONLY IN-HOUSE RAPID STRAIGHT TO LABORATORY At 12% 450 × $21.60 = $9,720 450 × $42.20 = $18,990 At 15%, top of the planning range 450 × $24.00 = $10,800 450 × $43.25 = $19,463 Swing from 12% to 15% $1,080 $473 Budget the higher figure. Add collection and lost time from Chapter 6 for the full cost. EXERCISE 7.1 1. Estimate next year's test count for your company by testing reason. heading: SECTION 7.2
body: SECTION 7.2 Levers that control cost The goal is not the lowest positive rate. It is paying only for the testing that serves a purpose, and paying for it efficiently. LEVER EFFECT ON COST Specimen by reason Use urine for high-volume screening, oral fluid where recent use or cheating is the concern, and hair only for the roles that need long-term history. Panel design Every drug added can add positives. Match the panel to real risk and to state law, especially for marijuana. Delivery model Rapid testing where speed and volume matter, straight-to-laboratory testing where predictability, regulation, or panel breadth matter (Chapter 6). Laboratory pricing Bundled pricing removes positive-rate risk from the laboratory fee. Unbundled pricing puts it back. Objective reading For rapid testing, fewer misread non-negatives means fewer unnecessary confirmations. Collection strategy Self-collection costs least. Mobile collection costs most. Match the option to the testing reason (Chapter 6, Section 6.5). Electronic custody forms Fewer cancelled tests and less staff time chasing paper. Collection quality Fewer rejected specimens, invalid results, and recollections in both models. Contract structure Choose per-positive or per-test MRO pricing knowingly, and confirm what the laboratory bundles. GOVERNING RULE Never save money by skipping confirmation or medical review. Those steps are what make a result safe to act on. Chapter 7: Budgeting and Controlling Cost © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. LabbHR Drug Testing Cost Guidebook | Q4 2026 Page 49 of 57

heading: SECTION 7.3
body: SECTION 7.3 Hidden costs Some of the largest costs of a testing program never appear on a testing invoice. HIDDEN COST WHERE IT COMES FROM Chasing paper Staff time faxing, scanning, correcting, and filing paper custody forms, and tests cancelled for form errors Lost work time Workers and applicants traveling to and waiting at outside collection sites Lost applicants Candidates who take another job while waiting for results Delayed starts Open shifts covered by overtime or temporary labor Incidents Injuries, damage, and workers' compensation claims involving impaired workers who were never detected Disputes and claims Results that cannot be defended because they were misread, poorly documented, or never medically reviewed THE FINANCE VIEW A positive rate is not a cost to minimize. Each positive found before hire or before an incident is a cost avoided. The right question is whether the program finds the risk it should, at a cost per positive the business can justify. heading: SECTION 7.4
body: SECTION 7.4 Questions to ask every vendor # QUESTION What is included in the screen price, and what is billed separately? Does the laboratory fee bundle confirmation, shipping, and supplies? If not, what does each cost? How is the MRO billed: per positive, per test, or a program fee? Is there any charge for negatives? Who pays for shipping and supplies for specimens sent to the laboratory? Do your collectors and laboratory use electronic custody forms? What do invalid results, recollections, and cancelled tests cost? What positive rate does your pricing assume, and what happens if ours is higher? Can you report our monthly non-negative and confirmed positive rates by specimen and reason? For rapid testing: how are results read, and what record exists if a result is challenged? For laboratory testing: what are collection site fees and turnaround times? heading: Appendix A: Glossary
body: Appendix A: Glossary APPENDICES A Glossary Terms used in this guidebook. Section references point to where each term is explained. B Break-even rate. The positive rate at which rapid and laboratory testing cost the same per test (6.3). Bundled pricing. A laboratory price that includes both the screen and confirmation (5.1, 5.3). C Collection site fee. A per-donor fee charged by an outside site that collects specimens (5.4, 6.4). Confirmation. A second, more specific laboratory test on a specimen that did not screen negative (3.1). MRO (Medical Review Officer). A licensed physician who reviews laboratory positives, interviews donors, and reports verified results (3.2). N Negative. A result showing no drug above the cut-off. A negative needs no MRO interview (3.3). Non-negative. A screen result that is not negative and must be confirmed by a laboratory. It is not yet a positive (3.1). P Panel. The list of drugs a test detects (2.3, 7.2). Cost per positive found. Total program cost divided by the number of positives it finds (4.2, 5.2, 6.2). Patient service center (PSC). A laboratory-owned collection site (6.5). Cost per test. Total program cost divided by the number of tests (1.2, 4.2, 5.2). Planning rate. The positive rate used to build a budget (2.3). F S eCCF (electronic custody and control form). A digital chain of custody form that replaces the paper form (6.5, 7.3). Screen. The first test on a specimen, rapid or laboratory (1.1). Fixed cost. A cost every test carries, such as the screen and collection (1.2). H Hidden cost. A cost of testing that does not appear on a testing invoice, such as lost work time (6.4, 7.3). I In-house rapid testing. Rapid screening performed on site, with only non-negatives sent to the laboratory (1.3, 4.1, 6.1). L Positive rate (positivity). The share of tests that are positive (2.1). Sensitivity analysis. Recalculating cost at different positive rates (4.3, 5.3, 6.3). V Straight-to-laboratory testing. Testing in which every specimen is sent to the laboratory for screening and any confirmation. Also called laboratory-based testing (1.3, 5.1, 6.1).

heading: Appendix A: Glossary
body: Unbundled pricing. Laboratory pricing that bills the screen and the confirmation separately (5.3). Variable cost. A cost that applies only to some tests, such as confirmation and MRO review (1.2). Verified result. The final result reported by the MRO (3.2). M Mobile collection. A collector who travels to the worksite, usually for a trip fee plus a per-donor fee (6.5). Appendix A: Glossary © 2026 Ramsey Diagnostics Corporation d/b/a Labb. All rights reserved. heading: OVERVIEW
body: OVERVIEW How to read this report THC drives positives everywhere. The regional difference is in the second and third drug: cocaine in the Northeast and Texas, methamphetamine in the West and rural Midwest/South, fentanyl highest in the West, and veterinary sedatives concentrated in the Northeast and Great Lakes. WORKFORCE % Estimated share of general-workforce urine tests positive for that drug in the region. National figures are sourced (Quest 2026 Drug Testing Index, 2025 data). Regional splits are Labb estimates (approximate), built by adjusting the national rate using CDC clinical, ONDCP wastewater, and NFLIS regional signals. Use them for panel design and sales positioning, not as citable statistics. HIGH-RISK % Share of clinical urine tests positive among patients in substance use disorder care (CDC Clinical Drug Test Dashboard, Millennium Health data, Oct to Dec 2025). Sourced, but a convenience sample; CDC cautions against comparing regions directly. This approximates what treatment, court, and justice programs will see. REGIONS (US CENSUS) Northeast: CT, ME, MA, NH, NJ, NY, PA, RI, VT. Midwest: IL, IN, IA, KS, MI, MN, MO, NE, ND, OH, SD, WI. South: AL, AR, DE, DC, FL, GA, KY, LA, MD, MS, NC, OK, SC, TN, TX, VA, WV. West: AK, AZ, CA, CO, HI, ID, MT, NV, NM, OR, UT, WA, WY. NATIONAL BASELINE 2025 workforce positivity Overall general-workforce urine positivity was 4.3% in 2025; hair caught 19.1%, so specimen choice changes detection more than geography does. Measure Urine Any drug, general workforce 4.3% Marijuana (THC) 4.4% Oral fluid Hair 19.1% 11.1% 15.1% Cocaine 4.0% Methamphetamine 2.5% Fentanyl, general workforce 0.28% (0.55% in 2024) Blank cells: not reported in the sources used. Healthcare had the highest industry positivity at 5.8%. Fentanyl positivity in random testing has run roughly 400% higher than in pre-employment testing. High-risk (clinical) national picture, Oct to Dec 2025: fentanyl 12.8%, cocaine 8.5%, heroin 2.6%; 84.6% of fentanyl positives also contained cocaine or methamphetamine, so any panel that tests fentanyl must also test both stimulants.
